lessons.title: Read this first: you need no experience
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
You do not need to know anything about computers or programming to
start. This module starts at zero. Take it slowly. One lesson a day
is fine.

▸  WHAT YOU WILL LEARN HERE
How to write small programs in a language called Go. A PROGRAM is a
list of instructions for a computer. CODE is the text of those
instructions. You write code. The computer follows it.

▸  THE COMPUTER IS LITERAL
A computer does exactly what you write. Not what you meant. One
missing quote mark and it stops and complains. That is normal. Every
programmer sees errors many times a day.

▸  HOW EACH LESSON WORKS
    1. Read the notes (this text).
    2. If there is code, press Run and look at the result.
    3. Change something small. Run it again. See what changed.
    4. Answer the quiz at the end.
Lessons named "Your turn" ask you to write the program yourself. The
app checks your answer.

▸  ONE HABIT THAT HELPS MOST
Before you press Run, guess what will happen. Then check. Wrong guesses
teach you the most.

▸  NEW WORDS
    program  - a list of instructions for a computer
    code     - the written text of a program
    run      - tell the computer to follow the instructions

quiz.q: What does a computer do with the code you write?
options: It guesses what you meant and fixes mistakes
It only follows the parts it understands
It follows it exactly as written
It asks you to confirm each instruction
quiz.explain: A computer follows instructions literally. It does not guess. That is why small typing mistakes cause errors.
quiz.hint: Re-read "THE COMPUTER IS LITERAL".

lessons.title: Set up your computer (one time only)
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
To run code, your computer needs the Go tools. You install them once.
It takes about five minutes.

▸  STEP 1: INSTALL GO
    On Kali, Debian or Ubuntu Linux:
        1. Open the Terminal app.
        2. Type this line and press Enter:
               sudo apt update && sudo apt install golang-go
        3. Type your password if it asks. (Nothing shows while you
           type it. That is normal.)
    On Windows or Mac:
        Download the installer from https://go.dev/dl/ and run it.

▸  STEP 2: RESTART THIS APP
Close this course window. Open it again. It will now find Go.

▸  STEP 3: CHECK
Press the Run button on this lesson. You should see two lines appear
below the code. The second line shows your Go version.

▸  IF IT SAYS "GO NOT FOUND"
Restart your computer and open the app again. Until then you can still
read every lesson and do every quiz.

▸  NEW WORDS
    install  - put a program on your computer so you can use it
    terminal - a window where you type commands instead of clicking

quiz.q: After installing Go, why should you close and reopen this app?
options: To delete your saved progress
Because Go only works the next day
To switch the app to Go mode
So the app can find the new Go tools
quiz.explain: The app looks for Go when it starts. Restarting it lets it see the tools you just installed.
quiz.hint: Step 2.

lessons.title: Your first program, line by line
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Every Go program has the same frame. You put your instructions inside
it. Press Run now and look at the result.

▸  THE FRAME, LINE BY LINE
    package main
        "This file is a program you can run." Always the first line.

    import "fmt"
        "I want to use the fmt tools." fmt is a toolbox for showing
        text on the screen. (Say it "fumpt" or "format".)

    func main() {
        "The program starts here." Everything between { and } runs,
        top to bottom.

    fmt.Println("Hello!")
        "Show the text Hello! on the screen, then go to a new line."
        Println means "print line".

    }
        "The program ends here."

▸  FOR NOW
Treat the first lines as a fixed frame. Copy them each time. You will
learn what each part really does later. Your work goes between { and }.

▸  TRY IT
    1. Change "Hello!" to your name. Run.
    2. Copy the Println line so it appears twice. Run.
    3. Remove one quote mark. Run. Read the red message. Put it back.

▸  NEW WORDS
    print - show something on the screen
    line  - one row of code or of output
lessons.expected:
Hello!
This is my first program.

quiz.q: In which part of the program do you write your own instructions?
options: Above the line "package main"
Between the { and } of func main()
After the very last } of the file
Inside the quotes after import
quiz.explain: The program starts at func main() { and runs everything until the matching }. Your instructions go there.
quiz.hint: Where does the program start?

lessons.title: Printing text and numbers
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Text goes inside double quotes. Numbers do not. You can print several
things at once by separating them with commas.

▸  TEXT
    fmt.Println("I like Go")
The quotes tell Go: "this is text, show it as it is." Text in quotes
is called a STRING (a string of letters).

▸  NUMBERS
    fmt.Println(42)
No quotes. Go knows this is a number.

▸  SEVERAL THINGS AT ONCE
    fmt.Println("I am", 30, "years old")
Commas separate the items. Println puts ONE SPACE between items.

▸  WATCH OUT
    fmt.Println("5 + 5")   shows  5 + 5   (it is text)
    fmt.Println(5 + 5)     shows  10      (Go does the sum)

▸  TRY IT
Predict each output line, then press Run. Were you right?

▸  NEW WORDS
    string - a piece of text, written inside double quotes
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("I like Go")
	fmt.Println(42)
	fmt.Println("I am", 30, "years old")
	fmt.Println("5 + 5")
	fmt.Println(5 + 5)
}
lessons.expected:
I like Go
42
I am 30 years old
5 + 5
10

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println("2 + 3") show?
options: An error
quiz.explain: The quotes make it text. Go shows text exactly as written, without the quote marks. It does no maths on text.
quiz.hint: Quotes mean text.

lessons.title: Your turn: print a name card
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Now you write a program yourself. The editor starts almost empty. The
box above shows the EXACT output you must produce.

▸  YOUR TASK
Print these three lines, exactly:
    Name: Gopher
    Language: Go
    Lessons done: 5
The last line must print the number 5 WITHOUT quotes around it (use a
comma: "Lessons done:", 5).

▸  HOW
    1. Keep the frame: package main, import "fmt", func main() { }.
    2. Inside main, write three fmt.Println lines.
    3. Press Run. Compare your output with the box, letter by letter.
       Capital letters and spaces matter.

▸  STUCK?
Press "Show solution". Read it. Then close it and type it yourself.
Typing it yourself is how you learn.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Name: Gopher")
	fmt.Println("Language: Go")
	fmt.Println("Lessons done:", 5)
}
lessons.expected:
Name: Gopher
Language: Go
Lessons done: 5

quiz.q: Your output says "name: Gopher" but the task says "Name: Gopher". Will it pass?
options: No, capital letters must match
Yes, the words are the same
Yes, if the rest is correct
No, because Gopher is wrong
quiz.explain: The computer compares the text exactly. "name" and "Name" are different to a computer.
quiz.hint: The computer is literal.

lessons.title: Errors are normal: how to read one
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
An error message is help, not a punishment. It tells you WHERE the
problem is and WHAT is wrong. Read it, go to that line, fix one thing.

▸  WHAT AN ERROR LOOKS LIKE
    ./main.go:6:14: newline in string
       |      | |    |
       file   | |    what is wrong
              | column (position in the line)
              line number
This means: "line 6, about 14 characters in, a string was never
closed."

▸  THE THREE MOST COMMON BEGINNER ERRORS
    newline in string
        You forgot the closing quote mark ".
    undefined: fmt.println
        Wrong capital letter. It is Println with a capital P.
    imported and not used: "fmt"
        You wrote import "fmt" but never used fmt. Add a fmt.Println,
        or remove the import.

▸  TRY IT (break it on purpose)
    1. Press Run. It works.
    2. Delete the last quote mark on line 6. Run. Read the error.
    3. Put the quote back. Run.
    4. Change Println to println (small p) on line 7. Run. Read the
       error. Fix it.
Breaking code on purpose is a great way to learn the error messages.

▸  RULE
Fix the FIRST error first. The others are often caused by it.
lessons.expected:
Errors are just messages
I can fix them

quiz.q: The error says "./main.go:9:2: ...". Where should you look?
options: Line 2, character 9
The ninth file you opened
Anywhere, the numbers are random
Line 9, near the start
quiz.explain: The first number after the file name is the line. The second is the position in that line. So: line 9, column 2.
quiz.hint: file:line:column.

lessons.title: Go as a calculator
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Go can do maths. Use + - * / just like a calculator. One surprise:
dividing two whole numbers gives a whole number.

▸  THE SIGNS
    +   add          7 + 2   is 9
    -   subtract     7 - 2   is 5
    *   multiply     7 * 2   is 14   (a star, not x)
    /   divide       7 / 2   is 3    (!)
    %   remainder    7 % 2   is 1    (what is left over)

▸  THE SURPRISE: 7 / 2 IS 3
When both numbers are whole numbers, Go gives a whole-number answer
and throws away the part after the point. To get 3.5, use a decimal
number: 7.0 / 2.

▸  REMAINDER
% gives what is left after dividing. 7 % 2 is 1 because 7 = 2 + 2 + 2,
with 1 left over. It is useful to test "is this number even?": if
n % 2 is 0, n is even.

▸  ORDER
Multiply and divide happen before add and subtract, like in school:
2 + 3 * 4 is 14. Use brackets to change the order: (2 + 3) * 4 is 20.

▸  TRY IT
Predict all six lines before pressing Run.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println(7 + 2)
	fmt.Println(7 * 2)
	fmt.Println(7 / 2)
	fmt.Println(7.0 / 2)
	fmt.Println(7 % 2)
	fmt.Println(2+3*4, (2+3)*4)
}

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println(9 / 2) show?
quiz.explain: 9 and 2 are both whole numbers, so the answer is a whole number: 4. The .5 is thrown away. Use 9.0 / 2 to get 4.5.
quiz.hint: Whole number divided by whole number.

lessons.title: Variables: boxes with names
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A VARIABLE is a box with a name. You put a value in it. Later you use
the name to get the value back.

▸  MAKING A VARIABLE
    age := 30
Read it as: "make a box called age and put 30 in it." The := sign
means "make a new box and fill it."

    name := "Sara"
A box can hold text too.

▸  USING A VARIABLE
    fmt.Println(name, "is", age)
Go looks inside the boxes and prints:  Sara is 30
Note: no quotes around name. With quotes, "name" would just be the
word name.

▸  WHY BOTHER?
    - Give values a meaning: price is clearer than 25.
    - Change a value in ONE place instead of many.
    - Save results to use later.

▸  NAMING RULES
Names use letters, digits and _. They cannot start with a digit and
cannot contain spaces. Go style joins words like this: totalPrice,
userName. Capital letters matter: age and Age are different boxes.

▸  A GO RULE
If you make a variable and never use it, Go refuses to run the program
("declared and not used"). This keeps code tidy.

▸  NEW WORDS
    variable - a named box that holds a value
    value    - the thing in the box: a number, some text...
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name := "Sara"
	age := 30
	city := "Cairo"
	fmt.Println(name, "is", age)
	fmt.Println(name, "lives in", city)
	fmt.Println("name")
}
lessons.expected:
Sara is 30
Sara lives in Cairo
name

quiz.q: After pet := "cat", what does fmt.Println("pet") show?
options: cat
pet
"cat"
An error
quiz.explain: With quotes, "pet" is just the text pet. To show what is inside the box, write the name without quotes: fmt.Println(pet).
quiz.hint: Quotes make text.

lessons.title: Changing what is in a box
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
You can put a new value in an existing box with = (one equals sign).
The old value is gone.

▸  := OR = ?
    score := 0        make a NEW box called score, put 0 in it
    score = 10        put 10 in the EXISTING box score
Use := the first time. Use = after that.

▸  USING THE OLD VALUE
    score = score + 5
Read it right to left: "take what is in score, add 5, put the result
back in score." This is how programs count and add up totals.

▸  SHORTCUTS
    score += 5     same as  score = score + 5
    score -= 2     same as  score = score - 2
    score++        same as  score = score + 1

▸  TRY IT
Follow the program line by line with a pencil. Write down what is in
the box after each line. Then press Run to check.

    line              score
    score := 0          0
    score = score + 10  ?
    ...
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	score := 0
	fmt.Println("start:", score)
	score = score + 10
	fmt.Println("after +10:", score)
	score += 5
	fmt.Println("after +=5:", score)
	score++
	fmt.Println("after ++:", score)
	score = 100
	fmt.Println("reset:", score)
}
lessons.expected:
start: 0
after +10: 10
after +=5: 15
after ++: 16
reset: 100

quiz.q: x := 4, then x = x * 3. What is in x now?
quiz.explain: Take what is in x (4), multiply by 3 (12), put it back in x. x is now 12.
quiz.hint: Right side first, then store.

lessons.title: Kinds of values: numbers, text, true and false
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Every value has a KIND, called its TYPE. A box can only hold one type.
You cannot add a number to a piece of text.

▸  THE FOUR TYPES YOU NEED NOW
    int       whole numbers          42, -7, 0
    float64   numbers with a point   3.14, 0.5, -2.0
    string    text in quotes         "hello", "42"
    bool      true or false          true, false

Go works out the type for you:
    count := 3          int
    price := 2.5        float64
    word := "Go"        string
    ready := true       bool

▸  WHY TYPES MATTER
    "5" + 5      error: text and number cannot be added
    "Go" + "pher"    is "Gopher": + joins two strings
    10 + 2.5     works when written directly like this
But two VARIABLES of different types cannot be mixed:
    count + price      error: int and float64
Convert one first: float64(count) + price.

▸  "42" IS NOT 42
"42" in quotes is text: two characters, 4 and 2. 42 without quotes is
a number you can do maths with.

▸  NEW WORDS
    type   - the kind of a value (int, float64, string, bool)
    bool   - a true-or-false value (named after George Boole)
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	count := 3
	price := 2.5
	word := "Go"
	ready := true
	fmt.Println(count, price, word, ready)
	fmt.Println(word + "pher")
	total := float64(count) * price
	fmt.Println("total:", total)
	fmt.Println("42" + "1")
	fmt.Println(42 + 1)
}
lessons.expected:
3 2.5 Go true
Gopher
total: 7.5
421
43

quiz.q: What does fmt.Println("7" + "3") show?
options: An error
quiz.explain: Both are text, so + joins them: "73". With numbers (7 + 3) you would get 10.
quiz.hint: Quotes mean text; + joins text.

lessons.title: Your turn: a shopping bill
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Use variables and maths together, like a real program.

▸  YOUR TASK
You buy 3 notebooks at 12 pounds each and 2 pens at 5 pounds each.
    1. Make four variables:
           notebooks := 3
           notebookPrice := 12
           pens := 2
           penPrice := 5
    2. Make a variable total that adds up the cost.
    3. Print exactly:
           Notebooks: 36
           Pens: 10
           Total: 46
           Change from 100: 54
Work out each number with code (notebooks * notebookPrice, and so on),
not by typing 36 yourself. Then if a price changes, only one line
changes.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	notebooks := 3
	notebookPrice := 12
	pens := 2
	penPrice := 5
	total := notebooks*notebookPrice + pens*penPrice
	fmt.Println("Notebooks:", notebooks*notebookPrice)
	fmt.Println("Pens:", pens*penPrice)
	fmt.Println("Total:", total)
	fmt.Println("Change from 100:", 100-total)
}
lessons.expected:
Notebooks: 36
Pens: 10
Total: 46
Change from 100: 54

quiz.q: Why calculate the totals with code instead of typing the answers?
options: Typed numbers are slower to print
Go does not allow typed numbers
If a price changes, the answers update
It makes the output look different
quiz.explain: When the numbers come from the variables, you change one price and every result is correct again. Typed answers would all need fixing by hand.
quiz.hint: Imagine the pen price goes up.

lessons.title: Asking the user for input
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A program can ask the person using it for information. fmt.Scan reads
what they type.

▸  HOW IT WORKS
    var name string
    fmt.Scan(&name)
Line 1 makes an empty text box called name. (var is the other way to
make a box: you give the type and it starts empty.)
Line 2 waits for the user to type a word, then puts it in the box.

The & means "put the answer INTO this box". Don't worry about why yet;
just always write & before the box name in fmt.Scan.

▸  IN THIS APP
Below the editor is a box labelled stdin. Whatever is written there
is what the program "types in". It is filled in for this lesson. Change
it and press Run again.

▸  READING A NUMBER
    var age int
    fmt.Scan(&age)
Because age is an int box, Scan reads a number.

▸  NEW WORDS
    input - information that goes INTO a program
    output - what the program shows (prints)
    stdin - "standard input": the keyboard, or here, the stdin box
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var name string
	var age int
	fmt.Scan(&name)
	fmt.Scan(&age)
	fmt.Println("Hello,", name)
	fmt.Println("Next year you will be", age+1)
}
lessons.expected:
Hello, Omar
Next year you will be 25

quiz.q: In fmt.Scan(&age), what does the & tell Go?
options: That age is a secret value
To add age to something
That age must be a word
To put what is typed into age
quiz.explain: fmt.Scan needs to know WHERE to store what the user typed. &age points it at the box called age.
quiz.hint: Into this box.

lessons.title: Repeating with for
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A LOOP repeats instructions. Go has one loop word: for. Instead of
writing the same line 10 times, you write it once inside a loop.

▸  COUNTING FROM 1 TO 5
    for i := 1; i <= 5; i++ {
        fmt.Println(i)
    }
It has three parts, separated by semicolons (;):
    i := 1     START:  make a counter box i, put 1 in it
    i <= 5     CHECK:  keep going while this is true
    i++        STEP:   after each round, add 1 to i
Then the block { } runs once per round.

▸  FOLLOW IT BY HAND
    round   i    i <= 5?   prints
      1     1    true        1
      2     2    true        2
     ...
      5     5    true        5
      -     6    false     (loop ends)

▸  ADDING UP WITH A LOOP
    total := 0
    for i := 1; i <= 100; i++ {
        total += i
    }
Adds 1 + 2 + ... + 100. (The answer is 5050.)

▸  NEW WORDS
    loop      - code that repeats
    counter   - a variable that counts the rounds (often called i)
lessons.expected:
round 1
round 2
round 3
round 4
round 5
1 + 2 + ... + 100 = 5050
countdown 10
countdown 7
countdown 4
countdown 1

quiz.q: How many times does "for i := 0; i < 3; i++" run its block?
options: 3 times
2 times
4 times
Forever
quiz.explain: i takes the values 0, 1 and 2. When i becomes 3, i < 3 is false and the loop stops. That is 3 rounds.
quiz.hint: Write the values of i down.

lessons.title: Your turn: a times table
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Use a loop to do work you would never type by hand.

▸  YOUR TASK
    1. Print the 7 times table from 1 to 10, one line each, like this:
           7 x 1 = 7
           7 x 2 = 14
           ...
           7 x 10 = 70
       Use a loop with a counter i from 1 to 10, and print
       7, "x", i, "=", 7*i  (Println puts the spaces in for you).
    2. After the loop, print the sum of all ten answers:
           Sum: 385

▸  HINT
Make sum := 0 BEFORE the loop. Inside the loop, add 7*i to it. Print
it AFTER the loop's closing }.

quiz.q: Why must sum := 0 come BEFORE the loop and not inside it?
options: Go does not allow variables inside loops
Inside, it would reset to 0 every round
Before the loop it runs faster
It does not matter where it goes

lessons.title: Lists: many values in one name
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A SLICE is a list of values of the same type, kept in order. Use it
when you have many things: names, prices, scores.

▸  MAKING A LIST
    fruits := []string{"apple", "banana", "cherry"}
[]string means "a list of strings". The values go inside { }.

▸  GETTING ONE ITEM
Items are numbered from ZERO, not one:
    fruits[0]   is "apple"
    fruits[1]   is "banana"
    fruits[2]   is "cherry"
    fruits[3]   CRASH: there is no fourth item
The number in [ ] is called the INDEX (the position).

▸  HOW MANY ITEMS?
    len(fruits)    is 3      (len = length)

▸  ADDING AN ITEM
    fruits = append(fruits, "date")
append makes the list longer by one.

▸  GOING THROUGH EVERY ITEM
    for i, f := range fruits {
        fmt.Println(i, f)
    }
range gives you each position (i) and item (f), one per round.
If you don't need the position, write _ instead of i:
    for _, f := range fruits { ... }

▸  NEW WORDS
    slice - a list of values
    index - the position of an item, starting at 0

[apple banana cherry]
first: apple last: cherry
how many: 3
0 apple
1 banana
2 cherry
3 date
total price: 8

options: red
blue

quiz.explain: Positions start at 0. colors[0] is red, colors[1] is green, colors[2] is blue.

lessons.title: Functions: name a job, use it many times
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A FUNCTION is a named piece of code that does one job. You write it
once and use it ("call" it) as often as you like. You already use
functions: fmt.Println is one.

▸  A FUNCTION THAT DOES SOMETHING
    func greet(name string) {
        fmt.Println("Hello,", name)
    }
    greet("Ali")       prints  Hello, Ali
    greet("Mona")      prints  Hello, Mona
name is an INPUT (called a PARAMETER). Each call can give a different
value.

▸  A FUNCTION THAT GIVES BACK AN ANSWER
    func double(n int) int {
        return n * 2
    }
    x := double(21)    x is now 42
The int after the brackets says "this function gives back an int".
return sends the answer back to whoever called it.

▸  WHERE THEY GO
Write your functions OUTSIDE main, above or below it. main is itself a
function: the one Go runs first.

▸  WHY USE FUNCTIONS?
    - No copy-paste: fix a mistake in one place.
    - Give a job a clear name: isEven(n) reads like English.
    - Break a big problem into small pieces.

▸  NEW WORDS
    function  - a named piece of code that does one job
    call      - use a function: double(21)
    parameter - an input to a function
    return    - give an answer back from a function
lessons.expected:
Hello, Ali
Hello, Mona
42 10
true false

Restarts the function from the top
Deletes the function after use
Sends an answer back to the caller
quiz.explain: return ends the function and hands a value back. x := double(21) catches that value in x. Printing is a separate job.

lessons.title: What you know now, and where to go next
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
You can now write real small programs. Next, go to module
"1 - Foundations". It covers the same ideas in more depth, then adds
new ones. Expect to see familiar things there: that is the plan.

▸  WORDS YOU NOW KNOW
    program, code, run         instructions, their text, following them
    print, output              show on screen; what was shown
    input, stdin               information given to the program
    variable, value            named box; what's in it
    := and =                   make a new box; change an existing box
    type                       int, float64, string, bool
    if / else                  choose
    ==  !=  <  >  &&  ||        compare and combine
    for, loop                  repeat
    slice, index, len, range   list; position from 0; length; go through
    function, parameter,       named job; its input; give an answer
    return, call               back; use it

▸  A SENSIBLE ORDER FOR THE REST OF THE COURSE
    1. 1 - Foundations            (go slowly, do every "Challenge")
    2. 2 to 6                     pointers, text, lists and maps, your
                                  own types, errors
    3. 7 to 12                    algorithms, files, packages, generics,
                                  concurrency (doing many things at once)
    4. G1 and G2 Go Anatomy       a tour of the language's grammar
    5. 33 - Practice Gym          small exercises - start these any time
                                  after module 6
    6. 13 to 32                   the rest, in any order that interests you

▸  YOU CAN SAFELY SKIP FOR NOW
Modules 20 to 23 (performance, runtime internals, security, operating
system) are for people who already work with Go. Come back to them
after the first twelve modules.

▸  WHEN YOU ARE STUCK

    2. Make the program smaller until it works, then add back slowly.
    3. Add fmt.Println lines to see what is in your boxes.
    4. Take a break. Many problems solve themselves after a walk.

lessons.title: Syntax: the shape of every Go program
lessons.concept:
Every Go program is a set of text files ending in .go. Each file has the same three-part shape:

1. A package clause: `package main`. It says which package this file belongs to. A program you can run always lives in package main.
2. Imports: `import "fmt"` brings in code other people wrote. fmt ("format") prints text.
3. Declarations: functions, variables, constants and types. A runnable program must declare `func main()`. Go starts running your program at the first line inside main and stops when main ends.

Curly braces { } mark where something starts and ends. The opening brace must be on the same line as the thing it belongs to (`func main() {`), because of Go's semicolon rule (a later lesson). Code inside braces is indented with one tab. The `go fmt` tool does that for you, so every Go program looks the same.

`fmt.Println(...)` means: from package fmt, use the function Println. It prints its arguments with spaces between them and ends the line.
lessons.eli5: Think of a Go file like a letter. At the top you write who it's from (package main). Then you list the helpers you need (import "fmt" is the helper that can talk to the screen). Then you write the instructions (func main). The computer reads the instructions inside main from top to bottom, like reading a recipe, and does each step.
lessons.expected:
Hello, Go!
2 + 3 = 5

quiz.q: Where does a Go program start running?
options: At the first line of the file
At the first line inside func main()
At the import statement
At whichever function is written last
quiz.explain: Execution starts inside main() in package main, and the program ends when main returns.
quiz.hint: Look for the special function every runnable program must have.

lessons.title: Package declarations
lessons.concept:
The first line of every Go file is a package clause: `package name`. A package is a folder of .go files that are compiled together and share their names: a function declared in one file can be used in another file of the same package.

There are two kinds of packages:
- `package main` is special: it builds into a program you can run, and it must contain `func main()`.
- Every other name (`package geometry`, `package strings`) is a library: code that other packages import and use. A library has no main function.

All files in one folder must use the same package name. By convention the package name is short, lower case, one word, and matches the folder name. When you write `fmt.Println`, `fmt` is the package name and Println is something that package offers.
lessons.eli5: A package is like a toy box with a label on it. Every toy (file) inside says on its tag which box it belongs to. The box labelled "main" is the special one: it's the box you open to start playing. Other boxes hold toys you can borrow.

This file belongs to package main.
Only package main can be run as a program.

quiz.q: Which package must contain func main()?

quiz.explain: Only package main builds into a runnable program, and it must declare func main().

lessons.title: Imports
lessons.concept:
`import` lets a file use another package's exported names. The standard library ships with Go and has hundreds of packages: fmt for printing, math for maths, strings for text, os for files and the operating system, time for clocks.

You can import one package:

    import "fmt"

or several in a group (the usual style):

    import (
        "fmt"
        "math"
    )

After importing, you use the package's last path element as a prefix: `math.Sqrt(16)`, `math.Pi`. You can rename an import with an alias: `import m "math"` then call `m.Sqrt`.

Two strict rules: you may only use packages you import, and Go refuses to compile if you import something you don't use. That keeps programs tidy and builds fast. The blank import `import _ "pkg"` runs a package's setup code without using its names (rarely needed).
lessons.eli5: Importing is like asking a friend to come help. If you need someone good at maths, you invite "math". But Go is strict: if you invite a friend and then never ask them for help, Go says "why did you invite them?" and won't start until you send them home.

square root of 16 is 4
pi is about 3.141592653589793
2 to the power 10 is 1024

options: Nothing, it is ignored

It is automatically removed at run time
quiz.explain: An unused import is a compile error in Go. Remove it (or use the blank identifier _ if you only need its side effects).

lessons.title: Comments
lessons.concept:
Comments are notes for humans; the compiler ignores them.

- `//` starts a line comment that runs to the end of the line.
- `/* ... */` is a block comment that can span lines (mostly used to disable code temporarily or for package documentation).

A comment directly above a declaration is its doc comment. Tools like `go doc` and pkg.go.dev show it, so start it with the name being described:

    // Area returns the area of a circle with radius r.
    func Area(r float64) float64 { ... }

Good comments explain WHY, not WHAT: the code already says what it does. Comments that start with `//go:` (no space) are directives to the tools, such as `//go:embed`; they are not ordinary comments.
lessons.eli5: Comments are sticky notes you put on your code. The computer doesn't read sticky notes, only people do. You write them to remind yourself (or a friend) why you did something.
lessons.expected:
comments are for people
the computer skips them

lessons.title: Semicolons
lessons.concept:
Go's grammar uses semicolons to end statements, but you almost never type them. The lexer inserts a semicolon automatically at the end of a line when the line's last token is:
- an identifier or a literal (a name, a number, a string),
- one of the keywords break, continue, fallthrough, return,
- `++`, `--`, `)`, `]` or `}`.

That one rule explains a famous Go requirement: the opening brace must be on the same line.

    func main()   // a semicolon is inserted after ")" here...
    {             // ...so this brace starts nothing: compile error

You only write semicolons yourself to put several statements on one line, or inside `for` and `if` headers: `for i := 0; i < 3; i++`.
lessons.eli5: Semicolons are like full stops at the end of sentences. Go is a polite helper that writes the full stops for you at the end of each line. But because it does that, you must keep the { on the same line, or Go puts a full stop in the wrong place and gets confused.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("one statement per line: no semicolons needed")
	fmt.Println("two")
	fmt.Println("on one line need one")
}
lessons.expected:
one statement per line: no semicolons needed
two
on one line need one

quiz.q: Why must the { of a function be on the same line as func main()?
options: It is just a style rule
Go inserts a semicolon at the end of the line after ), ending the declaration early
Because of the 80-column limit
So that comments can be added
quiz.explain: A semicolon is inserted after a line ending in ), so a brace on the next line would be separated from the function header.

lessons.title: Keywords
lessons.concept:
Go has only 25 keywords. They are reserved: you cannot use them as names.

    break     default      func    interface  select
    case      defer        go      map        struct
    chan      else         goto    package    switch
    const     fallthrough  if      range      type
    continue  for          import  return     var

Grouped by job:
- Declaring things: const, var, type, func, package, import
- Composite types: struct, interface, map, chan
- Control flow: if, else, for, range, switch, case, default, fallthrough, break, continue, goto, return
- Concurrency: go, select, defer

Words like int, string, true, false, nil, len and append are NOT keywords. They are predeclared identifiers: names Go defines for you, which you could (but shouldn't) shadow.
lessons.eli5: Keywords are Go's 25 magic words, like "abracadabra". Each one makes Go do something special, so you're not allowed to use them as names for your own things, just like you can't name your dog "Stop" if "Stop" is the word that makes the game end.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println("Go has 25 keywords, for example:")
	fmt.Println("func package import var const type")
	fmt.Println("if else for range switch case")
	fmt.Println("go select chan defer map struct interface")
}

Go has 25 keywords, for example:
func package import var const type
if else for range switch case

quiz.explain: range is one of the 25 keywords. int, true and len are predeclared identifiers, not keywords.
quiz.hint: Types and built-in functions are predeclared names, not keywords.

lessons.title: Built-in types
lessons.concept:
Go predeclares these types; you can use them anywhere without importing anything:

- bool: true or false
- string: text (an immutable sequence of bytes, usually UTF-8)
- Signed integers: int8, int16, int32, int64 and int (32 or 64 bits, the one you normally use)
- Unsigned integers: uint8, uint16, uint32, uint64, uint and uintptr (big enough to hold a pointer's bits)
- Floating point: float32, float64 (the one you normally use)
- Complex numbers: complex64, complex128
- byte: another name (alias) for uint8; used for raw data
- rune: another name for int32; holds one Unicode character (code point)
- error: the built-in interface for errors
- any: another name for interface{}, a value of any type
- comparable: a constraint used only in generics

The numbers in the names are sizes in bits. A bigger size holds a bigger range: int8 is -128..127, uint8 is 0..255, int64 reaches about 9.2 quintillion.
lessons.eli5: Built-in types are the different kinds of boxes Go gives you for free. A bool box holds yes/no. A string box holds words. An int box holds whole numbers. A float64 box holds numbers with a dot, like 3.5. Small boxes (int8) hold small numbers; big boxes (int64) hold huge ones.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println(true, false) // bool
	fmt.Println("hello")     // string
	fmt.Println(42, -7)      // int
	fmt.Println(3.14)        // float64
	fmt.Println('A')         // rune: prints its number, 65
	fmt.Println(2 + 3i)      // complex128
}
lessons.expected:
true false
hello
42 -7
3.14
65
(2+3i)

uint8

string
quiz.explain: byte = uint8 (0..255). rune = int32 and holds a Unicode code point.

lessons.title: Data types
lessons.concept:
A data type tells Go two things about a value: how much memory it uses and which operations are allowed. 3 + 4 is fine for numbers; "a" * 2 is a compile error for strings. Go is statically typed: every variable has one fixed type, checked before the program runs.

Go's types come in families:
- Basic types: booleans, numbers (integers, floats, complex), strings
- Composite types built from other types: arrays [3]int, slices []int, maps map[string]int, structs, pointers *int, functions func(int) int, interfaces, channels chan int
- Your own named types: type Celsius float64

`fmt.Printf` prints using a format string. The verb %T prints a value's type, %v prints the value itself, and \n ends the line. You will meet many more verbs later. Printing %T is the quickest way to ask Go "what type is this?".
lessons.eli5: A data type is the label on a box that says what can go inside. A box labelled "numbers" only takes numbers; you can't put a word in it. Go checks every label before your program starts, so mix-ups are caught early, like a teacher checking homework before you hand it in.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", 42, 42)
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", 3.5, 3.5)
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", "Go", "Go")
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", true, true)
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", 'x', 'x')
	fmt.Printf("%v is a %T\n", 2+3i, 2+3i)
}
lessons.expected:
42 is a int
3.5 is a float64
Go is a string
true is a bool
120 is a int32
(2+3i) is a complex128

quiz.explain: %T prints the Go type of the operand, e.g. int, float64, []int.

lessons.title: Identifiers
lessons.concept:
An identifier is a name you give to something: a variable, constant, type, function or package.

Rules:
- It starts with a letter (any Unicode letter) or underscore, followed by letters, digits or underscores: total, x2, _tmp, π are fine; 2x and my-name are not.
- It is case sensitive: count and Count are different names.
- It cannot be one of the 25 keywords.

Conventions Go programmers follow:
- mixedCaps (camelCase), not snake_case: userName, maxValue.
- Short names for short scopes (i, n, err), longer names for wider scopes.
- Acronyms keep one case: userID, HTTPServer.
- The first letter matters: a name starting with an upper-case letter is visible to other packages (exported). More on that later.

The blank identifier `_` is special: it means "I don't need this value".
lessons.eli5: An identifier is a name tag. Go has a few rules for name tags: they must start with a letter, can't have spaces or dashes, and "Cat" and "cat" are two different tags. The underscore _ is a special tag that means "throw this away, I don't need it".
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var userName = "ada"
	var UserName = "ADA" // a different identifier: case matters
	var π = 3.14159      // Unicode letters are allowed
	var _ = "ignored"    // the blank identifier discards a value
	fmt.Println(userName, UserName, π)
}
lessons.expected: ada ADA 3.14159

quiz.q: Which is a valid Go identifier?
options: 2fast
my-name

quiz.explain: Identifiers start with a letter or underscore; they cannot contain dashes or be keywords.

lessons.title: Short variable declarations
lessons.concept:
Inside a function you will usually declare variables with `:=` instead of var:

    name := "Ada"     // same as: var name = "Ada"
    x, y := 1, 2      // two at once

`:=` declares AND assigns, and the type comes from the value on the right. Rules:
- It only works inside functions. At package level you must use var.
- At least one variable on the left must be new in this scope. `a, err := f()` is allowed when a is new even if err already exists; err is then just assigned.
- `=` assigns to an existing variable; `:=` creates one. Mixing them up is a common beginner error ("no new variables on left side of :=").
lessons.eli5: `:=` is the shortcut way to make a new box and put something in it at the same time. Go looks at what you're putting in ("Ada" is words) and writes the right label on the box for you. You only use := the first time; after that you use = to swap what's inside.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name := "Ada"
	year := 1815
	x, y := 3, 4
	fmt.Println(name, year, x, y)

	year = 1843 // = changes an existing variable
	fmt.Println(name, year)
}

quiz.q: Where can you NOT use := ?
options: Inside func main
Inside an if block
At package level, outside any function
Inside a for loop
quiz.explain: Short variable declarations are only allowed inside functions; package-level variables need var.

lessons.title: Multiple assignment
lessons.concept:
Go can assign several variables in one statement:

    a, b := 1, 2
    a, b = b, a    // swap! no temporary variable needed

All the values on the right are evaluated first, then assigned left to right. That is why the swap works: Go reads b and a, then stores them.

You'll see multiple assignment everywhere because functions can return several values (`value, err := strconv.Atoi("42")`, a later lesson). Use the blank identifier to drop values you don't need:

    _, b = 10, 20   // keep only the second
lessons.eli5: Imagine you're holding a red ball in one hand and a blue ball in the other, and you want to switch them. Go lets you say "swap!" and both hands switch at the exact same moment, so you never drop a ball.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b := 1, 2
	fmt.Println("before:", a, b)
	a, b = b, a
	fmt.Println("after: ", a, b)

	x, y, z := "one", 2, 3.0
	fmt.Println(x, y, z)

	_, last := 10, 20
	fmt.Println(last)
}

before: 1 2
after:  2 1
one 2 3
20

quiz.explain: The right side is evaluated before any assignment, so the values swap: a=2, b=1.

lessons.title: Zero values
lessons.concept:
In Go a variable is never "uninitialised". If you don't give it a value, it gets its type's zero value:

- numbers (int, float64, ...): 0
- bool: false
- string: "" (empty)
- pointers, slices, maps, channels, functions, interfaces: nil (means "nothing yet")
- arrays and structs: every element/field set to its own zero value

This makes code safer (no garbage memory) and simpler: a counter can start at zero without writing `= 0`. Good Go types are designed so their zero value is ready to use.

`%q` in Printf prints a string in quotes, which is handy to see an empty string.
lessons.eli5: When you get a new box in Go, it's never full of random junk. A number box starts with 0, a yes/no box starts with "no" (false), and a word box starts empty. It's like getting a fresh notebook: clean pages, ready to use.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var i int
	var f float64
	var b bool
	var s string
	var r rune
	fmt.Println(i, f, b, r)
	fmt.Printf("%q\n", s)
	fmt.Println(s == "", b == false)
}
lessons.expected:
0 0 false 0
""
true true

quiz.q: What is the zero value of a string?
options: nil
" " (a space)
"" (empty string)
quiz.explain: Strings start as the empty string "". Only pointer-like types (pointers, slices, maps, channels, funcs, interfaces) are nil.

lessons.title: Type inference
lessons.concept:
Type inference means Go works out a type from the value, so you don't have to write it.

    x := 42        // int
    y := 3.0       // float64
    z := "hi"      // string
    w := x         // int, same as x

Number literals have default types: a whole number becomes int, a number with a dot or exponent becomes float64, a rune literal like 'a' becomes rune, and 2i becomes complex128.

Inference never makes a variable "dynamic": the type is decided once, at compile time, and fixed forever. If you need a different type than the default, say so: `var small int8 = 42` or `big := float32(1.5)`.

Inference also works for generic functions (later): Go deduces the type parameters from the arguments.
lessons.eli5: Type inference is Go being a good guesser. If you put a 5 in a box, Go thinks "that's a whole number" and labels the box for whole numbers. If you put 5.5, Go labels it "number with a dot". Once the label is on, it stays.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := 42
	b := 3.0
	c := "hi"
	d := 'g'
	e := a
	var small int8 = 42 // override the default type
	fmt.Printf("%T %T %T %T %T %T\n", a, b, c, d, e, small)
}
lessons.expected: int float64 string int32 int int8

quiz.q: What type does `v := 2.0` get?
options: int
float32
float64
it depends on the machine
quiz.explain: Untyped floating-point constants default to float64.

lessons.title: Constants
lessons.concept:
A constant is a value fixed at compile time; it can never change while the program runs.

    const pi = 3.14159
    const greeting = "hello"
    const (
        maxUsers = 100
        timeout  = 30
    )

Constants can be numbers, strings, booleans or runes. They must be computable by the compiler: `const n = len("abc")` is fine, but the result of a function call is not.

Untyped constants are special. `const big = 1 << 40` has no fixed type yet and is exact (arbitrary precision); it takes a type only when used, so `const x = 5` works with int, float64 or int8 variables. This is why `var f float64 = 5` and `var i int = 5` both compile.
lessons.eli5: A constant is a box that gets glued shut. You put the value in when you write the program, and nobody can ever change it afterwards. Good for things that never change, like how many days are in a week.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

const daysInWeek = 7

func main() {
	const pi = 3.14159
	const name = "Go"
	radius := 2.0
	fmt.Println("area:", pi*radius*radius)
	fmt.Println(name, "has", daysInWeek, "days per week of fun")

	var small int8 = daysInWeek // an untyped constant fits any numeric type
	var ratio float64 = daysInWeek
	fmt.Println(small, ratio)
}
lessons.expected:
area: 12.56636
Go has 7 days per week of fun
7 7

quiz.q: What happens if you write `pi = 3` after `const pi = 3.14`?
options: pi becomes 3
A run-time panic
A compile error: cannot assign to pi
pi becomes 3.14 again
quiz.explain: Constants cannot be assigned; the compiler rejects it.

lessons.title: Constants with iota
lessons.concept:
Inside a const block, `iota` is a counter: 0 on the first line, 1 on the next, and so on. A line with no value repeats the previous expression with the next iota. That makes numbered lists (enumerations) easy:

    const (
        Sunday = iota   // 0
        Monday          // 1
        Tuesday         // 2
    )

You can use iota in an expression: `KB = 1 << (10 * (iota + 1))` gives 1024, 1048576, ... Skip a value with the blank identifier `_ = iota`. iota restarts at 0 in every new const block.
lessons.eli5: iota is like a kid counting out loud while you point at things: "zero, one, two, three...". Each new line in a const group gets the next number, so you don't have to write the numbers yourself.

quiz.q: In `const ( A = iota; B; C )`, what is C?
quiz.explain: iota is 0, 1, 2 on successive lines, and B and C repeat the expression iota.

lessons.title: Operators
lessons.concept:
Operators combine values.

Arithmetic: + - * / % (remainder). Integer division throws away the fraction: 7/2 is 3, 7%2 is 1. With floats, 7.0/2 is 3.5. `+` also joins strings.

Comparison (result is bool): == != < <= > >=

Logical (on bools): && (and), || (or), ! (not). && and || short-circuit: the right side is only evaluated if needed.

Bitwise (on integers): & (and), | (or), ^ (xor, or "not" with one operand), &^ (and-not), << and >> (shifts).

Assignment operators combine an operator with =: x += 5, x *= 2, x %= 3. And x++ / x-- add or subtract 1 (they are statements in Go, not expressions: you can't write y = x++).

Precedence, from highest: * / % << >> & &^, then + - | ^, then comparisons, then &&, then ||. Use parentheses when in doubt.
lessons.eli5: Operators are the little symbols that do jobs: + adds, - takes away, * multiplies, / shares out equally. == asks "are these the same?" and gets a yes or no. && means "both must be true", || means "at least one is true".
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println(7+2, 7-2, 7*2, 7/2, 7%2)
	fmt.Println(7.0 / 2)
	fmt.Println("Go" + "pher")
	fmt.Println(3 < 5, 3 == 5, 3 != 5)
	fmt.Println(true && false, true || false, !true)
	fmt.Println(6&3, 6|3, 6^3, 1<<4)

	x := 10
	x += 5
	x++
	fmt.Println(x)
}
lessons.expected:
9 5 14 3 1
3.5
Gopher
true false true
false true false
2 7 5 16
16

quiz.q: What is 7 / 2 in Go when both are ints?
options: a compile error
quiz.explain: Integer division truncates toward zero, so 7/2 is 3 (and 7%2 is 1).

lessons.title: Expressions
lessons.concept:
An expression is anything that produces a value: 42, x, x + 1, len("go"), a > b, a function call that returns something.

Expressions are built from operands (values, names) and operators, and can be nested with parentheses: (a + b) * c.

Every expression has a type, decided at compile time. `x + 1` has the type of x. A comparison like `a < b` has type bool. Mixing types is an error: an int plus a float64 does not compile; convert one of them first (next lessons).

Constant expressions are evaluated by the compiler: `const seconds = 60 * 60 * 24` is computed before the program even runs.
lessons.eli5: An expression is a little maths problem that turns into one answer. "2 + 3" turns into 5. "Is 4 bigger than 9?" turns into "no". Go works out the answer and you can use it anywhere you could use the answer itself.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b, c := 2, 3, 4
	fmt.Println(a + b*c)
	fmt.Println((a + b) * c)
	fmt.Println(a < b && b < c)

	const secondsPerDay = 60 * 60 * 24
	fmt.Println(secondsPerDay)
	fmt.Println(len("gopher") * 2)
}

quiz.q: What does `2 + 3*4` evaluate to?
quiz.explain: * has higher precedence than +, so it's 2 + 12 = 14.

lessons.title: Type conversions
lessons.concept:
Go never converts between types automatically. You convert explicitly with `T(value)`:

    i := 42
    f := float64(i)      // int -> float64
    price := 3.99
    n := int(price)      // float64 -> int: truncates to 3
    big := 300
    u := uint8(big)      // 300 doesn't fit in a byte: wraps to 44

Constants are checked by the compiler instead: int(3.99) and uint8(300) written with literal numbers are compile errors, because the exact value can't be represented.

Numbers to strings are different. `string(65)` gives "A" (the character with that code), which surprises people, and `go vet` warns about it. To get "65" use the strconv package:

    s := strconv.Itoa(65)          // int -> "65"
    n, err := strconv.Atoi("123")  // "123" -> 123, plus an error if it isn't a number

Strings convert to and from []byte and []rune (see the Slices lesson).
lessons.eli5: Converting is like pouring water from a round cup into a square cup: you have to do it on purpose. Go won't mix a whole-number box with a dot-number box until you say "pour this into the other kind". Sometimes a bit spills: turning 3.99 into a whole number gives 3.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
)

func main() {
	i := 42
	f := float64(i) / 5
	fmt.Println(f)
	price := 3.99
	fmt.Println(int(price))
	big := 300
	fmt.Println(uint8(big))

	s := strconv.Itoa(2026)
	fmt.Println(s + "!")
	n, err := strconv.Atoi("123")
	fmt.Println(n+1, err)
	_, err = strconv.Atoi("abc")
	fmt.Println(err)
}
lessons.expected:
8.4
3
44
2026!
124 <nil>
strconv.Atoi: parsing "abc": invalid syntax

quiz.q: price := 3.99; what does int(price) give?
options: a compile error
quiz.explain: Converting a float variable to an integer truncates toward zero. (With a constant, int(3.99) would be a compile error.)

lessons.title: Switch statements
lessons.concept:
`switch` picks one case out of many. It is cleaner than a long else-if chain.

    switch day {
    case "Sat", "Sun":
        fmt.Println("weekend")
    case "Mon":
        fmt.Println("ugh")
    default:
        fmt.Println("weekday")
    }

Go's switch differs from C's: cases do not fall through, so no break is needed. A case can list several values. Use the `fallthrough` keyword if you really want to continue into the next case.

A switch with no value is a clean if-else chain: each case is a condition, checked top to bottom.

    switch {
    case score >= 90: grade = "A"
    case score >= 80: grade = "B"
    default:          grade = "C"
    }
lessons.eli5: switch is like a sorting machine with labelled slots. You drop a value in, and it slides into the one slot whose label matches. If no label matches, it goes into the "default" slot.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	day := "Sun"
	switch day {
	case "Sat", "Sun":
		fmt.Println("weekend")
	case "Mon":
		fmt.Println("start of the week")
	default:
		fmt.Println("weekday")
	}

	score := 84
	switch {
	case score >= 90:
		fmt.Println("A")
	case score >= 80:
		fmt.Println("B")
	default:
		fmt.Println("C")
	}
}
lessons.expected:
weekend
B

quiz.q: In Go, after a matching case runs, what happens?
options: It falls through to the next case
The switch ends (no fallthrough unless you write fallthrough)
default always runs too
It loops back to the top
quiz.explain: Go cases break automatically; fallthrough must be explicit.

lessons.title: For loops
lessons.concept:
`for` is Go's only loop keyword, and it covers every kind of loop:

    for i := 0; i < 3; i++ { }   // classic: init; condition; post
    for n < 100 { n *= 2 }       // like "while"
    for { }                      // forever (until break or return)
    for i := range 3 { }         // 0, 1, 2 (Go 1.22+)

The three-part form runs init once, checks the condition before each round, and runs the post statement after each round. Since Go 1.22 each iteration gets its own copy of the loop variable, which removes a classic bug.

There are no parentheses, and braces are required.
lessons.eli5: A for loop is "do this again and again". Like counting jumping jacks: "start at 1, keep going while you're under 10, add 1 each time". When the rule says stop, the loop stops.

lessons.title: Goto statements
lessons.concept:
`goto label` jumps to a labelled statement in the same function. A label is a name followed by a colon:

        i := 0
    loop:
        if i < 3 {
            i++
            goto loop
        }

Restrictions keep goto from being too dangerous: you can't jump into a block from outside it, and you can't jump over a variable declaration. In practice goto is rare in Go; loops with labelled break and continue are clearer. You will mostly see goto in generated code and in a few low-level standard library functions.
lessons.eli5: goto is a "teleport to this spot" sign. You put a named flag somewhere and say "goto flag" to jump straight there. It's powerful but can make code like a maze, so Go programmers hardly ever use it.

lessons.title: Statements
lessons.concept:
A statement is one instruction: it does something rather than producing a value. Kinds you'll use constantly:

- Declarations: var x int, const n = 3, type T int
- Assignments: x = 5, a, b = b, a, x += 1
- Increment/decrement: x++, x--
- Expression statements: a function call on its own line, fmt.Println("hi")
- Control flow: if, switch, for, break, continue, goto, return
- Blocks: { ... } groups statements
- go, defer and select (concurrency and cleanup, later)

Statements run one after another, top to bottom, unless a control-flow statement changes the order. Only some expressions may stand alone as statements: calls and receives, yes; `x + 1` on its own line, no ("x + 1 evaluated but not used").
lessons.eli5: A statement is one step in a recipe: "crack the egg", "stir", "bake". The computer does the steps in order, one at a time. Some steps, like "if the cake is done, take it out", decide which step comes next.

package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var count int      // declaration
	count = 10         // assignment
	count++            // increment
	count -= 3         // assignment operator
	fmt.Println(count) // expression statement (a call)
	if count > 5 {     // control flow
		fmt.Println("big")
	}
}

lessons.title: Blocks
lessons.concept:
A block is a sequence of statements inside braces { }. Blocks can nest. Besides the blocks you write, Go has implicit blocks:

- the universe block (holds predeclared names like int, true, len)
- the package block (everything declared at top level in the package)
- the file block (imports)
- each if, for and switch statement is its own block, and each case clause is a block

Blocks matter because they define scope: a name declared in a block exists only until that block's closing brace. You can open a bare block { } anywhere to limit a variable's lifetime.
lessons.eli5: A block is a room with walls { }. Anything you make inside the room stays in the room. When you walk out through the closing }, the things made inside are left behind.

lessons.title: Scope
lessons.concept:
Scope is the region of code where a name can be used.

- Universe scope: predeclared names (int, len, true, nil) are visible everywhere.
- Package scope: names declared at top level (outside functions) are visible in every file of the package.
- Function and block scope: names declared inside a function or block are visible from the declaration to the end of that block.

Shadowing: an inner block may declare a name that already exists in an outer scope. Inside the inner block the new name hides the outer one; the outer variable is untouched. Shadowing by accident (especially with := ) is a classic bug, which go vet can help catch.
lessons.eli5: Scope is "who can see this?". A name made outside every function is like a poster in the hallway: every room can see it. A name made inside a room is like a note on the room's own whiteboard: only people in that room can see it. If a room has a note with the same name as the hallway poster, people in that room see their own note first.

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.concept:
A function is a named, reusable piece of code.

    func add(a int, b int) int {
        return a + b
    }

- `func` keyword, the name, the parameter list in ( ), then the result type, then the body.
- Parameters of the same type can share it: `func add(a, b int) int`.
- `return` sends a value back to the caller and ends the function.
- Call it with `add(2, 3)`.

Functions are declared at package level (not inside other functions; for that you use function literals, later). The order of declarations doesn't matter: main can call a function written below it.
lessons.eli5: A function is a little machine you build once and use many times. You give it something (like two numbers), it does its job (adds them) and gives you something back (the total). Instead of doing the same work over and over, you just press the machine's button.

lessons.title: Parameters
lessons.concept:
Parameters are the inputs a function declares; arguments are the values you pass when calling it.

In Go every argument is passed by value: the function receives a copy. Changing a parameter inside the function does not change the caller's variable.

    func double(n int) { n = n * 2 }   // changes only the copy

To let a function change the caller's data, pass a pointer (Pointers lesson) or return the new value. Types like slices and maps contain internal pointers, so a function can change their contents even though the slice/map header itself is copied; that is covered in their lessons.
lessons.eli5: Parameters are the empty slots on the machine where you put things in. When you put a number in, Go gives the machine a photocopy, not your original. So if the machine scribbles on it, your original paper stays clean.

lessons.title: Return values
lessons.concept:
A function can return zero, one or many values.

    func divide(a, b int) (int, int) {
        return a / b, a % b
    }
    q, r := divide(7, 2)

Multiple results are how Go reports errors: the last result is an error (covered later), as in `n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)`.

Results can also be named. Named results are variables that start at their zero value; a bare `return` returns their current values. Use named results for documentation and short functions; avoid bare returns in long functions, because they make it hard to see what is returned.
lessons.eli5: Return values are what the machine hands back. Some machines hand back one thing; Go machines can hand back two or three at once, like a vending machine that gives you a drink AND your change.

lessons.title: Recursion (A–Z)
lessons.concept:
A recursive function calls itself. Every recursive function needs:
1. A base case that stops the recursion.
2. A recursive case that moves toward the base case.

    func factorial(n int) int {
        if n <= 1 { return 1 }          // base case
        return n * factorial(n-1)       // smaller problem
    }

Each call gets its own copy of the parameters on the stack. Go's goroutine stacks grow as needed, so deep recursion is fine until it's truly huge. Without a base case the program eventually crashes with "goroutine stack exceeds limit". Many recursive problems can also be solved with a loop.
lessons.eli5: Recursion is like Russian nesting dolls. To open the big doll, you open it and find a smaller doll, and you do the same thing again, until you reach the tiniest doll that doesn't open. That tiniest doll is the "base case" that tells you to stop.
lessons.expected:
120
3
2
1
liftoff!

quiz.q: What does every recursive function need to avoid running forever?
options: A loop
A base case
A global variable
A pointer
quiz.explain: The base case returns without recursing, stopping the chain of calls.

lessons.title: Pointers
lessons.concept:
A pointer holds the memory address of a value instead of the value itself.

- `&x` gives the address of x. Its type is `*int` if x is an int.
- `*p` follows the pointer to read or change the value it points at (dereferencing).
- The zero value of a pointer is `nil`, meaning it points at nothing. Dereferencing nil crashes the program (a panic).
- `new(T)` allocates a zero T and returns a pointer to it.

Why pointers? Arguments are copied, so to let a function change the caller's variable, pass its address:

    func reset(n *int) { *n = 0 }
    reset(&count)

Go has no pointer arithmetic (you can't do p+1), which keeps pointers safe. Go's garbage collector frees memory once no pointer refers to it.
lessons.eli5: A pointer is a treasure map. Instead of carrying the treasure (the value) around, you carry a map that says where it's buried. &x means "draw me a map to x". *p means "follow the map and dig up what's there". If two people have the same map, they find the same treasure.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func reset(n *int) {
	*n = 0
}

func main() {
	count := 42
	p := &count
	fmt.Println(*p)
	*p = 100
	fmt.Println(count)

	reset(&count)
	fmt.Println(count)

	q := new(int)
	fmt.Println(*q, q != nil)
}

quiz.q: If p := &x, what does *p = 5 do?
options: Makes p point to 5
Sets x to 5
Copies x
Compile error
quiz.explain: *p is the variable p points to, i.e. x itself.

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.concept:
An array is a fixed-length sequence of elements of one type. The length is part of the type: [3]int and [4]int are different types.

    var a [3]int              // [0 0 0]
    b := [3]string{"a", "b", "c"}
    c := [...]int{1, 2, 3, 4} // the compiler counts: [4]int

`len(a)` gives the length. Elements are numbered from 0.

Arrays are values: assigning or passing an array copies all of its elements. That makes them predictable but expensive when large. In everyday Go you mostly use slices (next lesson), which are built on top of arrays.
lessons.eli5: An array is an egg carton with a fixed number of cups. A 12-cup carton always has 12 cups, numbered from 0. You can't make it bigger. If you give a friend your carton, Go gives them a full copy, eggs and all.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var a [3]int
	a[0] = 10
	fmt.Println(a, len(a))

	colors := [3]string{"red", "green", "blue"}
	fmt.Println(colors)

	copyOf := colors // arrays are copied
	copyOf[0] = "pink"
	fmt.Println(colors[0], copyOf[0])

	nums := [...]int{5, 6, 7, 8}
	fmt.Printf("%T\n", nums)
}
lessons.expected:
[10 0 0] 3
[red green blue]
red pink
[4]int

quiz.q: Are [3]int and [4]int the same type?
options: Yes
No, the length is part of an array's type
Only if both are empty
Only in Go 1.22+
quiz.explain: Array length is part of the type, so they are distinct types.

lessons.title: Slices
lessons.concept:
A slice is a flexible, growable view of an array. It is the list type you will use most.

    s := []int{1, 2, 3}       // a slice literal (no length in the brackets)
    s = append(s, 4, 5)       // append returns the new slice: always assign it back
    fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))

A slice has three parts: a pointer to an underlying array, a length (how many elements you can use) and a capacity (room before append needs a bigger array). When capacity runs out, append allocates a bigger array and copies.

- `make([]int, 3)` creates a slice of length 3 filled with zero values; `make([]int, 0, 10)` reserves capacity 10.
- The zero value of a slice is nil, and a nil slice works with len, append and range.
- Copying a slice copies the header, not the elements: two slices can share one array.
lessons.eli5: A slice is like a stretchy line of kids holding hands. You can add more kids at the end with append. Behind the scenes there's a row of chairs (the array); when the chairs run out, Go quietly finds a bigger row and moves everyone over.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := []int{1, 2, 3}
	s = append(s, 4, 5)
	fmt.Println(s, len(s))

	m := make([]string, 2)
	m[0] = "go"
	fmt.Printf("%q %d\n", m, len(m))

	var empty []int
	fmt.Println(empty == nil, len(empty))
	empty = append(empty, 7)
	fmt.Println(empty)
}

quiz.q: Why must you write s = append(s, x)?
options: Style only
append may return a new slice header (new array, new length); you must keep it
append modifies in place and returns nothing
To avoid a copy
quiz.explain: append returns the updated slice; the old header still has the old length.

lessons.title: Array and slice indexing
lessons.concept:
Use `a[i]` to read or write element i of an array, slice or string. Indexes start at 0 and the last one is len(a)-1.

    nums := []int{10, 20, 30}
    nums[1] = 25             // write
    last := nums[len(nums)-1]

Indexes are checked: an index outside 0..len-1 stops the program with a panic, "index out of range". With constant indexes on arrays the compiler catches it before you run.

Indexing a string gives a byte (one 8-bit piece of UTF-8), not a character. For characters, use range or convert to []rune (later lessons).
lessons.eli5: Indexing is finding a seat by its number. Seat 0 is the first seat. If you ask for seat number 10 in a row of 3 seats, Go shouts "that seat doesn't exist!" and stops.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	nums := []int{10, 20, 30}
	fmt.Println(nums[0], nums[2])
	nums[1] = 25
	fmt.Println(nums)
	fmt.Println("last:", nums[len(nums)-1])

	word := "Go!"
	fmt.Println(word[0], string(word[0]))
}

quiz.q: What happens when you read nums[5] from a 3-element slice?
options: It returns 0
It returns nil
The program panics: index out of range
It grows the slice
quiz.explain: Go checks bounds at run time and panics on an out-of-range index.

lessons.title: Slice expressions
lessons.concept:
`a[low:high]` makes a new slice of elements low up to (but not including) high. Either bound may be left out:

    s := []int{0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
    s[1:3]   // [1 2]
    s[:2]    // [0 1]
    s[3:]    // [3 4]
    s[:]     // all

The result shares the original's underlying array: changing an element through one is visible through the other. The new length is high-low.

A full slice expression `a[low:high:max]` also limits capacity to max-low, so a later append is forced to copy instead of overwriting the original.

Strings can be sliced too, `"golang"[0:2]` is "go" (by bytes).
lessons.eli5: Slicing is cutting a piece out of a long loaf of bread. s[1:3] means "start at slice 1, stop before slice 3". But it's a magic loaf: the piece is still connected to the loaf, so if you put jam on the piece, the loaf gets jam too.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := []int{0, 1, 2, 3, 4}
	fmt.Println(s[1:3], s[:2], s[3:], s[:])

	part := s[1:3]
	part[0] = 99 // shares the array with s
	fmt.Println(s)

	safe := s[1:3:3] // capacity limited to 2
	safe = append(safe, 7)
	fmt.Println(s, safe)

	fmt.Println("golang"[0:2])
}

quiz.explain: low is included, high is excluded: elements 1 and 2.

lessons.title: Maps
lessons.concept:
A map stores key/value pairs and finds a value by its key very quickly (hash table).

    ages := map[string]int{"ada": 36, "alan": 41}
    ages["grace"] = 85          // add or update
    fmt.Println(ages["ada"])     // 36

- The type is map[KeyType]ValueType. Keys must be comparable (strings, numbers, bools, pointers, arrays and structs of comparable fields); slices and maps can't be keys.
- Create with a literal or make(map[string]int). The zero value is nil: reading a nil map is fine, writing to it panics.
- A map is a reference to its data: passing it to a function lets the function change it.
- Iteration order is deliberately random.
lessons.eli5: A map is a dictionary. You look up a word (the key) and find its meaning (the value). You don't flip through pages in order; you jump straight to the word you want.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	ages := map[string]int{"ada": 36, "alan": 41}
	ages["grace"] = 85
	ages["ada"] = 37
	fmt.Println(ages["ada"], ages["grace"], len(ages))

	scores := make(map[string]int)
	scores["go"] = 10
	fmt.Println(scores)
	fmt.Println(ages["nobody"]) // a missing key gives the zero value
}

quiz.q: What do you get reading a key that isn't in a map[string]int?
options: A panic
nil
0 (the value type's zero value)
quiz.explain: Reading a missing key returns the zero value; use the comma-ok form to tell the difference.

lessons.title: Map operations
lessons.concept:
Everything you can do with a map:

    m[k] = v              // insert or update
    v := m[k]             // read (zero value if missing)
    v, ok := m[k]         // comma-ok: ok is false if k is missing
    delete(m, k)          // remove (no error if k is missing)
    n := len(m)           // number of entries
    clear(m)              // remove everything (Go 1.21+)
    for k, v := range m   // visit every entry, in random order

The comma-ok form is how you tell "missing" apart from "present with value 0". You can't take the address of a map element (&m[k] is an error) because entries move when the map grows. To print a map in a stable order, collect and sort its keys (fmt.Println already prints maps sorted by key).
lessons.eli5: Map operations are the things you can do with your dictionary: write a new word, look one up, ask "is this word even in here?", rip a page out (delete), and count the pages (len).
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	stock := map[string]int{"apple": 5, "pear": 0}

	n, ok := stock["pear"]
	fmt.Println(n, ok)
	n, ok = stock["kiwi"]
	fmt.Println(n, ok)

	stock["kiwi"] = 3
	delete(stock, "apple")
	fmt.Println(stock, len(stock))

	clear(stock)
	fmt.Println(len(stock))
}
lessons.expected:
0 true
0 false
map[kiwi:3 pear:0] 2
0

quiz.q: How do you tell a missing key from a key whose value is 0?
options: Compare with nil
v, ok := m[k] and check ok
Use len(m)
Use delete
quiz.explain: The comma-ok form returns ok=false when the key is absent.

lessons.title: Type declarations
lessons.concept:
`type` creates a new named type. Two forms:

    type Celsius float64        // a defined type based on float64
    type Point struct{ X, Y int } // a defined type based on a struct

A defined type is a brand-new type: Celsius and float64 have the same underlying type, but they are different, so you can't mix them without converting: `Celsius(20) + Fahrenheit(3)` is a compile error. That catches unit mix-ups.

The new type keeps its underlying type's operations (you can add Celsius values) but none of its methods, and you can attach your own methods to it (Methods lesson). Group several declarations with type ( ... ).
lessons.eli5: type is like inventing a new label. "Celsius" boxes and "Fahrenheit" boxes both hold numbers, but they have different labels, so Go won't let you mix them up by accident, just like you wouldn't pour apple juice into the orange-juice jug.
lessons.expected:
212
main.Celsius main.Fahrenheit
22.5

quiz.q: type Meters float64; can you add a Meters and a float64 variable directly?
options: Yes
No, they're different types; convert first
Only if both are positive
Only with +=
quiz.explain: A defined type is distinct from its underlying type; mixing them needs a conversion.

lessons.title: Type aliases
lessons.concept:
An alias gives an existing type a second name. Note the `=`:

    type Text = string    // alias: Text IS string
    type Name string      // defined type: Name is a NEW type

With an alias the two names are fully interchangeable; nothing new is created. byte (= uint8), rune (= int32) and any (= interface{}) are aliases built into Go.

Aliases exist mainly to move a type between packages without breaking code that still uses the old name. Since Go 1.24 aliases can even have type parameters. For your own designs, a defined type is usually what you want.
lessons.eli5: An alias is a nickname. If your friend Robert is also called Bob, "Bob" and "Robert" are the same person. A type alias is a nickname for a type: two names, one thing.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Text = string // alias
type Name string   // new defined type

func shout(s string) string {
	return s + "!"
}

func main() {
	var t Text = "hello"
	fmt.Println(shout(t)) // fine: Text is string

	var n Name = "ada"
	fmt.Println(shout(string(n))) // Name needs a conversion
	fmt.Printf("%T %T\n", t, n)
}
lessons.expected:
hello!
ada!
string main.Name

quiz.q: What's the difference between `type A = int` and `type B int`?
options: None
A is an alias for int; B is a new, distinct type
B is an alias; A is new
A is a constant
quiz.explain: The = makes an alias; without it you define a new type.

lessons.title: Structs
lessons.concept:
A struct groups named fields into one value. It's how you model things:

    type Person struct {
        Name string
        Age  int
    }
    p := Person{Name: "Ada", Age: 36}
    p.Age++                  // fields are accessed with a dot
    fmt.Println(p.Name)

- Fields can be any type, including other structs, slices and maps.
- The zero value of a struct has every field at its zero value.
- Structs are values: assigning copies every field. Use a pointer (*Person) to share one.
- With a pointer, p.Name works directly; Go dereferences automatically.
- Structs are comparable with == if all their fields are.
lessons.eli5: A struct is a form with blanks to fill in: Name ___, Age ___. Each filled-in form is one value. A "Person" form always has the same blanks, but every person fills in different answers.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Person struct {
	Name string
	Age  int
}

func main() {
	p := Person{Name: "Ada", Age: 36}
	p.Age++
	fmt.Println(p.Name, p.Age)
	fmt.Printf("%v %+v\n", p, p)

	var empty Person
	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", empty)

	ptr := &p
	ptr.Name = "Ada Lovelace" // auto-dereference
	fmt.Println(p.Name)
}

quiz.q: How do you read the Age field of a struct p?
options: p->Age
p[Age]
p.Age
Age(p)
quiz.explain: Fields use dot notation, both for values and pointers.

lessons.title: Composite literals
lessons.concept:
A composite literal builds a value of a composite type (array, slice, map or struct) in one expression: the type followed by braces.

    [3]int{1, 2, 3}                    // array
    []string{"a", "b"}                 // slice
    map[string]int{"x": 1}             // map
    Point{X: 1, Y: 2}                  // struct with field names
    Point{1, 2}                        // positional (fragile; prefer names)
    &Point{X: 1}                       // address of a new struct
    []Point{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}            // inner type can be left out

Fields or elements you leave out get zero values. Trailing commas are required when the closing brace is on its own line. Indexed elements are allowed too: `[5]int{2: 10}` puts 10 at index 2.
lessons.eli5: A composite literal is building something with blocks all at once. Instead of making an empty box and filling it piece by piece, you say "here's a box with these three things in it" in one go.

quiz.q: In Point{X: 3}, what is Y?
options: Undefined
nil
0 (zero value)
quiz.explain: Omitted fields get their zero value.

lessons.title: Exported and unexported identifiers
lessons.concept:
Go has no public/private keywords. Visibility is decided by the first letter of a name:

- Upper case (Println, Person, Name): exported, usable from other packages.
- Lower case (helper, age): unexported, usable only inside its own package.

This applies to functions, types, variables, constants, struct fields and methods. That's why you call fmt.Println (exported) and can't call fmt's internal helpers.

Struct fields follow the same rule: a lower-case field is invisible outside the package, including to packages like encoding/json, so JSON skips it. Inside a single-package program (package main) everything is visible, but the habit matters as soon as you write libraries.
lessons.eli5: Capital letters are like a front door, lowercase letters are like a bedroom door. Things with a capital letter can be seen by everyone who visits (other packages). Things with a lowercase letter are private, only for the family living in that package.
lessons.expected: ada 100

quiz.q: Which name is exported from its package?

quiz.explain: A name is exported if it starts with an upper-case letter.

lessons.title: Struct tags
lessons.concept:
A struct tag is a string literal after a field, read by packages at run time to customise how they treat the field:

    type User struct {
        Name  string `json:"name"`
        Email string `json:"email,omitempty"`
        pass  string // unexported: json ignores it
    }

The convention is key:"value" pairs separated by spaces. encoding/json uses the json key: rename the field in JSON, `omitempty` drops it when it's the zero value, and "-" skips it. Other libraries use db:"...", yaml:"...", validate:"...".

json.Marshal turns a value into JSON bytes (plus an error), and json.Unmarshal does the reverse. Tags are just strings: a typo in one is silently ignored, which go vet checks for.
lessons.eli5: Struct tags are little stickers on each blank of your form. The sticker says "when you write this form in JSON language, call this blank 'name'". The computer reads the stickers when it translates your form.

{"name":"Ada"} <nil>
{Name:Alan Email:a@x.org Age:0} <nil>

options: Makes the field required
Names it email and leaves it out when it's empty/zero
Encrypts the field
Ignores the field always
