lessons.title: Methods
lessons.concept:
A method is a function attached to a type. The receiver goes before the name:

    type Rect struct{ W, H float64 }
    func (r Rect) Area() float64 { return r.W * r.H }   // value receiver
    func (r *Rect) Scale(k float64) { r.W *= k; r.H *= k } // pointer receiver
    r := Rect{2, 3}
    r.Scale(2)        // Go takes &r for you
    r.Area()          // 24

- A value receiver works on a copy; use it for small types that don't change.
- A pointer receiver can modify the original and avoids copying big structs. If any method needs a pointer receiver, make them all pointer receivers for consistency.
- You can declare methods on any named type defined in your package, not just structs: `func (c Celsius) String() string`.
- Methods of embedded types are promoted to the outer type.
lessons.eli5: A method is a special trick that belongs to one kind of thing. A dog knows the trick "Bark", a car knows the trick "Honk". You ask the thing to do its trick with a dot: dog.Bark(). Some tricks just look at the thing; others (pointer receivers) can change it, like painting the car a new colour.

quiz.q: Which receiver lets a method change the original struct?
options: (r Rect)
(r *Rect)
Either
Neither; methods can't change data
quiz.explain: A pointer receiver points at the original; a value receiver gets a copy.

lessons.title: Type assertions
lessons.concept:
An interface value holds a concrete value inside it. A type assertion gets it back out:

    var v any = "hello"
    s := v.(string)          // s is "hello"
    n := v.(int)             // wrong type: PANIC

Use the comma-ok form to check safely:

    n, ok := v.(int)         // ok is false, n is 0, no panic

You can also assert to another interface: `str, ok := v.(fmt.Stringer)` asks "does the value inside have a String method?". Assertions only work on interface values.
lessons.eli5: A type assertion is opening a mystery box and checking what's inside. "I bet this box has a string in it!" If you're right, you get the string. If you're wrong, things go boom, unless you asked politely with ", ok", which just tells you "nope, wrong guess".
lessons.expected:
hello
0 false
it is a string of length 5

quiz.q: What happens with v.(int) when v holds a string and you don't use comma-ok?
options: Returns 0
Returns nil
Panics
Converts the string
quiz.explain: A single-result assertion panics on mismatch; comma-ok returns ok=false instead.

lessons.title: Type switches
lessons.concept:
A type switch checks an interface value against several types at once:

    switch x := v.(type) {
    case int:
        fmt.Println("int, doubled:", x*2)     // x is an int here
    case string:
        fmt.Println("string of length", len(x))
    case nil:
        fmt.Println("nothing")
    default:
        fmt.Printf("other: %T\n", x)
    }

`v.(type)` is only legal inside a switch. In each case, x has that case's type, so you can use it directly. A case listing several types (case int, int64:) leaves x as the interface type.
lessons.eli5: A type switch is a sorting machine for mystery boxes. It peeks inside and says "a number? go left. Words? go right. Nothing? go in the bin." And once the box is sorted, you know exactly what's inside.
lessons.expected:
int, doubled: 42
string of length 6
nothing at all
something else: float64

quiz.q: Where can you write v.(type)?
options: Anywhere
Only in a type switch
Only in if statements
Only with generics
quiz.explain: The .(type) form exists only as the switch guard of a type switch.

lessons.title: Defer statements
lessons.concept:
`defer f()` schedules a call to run when the surrounding function returns, however it returns: normally, through an early return, or during a panic.

    f, err := os.Open(name)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer f.Close()        // runs when this function ends

Rules:
- Deferred calls run in last-in, first-out order (a stack).
- The arguments are evaluated immediately, when the defer statement runs; only the call is delayed.
- Deferred functions can read and change named results, which is how cleanup code can adjust a return value.

Put the defer right after acquiring a resource, so the release can never be forgotten. Avoid defer inside long loops: the calls pile up until the function ends.
lessons.eli5: defer is a "do this when we leave" note. When you walk into a room you write "turn off the light on the way out" and stick it on the door. No matter how you leave the room, the light gets turned off. If you write several notes, the last one you wrote is done first.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func work() {
	defer fmt.Println("3: deferred first, runs last")
	defer fmt.Println("2: deferred second, runs first")
	fmt.Println("1: normal work")
}

func main() {
	work()
	x := 1
	defer fmt.Println("x was", x) // argument evaluated now
	x = 100
	fmt.Println("x is now", x)
}
lessons.expected:
1: normal work
2: deferred second, runs first
3: deferred first, runs last
x is now 100
x was 1

quiz.q: In which order do deferred calls run?
options: In the order they were deferred
Last deferred runs first
Randomly
All at the same time
quiz.explain: Deferred calls form a stack: last in, first out.

lessons.title: Built-in functions
lessons.concept:
Go predeclares a handful of functions you can call without importing anything:

- len(x): length of a string, array, slice, map or channel
- cap(x): capacity of a slice, array or channel
- make(T, ...): create a slice, map or channel
- new(T): allocate a zero T and return *T
- append(s, ...): add elements to a slice
- copy(dst, src): copy slice elements, returns how many
- delete(m, k): remove a map key
- clear(x): empty a map or zero a slice's elements (Go 1.21)
- min(...), max(...): smallest / largest of their arguments (Go 1.21)
- close(ch): close a channel (Channels lesson)
- panic(v), recover(): see Panic and recover
- complex(r, i), real(c), imag(c): build and take apart complex numbers
- print, println: low-level printing to standard error, for debugging the runtime only; use fmt instead.
lessons.eli5: Built-in functions are the tools that come already in the toolbox. You don't need to borrow them from anyone. len counts things, append adds things, min and max pick the smallest and biggest, copy makes a copy. They're always there.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := make([]int, 3, 10)
	fmt.Println(len(s), cap(s))
	s = append(s, 4)
	dst := make([]int, 2)
	n := copy(dst, s)
	fmt.Println(dst, n)

	m := map[string]int{"a": 1, "b": 2}
	delete(m, "a")
	fmt.Println(len(m))
	clear(m)
	fmt.Println(len(m))

	fmt.Println(min(3, 1, 2), max(3, 1, 2))
	c := complex(1, 2)
	fmt.Println(real(c), imag(c))
	p := new(int)
	fmt.Println(*p)
}

options: remove

quiz.explain: delete(m, key) removes one key; clear(m) removes all of them.

lessons.title: Constraints
lessons.concept:
A constraint is an interface that limits which types a type parameter accepts.

- `any`: every type.
- `comparable`: types that support == and != (needed for map keys).
- A type set: `interface{ int | float64 }` allows exactly those types.
- `~int` means "int or any type whose underlying type is int" (so type Celsius int fits).
- The cmp package's `cmp.Ordered` allows every type that supports < and > (integers, floats, strings).

    func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T {
        if a > b { return a }
        return b
    }

The constraint decides which operations you may use on T inside the function: with any you can't use + or <, with cmp.Ordered you can. Constraints may also require methods: interface{ ~int; String() string }.
lessons.eli5: A constraint is the rule on the cookie cutter: "only for soft dough". If someone tries to use it on a rock, Go says no. comparable means "only things you can check are the same". Ordered means "only things you can line up from small to big".

quiz.q: Which constraint lets you use < on T?
options: any
comparable
cmp.Ordered
error
quiz.explain: cmp.Ordered includes every type supporting the ordering operators.

lessons.title: Goroutines
lessons.concept:
A goroutine is a function running concurrently with the rest of the program. Start one with the go keyword:

    go doWork(1)

Goroutines are very cheap (a few KB of stack that grows as needed), so programs can run thousands. The Go runtime schedules them onto operating-system threads.

When main returns, the whole program ends, even if goroutines are still running. So you need a way to wait: sync.WaitGroup counts running goroutines.

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    wg.Add(1)              // before starting
    go func() {
        defer wg.Done()    // when finished
        ...
    }()
    wg.Wait()              // blocks until the count is zero

Goroutines run in an unpredictable order. Never let two goroutines write the same variable without synchronisation (channels or a mutex): that's a data race. The example writes each result to its own slot, which is safe.
lessons.eli5: A goroutine is a helper you send off to do a chore while you keep doing your own. "go wash the dishes!" and off they go. The WaitGroup is a checklist: you tick off each helper as they finish, and you wait until every box is ticked before you leave the house.

quiz.q: What happens to running goroutines when main returns?
options: They keep running
The program exits and they stop
main waits for them automatically
They are restarted
quiz.explain: The program ends when main returns; use a WaitGroup (or channels) to wait.

lessons.title: Channels
lessons.concept:
A channel is a typed pipe that goroutines use to send values to each other safely.

    ch := make(chan int)      // unbuffered
    go func() { ch <- 42 }()  // send
    v := <-ch                 // receive (waits for a value)

- On an unbuffered channel a send waits until a receiver takes the value: the two goroutines meet, which also synchronises them.
- `make(chan int, 3)` is buffered: sends only wait when the buffer is full.
- `close(ch)` says "no more values". Receivers then drain the rest, and `for v := range ch` stops after the last one. `v, ok := <-ch` gives ok=false once closed and empty. Only the sender should close, and sending on a closed channel panics.
- Directional types restrict use: `chan<- int` can only send, `<-chan int` can only receive.

Go's motto: don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating.
lessons.eli5: A channel is a tube between two kids. One kid drops a marble in one end (send), the other kid catches it at the other end (receive). If the tube has no room (unbuffered), the first kid waits until the second kid is ready to catch. When the first kid is done, they put a cap on the tube (close).

a b 0
got 10
got 20
got 30

quiz.q: When does a send on an unbuffered channel complete?
options: Immediately
When a receiver takes the value

After 1 second
quiz.explain: Unbuffered sends block until another goroutine receives.

lessons.title: Select statements
lessons.concept:
`select` waits on several channel operations at once and runs the first one that is ready:

    select {
    case msg := <-messages:
        fmt.Println("got", msg)
    case <-time.After(time.Second):
        fmt.Println("timed out")
    }

- If several cases are ready, select picks one at random.
- A default case runs immediately when nothing is ready, which makes non-blocking sends and receives.
- time.After(d) returns a channel that receives a value after duration d, a simple way to add timeouts. time.Second and time.Millisecond are durations from the time package.
- A select with no cases blocks forever.

select inside a for loop is the heart of most concurrent Go code: wait for work, a timeout or a "stop" signal, whichever comes first.
lessons.eli5: select is waiting at several doors at once. Whichever door someone knocks on first, you open that one. You can also set an egg timer (time.After): if nobody knocks before it rings, you stop waiting. And with default you peek at all the doors and, if nobody's there, you go do something else.
lessons.expected:
got hello
nothing ready, moving on
timed out waiting

quiz.q: What does a default case in select do?
options: Runs after all other cases
Runs immediately if no other case is ready
Runs on timeout
Closes the channels
quiz.explain: default makes select non-blocking.

lessons.title: Initialization functions (init)
lessons.concept:
Before main runs, Go initialises each package:

1. Imported packages are initialised first, each exactly once.
2. Package-level variables are initialised, in dependency order (a variable that uses another is set after it).
3. Every func init() in the package runs, in the order they appear (files are processed in the order the compiler is given them, usually alphabetical).

init takes no arguments, returns nothing, and can't be called by your code. A file may have several.

Use init sparingly: for setting up tables that can't be written as a variable initialiser, or registering a driver. Hidden work in init makes programs harder to test and understand; explicit setup in main is usually better.
lessons.eli5: init is the "get the classroom ready" job before the lesson starts. Before main (the lesson) begins, Go sets out the desks (package variables) and runs every init helper. Then the bell rings and main starts.
lessons.expected:
1. package variable initialised
2. init runs before main
3. main starts: hello

quiz.q: When does func init() run?
options: When you call it
After main returns
Before main, after package variables are initialised
Only in tests
quiz.explain: Package variables are initialised, then init functions run, then main.

lessons.title: Modules
lessons.concept:
A module is a collection of packages released and versioned together. Its root folder contains go.mod:

    module github.com/you/project

    go 1.24

    require github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0

- `go mod init github.com/you/project` creates go.mod. The module path is the prefix for importing your packages: package util in folder util/ is imported as "github.com/you/project/util".
- `go get example.com/pkg@v1.2.3` adds or upgrades a dependency; `go mod tidy` adds missing and removes unused ones.
- go.sum records cryptographic checksums so builds are reproducible and tamper-proof.
- Versions follow semantic versioning (v1.2.3). A new major version v2+ changes the import path (.../v2).

This app's runner creates a tiny module for every program you run (module lesson), which is why your code can import the standard library but nothing that needs downloading.
lessons.eli5: A module is a whole lunchbox: all the packages (sandwiches, fruit) that go together, with a label (go.mod) listing what's inside and which other lunchboxes it borrows from. The label also says exactly which version of each borrowed thing, so lunch tastes the same every day.

quiz.q: Which file declares a module's path and dependencies?
options: main.go
go.mod
go.sum
package.json
quiz.explain: go.mod holds the module path, Go version and requirements; go.sum holds checksums.

lessons.title: I/O (io, fmt, os)
lessons.concept:
Input/output in Go is built on two tiny interfaces from package io:

    type Reader interface { Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) }
    type Writer interface { Write(p []byte) (n int, err error) }

Files, network connections, buffers, HTTP bodies and the terminal all implement them, so the same code works with all of them.

- os.Stdin, os.Stdout and os.Stderr are the terminal's input, output and error streams (an *os.File is both a Reader and a Writer).
- fmt.Fprintln(w, ...) and fmt.Fprintf(w, ...) print to any Writer; fmt.Println is Fprintln(os.Stdout, ...).
- os.WriteFile and os.ReadFile handle whole small files; os.Open and os.Create return files for streaming.
- io.ReadAll reads a Reader to the end; io.Copy pipes a Reader into a Writer.
- bufio.Scanner reads input line by line.

Always check the error, and close files you open (defer f.Close()).
lessons.eli5: I/O is how a program talks to the outside world. Input is listening (reading from the keyboard or a file), output is talking (writing to the screen or a file). Go uses two simple jobs for all of it: "Reader" (can give you bytes) and "Writer" (can take bytes). A file, the screen and the internet all know both jobs.

lessons.title: Start here: what is a program?
lessons.concept:
A PROGRAM is a list of instructions for a computer, written in a language
precise enough that there is never any doubt what each instruction
means. Computers are fast and tireless but take everything literally:
they do exactly what you wrote, not what you meant.

▸  WHAT IS GO?
Go (often called 'Golang') is a programming language created at Google
in 2009. It's used for web servers, command-line tools, cloud
infrastructure (Docker and Kubernetes are written in Go) and much more.
It was designed to be SMALL - you can learn the whole language - and to
make programs that are fast, reliable and easy to read.

▸  SOURCE CODE AND COMPILING
You write instructions as plain text in a file ending in .go - the
SOURCE CODE. The computer's processor can't read that text directly. A
tool called the COMPILER translates it into MACHINE CODE the processor
runs. In Go the compiler is part of the 'go' tool:

    you write  ->  main.go  ->  go build  ->  a program you can run

▸  WHAT THIS COURSE GIVES YOU
Every lesson has a CONCEPT to read and a QUIZ. Most also have CODE in an
editor with a Run button: press it and the app compiles and runs the
program on your computer and shows what it printed. Lessons whose title
starts 'Challenge' ask you to write the program yourself; the app
checks your output automatically.

▸  HOW TO STUDY
Read the '0 · How to Learn' lessons first - they take 15 minutes and
roughly double what you'll remember. The short version: before pressing
Run, PREDICT what will happen.

quiz.q: What does the compiler do?
options: Uploads your program to Google's servers
Runs the program one line at a time as you type
Checks your spelling in comments and text
Translates your source code into machine code
quiz.explain: A compiler turns human-readable source code into the machine instructions the processor executes. Go compiles your whole program into a single runnable file.
quiz.hint: The processor can't read .go text directly.

lessons.title: What happens when you press Run
lessons.concept:
Behind the Run button, the app does exactly what a Go programmer does by
hand:

    1. Writes your editor text to a file called main.go in a fresh,
       temporary folder, together with a small go.mod file (Go's project
       description).
    2. Runs 'go build', which COMPILES it. If the code has a mistake, the
       compiler stops and explains what and where - shown in red as a
       BUILD ERROR, usually with a plain-English HINT on top.
    3. Runs the finished program, feeding it whatever you typed in the
       'stdin:' box as keyboard input.
    4. Shows everything it printed in OUTPUT.
    5. Deletes the temporary folder.

▸  READING A BUILD ERROR
    ./main.go:6:2: declared and not used: x
       file   line:column   what is wrong
Line 6, column 2 - go straight there. Fix the FIRST error first: later
ones are often caused by it.

▸  TRY IT

error and the HINT, fix it (one small change), and Run again until it
prints 'Fixed it!'.

lessons.title: Your first Go program
lessons.concept:
Every runnable Go program has the same skeleton:

    package main          // this file builds into a program
    import "fmt"          // use the fmt (format) package
    func main() {         // execution starts here
        fmt.Println("...")
    }

▸  YOUR TASK
Print the two lines shown above (YOUR TASK box). Start from the skeleton
in the editor; you only need fmt.Println, called twice.

▸  HOW IT WORKS
fmt.Println prints each argument, separated by spaces, followed by a
newline. Text in double quotes is a string literal. Each statement goes
on its own line - Go adds the semicolons for you.

▸  IF IT WON'T BUILD

lessons.title: Println, Print and Printf
lessons.concept:
The fmt package has three printing styles you'll use constantly:

    fmt.Print(a, b)       no newline; adds spaces only between operands
                          when neither side is a string
    fmt.Println(a, b)     ALWAYS a space between operands, then a newline
    fmt.Printf(f, a, b)   a FORMAT string with verbs filled in order:
                          %v any value   %d integer   %s string
                          %f float      %q quoted     %T the type
                          %t bool       %% a literal percent sign

Printf does NOT add a newline - end the format with \n yourself.

▸  Sprint-, Fprint- AND Errorf
Every printer has siblings: Sprintf returns the string instead of
printing it, Fprintf writes to any io.Writer (a file, os.Stderr, an HTTP
response), and fmt.Errorf builds an error.

▸  WATCH OUT
Printf with the wrong verb doesn't crash; it prints a marker like
%!d(string=hi). 'go vet' catches these mismatches at build time - this
course runs vet on every example.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	name, age := "Ada", 36
	fmt.Print("no", "space", 1, 2, "\n")
	fmt.Println("with", "spaces", 1, 2)
	fmt.Printf("%s is %d years old\n", name, age)
	fmt.Printf("%v | %q | %T | %t | 100%%\n", age, name, age, age > 30)
	msg := fmt.Sprintf("%05.1f", 3.14159)
	fmt.Println(msg)
}
lessons.expected:
nospace1 2
with spaces 1 2
Ada is 36 years old
36 | "Ada" | int | true | 100%
003.1

A single space and then a newline
A newline, exactly like Println does
A trailing %d marker for the verb
quiz.explain: Printf prints exactly the format string with verbs substituted. If you want a newline, include \n in the format.
quiz.hint: Println adds a newline. Does Printf?

lessons.title: Comments and documentation
lessons.concept:
Go has two kinds of comment:
    // to the end of the line          (by far the most common)
    /* a block comment */               (rare: mainly to disable code)

▸  DOC COMMENTS
A comment placed directly above a package, func, type, const or var -
with no blank line in between - is its DOCUMENTATION. 'go doc' and
pkg.go.dev display it. Convention: start with the name being documented:

    // Celsius converts a temperature from Fahrenheit.
    func Celsius(f float64) float64 { ... }

Every exported name in a library should have one; linters flag those
that don't.

▸  DIRECTIVES ARE NOT COMMENTS
Lines like //go:build linux or //go:embed file.txt look like comments
but instruct the tools. Note: no space after the slashes.

quiz.q: Which comment does 'go doc' show as Celsius's documentation?
options: The // comment at the end of the return line
The // comment directly above func Celsius
The first comment line of the package
A /* */ comment anywhere in the same file
quiz.explain: A doc comment is the comment block immediately preceding the declaration with no blank line between. Trailing comments inside the body are just notes.
quiz.hint: Doc comments are attached to declarations by position.

lessons.title: Variables: var, := and multiple assignment
lessons.concept:
▸  FOUR SHAPES
    var count int            // declared, zero value 0
    var name = "Go"          // type inferred: string
    var x, y float64 = 1, 2  // several at once
    total := 10              // short declaration (inside functions only)

▸  := RULES
    - Declares AND assigns; the type comes from the right-hand side.
    - Works only inside functions; at package level use var.
    - At least ONE name on the left must be new:
          a, err := f()      // declares a and err
          b, err := g()      // OK: b is new, err is just reassigned
    - Plain = assigns to variables that already exist.

▸  UNUSED VARIABLES ARE ERRORS
Declaring a local and never reading it fails to compile ('declared and
not used'). Use the blank identifier _ to discard a value on purpose:
    _, err := fmt.Println("hi")

▸  YOUR TASK
Declare the variables and print them exactly as shown in YOUR TASK.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	var city string = "Cairo"
	var year = 2026
	temp := 31.5
	lat, lon := 30.04, 31.24
	fmt.Println(city, year, temp)
	fmt.Println(lat, lon)
}

quiz.q: Where is the short declaration form x := 5 NOT allowed?
options: At package level, outside any function
In the init part of a for loop
Inside an if statement's init clause
Inside the body of func main
quiz.explain: Package-level declarations must start with a keyword (var, const, type, func). := is a statement and statements only live inside functions.
quiz.hint: Think: what kinds of things may appear at the top level of a Go file?

lessons.title: Zero values: no uninitialised memory
lessons.concept:
▸  BEGINNERS
The code below uses a struct, a slice and a map. You meet them in
modules 4 and 5. For now, notice one thing: every variable starts with
a sensible 'empty' value. Numbers start at 0, text starts empty.

Every variable in Go starts life holding its type's ZERO VALUE:

    numbers (int, float64, ...)   0
    bool                          false
    string                        "" (empty)
    pointers, slices, maps,
    channels, funcs, interfaces   nil
    arrays and structs            every element / field zeroed

▸  WHY IT MATTERS
Zero values are designed to be USEFUL. A zero sync.Mutex is an unlocked
mutex. A zero bytes.Buffer is an empty buffer ready to write. A nil slice
has length 0 and you can append to it. Good Go types follow the same
rule - 'make the zero value useful' is one of the Go proverbs - so you
rarely need constructors just to initialise.

▸  ONE TRAP
A nil MAP can be read (missing keys return zero) but writing to it
panics: 'assignment to entry in nil map'. Create maps with make or a
literal before writing.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Config struct {
	Name    string
	Retries int
	Verbose bool
	Tags    []string
}

func main() {
	var c Config
	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", c)
	c.Tags = append(c.Tags, "fast") // appending to a nil slice works
	fmt.Println(len(c.Tags), c.Tags)

	var counts map[string]int
	fmt.Println(counts["x"], len(counts)) // reading a nil map is fine
}

quiz.q: What happens when you write m["k"] = 1 to a nil map?
options: It's a compile error to index a nil map
The map is created automatically and stores 1
A runtime panic: assignment to entry in nil map
Nothing; the write is silently ignored
quiz.explain: A nil map has no hash table behind it. Reads return the zero value, but a write would have nowhere to go, so the runtime panics. Use make(map[K]V) or a map literal first.
quiz.hint: Reading and writing behave differently. Look at ONE TRAP.

lessons.title: Basic types and their sizes
lessons.concept:
▸  BEGINNERS
For now you only need four types: int, float64, string and bool. The
rest of this list is for reference. Skim it and move on.

▸  THE EVERYDAY TYPES
    int        whole numbers (64-bit on modern machines)
    float64    decimals (IEEE-754 double); prefer it over float32
    string     immutable UTF-8 text
    bool       true / false
    byte       = uint8, one raw byte
    rune       = int32, one Unicode code point ('a', 'é', '世')

▸  THE EXACT-SIZE FAMILY
    int8 int16 int32 int64      signed
    uint8 uint16 uint32 uint64  unsigned
    uintptr                     big enough to hold a pointer value
    complex64 complex128        complex numbers (1+2i)

▸  LIMITS
The math package has the bounds: math.MaxInt64, math.MinInt8,
math.MaxUint32, math.MaxFloat64, and unsafe.Sizeof reports how many
bytes a value occupies.

▸  CHOOSING
Use int for counts and indexes, float64 for measurements, the sized
types only when a file format, protocol or memory budget demands it.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"unsafe"
)

func main() {
	var r rune = 'é'
	var b byte = 'A'
	fmt.Println(r, b, string(r), string(b))
	fmt.Println(math.MaxInt8, math.MinInt8, uint8(math.MaxUint8))
	fmt.Println(unsafe.Sizeof(int32(0)), unsafe.Sizeof(int64(0)), unsafe.Sizeof(true))
	c := complex(1, 2)
	fmt.Println(c*c, real(c), imag(c))
}

quiz.q: What is a rune in Go?
options: An alias for byte holding one ASCII character
An alias for int32 holding one Unicode code point
A string of length one
A special type usable only inside string literals
quiz.explain: rune = int32 and represents a single Unicode code point; a rune literal like 'é' is its numeric value (233). byte = uint8 is a single raw byte.
quiz.hint: Look at what the program prints for r.

lessons.title: Constants and iota
lessons.concept:
const declares values fixed at compile time:
    const Pi = 3.14159
    const Greeting = "hi"

▸  UNTYPED CONSTANTS
Pi above has no fixed type - it is an exact 'untyped float constant'
that takes whatever type its use needs. That's why 'radius * 2' works for
any numeric radius. Untyped constants are arbitrarily precise: the
expression 1 << 100 >> 98 is legal and equals 4.

▸  iota: AUTO-NUMBERING
Inside a const ( ... ) block, iota is 0 on the first line and goes up by
one per line. An omitted expression repeats the previous one:

    type Weekday int
    const (
        Sunday Weekday = iota  // 0
        Monday                 // 1
        Tuesday                // 2
    )

This is Go's enum. Use _ to skip a value, and expressions for bit flags:
    const (
        Read = 1 << iota       // 1
        Write                  // 2
        Exec                   // 4
    )

▸  YOUR TASK
Reproduce the output: a weekday enum plus a set of permission flags.
lessons.expected:
0 1 2
1 2 4
5 false true

quiz.q: In const ( A = iota; B; C ), what is C?
options: iota
quiz.explain: iota starts at 0 on the first line of the block and increments per line; B and C repeat the expression 'iota' so they are 1 and 2.
quiz.hint: Count lines from zero.

lessons.title: Arithmetic: integer division, remainder, precedence
lessons.concept:
▸  OPERATORS
    + - * /    arithmetic          % remainder (integers only)
    & | ^ &^   bitwise AND OR XOR AND-NOT
    << >>      shifts

▸  INTEGER DIVISION TRUNCATES TOWARD ZERO
    7 / 2   == 3          -7 / 2   == -3
    7 % 2   == 1          -7 % 2   == -1   (sign follows the dividend)
Dividing an integer by a zero VARIABLE panics at run time; dividing by a
constant 0 is a compile error. Floats follow IEEE: 1.0/0 is +Inf.

▸  PRECEDENCE: ONLY FIVE LEVELS
    5:  *  /  %  <<  >>  &  &^
    4:  +  -  |  ^
    3:  ==  !=  <  <=  >  >=
    2:  &&
    1:  ||
Only five levels, so you rarely need to memorise anything. Note that &
and << bind like * - so a&b == c means (a&b) == c, which is what you
nearly always meant. When in doubt, add parentheses.

▸  ASSIGNMENT OPERATORS
x += 3, x *= 2, x <<= 1 ... and x++ / x-- as STATEMENTS only.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println(7/2, -7/2, 7%2, -7%2)
	fmt.Println(7.0/2, 1+2*3, (1+2)*3)
	flags := 0b1010
	fmt.Println(flags&0b0010 == 2) // & binds tighter than ==
	x := 10
	x += 5
	x *= 2
	x--
	fmt.Println(x)
}

quiz.q: What does -7 % 3 evaluate to in Go?
quiz.explain: Go's % takes the sign of the dividend: -7 = -2*3 + (-1), so the remainder is -1 (division truncates toward zero).
quiz.hint: Integer division truncates toward zero; what remainder makes q*3 + r == -7?

lessons.title: Type conversions: T(v)
lessons.concept:
Go never converts between types for you. You convert explicitly by
writing the target type like a function: T(v).

    i := 42
    f := float64(i)        // int -> float64
    u := uint8(300)        // DOESN'T compile: constant 300 overflows uint8
    n := 300
    u := uint8(n)          // compiles: wraps to 44 at run time
    t := int(3.99)         // ERROR: constant truncated... (constant case)
    g := 3.99
    t := int(g)            // 3 - float->int TRUNCATES toward zero

▸  STRINGS ARE SPECIAL
    string(65)             "A"  (!) - converts a code point, not a number
                                   (go vet warns about this)
    strconv.Itoa(65)       "65" - the number as decimal text
    strconv.Atoi("65")     65, nil
    []byte("hi")           the bytes  [104 105]
    []rune("héllo")        the code points

▸  YOUR TASK
Compute an average of ints as a float and print it with two decimals,
then show the truncating float->int conversion.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"strconv"
)

func main() {
	total, count := 17, 4
	avg := float64(total) / float64(count)
	fmt.Printf("average: %.2f\n", avg)
	fmt.Println("truncated:", int(avg))
	s := strconv.Itoa(total)
	fmt.Println("as text:", s+"!")
	n, err := strconv.Atoi("123")
	fmt.Println(n+1, err)
}
lessons.expected:
average: 4.25
truncated: 4
as text: 17!
124 <nil>

quiz.q: What does int(2.99) give for a float64 variable holding 2.99?
options: 2 - conversion truncates toward zero
3 - conversion rounds to nearest
A runtime panic: precision lost
A compile error: lossy conversion
quiz.explain: Converting a float to an integer type truncates the fractional part toward zero. (A CONSTANT like int(2.99) is a compile error, because constant conversions must be exact - the variable case truncates.) Use math.Round first if you want rounding.
quiz.hint: Look at what 'truncated:' prints.

lessons.title: Strings: length, indexing, slicing, concatenation
lessons.concept:
A string is an immutable sequence of BYTES (holding UTF-8 by convention).

    s := "Gopher"
    len(s)          6        bytes
    s[0]            71       a byte (uint8) - the code for 'G'
    string(s[0])    "G"
    s[1:4]          "oph"    a substring: bytes 1, 2, 3 (end excluded)
    s[:3], s[3:]    "Gop", "her"
    s + "s"         "Gophers" - a NEW string
    s == "Gopher"   true      compare with == < > directly

▸  IMMUTABLE
s[0] = 'g' does not compile. Strings are safe to share between
goroutines precisely because no one can change them.

▸  RAW STRINGS
Backquotes make a raw string: no escapes are processed and it may span
lines. Perfect for regexps, paths on Windows, JSON and SQL:
    re := `\d+\.\d+`
    path := `C:\temp\new`

▸  MULTI-BYTE CHARACTERS
Indexing works on BYTES, so for non-ASCII text use 'for i, r := range s'
or []rune(s). (The Strings module goes deep on this.)
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := "Gopher"
	fmt.Println(len(s), s[0], string(s[0]))
	fmt.Println(s[1:4], s[:3], s[3:])
	fmt.Println(s+"s", s == "Gopher", "apple" < "banana")
	raw := `C:\temp\new	line`
	fmt.Println(raw)
	fmt.Println(len("\t"), len(`\t`))
}
lessons.expected:
6 71 G
oph Gop her
Gophers true true
C:\temp\new	line
1 2

quiz.q: What does s[1:4] contain when s is "Gopher"?
options: "ophe" - indexes 1 to 4
"Gop" - the first three bytes
"oph" plus a terminator
"oph" - indexes 1, 2 and 3
quiz.explain: Slice expressions are half-open: s[low:high] includes low and excludes high, so s[1:4] is bytes 1, 2 and 3. Go strings have no terminator.
quiz.hint: The end index is excluded.

lessons.title: Reading input with fmt.Scan
lessons.concept:
fmt.Scan reads space- or newline-separated values from standard input
into the variables you pass by POINTER:

    var name string
    var age int
    n, err := fmt.Scan(&name, &age)

It returns how many items it filled and an error (for example when the
input isn't a number). Always check it - examples are read as templates.

▸  THE & IS REQUIRED
fmt.Scan(age) can't modify your variable (Go passes copies), so it needs
its address: &age (the Pointers module explains this fully).

▸  IN THIS APP
Type input in the 'stdin:' box under the editor. Use \n for a new line.
This lesson pre-fills it with:  Ada 36

It's only needed for ints, not strings
Go passes copies; Scan needs the address
The & turns the int into text for Scan
quiz.explain: Every Go argument is a copy. To fill your variable, Scan must receive its address so it can write through the pointer - for every type.
quiz.hint: Think about pass-by-value.

lessons.title: Reading lines with bufio.Scanner
lessons.concept:
fmt.Scan splits on whitespace. To read whole LINES, wrap standard input
in a bufio.Scanner:

    sc := bufio.NewScanner(os.Stdin)
    for sc.Scan() {             // false at EOF or on error
        line := sc.Text()       // the line, without the newline
        ...
    }
    if err := sc.Err(); err != nil { ... }   // distinguish error from EOF

▸  WHY THIS SHAPE
The loop condition IS the read, so you can't accidentally process one
phantom line after the end of the input. sc.Err() is
checked after the loop because EOF is not an error.

▸  OTHER SPLITS
sc.Split(bufio.ScanWords) reads words; bufio.ScanRunes reads
characters. Lines longer than 64 KB need sc.Buffer(...) to raise the
limit.

▸  YOUR TASK
Number each input line and report the total, as in YOUR TASK.

lines: 3

quiz.q: When should you call sc.Err()?
options: Only if sc.Text() returned an empty string
Before each call to sc.Scan()
After the for sc.Scan() loop ends
Never - Scan panics if reading fails
quiz.explain: Scan returns false both at EOF and on error. After the loop, sc.Err() is nil for a clean EOF and non-nil for a real failure.
quiz.hint: Scan returning false can mean two different things.

lessons.title: for range: slices, strings, maps and integers
lessons.concept:
range iterates over a collection, giving TWO values per step:

    for i, v := range slice    // index, copy of the element
    for i, r := range str      // BYTE index, rune (decoded UTF-8)
    for k, v := range m        // key, value (unordered!)
    for v := range ch          // values until the channel is closed
    for i := range 10          // Go 1.22+: 0..9

Drop the value with 'for i := range s', drop the index with '_'.

▸  v IS A COPY
Assigning to v does not change the slice. Write s[i] = ... instead.

▸  EACH ITERATION HAS ITS OWN VARIABLE (Go 1.22+)
Before Go 1.22, the loop variable was ONE variable reused every
iteration, so closures and goroutines that captured it all saw the last
value - a famous bug. Since 1.22, each iteration gets a fresh copy.
(Your go.mod's 'go' line selects the behaviour.)

quiz.q: In 'for _, v := range nums { v *= 10 }', what happens to nums?
options: Nothing - v is a copy of each element
Every element is multiplied by 10
It's a compile error to assign to v
Only the last element changes
quiz.explain: range copies each element into v. Changing v doesn't touch the slice; index into it (nums[i] *= 10) to modify the elements.
quiz.hint: Compare the two printed lines.

lessons.title: Functions: parameters and results
lessons.concept:
func add(a int, b int) int {
        return a + b
    }

▸  SHAPE
func, name, parameter list, result type(s), body. Consecutive parameters
of the same type can share it: func add(a, b int) int.

▸  ALWAYS PASS-BY-VALUE
Arguments are copied into the parameters. To let a function change the
caller's variable, pass a pointer (covered in the Pointers module).
Slices, maps and channels are small headers, so passing them is cheap,
and the callee sees the SAME underlying data.

▸  NO OVERLOADING, NO DEFAULT ARGUMENTS
Each name has one signature. Use different names (ParseInt, ParseFloat),
variadic parameters, or an options struct instead.

▸  ORDER DOESN'T MATTER
Functions can be called before they are declared in the file - no
prototypes.

▸  YOUR TASK
Write area and perimeter functions for a rectangle and print both.
lessons.expected: area=13.5 perimeter=15.0

quiz.q: Can you call a function that's declared further down the file?
options: Only from inside func main
Only if the function is exported
Yes - package-level declaration order doesn't matter
No - you must add a prototype above the call
quiz.explain: Go resolves package-level names across the whole package, in any order, across files. There are no prototypes or forward declarations.
quiz.hint: Remember: no header files, no prototypes.

lessons.title: Multiple return values
lessons.concept:
Go functions can return several values:

    func divmod(a, b int) (int, int) {
        return a / b, a % b
    }

▸  THE (value, error) CONVENTION
The most common use is returning a result plus an error - the last
result, by convention:

    func parse(s string) (int, error)

▸  THE COMMA-OK CONVENTION
Some operations return (value, bool):
    v, ok := m[key]          // was the key present?
    s, ok := x.(string)      // did the type assertion succeed?
    v, ok := <-ch            // was the channel still open?

▸  IGNORING ONE
Use the blank identifier: q, _ := divmod(17, 5). Multiple results can be
passed straight into a function with matching parameters:
f(divmod(17, 5)).

quiz.explain: The idiom is (results..., error). Tools and readers rely on it, and linters flag functions that put the error elsewhere.

lessons.title: Named results and bare return
lessons.concept:
Results can be named, which declares them as variables initialised to
their zero values:

    func split(sum int) (x, y int) {
        x = sum * 4 / 9
        y = sum - x

    - Documentation: (lo, hi int) says more than (int, int).
    - A deferred function can read and CHANGE named results after the
      return statement ran - the standard way to turn a panic into an
      error, or to wrap an error on every return path.

▸  WHEN THEY HURT
Bare returns in long functions make it hard to see what is returned.
Style guides say: name results for documentation, but prefer explicit
'return x, y' except in very short functions.

lessons.title: Variadic functions and the ... spread
lessons.concept:
A final parameter written ...T accepts any number of T values, which
arrive as a slice []T:

    func sum(nums ...int) int {

        for _, n := range nums { total += n }

    sum(1, 2, 3)     // 6

▸  SPREADING A SLICE
If you already have a slice, pass it with ...:
    xs := []int{4, 5}
    sum(xs...)       // the slice itself is passed - no copy

fmt.Println(a ...any) and append(s, xs...) are the variadics you use
every day.

arguments, and print the results shown.

    type Transform func(int) int

▸  WHY IT MATTERS
Sorting with a comparison function (slices.SortFunc), HTTP handlers,
middleware, callbacks, strategies, and goroutines started with
'go func() { ... }()' all rely on function values. The zero value of a
function type is nil; calling a nil function panics.

lessons.title: Closures: functions that remember
lessons.concept:
A function literal can refer to variables from the scope it was created
in. It doesn't copy them - it CAPTURES them, keeping them alive as long
as the closure exists:

    func counter() func() int {
        n := 0
        return func() int {
            n++
            return n
        }
    }
    next := counter()
    next(); next()      // 1, 2   n lives on, inside the closure

Each call to counter() creates a fresh n, so two counters are
independent.

▸  WHERE YOU'LL SEE IT
Generators, memoisation, middleware that wraps a handler, and
'go func() { ... }()' goroutines that use surrounding variables.

▸  YOUR TASK
Write a counter factory and show two independent counters, matching
YOUR TASK exactly.

quiz.q: Why does 'a' keep counting after counter() has returned?
options: counter() keeps running in the background
Go copies n into the closure on every call
n is a global variable shared by all counters
The closure captured n, which stays alive with it
quiz.explain: The returned function refers to n, so n escapes to the heap and lives as long as the closure does. Each counter() call creates its own n, which is why b starts at 1.
quiz.hint: How many different n variables exist?

lessons.title: Recursion
lessons.concept:
A function may call itself. Every recursive function needs:
    1. a BASE CASE that returns without recursing, and
    2. a step that moves toward it.

    func fact(n int) int {
        if n <= 1 { return 1 }      // base case
        return n * fact(n-1)        // smaller problem
    }

▸  GO-SPECIFIC NOTES
    - Goroutine stacks GROW on demand (up to 1 GB by default), so deep
      recursion that would overflow a fixed-size stack often just works.
      Infinite recursion still ends with 'goroutine stack exceeds limit'.
    - Go does NOT promise tail-call optimisation. Prefer a loop when the
      depth could be huge.
    - Recursion shines on recursive data: trees, nested JSON, file
      systems (filepath.WalkDir), parsers.

▸  YOUR TASK
Print fact(0..5) and the first 10 Fibonacci numbers recursively.

quiz.q: What happens with infinitely deep recursion in Go?
options: It runs forever using constant memory
The stack grows until a limit, then a fatal error
It silently corrupts other memory
Go optimises it into a loop automatically
quiz.explain: Goroutine stacks grow dynamically, but there is a maximum (1 GB on 64-bit by default). Exceeding it aborts with 'goroutine stack exceeds limit' - a defined failure, not silent corruption.
quiz.hint: Go has no guaranteed tail calls.

lessons.title: Scope and shadowing
lessons.concept:
Every { } block creates a scope. A name declared inside it hides
('shadows') the same name from outer scopes:

    x := 1
    if true {
        x := 2          // a NEW x, only inside this block
        fmt.Println(x)  // 2
    }
    fmt.Println(x)      // 1

▸  THE := SHADOWING BUG
This bites everyone once:

    var cfg *Config
    if path != "" {
        cfg, err := load(path)   // := declares a NEW cfg here!
        ...
    }
    // cfg is still nil out here

Fix: declare err first and use plain =:
    var err error
    cfg, err = load(path)

▸  SCOPES, OUTSIDE IN
universe (int, len, true, nil...) > package > file (imports) > function
> each block. You can even shadow built-ins: 'len := 3' compiles, which
is why linters complain about it.
lessons.expected:
inner x: 2
outer x: 1
buggy cfg: ""
fixed cfg: "loaded" <nil>

quiz.q: Why is cfg still empty after the first if block in the example?
options: Strings can't be assigned inside an if block
The error was non-nil, so cfg was cleared
':=' inside the block declared a NEW cfg there
load() returned an empty string that time
quiz.explain: Inside the if block, 'cfg, err := load()' declares two new variables because := always declares in the CURRENT scope. The outer cfg is untouched. Use = with a pre-declared err.
quiz.hint: How many different cfg variables exist?

▸  os.Args

lessons.title: Big picture: values, addresses and who can see what
lessons.concept:
Before pointers make sense, fix the mental picture (the DIAGRAMS tab,
'pointer', draws it).

▸  EVERY VARIABLE IS A BOX
A box has a TYPE, a VALUE and a LOCATION (address). x := 42 creates a box
holding 42 somewhere in memory.

▸  ASSIGNMENT AND CALLS COPY
y := x copies the value into a new box. f(x) copies the value into f's
parameter box. There is no exception in Go: everything is passed by
value.

▸  SOME VALUES ARE SMALL HEADERS
Slices, strings, maps, channels, functions and interfaces are small
values that REFER to data stored elsewhere. Copying the header is cheap
and the copy refers to the SAME data. That's why changing a slice
element inside a function is visible to the caller, while reassigning
the whole slice is not.

▸  A POINTER IS A BOX HOLDING A LOCATION
p := &x stores x's address in p. *p reads or writes x through it.
Copying p copies the address, so every copy reaches the same x.

▸  WHERE DO BOXES LIVE?
You don't decide. The compiler puts a variable on the goroutine's stack
when it can prove nothing outlives the call, and on the garbage-
collected heap otherwise (escape analysis). Either way it lives exactly
as long as something can reach it.

quiz.q: You pass a slice to a function that sets s[0] = 9. What does the caller see?
options: s[0] is 9 - the copied header shares the same array
A compile error - slices must be passed by pointer
Nothing changes - the callee got a full copy
The callee's slice is reallocated automatically
quiz.explain: The slice header (pointer, len, cap) is copied, but both copies point at the same backing array, so element writes are shared. Reassigning s itself (s = append(...)) inside the callee would NOT be seen.
quiz.hint: Which part of a slice gets copied?

▸  THE ZERO VALUE IS nil

optional.

▸  POINTERS TO STRUCTS: NO ARROW

    pt.X = 10       // Go writes (*pt).X for you

exist.

with a helper that takes pointers.

}

func main() {

	p := &x
	*p = 7
	fmt.Println(x, *p, p == &x)

	a, b := 1, 2
	swap(&a, &b)
	fmt.Println(a, b)
}

lessons.title: Pointer parameters: when a function must change its argument
lessons.concept:
Because arguments are copied, a function can't change the caller's
variable - unless it receives that variable's ADDRESS.

    func reset(n *int) { *n = 0 }
    reset(&count)

▸  WHEN TO PASS A POINTER
    1. The function must modify the caller's value.
    2. The value is a LARGE struct and copying it on every call is
       wasteful (measure first - copying 100 bytes is very cheap).
    3. The value must not be copied at all (anything containing a
       sync.Mutex or sync.WaitGroup - go vet's copylocks check).
    4. 'Absent' must be representable (nil vs zero value).

▸  WHEN NOT TO
Slices, maps, channels, funcs and interfaces already refer to shared
data. Passing *[]int or *map[K]V is almost never needed - return the new
slice instead: s = appendAll(s, ...).

▸  RETURNING A RESULT IS OFTEN CLEARER
func double(n int) int beats func double(n *int) unless mutation is the
point.

quiz.q: Which parameter type is almost never needed in Go?

*Account - a pointer to a struct you modify
*sync.Mutex - a lock that mustn't be copied
*[]int - a slice already refers to shared data
quiz.explain: Slices are headers pointing at shared arrays; pass the slice and return the updated slice if its length may change. Pointers to structs, locks and buffers are all common and correct.

lessons.title: new, &T{} and composite literals
lessons.concept:
Three ways to get a pointer to a fresh value:

    p := new(int)            // *int pointing at a zeroed int
    pt := &Point{X: 1}       // address of a composite literal (most common)
    var v Point; pp := &v    // address of an existing variable

▸  new(T)
Allocates a zeroed T and returns *T. Rarely needed for structs (&T{} is
clearer and can set fields). Since Go 1.26, new also accepts an
EXPRESSION - new(42) or new(yearsSince(born)) - which is handy for
optional pointer fields (requires Go 1.26).

▸  COMPOSITE LITERALS
    Point{1, 2}              positional (fragile if fields change)
    Point{X: 1, Y: 2}        keyed (preferred; go vet nags about
                             positional literals of other packages' types)
    []int{1, 2, 3}
    map[string]int{"a": 1}
    &Node{Val: 1, Next: &Node{Val: 2}}

▸  NO make FOR STRUCTS
make is only for slices, maps and channels. new/& are for everything
else.

quiz.q: What does new(Point) return?
options: A *Point to a zeroed Point
A nil *Point
A Point allocated on the stack
A Point with zero fields
quiz.explain: new(T) allocates storage for a T, zeroes it, and returns its address. &Point{} does the same and also lets you set fields.
quiz.hint: new always returns a pointer.

lessons.title: Escape analysis: stack or heap?
lessons.concept:
Memory comes in two regions: the STACK (fast, per function call, freed
automatically when the call returns) and the HEAP (longer-lived, cleaned
up by the garbage collector). In Go you never choose - the COMPILER
decides, per variable:

    - If it can prove a variable is not referenced after the function
      returns, it goes on the goroutine's stack (cheap, freed instantly).
    - Otherwise it 'escapes' to the heap, managed by the garbage
      collector.

You can watch the decisions:
    go build -gcflags=-m .
    ./main.go:8:2: moved to heap: c
    ./main.go:14:13: ... does not escape

▸  COMMON REASONS TO ESCAPE
    - returning &local, or storing it in a global / a heap object
    - capturing it in a closure that outlives the call
    - passing it as an interface (often), e.g. to fmt.Println
    - sizes unknown at compile time (make([]int, n) with a variable n,
      if large)

▸  WHY YOU CARE (LATER)
Correctness never depends on it. Performance sometimes does: heap
allocations cost GC work. The Performance module shows how to measure
before optimising.

quiz.q: Who decides whether a Go variable lives on the stack or the heap?
options: You, by choosing new() versus :=
The operating system's allocator
The compiler, via escape analysis
The garbage collector, at run time
quiz.explain: Escape analysis at compile time decides placement. new(T) can live on the stack and := can escape to the heap - the syntax doesn't decide. See the decisions with go build -gcflags=-m.
quiz.hint: Is there any syntax in Go for 'put this on the heap'?

lessons.title: The garbage collector in one page
lessons.concept:
Go frees memory for you with a concurrent, tri-color, mark-and-sweep
garbage collector.

▸  WHAT IT DOES
Periodically it MARKS everything reachable from the roots (globals,
every goroutine's stack, registers), then SWEEPS the rest, reusing that
memory. Most of the work runs concurrently with your program; the
stop-the-world pauses are typically well under a millisecond.

▸  WHAT IT MEANS FOR YOU
    - No free(), no double-free, no use-after-free.
    - Memory is reclaimed when it's UNREACHABLE, not when you're 'done'
      with it. A global map that keeps growing is a leak; so is a
      goroutine blocked forever (its stack and everything it references
      stay alive).
    - Allocation-heavy code costs CPU in the collector.

▸  THE KNOBS (rarely touched)
    GOGC=100       collect when the heap grows 100% since the last cycle
    GOMEMLIMIT=1GiB  a soft memory ceiling (Go 1.19+): collect harder as
                   you approach it - useful in containers
Go 1.26 made the 'Green Tea' collector the default, cutting GC overhead
noticeably for allocation-heavy programs.

▸  NON-MEMORY RESOURCES
The GC frees memory, not files, sockets or locks. Those still need
explicit Close/Unlock - with defer.
lessons.expected:
collections ran: true
allocated a lot in total: true

quiz.q: Which of these is still a memory leak in a garbage-collected Go program?
options: A struct that nothing references any more
Returning the address of a local variable
Forgetting to call free() on a slice
A global map that only ever grows
quiz.explain: The GC frees UNREACHABLE memory. Anything still reachable - like entries in an ever-growing global map, or the stack of a goroutine blocked forever - stays alive. That's the Go meaning of a leak.
quiz.hint: The GC can only free what nothing can reach.

lessons.title: Value semantics vs pointer semantics
lessons.concept:
For each type you design, pick one 'semantics' and use it consistently.

▸  VALUE SEMANTICS (copy it)
Small, immutable-ish data: time.Time, a Point, a Money amount, a config
snapshot. Pass and return by value, use value receivers. Copies can't
surprise anyone, and they often stay on the stack.

▸  POINTER SEMANTICS (share it)
Things with identity or mutable state: a bank Account, a *os.File, a
*bytes.Buffer, a database handle, anything holding a mutex. Pass *T,
return *T from constructors (NewServer()), use pointer receivers.

▸  THE CONSISTENCY RULE
If any method needs a pointer receiver, give ALL methods pointer
receivers. Mixing them confuses readers and changes which types satisfy
which interfaces (see the Interfaces module).

▸  A QUICK TEST
'If I copy this, would I have two independent things that make sense?'
Two copies of a Point: fine. Two copies of an open file handle or a
lock: nonsense - use a pointer.

quiz.q: Which type should normally use POINTER semantics?
options: A time.Duration measuring an interval
A struct that contains a sync.Mutex
A Money amount stored in integer cents
A two-field Point used for geometry
quiz.explain: A mutex must never be copied - a copy is a different lock. Types with identity or internal locks are shared through pointers; small immutable values are passed by value.
quiz.hint: Would two independent copies make sense?

lessons.title: nil: one word, many meanings
lessons.concept:
nil is the zero value for SIX kinds of type. Each behaves differently:

    type            what works on nil                  what panics
    *T pointer      comparing to nil                   *p, p.Field
    []T slice       len, cap, range, append            s[0] (out of range)
    map[K]V         len, range, reading m[k]           m[k] = v
    chan T          -                                  close(nil chan);
                                                       send/recv block FOREVER
    func            comparing to nil                   calling it
    interface       comparing to nil                   calling a method

▸  NIL RECEIVERS CAN BE USEFUL
A method with a pointer receiver can be called on a nil pointer as long
as it doesn't dereference it - handy for 'empty tree' or 'no logger'
cases:
    func (t *Tree) Sum() int { if t == nil { return 0 } ... }

▸  THE NIL INTERFACE TRAP
An interface holding a nil POINTER is not nil (it still records the
type). The Errors module shows how this breaks 'if err != nil'.

quiz.q: Which operation on a nil slice PANICS?

append(s, 1)

quiz.explain: A nil slice behaves like an empty slice: length 0, range does nothing, append allocates. Indexing s[0] is out of range for any empty slice, so it panics.
quiz.hint: A nil slice is just an empty slice.

lessons.title: Pointer pitfalls: aliasing and loop variables
lessons.concept:
Go's pointers can't corrupt memory, but two LOGIC pitfalls remain.

▸  1. TAKING THE ADDRESS OF A RANGE VALUE
    for _, u := range users {
        ptrs = append(ptrs, &u)   // points at the loop variable, not users[i]
    }
Since Go 1.22 each iteration has its own u, so the pointers differ - but
they point at COPIES. Modifying *ptrs[0] won't change users[0]. To point
into the slice use &users[i].

▸  2. POINTERS INTO A SLICE THAT GROWS
    p := &s[0]
    s = append(s, 99)    // may move s to a new array
    *p = 7               // updates the OLD array; s doesn't see it
After an append that reallocates, old element pointers refer to the old
array. Re-take pointers after growing, or store indexes instead.

▸  THE GOOD NEWS
Neither is memory corruption: the old array stays alive and valid as
long as p references it. The bug is 'wrong data', never 'random crash'.

quiz.explain: The range value u is a copy of the element. &users[i] takes the address of the element inside the slice's backing array.

lessons.title: Bytes, runes and UTF-8
lessons.concept:
Three words to keep straight:

    byte    one 8-bit value (uint8). Strings are made of bytes.
    rune    one Unicode CODE POINT (int32): 'A' is 65, 'é' is 233,
            '世' is 19990, '😀' is 128512
    UTF-8   the encoding Go uses to store runes as bytes: ASCII takes 1
            byte, most European letters 2, CJK 3, emoji 4.

▸  WHAT EACH OPERATION SEES
    len(s)                  bytes
    s[i]                    the i-th BYTE
    for i, r := range s     i = byte offset, r = the rune starting there
    []rune(s)               decode everything into code points
    utf8.RuneCountInString  count runes without allocating
    string(r)               encode one rune back to UTF-8 text

▸  INVALID BYTES
A string may hold bytes that aren't valid UTF-8. range yields
U+FFFD (the replacement character, '�') for each bad byte instead of
failing. utf8.ValidString tells you whether a string is clean.

▸  'CHARACTERS' ARE HARDER STILL
A user-perceived character can be several runes ('é' can also be 'e' +
a combining accent; flags and family emoji are many runes). For true
grapheme handling you need a library (golang.org/x/text).

8 4

false [71 65533 111]

lessons.title: Building strings efficiently: strings.Builder
lessons.concept:
Strings are immutable, so s += x in a loop creates a brand-new string
each time and copies everything so far: O(n²) work for n pieces.

    var b strings.Builder
    for _, w := range words {
        b.WriteString(w)
        b.WriteByte(' ')
    }
    result := b.String()      // no extra copy

▸  OTHER TOOLS
    strings.Join(parts, sep)       when you already have a slice
    fmt.Fprintf(&b, "%d,", n)      a Builder is an io.Writer
    b.Grow(n)                      pre-size when you know the length
    bytes.Buffer                   when you need both writing AND reading

▸  WHEN += IS FINE
A handful of concatenations outside a loop: the compiler handles
'a + b + c' in one allocation. Optimise loops, not one-liners.

quiz.explain: Strings can't be modified, so every += allocates a new string and copies all previous bytes - quadratic total work. strings.Builder appends into a growing buffer instead.

lessons.title: Converting between string, []byte and []rune
lessons.concept:
b := []byte("héllo")     // copy the bytes out: [104 195 169 108 108 111]
    s := string(b)           // copy them back into a string
    r := []rune("héllo")     // decode: [104 233 108 108 111]
    s2 := string(r)          // encode back to UTF-8

Each conversion COPIES (strings are immutable, slices are mutable, so
they can't share memory - the compiler avoids the copy only in a few
safe cases, like map lookups m[string(b)]).

▸  WHEN TO USE WHICH
    string   keys, comparisons, storage, anything immutable
    []byte   I/O, network buffers, in-place edits, crypto
    []rune   character-level edits (reverse, per-letter transforms)

▸  THE bytes PACKAGE MIRRORS strings
bytes.Contains, bytes.Split, bytes.ToUpper, bytes.Buffer ... so you can
stay in []byte without converting back and forth.

lessons.title: Regular expressions with regexp
lessons.concept:
Go's regexp uses RE2 syntax: no backtracking, so matching is guaranteed
linear time - an attacker can't craft input that hangs your server
(ReDoS). The price: no backreferences or lookarounds.

    re := regexp.MustCompile(`(\w+)@(\w+)\.com`)   // compile once
    re.MatchString(s)                bool
    re.FindString(s)                 first match
    re.FindAllString(s, -1)          all matches
    re.FindStringSubmatch(s)         [whole, group1, group2]
    re.ReplaceAllString(s, "$2")     $1, $2 or ${name} refer to groups
    (?P<user>\w+)                    named group; re.SubexpIndex("user")

▸  HABITS
    - Use raw strings `...` so \d doesn't need doubling.
    - MustCompile at package level for constant patterns (panics at
      start-up on a typo - good); regexp.Compile for user input.
    - For plain substring checks, strings.Contains is far faster.

Go regexps only work on ASCII input text
quiz.explain: Go's regexp engine (RE2) uses automata rather than backtracking, guaranteeing linear-time matching. That's why it omits backreferences.

lessons.title: Slices: the header and the backing array
lessons.concept:
A slice is a 3-word HEADER describing a window onto an array:

    s := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
    t := s[1:3]          // header: ptr -> s[1], len 2, cap 4

    len(t) == 2          elements you can index: t[0], t[1]
    cap(t) == 4          room from t's start to the END of the array

▸  SLICING NEVER COPIES
t[0] = 99 changes s[1]. Every slice of the same array shares its
elements. The DIAGRAMS tab ('slice-share') draws it.

▸  BOUNDS
s[low:high] requires 0 <= low <= high <= cap(s). You may slice beyond
len (up to cap) to 'reveal' existing elements. Index out of range
panics.

▸  THE FULL SLICE EXPRESSION
s[low:high:max] also limits capacity to max-low. Handing out
s[0:2:2] guarantees the receiver's append can't overwrite s[2].
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	s := []int{10, 20, 30, 40, 50}
	t := s[1:3]
	fmt.Println(t, len(t), cap(t))
	t[0] = 99
	fmt.Println(s)

	u := t[:4] // extend within capacity
	fmt.Println(u)

	safe := s[0:2:2] // cap limited to 2
	safe = append(safe, -1)
	fmt.Println(s, safe)
}

quiz.q: For s := []int{1,2,3,4,5}; t := s[1:3], what is cap(t)?
quiz.explain: Capacity counts from the slice's start (index 1 of the array) to the end of the backing array: 5 - 1 = 4.
quiz.hint: Count from t's first element to the end of s's array.

lessons.title: append and growth
lessons.concept:
s = append(s, x)          // ALWAYS assign the result back
    s = append(s, a, b, c)
    s = append(s, other...)   // append a whole slice

▸  WHAT append DOES
    - If len < cap: write into the existing array, return a header with
      len+1. Same array!
    - If len == cap: allocate a bigger array (about 2x for small slices,
      ~1.25x for large ones), copy the elements, append, and return a
      header pointing at the NEW array.

▸  WHY YOU MUST ASSIGN THE RESULT
The returned header may point at a new array and always has a new
length. 'append(s, x)' on its own is a compile error: the result is
unused.

▸  PRE-SIZE WHEN YOU KNOW
    out := make([]int, 0, len(in))   // len 0, cap len(in): no regrowth

▸  YOUR TASK
Print len and cap as you append ten ints to an empty slice, and mark the
lines where the backing array was reallocated, as in YOUR TASK.
lessons.expected:
len= 1 cap= 1  <- new array
len= 2 cap= 2  <- new array
len= 3 cap= 4  <- new array
len= 4 cap= 4
len= 5 cap= 8  <- new array
len= 6 cap= 8
len= 7 cap= 8
len= 8 cap= 8
len= 9 cap=16  <- new array
len=10 cap=16

quiz.q: Why must you write s = append(s, x) rather than just append(s, x)?
options: append returns a new header that may use a new array
Go needs = to know which type append returns
append works on a copy that must then be freed
Without =, append would modify every other slice
quiz.explain: append can't change the caller's header (it was passed by value). It returns an updated header - longer, and possibly pointing at a freshly allocated array. The compiler rejects the bare call.
quiz.hint: Go passes the header by value.

lessons.title: The append aliasing trap
lessons.concept:
When a slice has spare capacity, two appends to it write into the SAME
slot:

    base := make([]int, 3, 10)
    a := append(base, 1)    // writes base's array[3] = 1
    b := append(base, 2)    // writes array[3] = 2  -- overwrites a's!
    fmt.Println(a[3])       // 2 (!)

This bites code that builds variations from a shared prefix (paths in a
search, permutations, request options).

▸  THE FIXES
    - Copy before branching:
          a := append(slices.Clone(base), 1)
    - Or hand out capacity-limited slices: base[:len(base):len(base)]
      forces append to allocate.

▸  THE RULE OF THUMB
Only append to a slice you OWN. If you received it from someone else,
or keep using the old variable afterwards, assume it might share memory.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

func main() {
	base := make([]int, 3, 10)
	a := append(base, 1)
	b := append(base, 2)
	fmt.Println("shared:", a[3], b[3])

	c := append(slices.Clone(base), 1)
	d := append(slices.Clone(base), 2)
	fmt.Println("cloned:", c[3], d[3])

	limited := base[:3:3]
	e := append(limited, 1)
	f := append(limited, 2)
	fmt.Println("cap-limited:", e[3], f[3])
}
lessons.expected:
shared: 2 2
cloned: 1 2
cap-limited: 1 2

quiz.q: After a := append(base, 1); b := append(base, 2) with spare cap, what is a[3]?
options: 1 - each append got its own copy
It panics: the index is out of range
2 - both wrote the same array slot
0 - a and b both start out empty
quiz.explain: With spare capacity append reuses base's backing array, so both write element 3 of the same array; the second write wins.
quiz.hint: Do a and b share a backing array?

lessons.title: make, copy and the slices package
lessons.concept:
▸  make
    make([]T, len)          len elements, all zero, cap == len
    make([]T, len, cap)     pre-reserve room for growth

▸  copy(dst, src)
Copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements and returns that count. It
handles overlapping slices correctly. dst must already have length!

    dst := make([]int, len(src))
    copy(dst, src)

▸  THE slices PACKAGE (Go 1.21+)  - use it instead of hand-written loops
    slices.Contains(s, v)        slices.Index(s, v)
    slices.Sort(s)               slices.SortFunc(s, cmp)
    slices.BinarySearch(s, v)    slices.Max(s) / Min
    slices.Reverse(s)            slices.Equal(a, b)
    slices.Clone(s)              slices.Compact(s)  (drop adjacent dups)
    slices.Insert(s, i, vs...)   slices.Delete(s, i, j)
Plus built-ins: min, max (Go 1.21) and clear(s) (zero all elements).
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"slices"
)

func main() {
	src := []int{5, 3, 8, 3, 1}
	dst := make([]int, 3)
	n := copy(dst, src)
	fmt.Println(n, dst)

	s := slices.Clone(src)
	slices.Sort(s)
	fmt.Println(s, slices.Contains(s, 8), slices.Index(s, 5))
	s = slices.Compact(s)
	fmt.Println(s)
	i, found := slices.BinarySearch(s, 5)
	fmt.Println(i, found, slices.Max(s), min(4, 2, 9))
	s = slices.Insert(s, 1, 2)
	s = slices.Delete(s, 0, 1)
	fmt.Println(s)
}

quiz.q: What does copy(dst, src) do when dst has length 0?
options: Grows dst to fit src, then copies
Copies into dst's spare capacity
Copies nothing and returns 0
Panics because dst is too short
quiz.explain: copy only fills existing elements: it copies min(len(dst), len(src)) of them. A zero-length dst receives nothing. Use make([]T, len(src)) or append(dst[:0], src...).
quiz.hint: copy never changes a slice's length.

lessons.title: 2-D slices and matrices
lessons.concept:
A 'matrix' is a slice of slices: [][]int. Each row is its own slice, so
rows can even have different lengths ('jagged').

    grid := make([][]int, rows)
    for i := range grid {
        grid[i] = make([]int, cols)
    }

▸  ONE ALLOCATION INSTEAD OF rows+1
For performance, allocate one big backing slice and carve rows out of
it - better locality, one allocation:

    cells := make([]int, rows*cols)
    for i := range grid {
        grid[i] = cells[i*cols : (i+1)*cols]
    }

▸  FIXED-SIZE GRIDS
If the size is a constant, a 2-D ARRAY ([3][3]int) is a single value
with no allocations at all.

▸  YOUR TASK
Build a 3x4 multiplication grid with the single-allocation technique and
print it, then print its transpose, matching YOUR TASK.

quiz.q: Why can rows of a [][]int have different lengths?
options: The outer slice stores the rows' lengths
Go pads short rows with zeros automatically
Each row is an independent slice header
Only the first row's length is enforced
quiz.explain: [][]int is a slice whose elements are slices. Each inner slice has its own pointer, len and cap - nothing ties them to one width.
quiz.hint: What is the element type of the outer slice?

lessons.title: Maps: create, read, write, delete
lessons.concept:
A map is a hash table from keys to values.

    ages := map[string]int{"ada": 36}   // literal
    m := make(map[string]int)           // empty, ready to use
    m["bob"] = 25                        // insert / update
    v := m["zoe"]                        // missing key -> zero value (0)
    v, ok := m["zoe"]                    // ok == false if absent
    delete(m, "bob")                     // no-op if absent
    len(m)                               // number of entries
    clear(m)                             // remove everything (Go 1.21)

▸  KEY TYPES
Keys must be COMPARABLE: numbers, strings, bools, pointers, channels,
arrays and structs of comparable fields. Slices, maps and functions
can't be keys.

▸  MAPS ARE REFERENCES
A map value is a pointer to the runtime's table. Passing it to a
function lets the function modify the same map.

▸  NOT SAFE FOR CONCURRENT WRITES
Two goroutines writing one map without a lock crash the program with
'fatal error: concurrent map writes'. Use a sync.Mutex (or sync.Map for
special cases).
lessons.expected:
15 7 2
zoe missing; v = 0
false 1

quiz.q: Why does scores[name] += pts work even for a brand-new name?
options: Maps reject += on missing keys at compile time
+= creates the key and sets it to 1 first
Go pre-fills every possible key with 0
A missing key reads as the zero value 0
quiz.explain: Reading a missing key returns the value type's zero value, so m[k] += 5 reads 0, adds 5 and stores 5. This makes counting with maps a one-liner.
quiz.hint: What does a missing key read as?

lessons.title: Map iteration order and sorted output
lessons.concept:
'for k, v := range m' visits every entry exactly once - in an order Go
deliberately RANDOMISES. Code that depends on map order is a bug waiting
for a different run.

▸  SORTED OUTPUT (Go 1.23+)
    for _, k := range slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) {
        fmt.Println(k, m[k])
    }
maps.Keys returns an iterator; slices.Sorted collects and sorts it.

▸  BEFORE 1.23
    keys := make([]string, 0, len(m))
    for k := range m { keys = append(keys, k) }
    sort.Strings(keys)

▸  MODIFYING WHILE RANGING
Deleting entries during range is allowed (deleted ones won't appear
later). Entries ADDED during range may or may not be visited.

▸  YOUR TASK
Print an inventory in alphabetical order and its total, as in YOUR TASK.
lessons.expected:

figs      7
kiwis     0
pears     4

quiz.q: Is the order of 'for k := range m' guaranteed?
options: Yes - keys come out sorted
Only for maps with string keys
No - Go randomises it on purpose
Yes - insertion order is preserved
quiz.explain: The spec leaves map iteration order unspecified, and the runtime randomises it so programs can't accidentally rely on it. Sort the keys when order matters.
quiz.hint: Run a range loop over a map twice and compare.

lessons.concept:

▸  HINTS

quiz.q: Why can rotate(m) change the caller's matrix without returning it?

The rows share backing arrays with the caller's
The caller's m is a global variable
Go passes [][]int by reference automatically

O(n²)
O(n log n)

lessons.title: Structs: bundling fields
lessons.concept:
type User struct {
        Name  string
        Email string
        Age   int
    }

    u := User{Name: "Ada", Age: 36}   // keyed literal; Email == ""
    u.Age++
    p := &u
    p.Email = "ada@example.com"       // dot works through the pointer

▸  ZERO VALUE
var u User gives every field its zero value - no constructor needed.

▸  COMPARABLE AND COPYABLE
Structs are VALUES: assignment copies all fields. Two structs are equal
with == if all their fields are comparable and equal.

▸  EXPORTED FIELDS
Upper-case field names are visible to other packages (and to
encoding/json); lower-case ones are private to the package.

▸  ANONYMOUS STRUCTS
For one-off groupings - test tables, JSON snippets:
    point := struct{ X, Y int }{1, 2}

▸  YOUR TASK
Define a Book struct, create two books, raise one's price by 10% through
a pointer, and print both as shown.

quiz.q: Why prefer Book{Title: "x", Price: 9} over Book{"x", "", 9}?
options: Positional literals don't compile for structs
Keyed literals allocate the struct on the heap
Positional literals skip the zero values
Keyed literals survive adding or reordering fields
quiz.explain: A positional literal must list every field in declaration order, so adding a field breaks every literal. Keyed literals keep working, and omitted fields get zero values. go vet flags positional literals of imported struct types.
quiz.hint: What happens to positional literals when the struct gains a field?

lessons.title: Methods and receivers
lessons.concept:
A method is a function with a RECEIVER parameter written before its
name:

    func (r Rect) Area() float64 { return r.W * r.H }       // value receiver
    func (r *Rect) Scale(f float64) { r.W *= f; r.H *= f } // pointer receiver

▸  VALUE vs POINTER RECEIVER
    value (r Rect)     the method gets a COPY. Use for small types the
                       method doesn't modify.
    pointer (r *Rect)  the method can modify the original and avoids
                       copying. Use when you mutate, when the struct is
                       big, or when it contains a lock.

▸  CALLING IS CONVENIENT
If v is addressable, v.Scale(2) is shorthand for (&v).Scale(2), and
p.Area() for (*p).Area(). You rarely write & or * at call sites.

▸  METHODS ON ANY NAMED TYPE
Not just structs: type Celsius float64 can have methods too. You can
only declare methods on types defined in YOUR package.

▸  YOUR TASK
Give Rect an Area method and a pointer-receiver Scale method and print
the results shown.

quiz.q: Scale has a pointer receiver. Why does r.Scale(2) work on a plain variable r?
options: Pointer receivers also accept copies of values
Scale secretly returns the new Rect
r was declared as a pointer variable
Go rewrites it to (&r).Scale(2) automatically
quiz.explain: When the variable is addressable, Go takes its address for you. The convenience doesn't apply to non-addressable values like map elements or function results.
quiz.hint: What would you have to write if Go didn't help?

lessons.title: Constructors and the useful zero value
lessons.concept:
Go has no constructors in the language. Two conventions replace them:

▸  1. MAKE THE ZERO VALUE USEFUL
Design types so 'var x T' works immediately: bytes.Buffer, sync.Mutex,
strings.Builder and http.Client all do. Lazily initialise inside
methods when needed (if s.items == nil { s.items = map... }).

▸  2. A NewT FUNCTION when there is real setup or validation:
    func NewServer(addr string, opts ...Option) (*Server, error)
Return *T for types with identity; return an error when inputs can be
invalid.

▸  ENFORCING USE OF THE CONSTRUCTOR
Unexport the type's fields (and optionally the type itself), so
outside code must go through NewT.

▸  YOUR TASK
Write a Stack with a useful zero value (Push/Pop/Len work on var s
Stack) and a NewStack(capacity) that pre-allocates. Print the results
shown.

quiz.q: What does 'make the zero value useful' mean for a type T?
options: var t T can be used right away without setup
T's methods must all use value receivers
T must provide a NewT constructor function
Every field of T must have the type int
quiz.explain: A well-designed Go type works when declared with var - like sync.Mutex or bytes.Buffer. Callers then need no constructor for the common case.
quiz.hint: Think of sync.Mutex: do you ever call NewMutex?

lessons.title: Embedding: composition instead of inheritance
lessons.concept:
A struct can EMBED another type by listing it without a field name:

    type Animal struct{ Name string }
    func (a Animal) Describe() string { return "I am " + a.Name }

    type Dog struct {
        Animal          // embedded
        Breed string
    }

    d := Dog{Animal{"Rex"}, "collie"}
    d.Name          // promoted field  (d.Animal.Name)
    d.Describe()    // promoted method (d.Animal.Describe())

▸  IT'S NOT INHERITANCE
A Dog is not an Animal: you can't pass a Dog where an Animal is
expected. Embedding is automatic DELEGATION. If Dog defines its own
Describe, it shadows the promoted one; the inner one is still reachable
as d.Animal.Describe().

▸  THE BIG WIN: INTERFACES
Promoted methods count toward satisfying interfaces. Embedding a
sync.Mutex gives your type Lock/Unlock; embedding an interface in a
struct lets you wrap ('decorate') an implementation and override just
one method.
lessons.expected:

WOOF!

quiz.q: Can you pass a Dog to a function that takes an Animal parameter?
options: Yes - Dog inherits from Animal
No - embedding is delegation, not subtyping
Only with a pointer: &Dog
Yes, but only if Dog has no methods
quiz.explain: Embedding promotes fields and methods, but Dog and Animal remain unrelated types. Pass d.Animal explicitly, or accept an INTERFACE both satisfy.
quiz.hint: Is there an 'is-a' relationship in Go's type system?
