lessons.title: Interfaces: behaviour as a type
lessons.concept:
An interface type lists METHODS. Any type that has those methods
satisfies it - implicitly:

    type Stringer interface { String() string }

▸  WHY IMPLICIT MATTERS
You can define an interface in YOUR package that types from OTHER
packages already satisfy, without changing them. Interfaces belong to
the CONSUMER, not the producer.

▸  SMALL IS BEAUTIFUL
The standard library's best interfaces have one or two methods:
    io.Reader       Read(p []byte) (n int, err error)
    io.Writer       Write(p []byte) (n int, err error)
    fmt.Stringer    String() string
    error           Error() string
    sort.Interface  Len, Less, Swap
'The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.' - Go proverb

▸  COMPILE-TIME CHECK
    var _ fmt.Stringer = Temp(0)   // fails to build if Temp lacks String()

▸  fmt AND Stringer
fmt calls String() automatically when printing a value that has it.

os.Stdout is an io.Writer too

quiz.q: Where should an interface usually be defined?
options: In the package that USES it (the consumer)
In a shared 'interfaces' package
In the package's main.go file only
Next to every type that implements it
quiz.explain: Because satisfaction is implicit, the consumer can declare exactly the small interface it needs. Producers return concrete types. This keeps interfaces small and packages decoupled.
quiz.hint: Implementers never mention the interface - so who needs it?

lessons.title: Interface values: the (type, value) pair
lessons.concept:
An interface VALUE holds two words:
    1. the dynamic TYPE stored in it (a pointer to type information)
    2. the dynamic VALUE (or a pointer to it)

    var s fmt.Stringer        // (nil, nil)  -> s == nil
    s = Temp(20)              // (Temp, 20)
    s = &Book{}               // (*Book, 0xc000...)

Calling s.String() looks up the method through the type word - that's
a lookup table of functions the compiler builds for you.

▸  WHAT YOU CAN DO WITH IT
    - call its methods
    - compare it with == (types must match, then values; comparing
      interfaces holding uncomparable values like slices PANICS)
    - get the concrete value back with a TYPE ASSERTION (next lesson)

▸  COST
Calling through an interface is an indirect call that the compiler
usually can't inline, and storing a non-pointer value often allocates.
Both are cheap - but in tight loops concrete types are faster.

quiz.q: What two things does an interface value contain?

Only a pointer to the concrete value
A pointer to the value and its length
The method table and the interface's name
quiz.explain: An interface value is a (type, value) pair. The type part identifies the concrete type and its method set; the value part holds the data. It's nil only when BOTH are absent.

lessons.title: Type assertions and type switches
lessons.concept:
To get a concrete value back out of an interface:

▸  TYPE ASSERTION
    t := s.(Temp)         // panics if s doesn't hold a Temp
    t, ok := s.(Temp)     // ok == false instead of panicking

▸  ASSERT TO ANOTHER INTERFACE ('does it also do X?')
    if w, ok := r.(io.WriterTo); ok { w.WriteTo(dst) }  // fast path
The standard library uses this everywhere to discover optional
capabilities.

▸  TYPE SWITCH
    switch v := x.(type) {
    case int:          // v is an int

Functions like fmt.Println take ...any. Prefer real types or generics
where you can - every 'any' gives up compile-time checking.

lessons.title: Method sets: why *T satisfies but T might not
lessons.concept:
Which methods belong to a type decides which interfaces it satisfies:

    value type T     has methods with receiver (t T)
    pointer *T       has methods with receiver (t T) AND (t *T)

So if Area has a POINTER receiver:
    func (c *Circle) Area() float64
then *Circle is a Shape, but Circle is NOT:
    var s Shape = Circle{1}    // compile error: Area has pointer receiver
    var s Shape = &Circle{1}   // OK

▸  WHY
An interface may hold a COPY of a value. Calling a pointer method on that
copy would modify the copy, not your variable - a silent bug, so the
compiler forbids it.

▸  THE PRACTICAL RULE
If any method has a pointer receiver, use pointers to that type
everywhere (constructors return *T; slices hold *T or call methods via
&s[i]).

quiz.explain: The method set of Clicks (a value) excludes pointer-receiver methods, so only *Clicks satisfies Counter. Otherwise Inc would increment a copy stored inside the interface.

lessons.title: Designing with small interfaces: accept interfaces, return structs
lessons.concept:
The most-quoted Go design rule:

    ACCEPT INTERFACES, RETURN STRUCTS (concrete types)

▸  ACCEPT INTERFACES
A function that only needs to READ should take an io.Reader, not an
*os.File. Then it works with files, network connections, gzip streams,
strings.NewReader in tests, and anything invented next year.

▸  RETURN CONCRETE TYPES
Constructors return *Server, not a Server interface. Callers get all the
methods and fields, and can define their own small interface if they
need to abstract it.

▸  DON'T PREDECLARE INTERFACES
Don't write an interface just because a type exists ('Java-style'). Wait
until you have a second implementation, or a test that needs a fake.
Discover interfaces; don't design them up front.

▸  TESTABILITY FALLS OUT
Because the consumer owns a small interface, tests pass a tiny fake
that implements just those methods - no mocking framework needed.

lessons.title: Struct tags and encoding/json
lessons.concept:
A struct field can carry a TAG - a string the compiler ignores but
libraries read through reflection:

    type User struct {
        ID       int       `json:"id"`
        Name     string    `json:"name"`
        Email    string    `json:"email,omitempty"`  // skip if empty
        Password string    `json:"-"`                // never serialise
        Created  time.Time `json:"created_at"`
    }

▸  MARSHAL / UNMARSHAL
    data, err := json.Marshal(u)            // struct -> JSON bytes
    data, err := json.MarshalIndent(u, "", "  ")
    err = json.Unmarshal(data, &u)          // JSON -> struct (pass a pointer!)

▸  RULES
    - Only EXPORTED fields are encoded (lower-case ones are invisible).
    - Unknown JSON keys are ignored on decode (use a json.Decoder with
      DisallowUnknownFields to reject them).
    - Decoding into any gives map[string]any / []any / float64.

with stricter defaults; v1 remains the stable API.

lessons.title: The error interface and errors.New
lessons.concept:

    type error interface { Error() string }

▸  CREATING ERRORS

    fmt.Errorf("open %s: %v", name, err)       a formatted message

    v, err := f()
    if err != nil {

default, report to the user) OR return it - but don't log it AND return
it, or it will be reported twice.

lessons.title: Wrapping errors with %w, errors.Is and errors.As
lessons.concept:
Wrapping adds context while preserving the original error:

    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("loading user %d: %w", id, err)
    }

The result's message includes both, AND it remembers the cause.

▸  errors.Is(err, target)
Walks the wrap chain looking for a specific VALUE:
    if errors.Is(err, fs.ErrNotExist) { ... create the file ... }

▸  errors.As(err, &target)
Walks the chain looking for a specific TYPE and copies it out:
    var pe *fs.PathError
    if errors.As(err, &pe) { fmt.Println(pe.Path) }
Go 1.26 adds a generic, type-safe version: pe, ok :=
errors.AsType[*fs.PathError](err).

▸  NEVER COMPARE MESSAGES
err.Error() == "not found" breaks as soon as anyone adds context.
Compare identities with errors.Is.

▸  %w vs %v
%v formats the error as text and CUTS the chain. Use %w unless you
deliberately want to hide the cause (e.g. at an API boundary).

quiz.explain: %w records the wrapped error so errors.Is and errors.As can walk the chain. %v only copies the text into a new, unrelated error.

lessons.title: The nil interface trap: returning a typed nil
lessons.concept:
This compiles, looks right, and is wrong:

    func check() error {
        var err *MyErr          // nil pointer
        if bad { err = &MyErr{} }
        return err              // !!! never nil as an error
    }
    if check() != nil { ... }   // ALWAYS true

▸  WHY
An interface value is (type, value). Returning a nil *MyErr produces
(*MyErr, nil): the type half is filled in, so the interface is NOT nil.
The DIAGRAMS tab ('nil-interface') draws it.

▸  THE FIX
Return a literal nil on the success path, and keep error-typed
variables declared as 'error', not as a concrete pointer type:

    func check() error {
        if bad { return &MyErr{} }
        return nil
    }

▸  THE GENERAL LESSON
'nil' in an interface means 'no type AND no value'. Any time you put a
nil pointer into an interface, you get a non-nil interface.

quiz.explain: An interface is nil only when both its type and value are empty. Storing a nil *MyErr sets the type, making the interface non-nil.

lessons.title: defer in depth: order, arguments and loops
lessons.concept:
▸  THE THREE RULES (recap)
    1. Deferred calls run when the surrounding FUNCTION returns -
       normally, early, or by panic.
    2. LIFO: the last deferred call runs first.
    3. Arguments are evaluated when the defer statement runs; the call
       happens later.

▸  CLOSURES SEE LATEST VALUES
    defer fmt.Println(x)          // prints x as it was at the defer
    defer func() { fmt.Println(x) }()   // prints x at return time

▸  LOOPS
A defer inside a loop doesn't run per iteration. Opening 10,000 files in
a loop with 'defer f.Close()' keeps all 10,000 open until the function
returns. Move the body into a helper function.

▸  COST
Since Go 1.14 most defers are 'open-coded' - nearly free. Use them
freely for correctness.

▸  YOUR TASK
Reproduce the output, which demonstrates all three rules plus the
closure difference.

closure sees late: 2
arg evaluated early: 1

quiz.q: Why move a loop body with 'defer f.Close()' into a helper function?
options: Because defer is forbidden inside for loops
So each file closes at the end of its own call
Helper functions run faster than loop bodies
To make the deferred calls run in FIFO order
quiz.explain: Defers are tied to the surrounding FUNCTION. Inside a helper, each call returns per item, so its deferred Close runs immediately rather than piling up until the outer function returns.
quiz.hint: When does a deferred call run?

lessons.title: panic and recover
lessons.concept:
panic stops normal execution of the current goroutine: deferred calls
run as the stack unwinds, and if nothing recovers, the program crashes
with the panic value and a stack trace.

▸  WHEN TO PANIC
For PROGRAMMER errors and impossible states: an index that can't be out
of range, a nil map you forgot to make, an unreachable switch case.
Also at start-up for broken configuration (regexp.MustCompile,
template.Must). NOT for 'file not found' or bad user input - those are
errors.

▸  recover
Only works inside a DEFERRED function. It returns the panic value and
stops the unwinding, letting the function return normally:

    defer func() {
        if r := recover(); r != nil {
            err = fmt.Errorf("internal error: %v", r)
        }
    }()

▸  WHERE RECOVER BELONGS
At boundaries: an HTTP server recovers per request (net/http does this
for you) so one bad request doesn't kill the server. A recover can't
catch a panic in ANOTHER goroutine - every goroutine needs its own.
lessons.expected:
<nil>
recovered: mustPositive: got -1
recovered: assignment to entry in nil map
recovered: custom

quiz.q: Where must recover() be called to stop a panic?
options: Directly after the line that panics
In a deferred func of the panicking goroutine
Anywhere in main, before the panic happens
In any goroutine, as long as it runs later
quiz.explain: recover only has an effect when called from a deferred function while the same goroutine is unwinding from a panic. Elsewhere it returns nil.
quiz.hint: Which code still runs while a panic unwinds the stack?

lessons.title: Error handling patterns that keep code readable
lessons.concept:
'if err != nil' everywhere can feel noisy. These patterns keep it
clean:

▸  1. HANDLE ONCE, EARLY RETURN
Indent the error path, keep the happy path on the left margin.

▸  2. WRAP AT EACH LAYER WITH CONTEXT
    return fmt.Errorf("parse %s line %d: %w", file, n, err)
The final message reads like a stack trace in plain English.

▸  3. THE STICKY ERROR (errWriter)
When many calls of the same kind may fail, record the first error and
skip the rest; check once at the end. bufio.Writer and bufio.Scanner
work this way (sc.Err(), w.Flush()).

▸  4. VALIDATE ALL, REPORT ALL
Collect problems and return errors.Join(problems...).

▸  5. DON'T PANIC ACROSS PACKAGE BOUNDARIES
Inside a package you may panic and recover to escape deep recursion
(encoding/json does) - but convert to an error before returning to
callers.

lessons.title: Binary search trees with generics
lessons.concept:
A BST keeps keys ordered: everything in a node's left subtree is
smaller, everything in the right is larger. Insert and lookup take
O(height) - O(log n) when balanced.

A generic BST needs ORDERED keys, which is a constraint:

    type Tree[K cmp.Ordered, V any] struct { root *node[K, V] }

cmp.Ordered (Go 1.21) permits every type that supports < <= > >=:
integers, floats and strings.

▸  IN-ORDER TRAVERSAL
Visiting left, node, right yields the keys in sorted order. Recursion is
the natural fit.

▸  IN PRACTICE
For an ordered map in production, consider a balanced tree library or
simply a map plus slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) at read time. Writing one
by hand is still the best way to learn generics plus pointers.

lessons.title: Memoisation and dynamic programming
lessons.concept:
Many recursive problems recompute the same sub-answers exponentially
often (naive fib(40) makes over 300 million calls). Two cures:

▸  MEMOISATION (top-down)
Cache results in a map, keyed by the arguments:
    memo := map[int]int{}
    var fib func(int) int
    fib = func(n int) int {
        if n < 2 { return n }
        if v, ok := memo[n]; ok { return v }
        memo[n] = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)
        return memo[n]
    }
(Declare 'var fib func(int) int' first so the closure can call itself.)

▸  TABULATION (bottom-up)
Fill a slice from the smallest case upward - no recursion, often less
memory.

▸  YOUR TASK
Solve the 'coin change' problem bottom-up: the minimum number of coins
from {1, 5, 10, 25} to make each amount shown in YOUR TASK.

quiz.explain: In 'fib := func(...) { ... fib(...) }' the name fib isn't in scope yet inside its own initialiser. Declaring the variable first lets the closure capture it.

lessons.title: os.Open, os.Create and the io.Reader / io.Writer interfaces
lessons.concept:

    f, err := os.Open(path)          // read-only
    f, err := os.Create(path)        // write; create or truncate

stream function in the library:

lessons.title: bufio: buffered reading and writing
lessons.concept:
Every Read/Write on an *os.File is a system call. bufio wraps a reader
or writer with an in-memory buffer so many small operations become a
few big ones.

▸  READING
    sc := bufio.NewScanner(f)        // lines (or words, runes)
    br := bufio.NewReader(f)
    line, err := br.ReadString('\n') // includes the '\n'; io.EOF at end

▸  WRITING
    bw := bufio.NewWriter(f)
    fmt.Fprintf(bw, "row %d\n", i)   // goes to the buffer
    if err := bw.Flush(); err != nil { ... }   // FORGET THIS = LOST DATA

Writing to a bufio.Writer and never calling Flush: the last (up to
4 KB) of output silently disappears. Flush before Close.

quiz.explain: bufio.Writer keeps up to its buffer size in memory. Nothing flushes it automatically at exit, so trailing output is silently lost.

lessons.concept:
CSV looks trivial until fields contain commas, quotes or newlines.
encoding/csv handles all of it:

    records, err := r.ReadAll()          // [][]string
    // or stream:  rec, err := r.Read()  until io.EOF

    w := csv.NewWriter(os.Stdout)
    w.Write([]string{"id", "name"})      // quotes fields when needed
    w.Flush()
    if err := w.Error(); err != nil {...}

to enforce a column count, r.TrimLeadingSpace.

compute the total of the amount column, and write a summary CSV, as in

lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/csv"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"strconv"
	"strings"
)

const data = `item,amount
coffee,3.50
"cake, chocolate",4.25
"the ""big"" lunch",12.00
`

func main() {
	records, err := csv.NewReader(strings.NewReader(data)).ReadAll()
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Println(err)
		return
	}
	total := 0.0
	for _, rec := range records[1:] {
		v, err := strconv.ParseFloat(rec[1], 64)
		if err != nil {
			fmt.Println("bad amount:", rec[1])
			continue
		}
		fmt.Printf("%-18s %6.2f\n", rec[0], v)
		total += v
	}
	w := csv.NewWriter(os.Stdout)
	w.Write([]string{"summary", "total"})
	w.Write([]string{"3 items, all paid", strconv.FormatFloat(total, 'f', 2, 64)})
	w.Flush()
}

lessons.title: Modules and go.mod
lessons.concept:
A MODULE is a versioned collection of packages - the unit you publish
and depend on. Its root holds go.mod:

    module github.com/you/inventory     // the module path (import prefix)

    go 1.25                             // language version / minimum toolchain

    require (
        github.com/google/uuid v1.6.0
        golang.org/x/sync v0.8.0
    )

▸  THE COMMANDS
    go mod init github.com/you/inventory   create go.mod
    go get github.com/google/uuid@latest   add / upgrade a dependency
    go mod tidy                            sync go.mod with your imports
    go list -m all                         every module in the build
    go mod why -m golang.org/x/sync        why is this here?

▸  go.sum
Holds cryptographic hashes of every dependency version; the checksum
database (sum.golang.org) makes sure everyone gets identical code.
Commit both go.mod and go.sum.

▸  THE 'go' LINE MATTERS
It selects language semantics (e.g. per-iteration loop variables need
go >= 1.22) and the minimum toolchain. Go 1.21+ can even download a
newer toolchain when a module requires it (GOTOOLCHAIN). This app sets
GOTOOLCHAIN=local so it never downloads anything.

quiz.q: What does 'go mod tidy' do?
options: Formats every .go file in the module
Upgrades all dependencies to their latest versions
Adds missing and removes unused dependencies
Deletes the module cache on your machine
quiz.explain: tidy makes go.mod and go.sum match the imports your code actually uses: it adds requirements that are missing and drops ones nothing imports. It does NOT upgrade versions - that's go get -u.
quiz.hint: Think 'sync go.mod with the source'.

lessons.title: Packages, directories and the internal rule
lessons.concept:
▸  ONE DIRECTORY = ONE PACKAGE
All .go files in a directory share a package name (plus optional
_test packages). The import path is module path + directory:
    github.com/you/inventory/store   ->   package store

▸  A TYPICAL LAYOUT
    inventory/
      go.mod
      cmd/inventory/main.go     package main (the binary)
      internal/store/store.go   package store
      internal/store/store_test.go
      api/handler.go            package api

There's no mandatory layout - start flat and add directories when a
package has a clear job.

▸  internal/
A package under a directory named internal can be imported ONLY by code
rooted at internal's parent. The compiler enforces it - your private
API stays private even in a public repository.

▸  NAMING
Short, lower-case, single-word package names (strconv, http, store).
Avoid util/common/misc. Don't stutter: store.Store is fine,
store.StoreItem should be store.Item.

▸  NO IMPORT CYCLES
Package A may not import B if B imports A - the compiler refuses. Cycles
usually mean a third, smaller package is waiting to be extracted.

quiz.q: Who can import github.com/you/app/internal/store?
options: Anyone - internal is just a naming convention
Only the package named main
Any package that has the store directory locally
Only packages inside github.com/you/app
quiz.explain: The go command enforces it: an internal/ directory is importable only by packages rooted at internal's parent directory - here, anything under github.com/you/app.
quiz.hint: The compiler checks the importer's path.

lessons.title: Multi-file packages and init()
lessons.concept:
A package can span many files; everything at package level is shared.
This lesson's program is split across main.go (in the editor) and
shapes.go (an extra file shipped with the lesson) - both are package
main, and main.go uses names defined in shapes.go without any import.

▸  INITIALISATION ORDER
    1. Imported packages are initialised first (depth-first, once each).
    2. Package-level variables are initialised in dependency order.
    3. Every func init() runs (a file may have several), in the order
       the files are presented to the compiler (alphabetical by name).
    4. main() runs.

▸  NOTICE THE OUTPUT
main.go's init() reports 0 shapes registered: main.go sorts before
shapes.go, so its init ran FIRST - before shapes.go's init filled the
registry. Code that depends on init order across files is fragile;
by the time main() runs, everything is ready.

▸  USE init() SPARINGLY
It runs implicitly, can't return errors, and makes tests harder.
Legitimate uses: registering drivers/codecs, computing lookup tables,
verifying invariants. Prefer explicit setup functions called from main.

quiz.explain: Package initialisation (variables, then every init function) completes before main starts. Imported packages are initialised before the packages that import them.

lessons.concept:

    go build            compile the package in this dir to ./name
    go build ./...      compile EVERYTHING (catches errors repo-wide)
    go install          build and copy the binary to $GOBIN (~/go/bin)
    go fmt ./...        = gofmt -l -w on all packages
    go vet ./...        static analysis for likely bugs

goimports, which also fixes import lists) on save. Every example in
this course is gofmt-clean.

▸  WHAT go vet CATCHES
Printf verb/argument mismatches, copied mutexes and WaitGroups, unkeyed
struct literals, unreachable code, lost context cancel functions,
suspicious shifts, self-assignment, misuse of sync/atomic, and (Go 1.25)
WaitGroup.Add inside the goroutine and fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d") host:port
building that breaks IPv6.

▸  go fix (Go 1.26)
Rewritten as a set of 'modernizers' that update old code to newer
idioms (e.g. interface{} -> any, manual loops -> slices functions).

lessons.title: Generic functions and type inference
lessons.concept:
func Map[T, U any](xs []T, f func(T) U) []U {
        out := make([]U, 0, len(xs))
        for _, x := range xs { out = append(out, f(x)) }
        return out
    }

    lens := Map([]string{"go", "gopher"}, func(s string) int { return len(s) })

▸  TYPE INFERENCE
You almost never write Map[string, int](...): the compiler infers T and
U from the arguments. Explicit instantiation is needed only when a type
appears in no argument (e.g. a zero-argument constructor).

▸  WHEN TO REACH FOR GENERICS
    - Containers (stacks, sets, trees, caches).
    - Algorithms over slices and maps (most now live in slices / maps).
    - Functions that would otherwise take 'any' and type-assert.
Not every function needs them: if an interface (io.Reader) already
expresses the behaviour, use the interface.

quiz.explain: Function argument type inference deduces type parameters from the types of the arguments ([]string -> T = string, the func's result -> U = int). Each instantiation is fully type-checked.

lessons.title: Constraints: any, comparable, cmp.Ordered and ~T
lessons.concept:
A constraint is an INTERFACE describing what a type parameter can do.

▸  BUILT-IN AND STANDARD CONSTRAINTS
    any            no requirements (only assignment, passing around)
    comparable     supports == and != (needed for map keys)
    cmp.Ordered    supports < <= > >= (ints, floats, strings)

▸  TYPE SETS
An interface can list types:
    type Number interface {
        ~int | ~int64 | ~float64
    }
The ~ means 'any type whose UNDERLYING type is int', so your
'type Celsius float64' satisfies ~float64. Without ~, only float64
itself would.

▸  METHODS IN CONSTRAINTS
    type Stringish interface { ~string; String() string }
Type sets and method requirements combine.

▸  WHAT YOU CAN'T DO (yet)
No type parameters on METHODS (only on the type), no specialisation for
particular types. Go 1.26 allows a generic type to refer to itself in
its own constraint list (type Adder[A Adder[A]] interface {...}).

lessons.title: reflect: inspecting types at run time
lessons.concept:
reflect lets a program examine values whose types it doesn't know at
compile time. encoding/json, fmt, text/template and ORMs are built on
it.

    t := reflect.TypeOf(x)        // the reflect.Type
    v := reflect.ValueOf(x)       // the reflect.Value
    t.Kind()                      // Struct, Slice, Map, Ptr, Int ...
    t.NumField(), t.Field(i)      // struct fields, incl. tags
    f.Tag.Get("json")             // read a struct tag
    v.Field(i).Interface()        // back to a normal value

▸  SETTING VALUES
You can only modify through a POINTER: reflect.ValueOf(&x).Elem() is
settable; reflect.ValueOf(x) is a copy and Set panics.

▸  USE IT RARELY
Reflection is slow-ish, loses compile-time type checking and panics on
mistakes. Prefer interfaces or generics; reach for reflect when writing
a general-purpose library. Go 1.26 adds iterator methods such as
Type.Fields() and Value.Fields().

lessons.title: unsafe: what it allows and why you avoid it
lessons.concept:
The unsafe package steps outside Go's type safety:

    unsafe.Pointer       convert between ANY pointer types
    unsafe.Sizeof(x)     bytes x occupies          (compile-time constant)
    unsafe.Alignof(x)    alignment requirement
    unsafe.Offsetof(s.f) field offset in a struct
    unsafe.Slice(p, n)   make a slice from a pointer and a length
    unsafe.String(p, n)  make a string from bytes without copying

▸  LEGITIMATE USES
Talking to C libraries (cgo), syscalls, reading binary layouts, zero-copy
string/[]byte conversions in measured hot paths, and the runtime
itself.

▸  WHY YOU AVOID IT
Everything the Go spec promises is off: the GC may move or free memory
you're pointing at incorrectly, layouts can change between versions,
and unsafe code is the one place where memory corruption becomes
possible again.
Importing unsafe makes a package non-portable by definition. go vet's
unsafeptr check catches some misuse.

▸  SIZES AND PADDING (safe to look at)
Field order affects struct size because of alignment padding: the CPU
wants an 8-byte value to start at an address divisible by 8.

quiz.q: Why is Loose 24 bytes but Tight only 16?
options: Go reorders fields only in Tight
bool fields are 8 bytes each in Go

quiz.explain: int64 needs 8-byte alignment. In Loose each bool is followed by padding to the next 8-byte boundary; in Tight the two bools sit together after the int64, needing only one block of padding. Go never reorders fields for you.
quiz.hint: Draw the bytes for each struct.

lessons.title: Big picture: concurrency is not parallelism
lessons.concept:
Rob Pike's distinction, worth memorising:

    CONCURRENCY  is about STRUCTURE: composing independently executing
                 tasks (handle 10,000 connections, each in its own flow).
    PARALLELISM  is about EXECUTION: doing several things at the same
                 instant on several CPU cores.

A concurrent program runs correctly on one core; given more cores, the
Go runtime runs goroutines in parallel automatically (GOMAXPROCS
defaults to the number of usable CPUs - and since Go 1.25 it respects a
container's CPU limit).

▸  THE GO TOOLKIT
    goroutines       cheap concurrent functions:   go f()
    channels         typed pipes that synchronise: ch <- v, <-ch
    select           wait on several channel operations
    sync             Mutex, RWMutex, WaitGroup, Once, Cond, Map, Pool
    sync/atomic      lock-free counters and flags
    context          cancellation and deadlines across goroutines

▸  THE THREE RULES THAT PREVENT MOST BUGS
    1. Know how every goroutine you start will END.
    2. Never touch shared memory from two goroutines without a channel,
       a lock or an atomic.
    3. Run your tests with -race.

quiz.q: Your program uses 50 goroutines on a 1-core machine. Is it concurrent? Parallel?
options: Concurrent, but not parallel
Both concurrent and parallel
Parallel, but not concurrent
Neither, with only one core
quiz.explain: The program is STRUCTURED as 50 independent tasks (concurrent), but with one core only one runs at any instant (not parallel). More cores would add parallelism without changing the code.
quiz.hint: Concurrency = structure; parallelism = simultaneous execution.

lessons.title: Goroutines and sync.WaitGroup
lessons.concept:
go doWork(i)              // starts doWork concurrently, returns at once
    go func() { ... }()       // a goroutine from a function literal

▸  WAITING FOR THEM
main doesn't wait for goroutines - when it returns, they die. Use a
sync.WaitGroup:

    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for i := range 3 {
        wg.Add(1)                 // BEFORE the go statement
        go func() {
            defer wg.Done()       // first line of the goroutine
            work(i)
        }()
    }
    wg.Wait()                     // blocks until the counter is 0

Go 1.25 adds wg.Go(func() { work(i) }), which does Add/Done for you.

▸  ORDER IS NOT GUARANTEED
Goroutines run in whatever order the scheduler picks. If output order
matters, have each goroutine write to its own slot (results[i] = ...)
and print after Wait.

▸  YOUR TASK
Compute the squares of 1..5 in five goroutines, store each result in
its own slot, and print them in order after waiting.

quiz.q: Why must wg.Add(1) come BEFORE 'go func()', not inside it?

Add can only be called from the main goroutine
go vet refuses to compile it the other way
quiz.explain: If the goroutine hasn't been scheduled yet, the counter is still 0 and Wait returns immediately - a race that 'works' on your laptop and fails in production. go vet (Go 1.25) now flags this.
quiz.hint: What does Wait see if Add hasn't happened yet?

lessons.title: Channels: synchronised communication
lessons.concept:
ch := make(chan int)      // unbuffered channel of int
    go func() { ch <- 42 }()  // send
    v := <-ch                 // receive

▸  UNBUFFERED = A HANDSHAKE
A send blocks until a receiver takes the value, and a receive blocks
until a sender delivers. The moment of transfer synchronises the two
goroutines - everything the sender did before sending is visible to the
receiver after receiving.

▸  DEADLOCK
If nobody will ever receive, the sender blocks forever. When EVERY
goroutine is blocked the runtime aborts with:
    fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!
Classic cause: sending on an unbuffered channel in main with no other
goroutine to receive.

▸  CHANNELS ARE VALUES
They can be passed to functions, stored in structs, sent over other
channels. Their zero value is nil (and nil channels block forever).

GOPHER HELLO
99

quiz.q: What happens when main sends on an unbuffered channel and no goroutine receives?
options: The value is dropped and main continues
The value waits in the channel until later
The send returns an error value
main blocks; the runtime reports a deadlock
quiz.explain: An unbuffered send waits for a receiver. With no other goroutine running, every goroutine is blocked and the runtime aborts with 'all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!'.
quiz.hint: An unbuffered channel stores nothing.

lessons.title: Buffered channels
lessons.concept:
ch := make(chan int, 3)   // capacity 3

A buffered channel holds up to cap values:
    - send blocks only when the buffer is FULL
    - receive blocks only when it is EMPTY
    len(ch) = values waiting, cap(ch) = capacity

▸  WHAT BUFFERS ARE FOR
    - Smoothing bursts between a producer and a consumer.
    - Letting N goroutines deliver results without waiting for the
      collector (cap = N).
    - A counting semaphore: make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrent).

▸  WHAT THEY ARE NOT FOR
Hiding a deadlock. If your program only works with a buffer of 'just
the right size', the design is wrong - the buffer will fill one day.
Start unbuffered; add a buffer with a reason.

lessons.title: Closing channels and ranging over them
lessons.concept:
close(ch) says 'no more values will be sent'.

    for v := range ch { ... }     // receives until ch is closed AND empty
    v, ok := <-ch                 // ok == false once closed and drained

▸  THE RULES
    - Only the SENDER closes (the receiver can't know whether more is
      coming). With several senders, close after all of them are done
      (WaitGroup + a closer goroutine).
    - Sending on a closed channel PANICS. Closing twice PANICS.
    - Receiving from a closed channel never blocks: buffered values first,
      then zero values with ok == false.
    - You don't HAVE to close a channel - only when a receiver needs to
      know the stream ended (range, or a 'done' broadcast).

▸  CLOSE AS A BROADCAST
Closing a channel wakes EVERY receiver at once - the basis of 'done'
channels and context cancellation.

lessons.title: select: waiting on several channels
lessons.concept:
select blocks until ONE of its cases can proceed, then runs it. If
several are ready, it picks one at random (fairness).

    select {
    case v := <-results:
        use(v)
    case err := <-errs:
        handle(err)
    case <-time.After(2 * time.Second):
        fmt.Println("timed out")
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    }

▸  default MAKES IT NON-BLOCKING
    select {
    case ch <- v:              // send if there's room
    default:                   // otherwise drop it / do something else
    }

▸  IDIOMS
    - Timeouts: case <-time.After(d)
    - Cancellation: case <-ctx.Done()
    - for { select { ... } } as an event loop
    - A nil channel case is never selected - set a channel to nil to
      disable its case once it's closed.

lessons.title: Data races and the race detector
lessons.concept:
A DATA RACE: two goroutines access the same variable concurrently, at
least one writes, and nothing orders the accesses. Results are
unpredictable - lost updates, torn values, impossible states - and they
vary between runs and machines.

    counter := 0
    for range 1000 {
        go func() { counter++ }()   // RACE: read-modify-write
    }

counter++ is three steps (read, add, write). Two goroutines can read the
same old value and both write old+1.

▸  THE RACE DETECTOR
    go run -race .
    go test -race ./...
It instruments every memory access and reports the two conflicting
goroutines' stacks. It finds races that HAPPEN during the run, so drive
it with tests that exercise concurrency. It costs 2-20x CPU, so it's for
tests and staging, not production. (It needs cgo, i.e. a C compiler.)

▸  THE FIXES
A mutex, an atomic, or redesign so only one goroutine owns the data and
others send it messages over a channel.

This lesson runs WITH -race on the FIXED version: no report appears.
Change it back to the racy version and run it in your own terminal with
'go run -race .' to see a report.
lessons.expected: counter: 1000

quiz.q: Why can 'counter++' from many goroutines lose updates?
options: Integers can only be changed by the main goroutine
It's a read, an add and a write that can interleave
The scheduler discards writes it considers duplicates
Go executes ++ on a copy of counter in each goroutine
quiz.explain: Two goroutines can both read 5, both compute 6, and both store 6 - one increment vanishes. Without synchronisation the result is undefined; the race detector reports it.
quiz.hint: How many machine steps is ++?

lessons.title: sync.Mutex and sync.RWMutex
lessons.concept:
A Mutex lets only one goroutine at a time into a critical section:

    type SafeCounter struct {
        mu sync.Mutex
        m  map[string]int
    }
    func (c *SafeCounter) Inc(k string) {
        c.mu.Lock()
        defer c.mu.Unlock()
        c.m[k]++
    }

▸  HABITS
    - Keep the mutex next to the data it guards, in the same struct,
      unexported.
    - Lock; defer Unlock - unless the critical section is tiny and hot.
    - Hold locks for as little time as possible; never do I/O or call
      unknown code while holding one.
    - NEVER copy a struct containing a mutex (pass *SafeCounter). go vet
      catches it.

▸  RWMutex
Many readers OR one writer:
    mu.RLock() / mu.RUnlock()   concurrent readers
    mu.Lock()  / mu.Unlock()    exclusive writer
Worth it only when reads vastly outnumber writes and the critical
section isn't trivial - measure.

▸  NOT RE-ENTRANT
Locking a mutex you already hold deadlocks. Go has no recursive mutex.
lessons.expected: k0=true k1=true k2=true k3=false 3

quiz.q: What happens if a goroutine calls mu.Lock() on a mutex it already holds?
options: It returns immediately without locking again
It succeeds and increments a lock counter
It deadlocks - Go mutexes are not re-entrant
It panics with 'mutex already locked'
quiz.explain: sync.Mutex has no notion of an owner, so the second Lock simply waits for an Unlock that will never come. Restructure so the inner code doesn't lock again (e.g. an unexported method that assumes the lock).
quiz.hint: Does a Go mutex know which goroutine holds it?

lessons.title: sync/atomic: lock-free counters and flags
lessons.concept:
For a single integer, pointer or flag, sync/atomic is simpler and faster
than a mutex:

    var hits atomic.Int64         // typed atomics (Go 1.19+)
    hits.Add(1)
    n := hits.Load()

    var ready atomic.Bool
    ready.Store(true)

    var cfg atomic.Pointer[Config]
    cfg.Store(newCfg)             // swap a whole config atomically
    cur := cfg.Load()

    old := v.Swap(new)            // set and return the old value
    ok := v.CompareAndSwap(old, new)

▸  WHEN NOT TO
Atomics protect ONE value. Two related fields that must change together
('balance and lastUpdated') need a mutex - two separate atomic updates
can be observed half-done.

▸  ZERO VALUE IS READY
atomic.Int64{} is 0 and usable. Like mutexes, don't copy them.
lessons.expected:
requests: 500
info -> debug
true false

quiz.q: When should you use a mutex instead of atomics?
options: When several values must change together
Whenever more than two goroutines share it
Whenever the counter is an int64
Atomics replace mutexes in every case
quiz.explain: Each atomic operation is indivisible on its own, but two atomic updates in a row aren't. Invariants spanning several fields need a lock around the whole update.
quiz.hint: Can another goroutine look between two atomic calls?

lessons.title: sync.Once and lazy initialisation
lessons.concept:
sync.Once runs a function exactly once, no matter how many goroutines
call it at the same time - perfect for lazy initialisation:

    var (
        once sync.Once
        db   *DB
    )
    func getDB() *DB {
        once.Do(func() { db = connect() })
        return db
    }

All callers block until the first Do finishes, so nobody sees a
half-initialised db.

▸  GO 1.21 HELPERS
    getConfig := sync.OnceValue(func() *Config { return load() })
    cfg := getConfig()                    // computed once, cached

    getConn := sync.OnceValues(func() (*Conn, error) { return dial() })
    conn, err := getConn()                // the error is cached too

▸  PANICS
If the function panics, Once considers it done (later calls do
nothing); OnceValue re-panics on every call.
lessons.expected:
loaded 1 time(s): prod eu
init with 0

quiz.q: Twenty goroutines call once.Do(f) simultaneously. How many times does f run?
options: At least once, possibly more under load
Once per CPU core available
Exactly once; the others wait until it finishes
Twenty times, but one at a time
quiz.explain: Once guarantees a single execution and makes every concurrent caller wait for it to complete, so all of them see the initialised state.
quiz.hint: It's in the name.

lessons.title: Goroutine leaks
lessons.concept:
A goroutine that blocks forever never ends: its stack and everything it
references stay in memory. In a server, a leak per request slowly eats
all RAM.

▸  THE CLASSIC LEAK
    func first(urls []string) string {
        ch := make(chan string)             // unbuffered
        for _, u := range urls {
            go func() { ch <- fetch(u) }()
        }
        return <-ch                         // only ONE receive...
    }   // ...the other senders block forever

▸  FIXES
    - Buffer the channel to len(urls), so every send completes.
    - Or pass a context and 'select { case ch <- r: case <-ctx.Done(): }'
      so senders give up when the caller stops listening.

▸  DETECTING LEAKS
runtime.NumGoroutine() in tests; goleak (go.uber.org/goleak); pprof's
goroutine profile. Go 1.26 adds an experimental 'goroutineleak' profile
that finds goroutines blocked on unreachable channels via the GC.
lessons.expected:
leaked goroutines: 9
after fixed version: 0

quiz.q: Why does buffering the channel to n fix the leak?
options: Every sender can complete even if nobody receives
It makes the first result arrive faster
The garbage collector kills idle buffered senders
Buffered channels close themselves automatically
quiz.explain: With capacity n, each of the n sends succeeds immediately into the buffer, so all goroutines finish. The unread values are collected with the channel once nothing references it.
quiz.hint: Why did the leaky senders block?

lessons.title: context: cancellation and deadlines
lessons.concept:
A context.Context carries a cancellation signal, a deadline and
request-scoped values down a call tree. Every blocking or long-running
API in Go takes one as its FIRST parameter:

    func fetch(ctx context.Context, url string) ([]byte, error)

▸  CREATING CONTEXTS
    ctx := context.Background()                     // the root
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)       // cancel() by hand
    ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parent, 2*time.Second)
    ctx, cancel := context.WithDeadline(parent, t)
    defer cancel()      // ALWAYS - releases timers and children

Cancelling a parent cancels every context derived from it.

▸  OBEYING A CONTEXT
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()     // context.Canceled or DeadlineExceeded
    case res := <-work:
        ...
    }

▸  RULES
    - Pass ctx explicitly; never store it in a struct field.
    - context.WithValue is for request-scoped data (trace IDs), NOT
      optional parameters.
    - context.Cause / WithCancelCause (Go 1.20) record WHY it was
      cancelled.
lessons.expected:
49 <nil>
0 context deadline exceeded true
child: context canceled

quiz.q: Why must you call the cancel function returned by WithTimeout?
options: It frees the timer and child resources early
It's needed to read the value of ctx.Err()
Go panics if a context is never cancelled
Without it the timeout never starts counting
quiz.explain: The context stays registered with its parent and keeps its timer until the deadline. defer cancel() releases them as soon as the work is done. go vet's lostcancel check flags forgotten cancels.
quiz.hint: What would linger until the deadline otherwise?

lessons.title: Worker pools
lessons.concept:
Start a FIXED number of workers that pull jobs from a channel. This
bounds concurrency (CPU, open files, API rate limits) no matter how many
jobs arrive.

    jobs := make(chan Job)
    results := make(chan Result)
    var wg sync.WaitGroup
    for w := range numWorkers {
        wg.Add(1)
        go func() { defer wg.Done(); for j := range jobs { results <- do(j) } }()
    }
    go func() { wg.Wait(); close(results) }()   // close when all workers end
    go func() { for _, j := range all { jobs <- j }; close(jobs) }()
    for r := range results { ... }

▸  THE THREE CLOSES
    - the job producer closes jobs -> workers' range loops end
    - a closer goroutine waits for workers, then closes results
    - main's range over results ends
Get these right and the pool shuts down cleanly with no leaks.

▸  YOUR TASK
Process 9 jobs with 3 workers; collect results, sort them, and print the
output in YOUR TASK.

quiz.q: In a worker pool, who should close the results channel?
options: main, right after sending the last job
The goroutine that produces the jobs
A goroutine that waits for every worker
Each worker, when its job loop ends
quiz.explain: Several workers send on results, so no single worker may close it (the others would panic). A dedicated goroutine does wg.Wait() then close(results).
quiz.hint: How many goroutines send on results?

lessons.title: Pipelines: stages connected by channels
lessons.concept:
A pipeline is a series of stages; each stage receives values from an
inbound channel, transforms them, and sends them on an outbound one:

    gen(1..n) -> square -> filter(even) -> sink

Each stage is a function that takes <-chan T and returns <-chan U,
starting its own goroutine and closing its output when its input is
exhausted:

    func square(in <-chan int) <-chan int {
        out := make(chan int)
        go func() {
            defer close(out)
            for v := range in { out <- v * v }
        }()
        return out
    }

▸  WHY
Stages run concurrently (a slow stage overlaps with the others), each is
simple and testable, and they compose like Unix pipes.

▸  CANCELLATION
In real pipelines every send should also watch ctx.Done(), so a consumer
that stops early doesn't leave upstream stages blocked forever.

quiz.q: Why does each pipeline stage close its output channel when done?
options: So the next stage's range loop can end
Unclosed channels can't be ranged over
Closing frees the memory of sent values
The Go runtime requires it for goroutines
quiz.explain: Closing is the 'end of stream' signal. The downstream stage's 'for v := range in' terminates only when in is closed, and then it closes its own output - the shutdown ripples through the pipeline.
quiz.hint: How does a range loop over a channel ever stop?

lessons.title: Fan-out and fan-in
lessons.concept:
FAN-OUT: start several goroutines reading from the SAME input channel to
parallelise a slow stage (the worker pool is fan-out).

FAN-IN (merge): combine several channels into one:

    func merge(cs ...<-chan int) <-chan int {
        out := make(chan int)
        var wg sync.WaitGroup
        for _, c := range cs {
            wg.Add(1)
            go func() { defer wg.Done(); for v := range c { out <- v } }()
        }
        go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()
        return out
    }

▸  ORDER
Fan-in loses ordering. If order matters, tag each item with its
sequence number and re-sort (or use an ordered results slice).

▸  HOW MANY WORKERS?
CPU-bound work: about runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0). I/O-bound work (network,
disk): more - limited by what the remote side or your file-descriptor
limit can take.
lessons.expected: 9 [a0 a1 a2 b0 b1 c0 c1 c2 c3]

quiz.q: What do you lose when you fan in several channels?
options: Some of the items, under load
Type safety of the channel values
The relative order of the items
The ability to close the output
quiz.explain: Values arrive in whatever order the merging goroutines manage to send. Nothing is lost, but ordering across (and sometimes within) sources isn't guaranteed.
quiz.hint: Why does the example sort before printing?

lessons.title: errgroup: goroutines that can fail
lessons.concept:
WaitGroup can't return errors or cancel siblings. The standard answer is
golang.org/x/sync/errgroup:

    g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
    for _, url := range urls {
        g.Go(func() error { return fetch(ctx, url) })
    }
    if err := g.Wait(); err != nil { ... }   // the FIRST error
    g.SetLimit(4)                             // bound concurrency

When any function returns an error, ctx is cancelled so the others can
stop early.

▸  THIS COURSE IS OFFLINE (stdlib only)
So the demo builds a minimal errgroup from WaitGroup + sync.Once +
context.WithCancelCause. It's ~25 lines - and shows exactly what the
real one does. In your projects: go get golang.org/x/sync.
lessons.expected:
first error: db failed
stopped early: true

quiz.q: What does errgroup add over a plain WaitGroup?
options: It retries any function that returns an error
It replaces the need for a context entirely
It runs the goroutines in a guaranteed order
It returns the first error and cancels the others
quiz.explain: errgroup.Wait returns the first non-nil error, and WithContext cancels the shared context when that happens, so sibling goroutines can stop instead of finishing pointless work.
quiz.hint: How long did the slow tasks actually run?

lessons.title: Semaphores and rate limiting
lessons.concept:
▸  A SEMAPHORE FROM A BUFFERED CHANNEL
Limit how many goroutines do something at once (say, 3 concurrent
downloads):

    sem := make(chan struct{}, 3)
    for _, u := range urls {
        go func() {
            sem <- struct{}{}        // acquire (blocks when 3 are busy)
            defer func() { <-sem }() // release
            download(u)
        }()
    }

▸  RATE LIMITING WITH A TICKER
Allow one operation per interval:
    tick := time.NewTicker(200 * time.Millisecond)
    defer tick.Stop()
    for _, req := range reqs {
        <-tick.C
        send(req)
    }
For bursts and per-client limits use golang.org/x/time/rate (a token
bucket).

▸  TIMERS SINCE GO 1.23
Unstopped Timers and Tickers are now garbage-collected, and their
channels are unbuffered - but calling Stop is still good hygiene.

quiz.q: How does make(chan struct{}, 3) limit concurrency?
options: A 4th send blocks until a slot is released
struct{} values expire after 3 sends
Channels can't have more than 3 receivers
The scheduler only runs 3 goroutines per channel
quiz.explain: Each worker sends into the buffer to acquire a slot. With 3 slots taken, the next send blocks until someone receives (releases).
quiz.hint: When does a buffered send block?

lessons.title: Timeouts, retries and backoff
lessons.concept:
Networks fail. Robust clients:

▸  1. ALWAYS HAVE A TIMEOUT
Via context.WithTimeout or http.Client{Timeout: ...}. 'Forever' is not a
timeout.

▸  2. RETRY ONLY WHAT'S SAFE TO RETRY
Idempotent operations (GET, a PUT of the same value) and errors that are
temporary (timeouts, 503, connection reset). Never blindly retry a
payment.

▸  3. BACK OFF EXPONENTIALLY, WITH JITTER
Wait 100ms, 200ms, 400ms ... (capped), plus randomness so a thousand
clients don't retry in lock-step and flatten the recovering server.

▸  4. RESPECT THE CALLER'S CONTEXT
Sleep with select on ctx.Done(), not time.Sleep, so cancellation stops
the retry loop immediately.

▸  YOUR TASK
Implement retry(ctx, attempts, base, op) with doubling backoff that
stops on success, on a non-retryable error, or on cancellation; run the
scenarios in YOUR TASK (jitter is omitted so the output is stable).
lessons.expected:
attempt 1 failed, retrying in 1ms
  attempt 2 failed, retrying in 2ms
flaky: <nil>
fatal: bad credentials
  attempt 1 failed, retrying in 1ms
  attempt 2 failed, retrying in 2ms
gave up: temporary failure

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to retry delays in real clients?
options: Random delays make each request faster
Servers reject requests at exact intervals
So many clients don't retry at the same instant
Go's timers need jitter to be accurate
quiz.explain: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together, creating waves of load (a 'thundering herd') that can knock a recovering service over again.
quiz.hint: Picture 10,000 clients that all failed at 12:00:00.

lessons.title: Testing concurrent code (and testing/synctest)
lessons.concept:
Concurrent code is hard to test because timing varies. Techniques:

▸  1. ALWAYS RUN WITH -race
    go test -race ./...

▸  2. AVOID time.Sleep IN TESTS
Sleeps make tests slow AND flaky. Synchronise on channels or WaitGroups,
or inject a clock / ticker interface so tests control time.

▸  3. testing/synctest (Go 1.25)
Runs a test in a 'bubble' with a FAKE clock: time only advances when
every goroutine in the bubble is blocked, so a 1-hour timeout test runs
instantly and deterministically:

    func TestTimeout(t *testing.T) {
        synctest.Test(t, func(t *testing.T) {
            ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(t.Context(), time.Hour)
            defer cancel()
            synctest.Wait()        // wait until bubble goroutines block
            <-ctx.Done()           // fake clock jumps 1h - instantly
        })
    }

▸  4. STRESS
go test -count=1000 -race -run TestPool  shakes out rare interleavings.

▸  5. DESIGN FOR IT
Pure functions for the logic, a thin concurrent shell around them.

quiz.q: What does testing/synctest's fake clock let you do?
options: Skip tests that use time.Sleep altogether
Test hour-long timeouts instantly
Run tests on several machines in parallel
Measure exactly how long each goroutine ran
quiz.explain: Inside a synctest bubble, time advances only when all goroutines are blocked, jumping straight to the next timer. Timeouts and tickers become instant and repeatable.
quiz.hint: What does the bubble's clock do while goroutines are blocked?

lessons.title: Number literals: bases, separators and the octal trap
lessons.concept:
Go accepts integer literals in four bases:

    42          decimal
    0x2A        hexadecimal  (0X also works)
    0o52        octal        (Go 1.13+, the clear form)
    052         octal too!   (a leading zero - the old form)
    0b101010    binary       (Go 1.13+)
    1_000_000   underscores separate digits anywhere between digits

▸  THE OCTAL TRAP  (100 Go Mistakes #17)
    perm := 0644      // 420 in decimal - correct for file modes
    n := 010          // 8, not 10!
A leading 0 silently means octal. Write 0o644 for permissions so the
intent is obvious, and never pad decimal numbers with zeros.

▸  FLOAT AND OTHER LITERALS
    1.5e3   1500        0x1p-2  0.25 (hex float)
    .5      0.5         1i      an imaginary literal
    'a'     a rune (97) '\n'    escape     '\x41'  'A'   'é' 'é'

▸  UNTYPED UNTIL USED
Literals are untyped constants; 1_000_000 fits an int but not an
int8 - assigning it to an int8 is a compile error, not a wraparound.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	fmt.Println(42, 0x2A, 0o52, 052, 0b101010)
	fmt.Println(1_000_000, 1.5e3, 0x1p-2)
	n := 010 // looks like ten...
	fmt.Println("010 is", n)
	fmt.Printf("%o %#o %O %x %#b\n", 420, 420, 420, 255, 5)
	fmt.Println('a', '\x41', string('é'))
}

quiz.q: What does the Go literal 010 equal?
options: 10, because Go ignores leading zeros
A compile error: leading zeros are illegal
8, because a leading zero means octal
2, because 010 is read as binary
quiz.explain: A leading 0 is the legacy octal prefix, so 010 is 1*8 + 0 = 8. Prefer the explicit 0o10 form so readers never have to guess.
quiz.hint: What does a leading 0 mean in the table above?

lessons.title: Integer overflow: silent wraparound
lessons.concept:
Integer arithmetic in Go WRAPS on overflow at run time - no panic,
no error (100 Go Mistakes #18):

    var x int8 = 127
    x++                 // -128
    var u uint8 = 0
    u--                 // 255

▸  CONSTANTS ARE CHECKED, VARIABLES ARE NOT
    var b int8 = 128    // compile error: constant overflows int8
    b := int8(n)        // run time: silently wraps if n > 127

▸  DETECTING OVERFLOW
For addition, the result has the 'wrong' sign or is smaller:
    func addInt(a, b int) (int, bool) {
        c := a + b
        if (c > a) == (b > 0) { return c, true }
        return 0, false
    }
math/bits gives carry-aware helpers: bits.Add64, bits.Mul64 return the
high and low words, so you can see the carry.

▸  WHEN IT MATTERS
Sizes from untrusted input (n * elemSize), counters that run for years,
converting int64 to int32 for a protocol. Use math/big when numbers can
grow without bound.

quiz.q: An int8 variable holding 127 is incremented. What happens?
options: It becomes 128, promoted to int16
The program panics with an overflow error
It stays at 127, saturating at the max
It wraps around to -128 with no error
quiz.explain: Go integers use two's-complement wraparound at run time. Only CONSTANT expressions are overflow-checked, at compile time.
quiz.hint: Does Go check arithmetic on variables at run time?

lessons.title: Floating point: precision, NaN and Inf
lessons.concept:
float64 is IEEE-754 binary floating point. Most decimal fractions can't
be stored exactly (100 Go Mistakes #19):

    0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3          false!   (0.30000000000000004)

▸  RULES OF THUMB
    - Never compare floats with ==; compare with a tolerance:
          math.Abs(a-b) <= 1e-9 * math.Max(math.Abs(a), math.Abs(b))
    - Never store money in floats: use integer cents (int64) or
      math/big.
    - Adding many small numbers to a big one loses the small ones;
      sum small values first.

▸  SPECIAL VALUES
    math.Inf(1), math.Inf(-1)   from 1/0.0 with variables
    math.NaN()                  'not a number', e.g. 0/0 or Sqrt(-1)
NaN is NOT equal to anything, even itself: x != x is true only for NaN.
Use math.IsNaN. A NaN map key can be inserted but never found again.

▸  FLOAT -> INT
int(f) truncates toward zero; out-of-range results are
implementation-defined - check bounds first. math.Round, math.Floor and
math.Ceil round explicitly.

lessons.title: Booleans, short-circuit and evaluation order
lessons.concept:
▸  && AND || SHORT-CIRCUIT
The right side is evaluated only if needed:
    if p != nil && p.Ready { ... }       // safe: p.Ready never runs on nil
    if len(s) > 0 && s[0] == '#' { ... } // safe indexing
Put the cheap or guarding test first.

▸  NO TRUTHINESS
Only bool values go in conditions: 'if n' or 'if ptr' don't compile.
There's no ternary operator ?: either - write an if/else.

▸  ORDER OF EVALUATION
In an expression, FUNCTION CALLS, method calls and channel operations
happen left to right:
    y := f() + g()       // f runs before g
But the order of other operand evaluation relative to those calls is
not specified - avoid expressions that both read and modify the same
variable:
    a[i] = i + inc(&i)   // legal, but hard to reason about

▸  ASSIGNMENT IS TWO-PHASE
    a, b = b, a          // all right-hand sides are evaluated first,
                         // then assigned - a swap needs no temp
    i, s[i] = 1, 9       // index expressions on the left are evaluated
                         // first too: s[0] gets 9 when i started at 0

A false
C true
2 1
1 [9 0]

quiz.q: In 'trace("A", false) && trace("B", true)', which calls run?
options: Only A, because the result is already false
B only, because && evaluates right to left
Both, because Go evaluates every operand
Neither, because the result is a constant
quiz.explain: && short-circuits: once the left side is false the whole expression is false, so the right side never runs. That is exactly why p != nil && p.Ready is safe.
quiz.hint: If the left side of && is false, can the right side change the answer?

lessons.title: Defined types vs type aliases
lessons.concept:
Two declarations that look alike and mean very different things
(gopl 2.5):

▸  A DEFINED TYPE creates a NEW, distinct type
    type Celsius float64
    type UserID int64
Celsius and float64 share an underlying type, so you CAN convert
(Celsius(x)), but you can't mix them without converting. Defined types
get their own method sets and catch unit mix-ups at compile time.
They do NOT inherit methods of the original type:
    type MyMutex sync.Mutex     // has no Lock/Unlock methods!

▸  AN ALIAS is just another NAME for the same type
    type byteAlias = byte       // note the =
byte and rune are aliases (for uint8 and int32); any is an alias for
interface{}. Aliases exist mainly for gradual refactoring - moving a
type between packages without breaking callers. Since Go 1.24 aliases
may be generic: type Set[T comparable] = map[T]struct{}.

▸  CHOOSING
Defined types for meaning (IDs, units, enums). Aliases almost never in
everyday code.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

type Celsius float64
type Fahrenheit float64

func (c Celsius) ToF() Fahrenheit { return Fahrenheit(c*9/5 + 32) }

type Temp = Celsius // alias: Temp IS Celsius

type UserID int64
type OrderID int64

func lookup(id UserID) string { return fmt.Sprint("user#", int64(id)) }

func main() {
	var c Celsius = 100
	var t Temp = c // no conversion needed: same type
	fmt.Println(c.ToF(), t.ToF())
	fmt.Printf("%T %T\n", c, t)

	oid := OrderID(7)
	// lookup(oid) would not compile: OrderID is not UserID
	fmt.Println(lookup(UserID(oid)))

	var b byte = 'G'
	var u uint8 = b // byte is an alias for uint8
	fmt.Println(u)
}

212 212
main.Celsius main.Celsius
user#7

lessons.title: Method values and method expressions
lessons.concept:
Methods can be turned into ordinary function values two ways
(gopl 6.4):

▸  METHOD VALUE: bound to a receiver
    p := Point{1, 2}
    f := p.Distance       // f is func(Point) float64, p is captured
    f(q)                  // same as p.Distance(q)
The receiver is evaluated (and copied, for value receivers) when the
method value is created - later changes to p don't affect f.

▸  METHOD EXPRESSION: the receiver becomes the first parameter
    g := Point.Distance   // func(Point, Point) float64
    g(p, q)
    h := (*Point).ScaleBy // func(*Point, float64)

▸  WHERE YOU USE THEM
    - Callbacks: time.AfterFunc(d, srv.Shutdown)
    - Goroutines: go w.run()  is really a method value call
    - Choosing an operation at run time:
          op := Point.Add; if sub { op = Point.Sub }
    - http.HandleFunc("/", app.home)  - a method value as a handler

quiz.q: What is the type of the method expression Point.Distance?
options: func(Point) float64
func(*Point, Point) float64
method Point.Distance
func(Point, Point) float64
quiz.explain: A method expression turns the receiver into an explicit first parameter. A method VALUE (p.Distance) already has its receiver bound, so its type is func(Point) float64.
quiz.hint: With no receiver bound yet, where does the receiver go?

lessons.title: Interface embedding: composing behaviours
lessons.concept:
Interfaces can embed other interfaces; the result has the union of
their methods:

    type Reader interface { Read(p []byte) (int, error) }
    type Writer interface { Write(p []byte) (int, error) }
    type ReadWriter interface {
        Reader
        Writer
    }

The io package is built this way: ReadCloser, WriteCloser,
ReadWriteCloser, ReadSeeker... Small pieces, composed as needed.

▸  WHY IT WORKS SO WELL
A function asks for exactly what it uses. A type that implements
Read, Write and Close satisfies ALL of these interfaces at once,
without declaring any of them.

▸  INTERFACE UPGRADES
Code often asks for the small interface and checks for a bigger one:
    if c, ok := r.(io.Closer); ok { defer c.Close() }
This is 'querying behaviour with a type assertion' (gopl 7.12).

▸  OVERLAPPING METHODS
Since Go 1.14, embedding two interfaces that share an identical method
(like Close() error in both) is allowed.
lessons.expected:
hello interfaces
write on closed buffer

quiz.q: Which types satisfy io.ReadWriter?
options: Only types that declare "implements io.ReadWriter"
Only types that embed io.Reader and io.Writer
Every type that has both Read and Write methods
Types with either a Read or a Write method
quiz.explain: An embedded interface just contributes its methods. Satisfaction stays implicit: having Read AND Write with the right signatures is all it takes.
quiz.hint: Does Go ever require a type to name the interfaces it implements?

lessons.title: Struct embedding pitfalls
lessons.concept:
Embedding promotes fields and methods - including ones you didn't
mean to expose (100 Go Mistakes #10):

▸  1. LEAKING METHODS
    type Cache struct {
        sync.Mutex             // embedded!
        data map[string]string
    }
Now every caller can write c.Lock() and c.Unlock() - your locking
discipline is part of the public API. Use a NAMED field instead:
    mu sync.Mutex

▸  2. SHADOWING
If the outer struct declares a field or method with the same name, it
wins; the embedded one is reached through the type name:
    c.Name          // outer
    c.Inner.Name    // embedded

▸  3. AMBIGUITY
Two embedded types at the same depth with the same field name compile
fine - until you USE that name: 'ambiguous selector c.ID'.

▸  4. INTERFACE SATISFACTION SURPRISES
Promoted methods make the outer type satisfy interfaces - e.g.
embedding *bytes.Buffer makes your type an io.Writer whether you
wanted it or not.

Rule: embed when you want the outer type to 'have the behaviour' of the
inner one publicly; otherwise use a named field.

1 99
base 1 base-name
0 1

It's a compile error: ambiguous selector
It returns the last embedded type, Audit.ID
It returns the sum of the two ID fields
quiz.explain: Two fields with the same name at the same embedding depth are ambiguous. The program still compiles as long as nobody writes u.ID; once you do, you must say u.Base.ID or u.Audit.ID.

lessons.title: Comparing values: ==, comparable and DeepEqual
lessons.concept:
Which values can you compare with == ? (100 Go Mistakes #29)

    COMPARABLE: bool, numbers, strings, pointers, channels, interfaces,
                arrays of comparable, structs whose fields are all
                comparable
    NOT:        slices, maps, functions (only against nil)

▸  STRUCTS AND ARRAYS
== compares field by field / element by element. Adding a slice field
to a struct makes == on it a COMPILE error.

▸  INTERFACES: COMPILE OK, RUN-TIME PANIC
Comparing two interfaces whose dynamic values are slices panics:
'comparing uncomparable type []int'. Also a map key of interface type
holding a slice panics on insert.

▸  WHAT TO USE INSTEAD
    slices.Equal(a, b)        element-wise, for comparable elements
    maps.Equal(m1, m2)        same keys, equal values
    bytes.Equal(x, y)         byte slices
    reflect.DeepEqual(a, b)   anything, recursively - slow, and it
                              treats nil and empty slices as DIFFERENT
In tests, prefer a dedicated diff library (go-cmp) in real projects.

▸  POINTERS
p == q compares ADDRESSES, not what they point to. Two separate
&Point{1,2} values are not equal.
lessons.expected:
true true
false true
true true
true false
recovered: runtime error: comparing uncomparable type []int

quiz.q: What does reflect.DeepEqual([]int(nil), []int{}) return?
options: false, because nil and empty are distinguished
true, because both have length zero
It panics on the nil slice
It won't compile: slices aren't comparable
quiz.explain: DeepEqual treats a nil slice and an empty non-nil slice as different. slices.Equal compares only lengths and elements, so it reports them equal.
quiz.hint: Look at the fourth line of output.

lessons.title: nil slices vs empty slices
lessons.concept:
Two slices that both have length 0 can still differ (100 Go Mistakes
#22-#23):

    var a []int          // nil slice:   a == nil is true
    b := []int{}         // empty slice: b == nil is false
    c := make([]int, 0)  // empty slice too

They behave the same for len, cap, range and append. They differ in:

▸  1. COMPARISON TO nil
So never test emptiness with 's == nil' - test 'len(s) == 0', which is
right for both.

▸  2. ENCODING
encoding/json writes a nil slice as null and an empty slice as [].
An API client expecting an array may break on null.

▸  3. reflect.DeepEqual (previous lesson)

▸  WHICH TO RETURN?
Idiomatic Go returns a nil slice for 'no results' (var out []T, then
append). If the result goes to JSON and clients need [], initialise
with []T{} or make([]T, 0).

lessons.title: Memory leaks with slices, substrings and maps
lessons.concept:
The garbage collector frees what is unreachable - and a tiny slice can
keep a huge array reachable (100 Go Mistakes #26, #28, #41).

▸  1. SUB-SLICES PIN THE WHOLE BACKING ARRAY
    func header(msg []byte) []byte { return msg[:5] }
If msg is 1 MB, the 5-byte result keeps the whole 1 MB alive. Copy:
    return bytes.Clone(msg[:5])          // or append([]byte(nil), ...)

▸  2. SUBSTRINGS DO THE SAME
s[:8] shares memory with s. When you keep a short piece of a long
string (an ID from a big log line), copy it: strings.Clone(s[:8]).

▸  3. SLICES OF POINTERS
Shrinking s = s[:n] leaves pointers in the hidden tail, still keeping
those objects alive. Set them to nil first, or use slices.Delete (which
clears the tail since Go 1.22).

▸  4. MAPS NEVER SHRINK
Deleting every key frees the VALUES but not the buckets: a map that
once held a million entries keeps its size. Re-create the map (m =
make(...)) after a big cleanup, or store pointers so values are small.

You won't see these in toy programs - they show up as a service whose
memory 'never goes down'. pprof's heap profile finds them.

HELLO 1048576 HELLO true
8
1 true true

quiz.q: You keep msg[:5] from a 1 MB message. How much memory stays reachable?
options: 5 bytes - the slice was copied out
Nothing - sub-slices are weak references
The whole 1 MB backing array
5 bytes plus a 24-byte slice header
quiz.explain: A sub-slice points into the original array, so the GC must keep the entire array alive. Copy the bytes you need (bytes.Clone) when the original is large and short-lived.
quiz.hint: What does the 5-byte slice point into?

lessons.title: Converting slices to arrays
lessons.concept:
Arrays and slices convert in both directions:

▸  ARRAY -> SLICE: slice it
    arr := [4]int{1, 2, 3, 4}
    s := arr[:]          // shares arr's memory

▸  SLICE -> ARRAY POINTER (Go 1.17)
    p := (*[4]int)(s)    // points INTO s's backing array

▸  SLICE -> ARRAY (Go 1.20)
    a := [4]int(s)       // COPIES the first 4 elements

Both panic if len(s) is smaller than the array length. A longer slice
is fine: only the first N elements are used.

▸  WHY YOU WANT ARRAYS
Arrays are comparable and usable as map keys, so converting a fixed-
size chunk (a 4-byte IPv4 address, a 32-byte hash, a 16-byte UUID)
lets you == it or index a map by it:
    seen := map[[32]byte]bool{}
    seen[[32]byte(sum)] = true

[192 168 1 10] 20
true

quiz.q: What does [4]int(s) do when s has 6 elements?
options: Panics, because the lengths differ
Copies all 6 elements into a bigger array
Returns a pointer into the slice
Copies the first 4 elements into a new array
quiz.explain: The conversion needs len(s) >= 4 and copies the first four elements. Only a SHORTER slice panics. The (*[4]int)(s) form shares memory instead of copying.

lessons.title: range semantics: copies, one evaluation and break targets
lessons.concept:
Three range details that cause real bugs (100 Go Mistakes #30-#34):

▸  1. THE RANGE EXPRESSION IS EVALUATED ONCE
    s := []int{1, 2, 3}
    for range s { s = append(s, 0) }   // runs 3 times, not forever
The loop works on a copy of the slice HEADER taken at the start.

▸  2. ARRAYS ARE COPIED
'for i, v := range arr' copies the whole ARRAY first; changes to arr
inside the loop aren't seen in v. Range over &arr or arr[:] to see
them.

▸  3. break INSIDE switch OR select
break exits the innermost for, switch OR select. Inside a switch in a
loop, a bare break only leaves the switch:
    for {
        switch x {
        case "quit":
            break       // leaves the switch, NOT the loop!
        }
    }
Use a labelled break (break loop) or return.

▸  4. MAPS: INSERTS DURING ITERATION
New entries added while ranging may or may not be visited.
Build a separate map if you need predictable results.
lessons.expected:
iterations: 3 len now: 6
copy saw 3
pointer saw 100
processed 1

options: The enclosing for loop
Both the switch and the loop
The whole function
Only the switch statement
quiz.explain: break applies to the innermost for, switch or select. To leave the loop from inside a switch, label the loop and write break label (or return).
quiz.hint: Which statement is innermost?

lessons.title: Encapsulation: exported names, getters and setters
lessons.concept:
Go's only access control is CAPITALISATION, and it works at PACKAGE
level, not type level (gopl 6.6):

    type Counter struct {
        n int          // unexported: invisible outside the package
    }
    func (c *Counter) N() int { return c.n }    // exported getter

▸  NAMING GETTERS (100 Go Mistakes #4)
The getter for field 'owner' is Owner(), not GetOwner(). A setter, if
needed, is SetOwner(). Don't write getters and setters by reflex: an
exported field is fine when there is no invariant to protect.

▸  WHEN TO HIDE A FIELD
    - It has invariants (balance must not go negative, a slice must
      stay sorted).
    - Changing it requires a lock.
    - You may want to change its representation later.

▸  THE PACKAGE IS THE UNIT
Code in the same package can touch unexported fields of any value -
that's why tests in the same package can inspect internals.

▸  UNEXPORTED TYPES, EXPORTED CONSTRUCTORS
func New() *client returns a type users can use but cannot name or
construct themselves. Use sparingly: it makes godoc harder to read.

quiz.explain: Effective Go: the getter is just the capitalised field name, Owner(). The setter, if you need one, is SetOwner().

lessons.title: Bit manipulation and a bit-vector set
lessons.concept:
Bitwise operators work on integers:

    &   AND        |   OR        ^   XOR (binary) / NOT (unary ^x)
    &^  AND NOT (bit clear): x &^ y clears the bits of y in x
    <<  >>  shifts (>> on signed ints is arithmetic: keeps the sign)

▸  COMMON MOVES
    x & (1 << i) != 0     is bit i set?
    x |= 1 << i           set bit i
    x &^= 1 << i          clear bit i
    x ^= 1 << i           toggle bit i
    x & (x - 1)           clear the lowest set bit
    x & -x                isolate the lowest set bit

math/bits gives fast helpers: OnesCount (popcount), LeadingZeros,
TrailingZeros, Len, RotateLeft, Reverse.

▸  A BIT-VECTOR SET (gopl 6.5)
A set of small non-negative ints as []uint64: element x lives in word
x/64, bit x%64. Membership, union and intersection become a few machine
instructions per 64 elements - far cheaper than a map.

▸  YOUR TASK
Implement IntSet with Add, Has, UnionWith, Len and String exactly as in
YOUR TASK.

quiz.explain: &^ is AND NOT: each bit of the result is set if it is set in x and NOT set in y. It is the idiomatic bit-clear operator.
quiz.hint: Read it as "x AND (NOT y)".

lessons.title: Run-time panics and reading a stack trace
lessons.concept:
Some mistakes can only be caught at run time. Each produces a panic
whose value implements runtime.Error:

    index out of range [5] with length 3
    slice bounds out of range [:9] with capacity 4
    invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
    assignment to entry in nil map
    integer divide by zero
    interface conversion: interface {} is string, not int
    comparing uncomparable type []int
    send on closed channel / close of closed channel
    all goroutines are asleep - deadlock!   (fatal, can't be recovered)
    concurrent map writes                   (fatal, can't be recovered)

▸  READING THE TRACE (Concurrency in Go, appendix)
    panic: runtime error: index out of range [5] with length 3

    goroutine 1 [running]:
    main.lookup(...)
            /src/main.go:9          <- the line that failed
    main.main()
            /src/main.go:14 +0x1d   <- who called it
    exit status 2
Read top-down: the panic message, the goroutine that died, then the
call stack from the failing frame outward. The first frame in YOUR
code is usually the bug.

▸  GOTRACEBACK
GOTRACEBACK=all prints every goroutine (useful for deadlocks);
GOTRACEBACK=crash also dumps core.

slice      runtime.Error: runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:5] with capacity 3

divide     runtime.Error: runtime error: integer divide by zero

lessons.title: defer with method receivers: what gets captured
lessons.concept:
'defer x.Method()' evaluates the RECEIVER immediately, like any other
argument (100 Go Mistakes #47):

▸  VALUE RECEIVER: a copy is taken at the defer
    type Report struct{ status string }
    func (r Report) Print() { fmt.Println(r.status) }
    r := Report{"starting"}
    defer r.Print()        // copies r NOW
    r.status = "done"      // the deferred call prints "starting"

▸  POINTER RECEIVER: the pointer is captured
    func (r *Report) Print()
    defer r.Print()        // captures &r; sees later changes: "done"

▸  A CLOSURE SEES THE LATEST STATE
    defer func() { r.Print() }()   // r is read when the defer RUNS

▸  WHY IT MATTERS
Deferred logging of a final status, a summary or an error value shows
stale data. The same rule applies to 'go x.Method()'.

closure:          done
pointer receiver: done
value receiver:  starting

options: The new status, read when the call finally runs
The status at the moment defer was executed
An empty string, since r was copied as zero
Nothing - value receivers cannot be deferred
quiz.explain: The receiver is an argument, evaluated when the defer statement executes. With a value receiver that means a copy of r at that moment.
quiz.hint: When are deferred arguments evaluated?

lessons.title: Shallow copies: structs with slices, maps and pointers
lessons.concept:
Assigning a struct copies its FIELDS - but a slice, map, pointer or
channel field is a reference, so the copy SHARES the underlying data:

    type Team struct {
        Name    string            // copied
        Members []string          // header copied, elements shared
        Scores  map[string]int    // the same map
    }
    b := a                        // b.Scores IS a.Scores

▸  CONSEQUENCES
    - Changing b.Members[0] or b.Scores["x"] changes a too.
    - Appending to b.Members may or may not affect a, depending on
      capacity (the append aliasing trap).
    - Returning an internal slice from a getter lets callers modify
      your private state.

▸  DEEP COPY WHEN YOU NEED INDEPENDENCE
    b.Members = slices.Clone(a.Members)
    b.Scores = maps.Clone(a.Scores)
Write a Clone() method for types that are copied often. (maps.Clone and
slices.Clone are themselves shallow for nested references.)

▸  NEVER COPY STRUCTS CONTAINING LOCKS
A copied sync.Mutex is a separate lock - go vet's copylocks check.
lessons.expected:
blue [ZED bob] map[ada:99]
[ZED bob] map[ada:99] | [ZED cy] map[ada:0]

quiz.q: After b := a, where a has a map field, what happens when you write b.Scores["x"] = 1?
options: a sees it too - both share the same map
Only b changes - assignment copies the map
It panics because the copied map is read-only
It does not compile without using maps.Clone
quiz.explain: A map value is a reference to the runtime table. Copying the struct copies that reference, so both structs share one map. Clone it for independence.
quiz.hint: What does a map variable actually hold?
