lessons.title: ⚛ Source code: characters, tokens and semicolons
lessons.concept:
The Go spec (go.dev/ref/spec) is short enough to read in an evening -
about 100 pages. This tree walks through it with runnable examples.

▸  SOURCE IS UTF-8
Identifiers may use any Unicode letter: π, größe, 名前 are legal names.
(Exported names must start with an UPPER-CASE letter, so non-Latin
scripts without case can't be exported.)

▸  TOKENS
The compiler splits source into identifiers, keywords, operators and
punctuation, and literals; whitespace and comments only separate them.

▸  AUTOMATIC SEMICOLONS
The lexer inserts a ';' at the end of a line whose last token is:
    an identifier, a literal, one of the keywords break continue
    fallthrough return, or one of ++ -- ) ] }
Consequences you already met:
    - '{' must be on the same line as if/for/func (otherwise a ';' is
      inserted after the condition).
    - A multi-line call or composite literal needs a trailing comma:
          f(a,
            b,      // without this comma, ';' is inserted after b
          )
    - A method chain must break AFTER the dot, not before it.
lessons.expected:
6.28318
ch4in c4lls
brace placement is part of the grammar

quiz.q: Why must a multi-line composite literal end its last line with a comma?
options: gofmt refuses to format it otherwise
Trailing commas mark the end of the slice length
A semicolon would be inserted after the last element
The compiler counts commas to size the array
quiz.explain: A line ending in an identifier or literal gets an automatic semicolon. A trailing comma means the line ends with "," so no semicolon is inserted, and the closing brace can sit on its own line.
quiz.hint: Which tokens trigger automatic semicolon insertion?

lessons.title: ✦ Keywords vs predeclared identifiers
lessons.concept:
Go has only 25 KEYWORDS - reserved words you can never use as names:

    break     default      func    interface  select
    case      defer        go      map        struct
    chan      else         goto    package    switch
    const     fallthrough  if      range      type
    continue  for          import  return     var

Everything else you think of as 'built in' is a PREDECLARED IDENTIFIER
living in the universe block, and CAN be shadowed:

    types:      bool byte comparable complex64 complex128 error
                float32 float64 int int8 int16 int32 int64 rune string
                uint uint8 uint16 uint32 uint64 uintptr any
    constants:  true false iota
    zero value: nil
    functions:  append cap clear close complex copy delete imag len
                make max min new panic print println real recover

So 'len := 3', 'true := false' or 'type int string' compile - and
confuse everyone. Linters (predeclared, shadow) flag it. The lesson:
know which names are truly reserved, and never reuse the others.

lessons.title: ⚛ Constants: exact, untyped and representable
lessons.concept:
Constants live at COMPILE TIME and follow different rules from
variables:

▸  EXACT ARITHMETIC
Constant expressions are evaluated exactly, with at least 256 bits of
precision. 1 << 100 is a fine intermediate value; 1.0/3*3 is exactly 1.

▸  UNTYPED vs TYPED
    const a = 10            untyped integer constant
    const b int64 = 10      typed: behaves like an int64 value
An untyped constant takes the type its use requires - that's why
'var f float32 = a' and 'time.Duration(a) * time.Second' just work.

▸  REPRESENTABILITY
When a constant meets a type, its value must be REPRESENTABLE in it,
or compilation fails:
    var x uint8 = 256       // constant 256 overflows uint8
    var y int = 2.5         // constant 2.5 truncated to integer
    var z int = 2.0         // OK: 2.0 is representable as an int

▸  KINDS
Untyped constants have a kind: boolean, rune, integer, floating-point,
complex or string. Mixing kinds yields the 'later' one in that list:
1 + 2.5 is an untyped float, 'a' + 1 is an untyped rune.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
	"time"
)

const huge = 1 << 100         // fine as long as it is never stored whole
const third = 1.0 / 3         // exact rational arithmetic at compile time
const timeout = 5             // untyped integer
const typed int64 = 7         // a typed constant
const pi2 = math.Pi * math.Pi // constant folding through math constants

func main() {
	fmt.Println(huge >> 98)            // 4
	fmt.Println(third*3 == 1)          // exact
	fmt.Println(timeout * time.Second) // untyped adapts to Duration
	var f float32 = timeout            // ...and to float32
	fmt.Println(f, typed+1)
	var whole int = 2.0 // representable as an int
	fmt.Println(whole, 'a'+1, string(rune('a'+1)))
	fmt.Printf("%.4f\n", pi2)
}

quiz.q: Why does "var z int = 2.0" compile but "var y int = 2.5" does not?
options: 2.0 is representable as an int; 2.5 is not
The compiler rounds 2.0 but not 2.5
Float literals ending in .0 are integer literals
int accepts floats only when they are positive
quiz.explain: An untyped constant can be assigned to a type only if its exact value is representable there. 2.0 equals the integer 2; 2.5 would need truncation, which constants never do silently.
quiz.hint: Representability is about the exact value.

lessons.title: ✦ Default types of untyped constants
lessons.concept:
When an untyped constant must become a value with no type context -
x := 1, or passed to a parameter of type any - it gets its DEFAULT
TYPE:

    kind            example     default type
    boolean         true        bool
    rune            'a'         rune (int32)
    integer         42          int
    floating-point  4.2         float64
    complex         4.2i        complex128
    string          "hi"        string

▸  THE CLASSIC SURPRISE
    var f float64 = 1 / 3      // 0 !  1/3 is INTEGER constant division
    var g float64 = 1.0 / 3    // 0.333...
Both operands of 1 / 3 are untyped integers, so the constant expression
is an integer division - before it ever meets float64.

▸  'a' IS NOT A STRING
fmt.Println('a') prints 97: its default type is rune, an integer.

▸  SHIFTS
In 'var x float64 = 1 << s' with a non-constant s, the untyped 1 takes
the type float64 from context - and shifting a float is an error. Give
the constant an explicit type: float64(int(1) << s).
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a, b, c, d, e := 1, 1.5, 'x', 2i, "s"
	fmt.Printf("%T %T %T %T %T\n", a, b, c, d, e)

	var f float64 = 1 / 3
	var g float64 = 1.0 / 3
	fmt.Println(f, g)

	var any1 any = 7
	var any2 any = 7.0
	fmt.Printf("%T %T\n", any1, any2)
	fmt.Println('a', string('a'))
}

int float64 int32 complex128 string
0 0.3333333333333333
int float64
97 a

quiz.q: What value does "var f float64 = 1 / 3" store?
options: A compile error
quiz.explain: 1 / 3 is evaluated as a constant expression first. Both operands are untyped integers, so it is integer division: 0. Only then is the result converted to float64. Write 1.0 / 3.
quiz.hint: What kind are the constants 1 and 3?

lessons.title: ⚛ Types: underlying types and type identity
lessons.concept:
Every type has an UNDERLYING TYPE:
    - for predeclared types (int, string...) and type literals
      ([]int, struct{...}, map[string]bool), it is the type itself
    - for 'type T X', it is X's underlying type

    type Celsius float64        underlying: float64
    type Temps []Celsius        underlying: []Celsius
    type Reading Temps          underlying: []Celsius (follows the chain)

▸  NAMED vs UNNAMED
int, Celsius and Temps are NAMED types. []int, map[K]V, func(int),
struct{X int} written out are type LITERALS (unnamed).

▸  TYPE IDENTITY
    - A named type is identical only to itself. Celsius and Fahrenheit
      are different types even with the same underlying type.
    - Two type literals are identical if they have the same structure:
      []int is []int everywhere; two struct literals are identical if
      they have the same field names, types, TAGS and order.

▸  CONVERSIONS
T(x) is allowed when x's type and T have identical underlying types
(ignoring struct tags), among other rules. That's how Celsius(f) and
[]byte(s) work.

1
main.A main.B

quiz.q: Are struct{X int `json:"x"`} and struct{X int} identical types?
options: Yes - tags are only comments for the compiler
Only when both struct types are unexported
Only when both appear inside the same package
No - struct tags are part of type identity
quiz.explain: Identity of struct types includes field names, types and tags. Conversion between them is still allowed, because conversion ignores tags - but they are different types.
quiz.hint: Identity vs convertibility.

lessons.title: ✦ Assignability: when no conversion is needed
lessons.concept:
A value x of type V is ASSIGNABLE to a variable of type T (no
conversion written) when any of these holds:

    1. V and T are identical.
    2. V and T have identical underlying types, and at least one of
       them is NOT a named type.
       -> Temps (named) to []Celsius (unnamed): OK
       -> Celsius to Fahrenheit (both named): needs a conversion
    3. T is an interface type and x implements it.
    4. x is a bidirectional channel, T is a channel type with the same
       element type, and one of them is unnamed (chan int -> <-chan int).
    5. x is nil and T is a pointer, func, slice, map, channel or
       interface type.
    6. x is an untyped constant representable by a value of type T.

Assignability governs assignments, passing arguments, returning
values, sending on channels, and map/slice/composite literal elements.

▸  WHY RULE 2 MATTERS
It lets a named slice type like http.Header (map[string][]string) or
sort.IntSlice flow into code expecting the plain literal type, while
still keeping named types apart from each other.

true 9 true 255

options: No - named types always need a conversion
Yes - same underlying type and []int is unnamed
Only if IDs has no methods
Only with the spread operator f(ids...)
quiz.explain: Assignability rule: identical underlying types, and at least one of the two types is not named. []int is a type literal, so IDs flows into it directly.
quiz.hint: Is []int a named type?

lessons.title: ⚛ Composite literals in full
lessons.concept:
A composite literal builds a struct, array, slice or map value. The
spec allows several shortcuts most people never learn:

▸  INDEXED ARRAY AND SLICE ELEMENTS
    days := [...]string{6: "sat", 0: "sun"}   // len 7, gaps are ""
    s := []int{5: 1}                           // len 6
After a keyed element, unkeyed ones continue from the next index.

▸  ELIDED TYPES IN NESTED LITERALS
Inside a literal of type []T, [N]T or map[K]T, element (and key)
literals may omit T:
    pts := []Point{{1, 2}, {3, 4}}
    m := map[Point]string{{0, 0}: "origin"}
And for pointer element types, &T is elided too:
    nodes := []*Node{{Val: 1}, {Val: 2}}      // each is a &Node{...}

▸  &T{} TAKES THE ADDRESS OF A FRESH VALUE
&Point{1, 2} is legal even though you can't take the address of most
expressions; each evaluation creates a new variable.

▸  RULES
Struct literals: either all fields keyed or all positional; keyed
fields may be omitted (zero value). Map literals: duplicate constant
keys are a compile error.

[0 0 0 30 40 0 0 70] 8
[{1 2} {3 0}] origin {2}
6 false true

quiz.q: What is len([...]string{4: "e", "f"})?
options: It does not compile
quiz.explain: "e" goes to index 4 and the unkeyed "f" continues at index 5. [...] makes the length the highest index plus one: 6.
quiz.hint: Where does the unkeyed element after a keyed one go?

lessons.title: ⚛ Struct types: fields, tags and blank fields
lessons.concept:
Spec details of struct types:

▸  FIELD DECLARATIONS
    struct {
        X, Y int              // several names, one type
        name string           // unexported field
        io.Reader             // embedded field: its name is Reader
        *Config               // embedded pointer: name is Config
        _    int              // blank field: padding, never accessible
        Tags []string `json:"tags,omitempty"`  // a tag
    }
Field names must be unique, counting embedded type names.

▸  THE BLANK FIELD TRICK
A '_ struct{}' field forces users to write KEYED literals:
    type Options struct { _ struct{}; Debug bool }
    Options{true}          // compile error: too few values
    Options{Debug: true}   // OK
Libraries use this to keep the freedom to add fields.

▸  THE EMPTY STRUCT
struct{} has size zero. All zero-size values may share one address,
so &struct{}{} == &struct{}{} is not guaranteed either way.

▸  COMPARABILITY AND KEYS
A struct is comparable if all its fields are - then it can be a map
key, compared with ==, and used as a comparable type argument.

quiz.q: What does adding a blank field "_ struct{}" to an options struct achieve?
options: It makes the struct incomparable
It hides all other fields from other packages
It forces callers to use keyed struct literals
It reserves memory for future fields
quiz.explain: A positional literal must supply every field, including the blank one - which cannot be written. So only keyed literals compile, and the library can add fields later without breaking callers.
quiz.hint: Try writing Options{true, 3}.

lessons.title: ✦ Method sets and addressability, formally
lessons.concept:
The spec defines METHOD SETS precisely:
    - The method set of a defined type T: all methods with receiver T.
    - The method set of *T: methods with receiver T AND *T.
    - An interface's method set is its interface (its methods).
    - A struct with embedded field S gets S's methods; with embedded *S
      it gets the methods of both S and *S. Embedding S in a struct
      reached through a pointer also promotes *S's methods.

▸  THE CALL SHORTHAND NEEDS ADDRESSABILITY
x.M() where M has a *T receiver is shorthand for (&x).M() - legal only
if x is ADDRESSABLE:
    addressable:   variables, pointer indirections *p, slice elements
                   s[i], fields of addressable structs, array elements
                   of addressable arrays
    NOT:           map elements m[k], function results f(), constants,
                   literals (except &T{} composite literals),
                   string bytes s[i]

▸  CONSEQUENCES
    m["a"].Inc()       // compile error: cannot take address of m["a"]
    s[0].Inc()         // fine: slice elements are addressable
    getT().Inc()       // compile error for a pointer method
Store pointers in maps (map[string]*T) when you need to mutate values in
place.

quiz.q: Inc has a pointer receiver. Which call compiles?
options: s[0].Inc() for s []Counter
m["a"].Inc() for m map[string]Counter
Counter{}.Inc() on a literal
newCounter().Inc() on a value result
quiz.explain: The shorthand x.Inc() means (&x).Inc() and needs x addressable. Slice elements are; map elements, plain literals and function results are not.
quiz.hint: Which expression can you take the address of?

lessons.title: ⚛ Blocks, scopes and declarations
lessons.concept:
The spec defines nested BLOCKS, each a scope:

    universe block      predeclared identifiers (int, len, nil...)
    package block       all package-level declarations, across files
    file block          import names (an import is visible only in
                        the file that imports it)
    function blocks     parameters and results live in the body's scope
    explicit { }        any brace block
    IMPLICIT blocks     each if, for and switch statement, and each
                        case / select clause, is its own block

▸  IMPLICIT BLOCKS IN PRACTICE
    if x := f(); x > 0 { } else { }   // x is visible in both branches
    switch v := y.(type) { case int: ... }  // each clause gets its own v
    for i := ...                       // i scoped to the loop

▸  REDECLARATION
':=' may 'redeclare' a variable only if it was declared earlier IN THE
SAME SCOPE with the same type, and at least one other variable is new.
In an inner scope, := always declares a fresh variable (shadowing).

▸  LABELS
Labels are scoped to the whole function body, are not shadowed by
blocks, and an unused label is a compile error.

▸  UNUSED VARIABLES AND IMPORTS
Compile errors by design - not warnings.

2 / 4 is an integer constant division evaluated first

lessons.title: ⚛ Selectors, index expressions and auto-dereference
lessons.concept:
Primary expressions, as the spec defines them:

▸  SELECTORS x.f
x.f finds field or method f at the SHALLOWEST embedding depth. If x is
a pointer to a struct, x.f means (*x).f automatically - which is why Go
has no '->'. The same automatic dereference applies one level for
pointers to arrays.

▸  INDEX EXPRESSIONS a[x]
    array or pointer to array   a[i], p[i] == (*p)[i]
    slice                       s[i]
    string                      s[i] is a BYTE, not addressable
    map                         m[k]; m[k] with comma-ok; absent -> zero
Indexes must be integers (any integer type) in range; constant indexes
are checked at COMPILE time:
    arr := [3]int{}; arr[5] = 1    // compile error: index out of bounds

▸  POINTER-TO-ARRAY CONVENIENCES
For p *[N]T: p[i], len(p), cap(p), p[:], and 'for i, v := range p' all
work without writing *p.

▸  MAP INDEX ON A NIL MAP
Reading returns the zero value; assigning panics.

lessons.title: ✦ Slice expressions in full
lessons.concept:
▸  SIMPLE SLICE EXPRESSIONS a[low:high]
    operand               result type
    array (addressable)   slice []T sharing the array
    pointer to array      slice []T
    slice                 slice
    string                STRING (a substring sharing the bytes)
Defaults: low = 0, high = len(a). Bounds: 0 <= low <= high <= cap(a)
(for strings, <= len). Slicing beyond len up to cap is legal - it
'reveals' elements that are already there.

▸  FULL SLICE EXPRESSIONS a[low:high:max]
Sets the result's capacity to max-low. Only for arrays, pointers to
arrays and slices - NOT strings (strings have no capacity). Used to
make sure a later append can't overwrite the original's elements.

▸  CONSTANT INDEXES ARE CHECKED AT COMPILE TIME
s[3:1] with constant indexes is a compile error; with variables it is
a run-time panic 'slice bounds out of range [3:1]'.

▸  SLICING A NON-ADDRESSABLE ARRAY
f()[1:] is an error if f returns an array (the array isn't addressable)
but fine if it returns a slice.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	base := make([]int, 3, 8)
	ext := base[:6] // reveal elements up to cap
	fmt.Println(len(ext), cap(ext))

	full := base[1:3:4]
	fmt.Println(len(full), cap(full))
	full = append(full, 7) // fits: cap is 3
	full = append(full, 8) // exceeds cap: new array, base untouched
	fmt.Println(base[:4], full)

	s := "gopher"
	sub := s[1:4]
	fmt.Printf("%q %T\n", sub, sub)

	arr := [4]string{"a", "b", "c", "d"}
	fmt.Println(arr[2:], (&arr)[:2])

	lo, hi := 3, 1
	defer func() { fmt.Println("recovered:", recover()) }()
	_ = base[lo:hi]
}

quiz.q: Which operand does NOT allow a full slice expression a[1:2:3]?

A string
A slice
A pointer to an array
quiz.explain: The third index sets capacity, and strings have no capacity (they are immutable, so append can never write into them). The spec allows full slice expressions only on arrays, pointers to arrays and slices.

lessons.title: ⚛ Calls, variadic arguments and multiple results
lessons.concept:
▸  ARGUMENT EVALUATION
In f(a, b, c) the function value and all arguments are evaluated in
the usual order, then COPIED into new parameter variables. A function
call never sees the caller's variables, only copies.

▸  f(g()) - PASSING MULTIPLE RESULTS
If g returns several values, f(g()) passes them as f's arguments - but
only when g() is the ONLY argument. f(g(), x) is a compile error.

▸  VARIADIC RULES
For func f(prefix string, xs ...int):
    f("a")                 xs is nil
    f("a", 1, 2)           xs is a new []int{1, 2}
    f("a", s...)           xs IS s (same backing array!) - and s...
                           must be the last argument, alone
    f("a", 1, s...)        compile error: can't mix
Because f("a", s...) shares s, a variadic function that modifies xs
modifies the caller's slice.

▸  METHOD CALLS
x.m() where x's method set lacks m but &x's has it: rewritten to
(&x).m() if x is addressable.

list [0 6] false
spread [0 2 3] false
caller now has [0 2 3]

options: s[0] becomes 0, because xs is the same slice
Nothing - variadic arguments are always copied
The program panics
A copy of s is modified and then discarded
quiz.explain: With the spread form the slice itself is passed (its header is copied, the elements are shared). With f(1, 2, 3) Go builds a fresh slice instead.

lessons.title: ⚛ Operators and shifts, formally
lessons.concept:
Spec details of operators beyond the basics:

▸  SHIFTS
    x << n, x >> n
    - the right operand must be an INTEGER (signed allowed since Go
      1.13); a negative count PANICS at run time
    - shifting by >= the width gives 0 (or -1 for >> on negative signed)
    - >> on signed integers is arithmetic (copies the sign bit)
    - in '1 << n' with non-constant n, the untyped 1 takes its type from
      the context

▸  INTEGER DIVISION
q = x / y truncates toward zero, and x == q*y + x%y always holds.
Exception: the most negative value divided by -1 gives itself (no
panic), and x % -1 is 0.

▸  COMPARISON RULES
== works on comparable operands of the same type (or assignable to
each other); <, <= etc. only on ordered types (integers, floats,
strings). Comparing an interface with a non-interface value compares
dynamic type and value.

▸  STRING CONCATENATION
+ on strings creates a new string; += in loops is quadratic (use a
Builder).

▸  &^ AND UNARY ^
x &^ y is bit clear; ^x is bitwise NOT (no ~ operator in expressions -
~ only appears in constraints).
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"math"
)

func main() {
	var x int8 = -16
	fmt.Println(x>>2, uint8(x)>>2) // arithmetic vs logical shift

	n := 3
	var f int64 = 1 << n // the untyped 1 becomes int64
	fmt.Printf("%T %d\n", f, f)

	q, r := -7/2, -7%2
	fmt.Println(q, r, q*2+r == -7)

	minInt := math.MinInt64
	neg := -1
	fmt.Println(minInt/neg == minInt, minInt%neg)

	var any1 any = 3
	fmt.Println(any1 == 3, any1 == int64(3)) // dynamic type matters

	fmt.Printf("%04b %04b\n", 0b1101&^0b0101, ^0b1010&0b1111)

	defer func() { fmt.Println("recovered:", recover()) }()
	k := -1
	fmt.Println(1 << k)
}

quiz.explain: Comparing an interface with a concrete value compares the dynamic TYPE as well as the value. The untyped constant 3 stored in any has default type int, which is not int64.

lessons.title: ✦ Order of evaluation, precisely
lessons.concept:
The spec guarantees less than people assume:

▸  WHAT IS SPECIFIED
At package level, initialisation follows dependency order. Inside
functions, when evaluating the operands of an expression, assignment or
return statement: all FUNCTION CALLS, METHOD CALLS, RECEIVE operations
and binary logical operations happen in LEXICAL LEFT-TO-RIGHT ORDER.

    y[f()], ok = g(z || h(), i()+x[j()], <-c), k()
order: f(), h() (if z is false), i(), j(), <-c, g(), k()

▸  WHAT IS NOT SPECIFIED
The order of those events relative to the evaluation of ordinary
variable reads and index expressions:
    a := 1
    f := func() int { a++; return a }
    x := []int{a, f()}     // [1 2] or [2 2]? Not specified!

▸  ASSIGNMENTS HAPPEN IN TWO PHASES
    1. index expressions and pointer indirections on the left, and all
       expressions on the right, are evaluated (in the usual order)
    2. assignments are carried out left to right

▸  THE PRACTICAL RULE
Never read and modify the same variable within one expression via a
function call. Split it into separate statements.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func trace(name string, v int) int {
	fmt.Print(name, " ")
	return v
}

func main() {
	total := trace("a", 1) + trace("b", 2)*trace("c", 3)
	fmt.Println("=", total) // calls run left to right regardless of precedence

	s := []int{0, 0, 0}
	i := 0
	i, s[i] = 2, 9 // s[i] uses the OLD i (index evaluated in phase 1)
	fmt.Println(i, s)

	x, y := 1, 2
	x, y = y, x+y // right side fully evaluated first
	fmt.Println(x, y)
}

quiz.q: In "f() + g() * h()", in what order are the three functions called?
options: g, h, then f - multiplication binds tighter
h, g, f - right to left
The order is unspecified
f, g, h - calls run left to right
quiz.explain: Precedence decides how the RESULTS combine, not when the calls happen. The spec guarantees function calls are evaluated in lexical left-to-right order.
quiz.hint: Look at the first line of output.

lessons.title: ⚛ switch and select, formally
lessons.concept:
▸  EXPRESSION SWITCH
    switch x := f(); tag { case e1, e2: ... }
The tag is evaluated once; case expressions are evaluated top to
bottom, left to right, stopping at the FIRST match. Case expressions
need not be constants. Duplicate CONSTANT cases are a compile error.
A missing tag means 'true'.

▸  fallthrough
Must be the last statement of a case, transfers control to the first
statement of the NEXT case without testing it, and can't be used in
the final case or in a type switch.

▸  TYPE SWITCH
    switch v := x.(type) {
    case int, int64:   // several types: v has x's (interface) type
    case nil:          // matches a nil interface
    case error:        // interface cases match any implementation
    }

▸  SELECT
All channel operands and send values are evaluated ONCE, top to
bottom, on entry. If several cases are ready, one is chosen
UNIFORMLY AT RANDOM - code must not depend on case order. With no
ready case and no default it blocks; 'select {}' blocks forever.
lessons.expected:
eval a; eval b; matched
big and also this
integer (int64) | nil | error: x
both cases chosen: true

quiz.q: Two cases of a select are ready at the same time. Which runs?
options: The first one written in the source
One chosen pseudo-randomly
The last one written in the source
Both, one after another
quiz.explain: The spec requires a uniform pseudo-random choice among ready cases, to prevent starvation. Code that relies on case order is wrong.
quiz.hint: Look at the last line of output.

lessons.title: ⚛ go, defer and recover, formally
lessons.concept:
▸  go AND defer EVALUATE EAGERLY
In 'go f(x)' and 'defer f(x)', the FUNCTION VALUE and the ARGUMENTS
are evaluated immediately, when the statement runs. Only the call is
postponed (or moved to a new goroutine).

▸  defer ORDER AND RESULTS
Deferred calls run in LIFO order after the return values are set and
before the function returns to its caller - so they can read and
modify NAMED results.

▸  DEFERRING A NIL FUNCTION
'var f func(); defer f()' is accepted when the defer statement runs,
but PANICS when the deferred call executes at function exit.

▸  recover RULES
recover returns non-nil only when:
    - called DIRECTLY by a deferred function (not by a function that
      the deferred function calls),
    - while the goroutine is panicking.
Otherwise it returns nil. After a successful recover the function
returns normally (with whatever its named results hold).

▸  runtime.Goexit
Ends the current goroutine after running its deferred calls, without
panicking - what t.FailNow uses internally.

nil defer: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference

options: nil - recover wasn't called by the deferred func
The panic value - any function can recover
An error value describing the call depth
It re-panics immediately with a new value
quiz.explain: The spec makes recover effective only when called directly by a deferred function. One level of indirection and it returns nil, leaving the panic in flight.

lessons.title: ⚛ Built-in functions: the complete list
lessons.concept:
Go has exactly these built-in functions (predeclared, so they're
not keywords):

    len(v)        length: string bytes, array, slice, map, channel
                  (queued elements), pointer to array
    cap(v)        capacity: array, slice, channel, pointer to array
    make(T, ...)  slices, maps, channels only
    new(T)        pointer to a fresh zero T (Go 1.26: new(expr) too)
    append(s, ...)   grow a slice; append([]byte, string...) works
    copy(dst, src)   returns count; copy([]byte, string) works
    clear(x)      (1.21) delete all map entries / zero slice elements
    delete(m, k)  remove a map key (no-op if absent or m is nil)
    close(ch)     close a channel
    min(...), max(...)  (1.21) ordered types, at least one argument
    complex(r, i), real(c), imag(c)
    panic(v), recover()
    print(...), println(...)   low-level, write to stderr; for
                  bootstrapping and debugging only - use fmt

▸  CONSTANT RESULTS
len and cap of arrays (and of constant strings) are CONSTANTS when no
function call or channel receive is involved: 'const n = len([4]int{})'
compiles.

▸  BUILT-INS AREN'T VALUES
You can't take a built-in's address or store it: f := len doesn't
compile. Wrap it: f := func(s string) int { return len(s) }.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

const size = len([4]int{}) // a constant
const greet = len("héllo") // constant too: 6 bytes

func main() {
	fmt.Println(size, greet)

	b := append([]byte("go"), "pher"...) // append a string to []byte
	n := copy(b, "GO")                   // copy from a string
	fmt.Println(string(b), n)

	m := map[string]int{"a": 1, "b": 2}
	delete(m, "zzz") // no-op
	s := []int{1, 2, 3}
	clear(m)
	clear(s)
	fmt.Println(len(m), s, len(s))

	ch := make(chan int, 5)
	ch <- 1
	ch <- 2
	fmt.Println(len(ch), cap(ch))
	close(ch)

	c := complex(3, 4)
	fmt.Println(real(c), imag(c), min(3, 1, 2), max("b", "a"))
	p := new([3]int)
	fmt.Println(len(p), cap(p))
}

quiz.q: Why does "f := len" not compile?
options: len is a reserved keyword, like for or if
Storing len would require a generic type
Built-ins have no value that can be stored
f needs an explicit function type annotation
quiz.explain: Built-ins are special forms handled by the compiler (len works on many unrelated types), so they cannot be used as function values. Wrap one in a function literal to pass it around.
quiz.hint: What would the type of f even be?

lessons.title: ⚛ Package initialization and program execution
lessons.concept:
▸  PACKAGE-LEVEL VARIABLES INITIALISE IN DEPENDENCY ORDER
Not declaration order! The spec repeatedly picks the earliest variable
(in declaration order) that is READY - whose initialiser doesn't depend
on uninitialised variables:
    var a = b + 1       // initialised second
    var b = f()         // initialised first
Dependencies are found through references, including through
functions and methods the initialiser calls. A cycle is a compile
error ('initialization cycle').

▸  THE FULL SEQUENCE
    1. Imported packages are initialised first (each exactly once, even
       if imported many times), dependencies before dependents.
    2. The package's variables, in dependency order.
    3. Every init() in the package, in the order the files are
       presented to the compiler (sorted by name with the go tool),
       top to bottom within a file.
    4. For package main: main() runs.

▸  PROGRAM EXIT
When main returns, the program exits immediately - it does NOT wait
for other goroutines. os.Exit exits without running deferred calls.

▸  init IS SPECIAL
A file may declare several init functions; they can't be called or
referenced by name.

quiz.q: Given "var a = b + 1" followed by "var b = f()", which initialiser runs first?
options: a, because it is declared first
They run concurrently
Neither - it is an initialization cycle
b, because a depends on it
quiz.explain: Package-level variables are initialised in dependency order. a cannot be ready until b has a value, so b goes first even though it is declared later.
quiz.hint: Look at the order of the "init var" lines.

lessons.title: ★ Boss: expressions, statements and execution
lessons.concept:
BOSS ROUND - finish level G2 and the Go Anatomy tree.

The program combines: left-to-right call order, two-phase assignment,
variadic spreading that shares memory, full slice expressions, defer
argument evaluation and named results, switch with fallthrough, the
dynamic type in interface comparison, and initialization order.

▸  HOW TO PLAY
Predict EVERY line on paper before running. Then, for each miss, name
the spec rule and revisit its lesson. When you can predict this
program perfectly, you know the core of the Go spec better than most
working Go programmers.

The boss is worth 25 XP.
lessons.code:
package main

import "fmt"

var first = second * 2
var second = 21

func touch(xs ...int) { xs[0] = -1 }

func id(s string, v int) int {
	fmt.Print(s)
	return v
}

func final() (r int) {
	defer func() { r++ }()
	r = 5
	return r * 2
}

func main() {
	fmt.Println(first)

	n := id("x", 1) + id("y", 2)*id("z", 3)
	fmt.Println("", n)

	base := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
	part := base[0:2:2]
	part = append(part, 9)
	touch(base...)
	fmt.Println(base, part)

	i := 1
	i, base[i] = 3, 7
	fmt.Println(i, base)

	switch {
	case i > 2:
		fmt.Print("A")
		fallthrough
	case i > 100:
		fmt.Println("B")
	}

	var v any = 'z'
	fmt.Println(final(), v == 'z', v == "z")
}

quiz.q: In the boss program, why is part[0] still 1 after touch(base...) set base[0] to -1?
options: append moved part to a new array (cap was 2)
touch received a copy of every element
Full slice expressions always copy the data
base and part never shared any memory at all
quiz.explain: part := base[0:2:2] limits capacity to 2, so appending 9 had to allocate a new array and copy 1 and 2 into it. After that, part no longer shares memory with base.
quiz.hint: What was cap(part) before the append?

lessons.title: go test: your first test
lessons.concept:
Go's testing tools are built in - no framework to install.

▸  THE CONVENTIONS
    - Tests live in files ending _test.go, next to the code.
    - A test is   func TestXxx(t *testing.T)   (Xxx starts upper-case).
    - 'go test' builds the package plus its tests and runs them.
    - 'go test -v' prints every test's name and result.

▸  REPORTING FAILURES
    t.Errorf(...)   record a failure and KEEP GOING (see all problems)
    t.Fatalf(...)   record a failure and STOP this test now (use when
                    continuing makes no sense, e.g. a nil result)
    t.Log(...)      extra output, shown with -v or on failure

▸  THE MESSAGE FORMAT
Write what was called, what you got and what you wanted:
    t.Errorf("Abs(%d) = %d, want %d", in, got, want)
Go tests use plain if statements - no assertion library needed.

▸  IN THIS APP
In lessons marked as tests, the editor holds the _test.go file and the
code under test ships alongside it (here, abs.go with Abs and Clamp).
Run executes 'go test -v'. Break Abs on purpose (edit the test's
expectation) and watch the FAIL output.

lessons.title: Test helpers: t.Helper, t.Cleanup, t.TempDir, t.Setenv
lessons.concept:
The testing.T type has helpers that remove most setup boilerplate:

▸  t.Helper()
Call it first in an assertion helper. Failures are then reported at
the CALLER's line instead of inside the helper:
    func assertEqual[T comparable](t *testing.T, got, want T) {
        t.Helper()
        if got != want { t.Errorf("got %v, want %v", got, want) }
    }

▸  t.Cleanup(func())
Registers teardown that runs when the test (and its subtests) finish,
in LIFO order - like defer, but usable from inside helpers.

▸  t.TempDir()
A fresh directory, deleted automatically after the test. Never write
test files into the source tree.

▸  t.Setenv(key, value)
Sets an environment variable for this test and restores it afterwards.
(Can't be combined with t.Parallel.)

▸  t.Context() (Go 1.24)
A context cancelled just before the test's cleanups run.

▸  t.Skip("reason")
Skip a test that can't run here (needs network, wrong OS, -short mode).

lessons.concept:
An Example function is documentation AND a test (gopl 11.6):

    func ExampleReverse() {

    ExampleStack            example for the type
    Example                 example for the whole package

belong to - the most-read part of most packages' documentation.

and go test compares the lines as a set.

lessons.title: Testing HTTP handlers with httptest
lessons.concept:
net/http/httptest tests handlers without opening real ports
(100 Go Mistakes #88):

▸  1. ResponseRecorder: call the handler directly
    req := httptest.NewRequest("GET", "/hello?name=ada", nil)
    rec := httptest.NewRecorder()
    handler.ServeHTTP(rec, req)
    rec.Code, rec.Body.String(), rec.Header()
Fast and simple - perfect for a single handler.

▸  2. httptest.NewServer: a real server on a loopback port
    srv := httptest.NewServer(handler)
    defer srv.Close()
    resp, err := http.Get(srv.URL + "/hello")
Exercises the full stack (routing, middleware, client code). Also the
way to FAKE an external API your client code calls: point the client
at srv.URL.

▸  WHAT TO ASSERT
Status code, important headers (Content-Type), and the body - decode
JSON bodies into structs rather than comparing raw strings when field
order or whitespace could change.

lessons.title: Fakes through small interfaces
lessons.concept:
You test code that talks to databases, clocks, payment providers or
email servers by depending on a SMALL INTERFACE and handing the test a
FAKE (Ultimate Go 5.5, Let's Go 13.6):

    type Mailer interface { Send(to, body string) error }

    type Signup struct { mail Mailer }       // production: SMTP mailer
    type fakeMailer struct { sent []string } // tests: records calls

▸  WHY THIS IS IDIOMATIC GO
The consumer owns the interface and it lists only the methods it uses,
so the fake is a few lines - no mocking framework or code generation.

▸  FAKE vs STUB vs MOCK (loosely)
    stub   returns canned answers
    fake   a working lightweight implementation (in-memory store)
    mock   also verifies HOW it was called
Hand-written fakes that record calls cover almost every need.

▸  INJECT ERRORS
Fakes make failure paths testable: a fake that returns an error on
demand lets you check that Signup reports it instead of panicking.
lessons.expected:
=== RUN   TestRegisterSendsWelcome
--- PASS: TestRegisterSendsWelcome
=== RUN   TestRegisterReportsMailFailure
--- PASS: TestRegisterReportsMailFailure
PASS

options: Go generates mocks automatically for each type
The testing package can replace any function
Small consumer-owned interfaces are easy to implement
Struct fields can be overwritten by reflection
quiz.explain: Because interfaces are satisfied implicitly and the consumer defines one listing only what it uses, a fake is a tiny struct with those few methods - no framework needed.

lessons.title: Controlling time in tests
lessons.concept:
Code that calls time.Now() directly is hard to test: the answer changes
every run, and testing 'expires after 24 hours' would take 24 hours
(100 Go Mistakes #86-#87).

▸  INJECT THE CLOCK
    type Session struct {
        created time.Time
        now     func() time.Time    // time.Now in production
    }
Tests pass a function returning whatever time they want, and move it
forward instantly.

▸  NEVER time.Sleep IN UNIT TESTS
Sleeping makes tests slow and FLAKY: on a busy CI machine 10ms isn't
always enough. Synchronise on channels or WaitGroups instead, and
inject time.

▸  testing/synctest (Go 1.25)
For concurrent code with timers, synctest.Test runs the test in a
bubble with a fake clock that jumps ahead whenever all goroutines are
blocked (see the Concurrency Patterns module).

▸  TIMEZONES
Build test times with time.Date(..., time.UTC) so tests don't depend
on the machine's local zone.

It is not allowed inside *testing.T functions
It always makes the race detector fail
It stops the test timer from counting
quiz.explain: A sleep is a guess about how long something takes. Too short and the test fails on slow machines; long enough to be safe and the suite crawls. Inject time and synchronise explicitly.

lessons.title: Fuzzing: let Go find the inputs that break you
lessons.concept:
A fuzz test (Go 1.18) generates inputs automatically, looking for ones
that crash your code or break a property:

    func FuzzReverse(f *testing.F) {
        f.Add("hello")                // seed corpus
        f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, s string) {
            r := Reverse(s)
            if Reverse(r) != s {      // a PROPERTY, not one answer
                t.Errorf(...)
            }
        })
    }

▸  TWO MODES
    go test               runs only the seeds (fast, every CI run)
    go test -fuzz=Fuzz    mutates inputs until it finds a failure or
                          you stop it (add -fuzztime=30s)

▸  FAILURES BECOME REGRESSION TESTS
A failing input is saved under testdata/fuzz/FuzzReverse/ and from then
on runs with every plain 'go test'.

▸  WHAT TO ASSERT
Fuzzing needs properties that hold for EVERY input: round trips
(decode(encode(x)) == x), no panics, output is valid UTF-8, a fast
implementation agrees with a slow obvious one.

▸  THE CLASSIC FIND
A byte-wise Reverse passes 'hello' but breaks on 'é'. Fuzzing finds
that in seconds; the fixed rune-wise version is shipped here.

=== RUN   FuzzReverse/seed#0
=== RUN   FuzzReverse/seed#1
=== RUN   FuzzReverse/seed#2
=== RUN   FuzzReverse/seed#3

    --- PASS: FuzzReverse/seed#0
    --- PASS: FuzzReverse/seed#1
    --- PASS: FuzzReverse/seed#2
    --- PASS: FuzzReverse/seed#3
PASS

quiz.q: What does a plain "go test" (without -fuzz) do with a fuzz test?
options: Skips it, because fuzzing needs the -fuzz flag
Fuzzes for ten seconds by default, then stops
Fuzzes until it finds a failing input
Runs only the seeds and saved failures
quiz.explain: Without -fuzz, the fuzz target acts like a table test over its seeds (f.Add) plus any failing inputs stored in testdata/fuzz. Mutation only happens with -fuzz.

lessons.title: Benchmarks: measuring instead of guessing
lessons.concept:
A benchmark (gopl 11.4) measures how long code takes:

    func BenchmarkJoin(b *testing.B) {
        b.ReportAllocs()
        for b.Loop() {               // Go 1.24+
            JoinPlus(words)
        }
    }

    go test -bench=. -benchmem          run all benchmarks
    go test -bench=Join -count=10       repeat for statistics

▸  b.Loop (Go 1.24) vs THE OLD FORM
Before 1.24: 'for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { ... }'. b.Loop is better: it
times only the loop, runs setup once, and keeps the compiler from
optimising the benchmarked call away.

▸  READING RESULTS
    BenchmarkJoinPlus-8     2000    5120 ns/op   12000 B/op   99 allocs/op
-8 = GOMAXPROCS; ns/op = time per iteration; B/op and allocs/op =
memory per iteration (with -benchmem or b.ReportAllocs).

▸  BENCHMARK HONESTLY (100 Go Mistakes #89)
    - Compare with benchstat over -count=10 runs, not one run.
    - Don't benchmark on a busy laptop with throttling.
    - Make sure the result is used, or the work may be optimised away
      (b.Loop protects you here).
    - Sub-benchmarks (b.Run) compare sizes or implementations.

This lesson runs 100 iterations each - numbers vary by machine, so the
output isn't graded. Compare the allocs/op columns.

quiz.q: Why prefer "for b.Loop()" (Go 1.24) over "for i := 0; i < b.N; i++"?
options: b.Loop runs the body exactly once, which is enough
It times only the loop and keeps the call alive
b.Loop disables the garbage collector while timing
b.Loop runs benchmarks in parallel automatically
quiz.explain: b.Loop excludes setup before the loop from timing, runs that setup only once, and prevents the compiler from eliminating the benchmarked call as dead code - two classic sources of wrong benchmark numbers.
quiz.hint: What are the two classic ways benchmarks lie?

lessons.title: Golden files and testdata
lessons.concept:
For outputs that are long or structured (a rendered report, generated
code, a CLI's help text), store the expected output in a file and
compare against it - a GOLDEN FILE.

▸  testdata/
The go tool ignores directories named testdata when building, and
tests run with the package directory as the working directory, so
    os.ReadFile("testdata/report.golden")
just works. Put fixtures, sample inputs and golden files there.

▸  THE -update FLAG PATTERN
    var update = flag.Bool("update", false, "rewrite golden files")
    ...
    if *update { os.WriteFile(golden, got, 0o644) }
Run 'go test -update' after an intended change, review the diff in
version control, commit. The diff IS the code review of the output.

▸  KEEP GOLDEN TESTS DETERMINISTIC
Sort map keys, fix timestamps (inject a clock), and normalise paths -
otherwise the file changes on every run.

The go tool ignores testdata when building packages
testdata is deleted after every test run

lessons.title: Testing failure paths with iotest and errors.Is
lessons.concept:
The error branches are where bugs hide, and they're the hardest to
trigger with real files and networks. testing/iotest provides readers
that misbehave on purpose:

    iotest.ErrReader(err)        every Read returns err
    iotest.TimeoutReader(r)      second Read returns ErrTimeout
    iotest.HalfReader(r)         reads at most half the buffer each time
    iotest.OneByteReader(r)      reads one byte per call
    iotest.DataErrReader(r)      returns the last data together with EOF
    iotest.TestReader(r, want)   checks a Reader implementation is correct

▸  WHY ONE-BYTE READS MATTER
Code that assumes one Read fills the buffer works on files and breaks
on networks. OneByteReader shakes that bug out (use io.ReadFull).

▸  CHECK WHICH ERROR, NOT JUST 'AN ERROR'
    if !errors.Is(err, ErrTruncated) { t.Errorf(...) }
A test that only checks err != nil passes even when the code fails
for the wrong reason.

=== RUN   TestReadHeader/one_byte_at_a_time
=== RUN   TestReadHeader/truncated
--- PASS: TestReadHeader

    --- PASS: TestReadHeader/one_byte_at_a_time
    --- PASS: TestReadHeader/truncated
=== RUN   TestReadHeaderDiskError
--- PASS: TestReadHeaderDiskError
PASS

quiz.q: Which bug does iotest.OneByteReader expose?
options: Code that forgets to close the reader
Code that reads past io.EOF
Code that never checks for errors at all
Code assuming one Read call fills the buffer
quiz.explain: Read may legally return fewer bytes than requested. Files usually fill the buffer so the bug hides; networks and pipes don't. Feeding one byte per Read reveals it - use io.ReadFull when you need an exact count.
quiz.hint: How many bytes is a single Read allowed to return?

lessons.title: Running tests: flags, coverage and categories
lessons.concept:
The everyday go test flags:

    go test ./...                 every package in the module
    go test -run 'Login|Signup'   tests whose names match the regexp
    go test -v                    verbose: every test name and t.Log
    go test -count=1              bypass the test-result cache
    go test -race                 the race detector (always in CI)
    go test -short                tests can check testing.Short() and
                                  skip slow work
    go test -shuffle=on           random test order - finds tests that
                                  depend on each other
    go test -parallel 8           max parallel tests (with t.Parallel)
    go test -timeout 30s          fail instead of hanging forever
    go test -failfast             stop at the first failure

▸  COVERAGE
    go test -cover                       percentage per package
    go test -coverprofile=c.out
    go tool cover -html=c.out            highlighted source in a browser
Coverage shows what was NOT executed. High coverage doesn't prove
correctness; 0% on an error path proves it was never tested.

▸  CATEGORISING TESTS (100 Go Mistakes #82)
    //go:build integration      at the top of slow tests' files;
                                run them with -tags integration
    if testing.Short() { t.Skip("slow") }
    an env var gate: if os.Getenv("DB_URL") == "" { t.Skip(...) }

▸  EXTERNAL TEST PACKAGES
A test file with 'package foo_test' sees only foo's EXPORTED API - it
tests the package the way users see it, and can break import cycles.

quiz.q: What does go test -shuffle=on help you find?
options: Tests that are slower than the average test
Benchmarks whose timings are unstable
Tests that depend on each other's order
Data races between goroutines in a test
quiz.explain: If test B only passes after test A set up some global state, a random order exposes it. Each test should stand alone.

lessons.title: Faking HTTP calls with a custom RoundTripper
lessons.concept:
Code that calls external APIs needs tests that don't hit the network.
Two stdlib options:

▸  1. httptest.NewServer (Testing module): a real local server.

▸  2. A FAKE TRANSPORT
An http.Client sends requests through its Transport, an
http.RoundTripper:
    type RoundTripper interface {
        RoundTrip(*http.Request) (*http.Response, error)
    }
Swap in a function that inspects the request and returns a canned
response - no sockets at all, and you can simulate failures that are
hard to produce with a real server (connection reset, timeouts).

    type roundTripFunc func(*http.Request) (*http.Response, error)
    func (f roundTripFunc) RoundTrip(r *http.Request) (*http.Response, error) { return f(r) }
    client := &http.Client{Transport: roundTripFunc(fake)}

▸  DESIGN FOR IT
Give your API client an *http.Client field (or accept one in its
constructor) instead of calling http.Get - injection again.

▸  ALSO USEFUL
Transports are how real middleware for clients works too: retries,
auth headers, logging and metrics wrap the default transport.

Use HTTPS without generating any certificates

Send requests that do not need a URL at all
quiz.explain: RoundTrip can return any error directly, so transport failures, timeouts and resets are one line each. A real httptest server can only produce HTTP responses.

lessons.title: Parallel tests and TestMain
lessons.concept:
▸  t.Parallel()
Marks a test (or subtest) as safe to run alongside other parallel
tests. go test pauses it until the sequential tests at its level have
finished, then runs the parallel ones together (up to -parallel N,
default GOMAXPROCS). In -v output you'll see '=== PAUSE' and
'=== CONT' lines.
    - Big win for slow, I/O-bound tests.
    - Parallel tests must not share mutable state, use t.Setenv or
      t.Chdir, or depend on order.
    - A parent test's cleanup (and the end of its function) waits for
      its parallel subtests.

▸  TestMain: package-level setup and teardown
    func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
        setup()               // start a container, create a temp DB...
        code := m.Run()       // run all tests
        teardown()
        os.Exit(code)         // (since Go 1.15 returning also works)
    }
Use it sparingly - most setup belongs in helpers with t.Cleanup.

▸  ORDER
Because parallel tests interleave, their output order varies from run
to run - this lesson's output isn't graded for that reason.

quiz.q: What happens when a subtest calls t.Parallel()?
options: It runs in a separate process of its own
It runs before every sequential test starts
It is skipped unless the -parallel flag is set
It pauses, then runs with its parallel siblings
quiz.explain: The subtest signals it is safe to run concurrently; go test pauses it and resumes all parallel siblings together once the sequential part of the parent has finished.
quiz.hint: Look for PAUSE and CONT in the output.

lessons.title: time: instants, durations and time zones
lessons.concept:
Two core types:

    time.Time       an instant (with a location / time zone)
    time.Duration   an int64 count of NANOSECONDS

▸  DURATIONS
    d := 90 * time.Second           // 1m30s
    d.Minutes()                     // 1.5
    time.ParseDuration("1h15m")
    WRONG: time.Sleep(5)            // 5 NANOSECONDS (100 Go Mistakes #75)
    RIGHT: time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)

▸  ARITHMETIC
    t.Add(d), t.Sub(u) Duration, t.AddDate(y, m, d)
    t.Before(u), t.After(u), t.Equal(u)   // not == (see below)
    t.Truncate(time.Hour), t.Weekday(), t.YearDay()

▸  MEASURING ELAPSED TIME
    start := time.Now(); ...; time.Since(start)
time.Now carries a MONOTONIC clock reading, so elapsed times stay
correct even if the wall clock is changed.

▸  TIME ZONES
    loc, err := time.LoadLocation("Africa/Cairo")
    t.In(loc), t.UTC(), t.Unix()
Store and compare in UTC; convert to local only for display. Use
t.Equal(u), not ==, because == also compares the location and the
monotonic reading.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	start := time.Date(2026, time.March, 30, 22, 15, 0, 0, time.UTC)
	end := start.Add(90 * time.Minute)
	fmt.Println(start)
	fmt.Println(end, end.Weekday())
	fmt.Println(end.Sub(start), end.Sub(start).Minutes())

	d, _ := time.ParseDuration("1h15m30s")
	fmt.Println(d, d.Seconds(), d.Round(time.Hour))

	nextMonth := start.AddDate(0, 1, 0)
	fmt.Println(nextMonth.Format(time.DateOnly), start.YearDay())

	fixed := time.FixedZone("EET", 2*60*60)
	local := start.In(fixed)
	fmt.Println(local, local.Equal(start), local == start)
	fmt.Println(start.Unix(), time.Unix(0, 0).UTC())
}

lessons.title: Formatting and parsing dates: the reference time
lessons.concept:
Go formats dates with an EXAMPLE instead of %Y-%m-%d codes. The
reference time is:

    Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006
     ^   ^  ^  ^  ^  ^  ^   ^
    day mon 2  15 04 05 zone year     (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 in order:
                                       01/02 03:04:05PM '06 -0700)

You write the layout as 'how would that moment look?':
    t.Format("2006-01-02")          2026-11-03
    t.Format("02 Jan 2006 15:04")   03 Nov 2026 13:12
    t.Format("3:04PM")              1:12PM

▸  PREDEFINED LAYOUTS
    time.RFC3339 ("2006-01-02T15:04:05Z07:00") - use for APIs and JSON
    time.DateTime, time.DateOnly, time.TimeOnly (Go 1.20)
    time.Kitchen ("3:04PM")

▸  PARSING
    t, err := time.Parse("2006-01-02", "2026-11-03")       // UTC
    t, err := time.ParseInLocation(layout, s, loc)          // local
Parsing with the wrong layout gives an error that quotes both.

▸  THE CLASSIC MISTAKE
"2006-02-01" swaps month and day; "YYYY-MM-DD" is printed literally.
Write the reference date in the shape you want.

quiz.q: Which layout prints a date like 2026-11-03?
options: "YYYY-MM-DD"
quiz.explain: Layouts are written using the reference time Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 2006: year 2006, month 01, day 02. "2006-02-01" would put the DAY in the middle.
quiz.hint: The reference month is January (01) and the day is 2 (02).

lessons.title: Timers, tickers and the time.After trap
lessons.concept:
▸  ONE-SHOT TIMERS
    t := time.NewTimer(2 * time.Second)
    <-t.C                      // fires once
    t.Stop()                   // cancel if it hasn't fired
    t.Reset(d)                 // reuse it
    time.AfterFunc(d, f)       // run f in its own goroutine later

▸  REPEATING TICKERS
    tk := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
    defer tk.Stop()
    for range tk.C { ... }

▸  THE time.After TRAP (100 Go Mistakes #76)
    for {
        select {
        case ev := <-events:
            handle(ev)
        case <-time.After(time.Minute):   // a NEW timer every loop!
            log.Println("idle")
        }
    }
Each iteration creates a timer. Before Go 1.23 none of them could be
collected until it fired - a busy loop leaked thousands. Go 1.23 made
unreferenced timers collectable, but you still pay an allocation per
iteration. Create ONE timer and Reset it, or use a context deadline.

▸  GO 1.23 TIMER CHANGES
Timer channels became unbuffered: after Stop or Reset returns, no stale
value will be received. Old 'drain the channel' code is no longer
needed (and is harmless).

stopped before firing: true

ticks: 3

quiz.q: Why avoid "case <-time.After(d):" inside a busy for-select loop?
options: It creates a new timer on every iteration
time.After only works outside select statements
It blocks the other select cases forever
It fires immediately after the first iteration
quiz.explain: time.After allocates a fresh Timer each time it is evaluated. In a hot loop that is constant allocation (and, before Go 1.23, memory that stayed alive until each timer fired). Reuse one Timer with Reset.
quiz.hint: How often is the select statement - and its case expressions - evaluated?

lessons.concept:
Go has two random-number packages - pick by purpose:

▸  math/rand/v2  (Go 1.22) - fast, NOT secure
    rand.IntN(10)            0..9, auto-seeded randomly
    rand.Float64()           [0.0, 1.0)
    rand.Shuffle(n, swap)
    rand.Perm(5)
    rand.N(10 * time.Second) a random Duration (generic N)
For reproducible simulations and tests, make your own seeded generator:
    r := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(seed1, seed2))
The same seeds always give the same sequence.

▸  crypto/rand - for anything secret
Tokens, session IDs, password-reset links, salts, keys:
    b := make([]byte, 32); crypto/rand.Read(b)
    crypto/rand.Text()       (Go 1.24) a random base32 string
math/rand output can be predicted from a few samples; never use it for
security.

▸  THE OLD PACKAGE
math/rand (v1) still exists. Since Go 1.20 it seeds itself and
rand.Seed is deprecated - the course linter flags rand.Seed.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	crand "crypto/rand"
	"fmt"
	"math/rand/v2"
)

func main() {
	r := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(42, 1024)) // seeded: same output every run
	fmt.Println(r.IntN(100), r.IntN(100), r.IntN(100))
	deck := []string{"A", "K", "Q", "J", "10"}
	r.Shuffle(len(deck), func(i, j int) { deck[i], deck[j] = deck[j], deck[i] })
	fmt.Println(deck, r.Perm(5))

	again := rand.New(rand.NewPCG(42, 1024))
	fmt.Println("reproducible:", again.IntN(100))

	n := rand.IntN(6) + 1 // auto-seeded: different every run
	fmt.Println("die in range:", n >= 1 && n <= 6)

	token := make([]byte, 16)
	crand.Read(token)
	fmt.Println("secure token bytes:", len(token))
}
lessons.expected:
94 49 90
[10 K A J Q] [2 1 0 4 3]
reproducible: 94
die in range: true
secure token bytes: 16

quiz.q: Which package should generate a password-reset token?
options: crypto/rand
math/rand seeded with time.Now()
math/rand/v2 with a PCG source
hash/fnv applied to the user ID
quiz.explain: Only crypto/rand draws from the operating system's cryptographically secure generator. math/rand variants are statistical generators whose future output can be predicted.
quiz.hint: Can an attacker predict the value?

lessons.title: math/big: numbers without limits
lessons.concept:
When int64 (max ~9.2e18) or float64 (~16 significant digits) isn't
enough, math/big gives arbitrary precision:

    big.Int     integers of any size (crypto, factorials, IDs)
    big.Float   floats with chosen precision (in bits)
    big.Rat     exact fractions (1/3 stays exactly 1/3)

▸  THE API STYLE
Methods store the result in the RECEIVER and return it, so values can
be reused without allocating:
    z := new(big.Int)
    z.Mul(x, y)              // z = x * y
    z.Add(z, big.NewInt(1))  // z = z + 1
Comparison uses x.Cmp(y) (-1, 0, +1), never ==.

▸  PARSING AND PRINTING
    n, ok := new(big.Int).SetString("123456789012345678901234567890", 10)
    fmt.Println(n)            // big types implement fmt.Formatter
    r := big.NewRat(1, 3)     r.FloatString(10)

▸  COST
Every operation allocates or loops over words - use big only where the
range demands it.

quiz.q: How do you compare two *big.Int values x and y for equality?
options: x == y
x.Cmp(y) == 0
x.String() == y
reflect.DeepEqual(x, y) only
quiz.explain: x == y compares POINTERS. Cmp compares numeric values and returns -1, 0 or +1.
quiz.hint: big.Int values are used through pointers.

lessons.newhere:
• big.Int.String - String returns the decimal representation of x as generated by x.Text(10).
  • big.Float.SetPrec - SetPrec sets z's precision to prec and returns the (possibly) rounded value of z.
  • big.Float.Text - Text converts the floating-point number x to a string according to the given format and precision prec.

lessons.title: Encodings: base64, hex and encoding/binary
lessons.concept:
Turning bytes into text, and numbers into bytes:

▸  encoding/hex
    hex.EncodeToString([]byte("Go"))  "476f"
    hex.DecodeString("476f")
    hex.Dump(b)                       a classic hex dump

▸  encoding/base64  (4 characters per 3 bytes)
    base64.StdEncoding     + and /, padded with =
    base64.URLEncoding     - and _ (safe in URLs and file names)
    base64.RawURLEncoding  no padding (JWTs use this)

▸  encoding/binary  - fixed-size numbers <-> bytes
Network protocols and file formats define a BYTE ORDER:
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(buf, 0xCAFEBABE)   network order
    binary.LittleEndian.Uint16(buf)               x86 order
    binary.Write(w, binary.LittleEndian, &header) whole structs
    binary.AppendUvarint(buf, n)                  compact varints
Go 1.23 added binary.Encode / binary.Decode / binary.Append.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/binary"
	"encoding/hex"
	"fmt"
)

type Header struct {
	Magic   uint32
	Version uint16
	Flags   uint16
}

func main() {
	data := []byte("Go?>")
	fmt.Println(hex.EncodeToString(data))
	fmt.Println(base64.StdEncoding.EncodeToString(data))
	fmt.Println(base64.URLEncoding.EncodeToString(data))
	fmt.Println(base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(data))

	buf := make([]byte, 4)
	binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(buf, 0xCAFEBABE)
	fmt.Printf("% x | little: % x\n", buf, binary.LittleEndian.AppendUint32(nil, 0xCAFEBABE))

	var w bytes.Buffer
	binary.Write(&w, binary.BigEndian, Header{Magic: 0x474F, Version: 2, Flags: 1})
	fmt.Printf("% x\n", w.Bytes())
	var h Header
	binary.Read(&w, binary.BigEndian, &h)
	fmt.Printf("%+v\n", h)

	v := binary.AppendUvarint(nil, 300)
	n, _ := binary.Uvarint(v)
	fmt.Println(len(v), "bytes for", n)
}
lessons.expected:
476f3f3e
R28/Pg==
R28_Pg==
R28_Pg
ca fe ba be | little: be ba fe ca
00 00 47 4f 00 02 00 01
{Magic:18255 Version:2 Flags:1}
2 bytes for 300

quiz.q: Which base64 encoding is safe to put directly in a URL path?
options: base64.StdEncoding
hex.EncodeToString
base64.URLEncoding (or RawURLEncoding)
Any of them - base64 is always URL-safe
quiz.explain: StdEncoding uses + and /, which have meaning in URLs. URLEncoding substitutes - and _; the Raw variants also drop the = padding.
quiz.hint: Which characters differ between the two outputs?

lessons.newhere:
• binary.littleEndian.AppendUint32 - appends a number as 4 bytes, least significant byte first
  • bytes.Buffer - A Buffer is a variable-sized buffer of bytes with Buffer.Read and Buffer.Write methods.
  • bytes.Buffer.Bytes - Bytes returns a slice of length b.Len() holding the unread portion of the buffer.
  • binary.Read - Read reads structured binary data from r into data.
  • binary.Uvarint - Uvarint decodes a uint64 from buf and returns that value and the number of bytes read (> 0).

lessons.title: Hashes and checksums: sha256, crc32, fnv
lessons.concept:
A hash function maps any input to a fixed-size value. Choose by job:

    crypto/sha256, sha512   cryptographic: integrity of downloads,
                            content addressing, signatures, HMAC
    hash/crc32, crc64       detect ACCIDENTAL corruption (zip, ethernet)
                            - fast, trivially forgeable
    hash/fnv, maphash       hash tables and sharding - fast, not secure

▸  TWO STYLES
    sum := sha256.Sum256(data)      // one shot, returns [32]byte
    h := sha256.New()               // streaming: implements io.Writer
    io.Copy(h, file)
    h.Sum(nil)

All hashes implement hash.Hash, so code can accept any of them.

▸  NOT FOR PASSWORDS
A plain SHA-256 of a password is crackable at billions of guesses per
second. Passwords need a slow, salted KDF (see the Security module).

▸  NOT md5/sha1 FOR SECURITY
Both are broken for collision resistance. Fine for a non-adversarial
cache key, never for integrity against attackers.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
	"hash"
	"hash/crc32"
	"hash/fnv"
	"io"
	"strings"
)

func digest(h hash.Hash, r io.Reader) string {
	io.Copy(h, r) // stream: works for any size
	return fmt.Sprintf("%x", h.Sum(nil))
}

func main() {
	data := "The quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
	fmt.Printf("%x\n", sha256.Sum256([]byte(data)))
	fmt.Println(digest(sha256.New(), strings.NewReader(data)))
	fmt.Printf("%08x\n", crc32.ChecksumIEEE([]byte(data)))

	f := fnv.New32a()
	f.Write([]byte("user-42"))
	fmt.Println("shard:", f.Sum32()%8)

	tampered := strings.Replace(data, "dog", "cog", 1)
	fmt.Println(sha256.Sum256([]byte(data)) == sha256.Sum256([]byte(tampered)))
}
lessons.expected:
d7a8fbb307d7809469ca9abcb0082e4f8d5651e46d3cdb762d02d0bf37c9e592
d7a8fbb307d7809469ca9abcb0082e4f8d5651e46d3cdb762d02d0bf37c9e592
414fa339
shard: 3
false

quiz.q: You need to detect ACCIDENTAL corruption in a file format, as fast as possible. Which fits?
options: crypto/sha512
A salted password KDF
math/rand with the file as seed
hash/crc32
quiz.explain: CRC32 is designed exactly for detecting random corruption and is extremely fast (hardware-accelerated). It offers no protection against deliberate tampering - that needs SHA-256 or an HMAC.
quiz.hint: Is anyone trying to fool the check on purpose?

lessons.newhere:
• crc32.ChecksumIEEE - ChecksumIEEE returns the CRC-32 checksum of data using the IEEE polynomial.
  • fnv.New32a - New32a returns a new 32-bit FNV-1a hash.Hash.
  • hash.Hash32.Sum32 - returns the 32-bit hash of everything written so far
  • strings.Replace - Replace returns a copy of the string s with the first n non-overlapping instances of old replaced by new.

lessons.title: net/url: parsing and building URLs
lessons.concept:
Never build or pick apart URLs with string concatenation - escaping
rules differ for paths, queries and fragments.

    u, err := url.Parse("https://user:pw@example.com:8080/a/b?q=go&n=1#top")
    u.Scheme   "https"         u.Host      "example.com:8080"
    u.Hostname() "example.com" u.Port()    "8080"
    u.Path     "/a/b"          u.RawQuery  "q=go&n=1"
    u.Fragment "top"           u.User.Username()

▸  QUERY PARAMETERS
    q := u.Query()             // url.Values = map[string][]string
    q.Get("q"), q["n"]
    q.Set("page", "2"); q.Add("tag", "a b")
    u.RawQuery = q.Encode()    // escaped and SORTED by key

▸  ESCAPING
    url.QueryEscape("a b&c")   "a+b%26c"
    url.PathEscape("a b/c")    "a%20b%2Fc"

▸  RELATIVE REFERENCES
    base.ResolveReference(ref)  -  how a browser resolves href="../x"
    u.JoinPath("v1", "users")   (Go 1.19)
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"net/url"
)

func main() {
	u, err := url.Parse("https://ada:secret@api.example.com:8443/v1/search?q=go+lang&tag=a&tag=b#results")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println(u.Scheme, u.Hostname(), u.Port(), u.Path, u.Fragment)
	fmt.Println(u.User.Username())

	q := u.Query()
	fmt.Println(q.Get("q"), q["tag"])
	q.Set("page", "2")
	q.Add("tag", "c&d")
	u.RawQuery = q.Encode()
	u.User = nil
	fmt.Println(u)

	fmt.Println(url.QueryEscape("a b&c"), url.PathEscape("a b/c"))
	base, _ := url.Parse("https://example.com/docs/guide/intro.html")
	ref, _ := url.Parse("../api/index.html")
	fmt.Println(base.ResolveReference(ref))
	fmt.Println(base.JoinPath("..", "faq"))
}

https api.example.com 8443 /v1/search results
ada
go lang [a b]
https://api.example.com:8443/v1/search?page=2&q=go+lang&tag=a&tag=b&tag=c%26d#results
a+b%26c a%20b%2Fc
https://example.com/docs/api/index.html
https://example.com/docs/guide/faq

options: Sorts the parameters by key
Removes duplicate keys
Lower-cases every key
Adds a leading ? character
quiz.explain: Encode escapes values and emits them sorted by key, which makes URLs deterministic - handy for caching and tests.

lessons.title: text/template: generating text from data
lessons.concept:
text/template fills a template with data (gopl 4.6, Go by Example).
It powers Helm charts, Hugo sites, code generators and go doc.

    {{.Name}}                 a field (or map key) of the current data
    {{.}}                     the current data itself
    {{if .Admin}}...{{else}}...{{end}}
    {{range .Items}}{{.}}{{else}}empty{{end}}
    {{with .Address}}{{.City}}{{end}}      changes the current data
    {{len .Items}}            built-in functions: len, index, printf,
                              and, or, not, eq, ne, lt, le, gt, ge
    {{.Price | printf "%.2f"}}  pipelines
    {{- .X -}}                trims whitespace around the action
    {{define "row"}}...{{end}} {{template "row" .}}   reusable pieces

▸  CUSTOM FUNCTIONS
    template.New("t").Funcs(template.FuncMap{"upper": strings.ToUpper})
Funcs must be added BEFORE Parse.

▸  PARSE ONCE
Parse at start-up with template.Must (panics on a syntax error), then
Execute many times. Execute writes to any io.Writer.

▸  FOR HTML, USE html/template
Same API, but it escapes data contextually to prevent XSS (Web module).

Invoice for ADA (VIP)
0. tea      2 x 1.50
1. cake     1 x 4.25
Lines: 2
Invoice for BOB
(no items)
Lines: 0

quiz.q: When must custom template functions be registered with Funcs?
options: After Parse but before Execute
Before Parse, so the parser knows the names
Inside the template with {{define}}
Any time - templates look functions up lazily
quiz.explain: The parser checks that every function name used in the template exists. Calling Funcs after Parse is too late: Parse would already have failed with "function not defined".
quiz.hint: Who needs to know that "upper" is a valid name?

lessons.title: Logging: log and log/slog
lessons.concept:
▸  THE log PACKAGE (simple)
    log.Println("starting")       // to stderr with a timestamp
    log.Fatalf(...)               // log, then os.Exit(1) - defers skip!
    l := log.New(w, "api: ", log.LstdFlags|log.Lshortfile)

▸  log/slog (Go 1.21) - STRUCTURED LOGGING
Logs as key/value pairs that machines can query:
    slog.Info("request", "method", "GET", "path", "/users", "ms", 12)
Handlers decide the format:
    slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stderr, nil)   key=value text
    slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stderr, nil)   one JSON object per line

▸  LEVELS AND CONTEXT
    Debug < Info < Warn < Error;  HandlerOptions{Level: slog.LevelDebug}
    logger.With("request_id", id)   attributes added to every line
    slog.Group("user", "id", 7, "role", "admin")
    slog.SetDefault(logger)         also redirects the old log package

▸  CUSTOMISING
HandlerOptions.ReplaceAttr can rename or remove keys - the demo drops
the time so the output is stable. Implement LogValuer on a type to
control how it's logged (e.g. redact a password).

quiz.q: Why is structured logging (slog) better than log.Printf for services?
options: It writes logs faster to the disk
It needs no configuration at all
Key/value fields can be filtered and queried
It automatically sends logs to the cloud
quiz.explain: With key/value attributes, log systems can filter on status=500 or sum ms per path instead of regex-scraping free text. The JSON handler makes each line a machine-readable record.
quiz.hint: Who reads logs in production: people, or tools?

A Fast Structured Logging Package - Jonathan Amsterdam

lessons.newhere:
• slog.Value - A Value can represent any Go value, but unlike type any, it can represent most small values without an allocation.
  • slog.StringValue - StringValue returns a new Value for a string.
  • slog.Attr - An Attr is a key-value pair.
  • slog.Attr.Key - the name of a log attribute (a key=value pair)
  • slog.TimeKey - TimeKey is the key used by the built-in handlers for the time when the log method is called.

lessons.title: Environment variables and configuration
lessons.concept:
Twelve-factor services read configuration from the environment:

    os.Getenv("PORT")              "" when unset - can't tell unset from empty
    v, ok := os.LookupEnv("PORT")  ok reports whether it is set
    os.Setenv / os.Unsetenv        (mostly for tests: use t.Setenv)
    os.Environ()                   all of them as "KEY=value"
    os.ExpandEnv("$HOME/data")     substitute variables in a string

▸  A CONFIG STRUCT, LOADED ONCE
Read everything at start-up into a struct, validate it, and pass the
struct down. Don't sprinkle os.Getenv through the code - it hides
dependencies and makes testing harder.

▸  PRECEDENCE
A common, predictable order:  flag  >  environment  >  default.
Fail fast with a clear message when a required setting is missing.

▸  SECRETS
Environment variables are visible to child processes and often end up
in crash dumps; never log them.
lessons.expected:
first try: DB_URL is required
{Port:8080 Env: Timeout:250ms DBURL:postgres://localhost/app} <nil>
timeout is 250ms

quiz.q: Why use os.LookupEnv instead of os.Getenv?
options: LookupEnv is faster because it skips a copy
Getenv is deprecated since Go 1.21
LookupEnv also reads values from .env files
It tells "unset" apart from "set to empty"
quiz.explain: Getenv returns "" both when the variable is missing and when it is set to the empty string. LookupEnv's second result tells them apart - note APP_ENV="" in the demo stays empty instead of defaulting.
quiz.hint: Look at the Env field in the second line.

lessons.title: os/exec: running other programs
lessons.concept:
os/exec starts external commands (Go by Example: Spawning Processes):

    out, err := exec.Command("git", "rev-parse", "HEAD").Output()
    out, err := cmd.CombinedOutput()       // stdout + stderr
    cmd.Stdin = strings.NewReader("data")  // feed input
    cmd.Dir, cmd.Env                       // working dir, environment
    exec.CommandContext(ctx, ...)          // killed when ctx is done
    cmd.Start(); ...; cmd.Wait()           // run in the background

▸  NO SHELL BY DEFAULT
exec.Command("ls", "-l", dir) passes arguments DIRECTLY - no globbing,
no pipes, and no shell injection. Only use "sh", "-c", script when you
truly need shell features, and never put user input inside script.

▸  ERRORS
    *exec.ExitError       the program ran and exited non-zero
                          (ExitCode(), Stderr when using Output)
    exec.ErrNotFound      not found on PATH (exec.LookPath to check)

▸  REPLACING THE PROCESS
syscall.Exec replaces the current program entirely (Go by Example:
Exec'ing Processes) - rarely needed.

This demo uses standard Unix tools (Kali/Linux/macOS).
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"os/exec"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	out, err := exec.Command("echo", "hello", "from", "echo").Output()
	fmt.Printf("%q %v\n", out, err)

	cmd := exec.Command("tr", "a-z", "A-Z")
	cmd.Stdin = strings.NewReader("shout this")
	out, _ = cmd.Output()
	fmt.Println(string(out))

	err = exec.Command("sh", "-c", "echo oops >&2; exit 3").Run()
	var ee *exec.ExitError
	if errors.As(err, &ee) {
		fmt.Println("exit code:", ee.ExitCode())
	}

	_, err = exec.Command("no-such-program-xyz").Output()
	fmt.Println(errors.Is(err, exec.ErrNotFound))

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 50*time.Millisecond)
	defer cancel()
	err = exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sleep", "5").Run()
	fmt.Println("killed:", err != nil, ctx.Err())
}

"hello from echo\n" <nil>
SHOUT THIS
exit code: 3
true
killed: true context deadline exceeded

options: rm is faster when called without a shell
No shell parses the argument, so no injection
The shell version needs root privileges
exec.Command escapes quotes inside userInput
quiz.explain: Without a shell, userInput is one argument - "; reboot" is just a strange file name. With sh -c, the shell parses the string and runs whatever commands an attacker wrote.

lessons.title: os/signal: Ctrl+C and graceful exit
lessons.concept:
Servers and CLIs should stop cleanly when the user presses Ctrl+C
(SIGINT) or the orchestrator sends SIGTERM (Go by Example: Signals).

▸  THE MODERN WAY: a context (Go 1.16)
    ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(),
        os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
    defer stop()
    <-ctx.Done()      // returns when a signal arrives
    ... shut down: finish requests, flush, close files ...
Pass ctx into your workers so they all see the cancellation.

▸  THE CLASSIC WAY: a channel
    sigs := make(chan os.Signal, 1)    // buffered! signal won't block
    signal.Notify(sigs, os.Interrupt)
    sig := <-sigs

▸  NOTES
    - After stop() a second Ctrl+C kills the program the default way -
      a useful escape hatch if shutdown hangs.
    - SIGKILL can't be caught. Kubernetes sends SIGTERM, waits a grace
      period (30s default), then SIGKILL.
    - context.Cause(ctx) reports which signal (Go 1.26 adds the signal
      as the cancellation cause).

The demo sends itself an interrupt so you can see it without pressing
keys (Unix only).
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"os/signal"
	"syscall"
	"time"
)

func worker(ctx context.Context, done chan<- struct{}) {
	defer close(done)
	tick := time.NewTicker(5 * time.Millisecond)
	defer tick.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			fmt.Println("worker: flushing and exiting")
			return
		case <-tick.C:
		}
	}
}

func main() {
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(), os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	done := make(chan struct{})
	go worker(ctx, done)

	go func() { // simulate the user pressing Ctrl+C
		time.Sleep(20 * time.Millisecond)
		p, _ := os.FindProcess(os.Getpid())
		p.Signal(os.Interrupt)
	}()

	<-ctx.Done()
	fmt.Println("main: got", ctx.Err())
	<-done
	fmt.Println("main: clean shutdown")
}
lessons.expected:
main: got context canceled
worker: flushing and exiting
main: clean shutdown

quiz.q: Which signal can a Go program NOT catch?
options: SIGINT (Ctrl+C)
SIGTERM
SIGHUP
SIGKILL
quiz.explain: SIGKILL (and SIGSTOP) are handled by the kernel and can never be intercepted. That is why graceful shutdown must happen on SIGTERM, before the orchestrator escalates.
quiz.hint: kill -9 ...

lessons.newhere:
• os.FindProcess - FindProcess looks for a running process by its pid.
  • os.Getpid - Getpid returns the process id of the caller.

lessons.title: encoding/xml

XML works like JSON: struct tags map fields to elements and attributes
