lessons.title: Streaming: gzip, io.Pipe and composable readers
lessons.concept:
Because everything speaks io.Reader / io.Writer, you can snap streams
together like pipe fittings:

    gz := gzip.NewWriter(file)        // compress as you write
    defer gz.Close()                  // Close writes the footer!
    io.Copy(gz, src)

    zr, err := gzip.NewReader(file)   // decompress as you read

▸  MORE FITTINGS
    io.MultiWriter(a, b)    write to several at once (tee)
    io.MultiReader(a, b)    read a then b as one stream
    io.TeeReader(r, w)      copy everything read from r into w
    io.LimitReader(r, n)    stop after n bytes (defend against bombs)
    io.SectionReader        a window into an io.ReaderAt

▸  io.Pipe: connect a writer to a reader in another goroutine
    pr, pw := io.Pipe()
    go func() { json.NewEncoder(pw).Encode(v); pw.Close() }()
    http.Post(url, "application/json", pr)   // streams, no big buffer
CloseWithError on the writer side passes an error to the reader.

▸  ALWAYS CLOSE COMPRESSORS
A gzip.Writer buffers data and writes a checksum footer on Close. Skip
it and the archive is truncated and corrupt.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bytes"
	"compress/gzip"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	text := strings.Repeat("gophers love streams. ", 200)

	var compressed bytes.Buffer
	gz := gzip.NewWriter(&compressed)
	io.Copy(gz, strings.NewReader(text))
	gz.Close() // writes the footer
	fmt.Println(len(text), "->", compressed.Len(), "bytes")

	zr, err := gzip.NewReader(&compressed)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	h := sha256.New()
	n, _ := io.Copy(h, io.TeeReader(zr, io.Discard))
	fmt.Println("decompressed", n, "bytes, intact:", fmt.Sprintf("%x", h.Sum(nil)) == fmt.Sprintf("%x", sha256.Sum256([]byte(text))))

	pr, pw := io.Pipe()
	go func() {
		for i := range 3 {
			fmt.Fprintf(pw, "line %d\n", i)
		}
		pw.Close()
	}()
	all, _ := io.ReadAll(io.MultiReader(strings.NewReader("header\n"), pr))
	fmt.Print(string(all))

	limited, _ := io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(strings.NewReader("0123456789"), 4))
	fmt.Println(string(limited))
}

4400 -> 73 bytes
decompressed 4400 bytes, intact: true
header
line 0
line 1
line 2
0123

Nothing - gzip flushes on every Write
The data is stored uncompressed
The program panics on exit
quiz.explain: The writer buffers compressed blocks and must write the final block plus the CRC-32 and size footer. Without Close, readers report an unexpected EOF.
quiz.hint: Where does the checksum footer get written?

lessons.title: bufio.Scanner in depth: custom split functions
lessons.concept:
A bufio.Scanner splits input into TOKENS using a SplitFunc:

    bufio.ScanLines    (default) lines without the newline (handles \r\n)
    bufio.ScanWords    whitespace-separated words
    bufio.ScanRunes    one UTF-8 character at a time
    bufio.ScanBytes    one byte at a time

▸  WRITING YOUR OWN
    func(data []byte, atEOF bool) (advance int, token []byte, err error)
Look at data: if it contains a complete token, return how many bytes
to consume and the token. If not, return 0, nil, nil to ask for more
data - unless atEOF, in which case return whatever remains.
bufio.ErrFinalToken stops scanning after the token you return.

▸  TOKEN SIZE LIMIT
Tokens are limited to 64 KB by default; a longer line fails with
'bufio.Scanner: token too long'. Raise it:
    sc.Buffer(make([]byte, 0, 64*1024), 10*1024*1024)

▸  WHEN NOT TO USE Scanner
For huge records or binary formats use bufio.Reader (ReadString,
ReadBytes, ReadRune) or io.ReadFull - Scanner keeps whole tokens in
memory.

-1, nil, nil - tell the Scanner to back up
quiz.explain: Returning zero bytes advanced and no token tells the Scanner to read more input and call the function again with a larger buffer.

lessons.title: Text transformations and the Trim trap
lessons.concept:
Handy strings functions beyond the basics:

    strings.NewReplacer("a", "1", "b", "2")   many replacements in ONE
                                              pass; build once, reuse
    strings.Map(f, s)                         transform or drop each rune
                                              (return -1 to drop)

    strings.ContainsFunc, IndexFunc, FieldsFunc

▸  THE TRIM TRAP (100 Go Mistakes #38)
    strings.TrimRight(s, "xo")   removes ANY of the characters x and o
                                  from the right, repeatedly - it takes
                                  a CUTSET, not a suffix
    strings.TrimSuffix(s, "xo")  removes the exact suffix "xo" once
So TrimRight("123oxo", "xo") is "123", not "123o".

EqualFold doesn't, and handles more Unicode cases.

▸  NORMALISATION

reliably, normalise with golang.org/x/text/unicode/norm.

lessons.title: JSON pitfalls
lessons.concept:
Four encoding/json surprises (100 Go Mistakes #77):

▸  1. EMBEDDED TYPES HIJACK MarshalJSON
    type Event struct {
        ID int
        time.Time            // embedded!
    }
time.Time's MarshalJSON is PROMOTED to Event, so json.Marshal(event)
outputs only the time and drops ID. Use a named field instead.

▸  2. NUMBERS IN map[string]any ARE float64
Large IDs lose precision above 2^53. Use dec.UseNumber() (json.Number)
or decode into a typed struct.

▸  3. COMPARING TIMES AFTER A ROUND TRIP
time.Now() carries a monotonic clock reading that JSON drops, so a
decoded time is != the original. Compare with t.Equal(u), and strip
the monotonic part with t.Round(0) when you need ==.

▸  4. CASE-INSENSITIVE FIELD MATCHING
Unmarshal matches JSON keys to fields CASE-INSENSITIVELY, so {"ID": 1}
and {"id": 1} both fill ID - and duplicate keys with different case
silently overwrite each other. (encoding/json/v2 makes matching
case-sensitive by default.)

▸  ALSO
Unexported fields are ignored; nil slices become null; unknown fields
are silently dropped unless DisallowUnknownFields.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

type EventBad struct {
	ID int
	time.Time
}

type EventGood struct {
	ID   int       `json:"id"`
	When time.Time `json:"when"`
}

func main() {
	when := time.Date(2026, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 0, time.UTC)
	bad, _ := json.Marshal(EventBad{ID: 42, Time: when})
	good, _ := json.Marshal(EventGood{ID: 42, When: when})
	fmt.Println(string(bad))
	fmt.Println(string(good))

	var m map[string]any
	json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"id": 9007199254740993}`), &m)
	fmt.Printf("%T %.0f\n", m["id"], m["id"])
	dec := json.NewDecoder(strings.NewReader(`{"id": 9007199254740993}`))
	dec.UseNumber()
	dec.Decode(&m)
	fmt.Printf("%T %v\n", m["id"], m["id"])

	now := time.Now()
	b, _ := json.Marshal(now)
	var back time.Time
	json.Unmarshal(b, &back)
	fmt.Println(now == back, now.Equal(back))

	var e EventGood
	json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"ID": 1, "id": 2}`), &e)
	fmt.Println(e.ID)
}

quiz.q: A struct embeds time.Time. What does json.Marshal produce for it?
options: Only the time: the promoted MarshalJSON wins
All fields, with the time as a nested object
An error about ambiguous embedded fields
All of the struct's fields except the time
quiz.explain: Embedding promotes time.Time's MarshalJSON method, so the whole struct now implements json.Marshaler and encodes as just the timestamp. Use a named field.
quiz.hint: Look at the first line of output.

lessons.title: http.Handler: the one interface behind every Go web app
lessons.concept:
Everything in net/http revolves around one interface (gopl 7.7):

    type Handler interface {
        ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request)
    }

    w   where you write the response: headers, status, body
    r   the incoming request: method, URL, headers, body, context

▸  HandlerFunc: functions as handlers
    func home(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) { ... }
    http.HandlerFunc(home)        // adapts a func to the interface
http.HandlerFunc is a function TYPE with a ServeHTTP method that calls
itself - a neat trick worth understanding.

▸  ServeMux: a router is also a Handler
    mux := http.NewServeMux()
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /{$}", home)       // exactly "/"
    mux.Handle("GET /static/", files)
    http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux)
Because a mux is a Handler, so is anything that wraps it - that's how
middleware composes.

▸  IN THESE LESSONS
Each demo starts the handler with httptest.NewServer (a real HTTP
server on a random local port) and calls it with a client, so you see
real requests and responses without leaving the program running.

net/http converts it automatically

quiz.explain: ServeMux implements ServeHTTP by finding the best-matching registered handler and calling it. Being a Handler itself is what lets you wrap a whole router in middleware.

lessons.title: Routing with Go 1.22 patterns: methods and wildcards
lessons.concept:

(Let's Go 2.3-2.5) - most apps no longer need a router library:

    mux.HandleFunc("GET /posts", list)
    mux.HandleFunc("POST /posts", create)
    mux.HandleFunc("GET /posts/{id}", show)        // one segment

lessons.title: Writing responses: headers, status codes and JSON
lessons.concept:
The ResponseWriter has three parts, and ORDER MATTERS:

    w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")   1. headers
    w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)                    2. status
    w.Write(body)                                        3. body

Once the status is written, header changes are ignored. If you call
Write without WriteHeader, Go sends 200 and sniffs a Content-Type.

▸  A JSON HELPER
    func writeJSON(w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
        w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        w.WriteHeader(status)
        json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v)
    }

▸  ERRORS
    http.Error(w, "message", http.StatusBadRequest)   plain-text error
Then RETURN (100 Go Mistakes #80):
    if bad {
        http.Error(w, "bad", 400)
        // forgetting return here keeps going and writes MORE output:
        // 'superfluous response.WriteHeader call' in the logs
    }

▸  STATUS CODES WORTH KNOWING
200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301/302/303 redirects,
400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden
(logged in, not allowed), 404, 405, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable,
429 Too Many Requests, 500, 503.

quiz.q: A handler calls w.WriteHeader(201) and THEN w.Header().Set("Location", "/x"). What happens?

▸  QUERY PARAMETERS

    page := q.Get("page")       // "" when absent

▸  JSON BODIES, DEFENSIVELY
    r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)   // 1 MB cap
    dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
    dec.DisallowUnknownFields()                      // catch typos
    if err := dec.Decode(&input); err != nil { 400 }

lessons.title: Middleware: wrapping handlers
lessons.concept:
Middleware is a function that takes a Handler and returns a Handler
that does something before and/or after calling it (Let's Go ch.6):

    func logRequests(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
        return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
            start := time.Now()

            log.Println(r.Method, r.URL.Path, time.Since(start))

▸  TYPICAL MIDDLEWARE
    - security headers on every response
    - request logging (wrap w to capture the status code)
    - panic recovery: defer + recover -> 500 instead of a dropped
      connection (net/http recovers too, but only logs)
    - authentication, rate limiting, CORS, request IDs, compression

▸  ORDER MATTERS
    handler := recoverPanic(logRequests(secureHeaders(mux)))
The OUTERMOST runs first. Recovery goes outside so it catches panics
from everything inside it. A tiny helper makes chains readable:
    func chain(h http.Handler, m ...func(http.Handler) http.Handler)

▸  CAPTURING THE STATUS
ResponseWriter doesn't expose the status, so logging middleware wraps
it in a struct that records WriteHeader calls.

recoverPanic runs after logRequests returns
Panics are invisible to every middleware
The panic unwound past logRequests' Printf

lessons.title: Request context: cancellation and request-scoped values
lessons.concept:
Every request carries a context.Context (Let's Go ch.11):

    ctx := r.Context()

▸  CANCELLATION FOR FREE
The context is cancelled when the client disconnects or the server
shuts down. Pass it to every database query and outgoing request so
abandoned work stops:
    rows, err := db.QueryContext(r.Context(), q)

▸  PASSING VALUES DOWN THE CHAIN
Authentication middleware identifies the user once; handlers read it:
    type ctxKey int                       // unexported key TYPE
    const userKey ctxKey = 0
    ctx := context.WithValue(r.Context(), userKey, user)
    next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
    ...
    user, ok := r.Context().Value(userKey).(*User)

▸  RULES
    - Use an unexported key type so no other package can collide.
    - Wrap access in small helpers (userFrom(ctx)) instead of
      scattering type assertions.
    - Only REQUEST-SCOPED data: user, request ID, trace span. Never
      config, loggers or optional parameters - pass those explicitly.

String keys are too slow for context lookups
context.WithValue rejects plain string keys
Integer keys use less memory than strings
quiz.explain: Context keys are compared by type and value. A key of your own unexported type can never equal a key from another package, even one that also uses 0 or "user".

lessons.title: Cookies and a tamper-proof session cookie
lessons.concept:
▸  SETTING AND READING COOKIES
    http.SetCookie(w, &http.Cookie{
        Name: "session", Value: v, Path: "/",
        HttpOnly: true,                  // JavaScript can't read it
        Secure:   true,                  // HTTPS only
        SameSite: http.SameSiteLaxMode,  // CSRF mitigation
        MaxAge:   3600,                  // seconds; <0 deletes
    })
    c, err := r.Cookie("session")        // http.ErrNoCookie if absent

▸  NEVER TRUST A COOKIE'S CONTENTS
Users can edit cookies. Either store only a random session ID (and
keep the data server-side), or SIGN the value with an HMAC so any
change is detected:
    sig = HMAC-SHA256(secretKey, value)
    cookie = value + "." + base64(sig)
Verify with hmac.Equal - a constant-time comparison, so attackers
can't learn the signature byte by byte from response timings.

▸  SESSIONS IN PRACTICE
Libraries such as alexedwards/scs or gorilla/sessions handle expiry,
rotation and storage. Signing hides nothing - encrypt (AES-GCM) if the
value is secret.

200 you are bob

quiz.q: Why compare signatures with hmac.Equal instead of ==?
options: == cannot compare two byte slices in Go
hmac.Equal also decrypts the cookie value
hmac.Equal is much faster for long values
Its timing reveals nothing about the bytes
quiz.explain: A normal comparison stops at the first differing byte, so response times reveal how many leading bytes were right. hmac.Equal always takes the same time.
quiz.hint: What can an attacker measure from outside?

lessons.title: The HTTP client done right
lessons.concept:
Calling other services is half of most backends (Go by Example: HTTP
Client; 100 Go Mistakes #79, #81).

▸  1. NEVER USE THE DEFAULT CLIENT IN PRODUCTION
http.Get uses http.DefaultClient, which has NO timeout. One stuck server
hangs your goroutine forever.
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 10 * time.Second}

▸  2. ALWAYS CLOSE THE BODY
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
An unclosed body leaks the connection (and its goroutines); also read it
to the end if you want the connection reused.

▸  3. A 404 IS NOT AN ERROR
err is only for transport failures. Check resp.StatusCode yourself.

▸  4. USE CONTEXTS FOR PER-REQUEST DEADLINES
    req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "GET", url, nil)

▸  5. LIMIT WHAT YOU READ
    io.ReadAll(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20))

▸  6. REUSE ONE CLIENT
Clients are safe for concurrent use and pool connections. Create one,
share it; tune Transport (MaxIdleConnsPerHost) for heavy traffic.

Yes - net/http should return an error for 5xx
Yes - the request must have been cancelled
No - a 500 status means the request succeeded
quiz.explain: The client got a valid HTTP response, so there is no transport error. Interpreting the status (4xx, 5xx) is the caller's job.

lessons.title: http.Server: timeouts and graceful shutdown
lessons.concept:
http.ListenAndServe(addr, h) has no timeouts: slow or malicious
clients can hold connections forever (Slowloris). Configure a server
(Let's Go ch.9; 100 Go Mistakes #81):

    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr:              ":8080",
        Handler:           mux,
        ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
        ReadTimeout:       10 * time.Second,
        WriteTimeout:      15 * time.Second,
        IdleTimeout:       time.Minute,
        MaxHeaderBytes:    1 << 20,
        ErrorLog:          slog.NewLogLogger(handler, slog.LevelError),
    }

▸  GRACEFUL SHUTDOWN
    go func() { srv.ListenAndServe() }()   // returns ErrServerClosed
    <-ctx.Done()                           // SIGINT / SIGTERM
    shutdownCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    srv.Shutdown(shutdownCtx)
Shutdown stops accepting new connections, waits for in-flight requests
to finish (or the context to expire), then returns. Deploys then drop
zero requests.

▸  HTTPS
srv.ListenAndServeTLS(certFile, keyFile), or a tls.Config with
MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12. In production a reverse proxy or
autocert often terminates TLS.

The demo listens on 127.0.0.1:0 (a random free port).
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"io"
	"net"
	"net/http"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /work", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		time.Sleep(100 * time.Millisecond) // an in-flight request
		fmt.Fprint(w, "finished work")
	})
	srv := &http.Server{
		Handler:           mux,
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
		ReadTimeout:       10 * time.Second,
		WriteTimeout:      15 * time.Second,
		IdleTimeout:       time.Minute,
	}
	ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	serveErr := make(chan error, 1)
	go func() { serveErr <- srv.Serve(ln) }()

	result := make(chan string)
	go func() {
		resp, err := http.Get("http://" + ln.Addr().String() + "/work")
		if err != nil {
			result <- "client error: " + err.Error()
			return
		}
		defer resp.Body.Close()
		b, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
		result <- string(b)
	}()

	time.Sleep(30 * time.Millisecond) // the request is now in flight
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	fmt.Println("shutdown:", srv.Shutdown(ctx)) // waits for /work
	fmt.Println("in-flight request got:", <-result)
	fmt.Println("Serve returned ErrServerClosed:", errors.Is(<-serveErr, http.ErrServerClosed))

	_, err = http.Get("http://" + ln.Addr().String() + "/work")
	fmt.Println("new requests refused:", err != nil)
}

shutdown: <nil>
in-flight request got: finished work
Serve returned ErrServerClosed: true
new requests refused: true

options: Aborts them immediately with a 503
Waits for them to finish, up to the context deadline
Moves them to a new server instance
Ignores them; they keep running after Shutdown returns
quiz.explain: Shutdown closes the listeners, then waits for active connections to go idle. If ctx expires first, it returns ctx.Err() and you can fall back to srv.Close().
quiz.hint: Look at what the in-flight request received.

lessons.title: Authentication: signup, login and sessions
lessons.concept:
Putting the pieces together the way Let's Go ch.10 does:

▸  SIGNUP
Validate the email and password length, hash the password with a slow
salted KDF (Security module), store the user. Never store or log the
plain password.

▸  LOGIN
Look up the user, verify the password in constant time, then create a
SESSION: a random token (crypto/rand, 128+ bits) mapped server-side to
the user ID, sent as a cookie:
    HttpOnly (no JavaScript access), Secure (HTTPS only),
    SameSite=Lax (CSRF mitigation), Path=/, a sensible MaxAge.
Use the SAME error message for 'no such user' and 'wrong password', so
attackers can't enumerate accounts.

▸  RENEW THE TOKEN ON LOGIN
Issue a fresh token whenever privilege changes, preventing session
fixation.

▸  AUTHORISATION
Middleware reads the cookie, looks up the session and puts the user in
the request context; protected handlers require it (401 if absent, 403
if not allowed).

▸  LOGOUT
Delete the server-side session and expire the cookie (MaxAge: -1).

In production use a session library (alexedwards/scs) backed by a
database or Redis, and argon2id/bcrypt for passwords.

Because both errors use the same status code anyway
So attackers cannot discover which emails have accounts
To keep the error messages short

lessons.title: CSRF: protecting state-changing requests
lessons.concept:
CROSS-SITE REQUEST FORGERY: a malicious page makes the victim's
browser send a request to YOUR site - with the victim's cookies
attached. If POST /transfer trusts the session cookie alone, the
attacker moves money (Let's Go 10.7).

▸  DEFENCE 1: SameSite COOKIES
SameSite=Lax (Go's http.SameSiteLaxMode) stops cookies on cross-site
POSTs in modern browsers. Use it always - but don't rely on it alone
(older browsers, subdomain attacks).

▸  DEFENCE 2: CHECK WHERE THE REQUEST CAME FROM
Browsers send Sec-Fetch-Site (same-origin / same-site / cross-site /
none) and Origin on POSTs. Reject unsafe methods whose Sec-Fetch-Site
is cross-site, or whose Origin isn't yours. Go 1.25 packages exactly
this as http.CrossOriginProtection:
    handler = http.NewCrossOriginProtection().Handler(mux)

▸  DEFENCE 3: TOKENS
Put a random token in the form (or a header) and in the session or a
cookie; reject unsafe requests where they don't match. Attackers can
make the browser SEND your cookies but can't READ them, so they can't
forge the token.

▸  SAFE METHODS
GET, HEAD and OPTIONS must never change state - CSRF defences only
check unsafe methods.

options: It can make the browser send it, but cannot read it
Browsers strip cookies from every cross-site request
CSRF tokens are encrypted end to end by TLS
Tokens always expire before an attacker can use them
quiz.explain: The same-origin policy stops other sites from READING your cookies and pages. The browser will SEND the cookie, but the attacker cannot copy the token into the header or form field, so the check fails.
quiz.hint: Sending versus reading.

lessons.title: TCP servers and clients with net
lessons.concept:
HTTP sits on TCP. The net package gives you the layer below
(gopl 8.2-8.3):

    ln, err := net.Listen("tcp", ":9000")
    for {
        conn, err := ln.Accept()       // blocks for the next client
        go handle(conn)                // one goroutine per connection
    }

    conn, err := net.Dial("tcp", "localhost:9000")
    fmt.Fprintf(conn, "hello\n")
    reply, _ := bufio.NewReader(conn).ReadString('\n')

▸  net.Conn IS AN io.ReadWriter
So bufio.Scanner, fmt.Fprintf, io.Copy and json.Encoder all work on
it. An echo server is literally io.Copy(conn, conn).

▸  GOROUTINE PER CONNECTION
Goroutines are cheap enough that thousands of concurrent clients are
routine - no event loop or callback style needed. The runtime uses
epoll/kqueue underneath (the 'netpoller').

▸  CLOSING
Always defer conn.Close() in the handler. Closing the listener makes
Accept return an error (net.ErrClosed) - the way to stop the loop.

▸  TCP IS A STREAM
There are no message boundaries: one Write can arrive as two Reads and
vice versa. Frame messages yourself (newline-delimited, or a length
prefix).
lessons.expected:

sent "gophers" got "GOPHERS\n"
sent "quit"   got "bye\n"

quiz.q: A client sends two Write calls of 5 bytes each over TCP. How many Read calls does the server need?
options: Exactly two: TCP keeps each Write separate
Exactly one: writes are always merged
Ten: TCP delivers one byte per Read call
Unknown: TCP is a stream with no boundaries
quiz.explain: TCP delivers an ordered stream of bytes, not messages. Reads may return any amount. That is why protocols use delimiters (newlines) or length prefixes, and why bufio is so useful.
quiz.hint: Does TCP know where your messages begin and end?

lessons.title: A broadcast chat server
lessons.concept:
gopl 8.10 builds a chat server with a beautiful structure: ONE
goroutine owns the set of clients, and everybody talks to it through
channels - no mutex at all.

    entering = make(chan client)   // a client joined
    leaving  = make(chan client)   // a client left
    messages = make(chan string)   // something to broadcast

    func broadcaster() {
        clients := map[client]bool{}       // owned by this goroutine only
        for {
            select {
            case msg := <-messages:
                for cli := range clients { cli <- msg }
            case cli := <-entering:
                clients[cli] = true
            case cli := <-leaving:
                delete(clients, cli); close(cli)
            }
        }
    }

Each connection gets two goroutines: one reading lines from the
socket into messages, one writing its own outgoing channel to the
socket. This 'confinement' pattern - state owned by one goroutine,
changes requested by message - is 'share memory by communicating'.

Joining also announces you to yourself, which gives the demo's clients
a sync point: each waits for the line it expects, so the output is
deterministic without any sleeps.

quiz.q: Why does the chat server need no mutex around its clients map?
options: Maps are safe for concurrent use in Go
net.Conn locks the map automatically
Only the broadcaster goroutine ever touches it

lessons.title: Deadlines and timeouts on connections
lessons.concept:
A network peer can stall forever. Every production read and write
needs a bound.

▸  DIALING
    net.DialTimeout("tcp", addr, 3*time.Second)
    d := net.Dialer{Timeout: 3 * time.Second, KeepAlive: 30 * time.Second}
    d.DialContext(ctx, "tcp", addr)

▸  DEADLINES ON A CONNECTION
    conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(10 * time.Second))
    conn.SetWriteDeadline(...)
    conn.SetDeadline(...)        // both
A deadline is an absolute TIME, not a duration. It applies to all
future operations, so for an idle timeout you push it forward before
each read.

▸  RECOGNISING A TIMEOUT
    if errors.Is(err, os.ErrDeadlineExceeded) { ... }
or check net.Error's Timeout() method.

▸  CANCELLING A BLOCKED READ
Setting a deadline in the past (or closing the conn) from another
goroutine makes a blocked Read return immediately - how servers stop
idle connections on shutdown.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"bufio"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"net"
	"os"
	"time"
)

func main() {
	ln, _ := net.Listen("tcp", "127.0.0.1:0")
	defer ln.Close()
	go func() {
		conn, err := ln.Accept()
		if err != nil {
			return
		}
		defer conn.Close()
		time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond) // a server that never answers in time
	}()

	conn, err := net.DialTimeout("tcp", ln.Addr().String(), time.Second)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer conn.Close()

	conn.SetReadDeadline(time.Now().Add(50 * time.Millisecond))
	start := time.Now()
	_, err = bufio.NewReader(conn).ReadString('\n')
	fmt.Println("timed out:", errors.Is(err, os.ErrDeadlineExceeded))
	var ne net.Error
	fmt.Println("net.Error with Timeout():", errors.As(err, &ne) && ne.Timeout())
	fmt.Println("waited about 50ms:", time.Since(start) < 300*time.Millisecond)

	_, err = net.DialTimeout("tcp", "127.0.0.1:1", time.Second)
	fmt.Println("closed port refused:", err != nil)
}
lessons.expected:
timed out: true
net.Error with Timeout(): true
waited about 50ms: true
closed port refused: true

quiz.q: conn.SetReadDeadline takes what kind of argument?
options: A time.Duration from now
A number of milliseconds
An absolute time.Time
A context.Context
quiz.explain: Deadlines are points in time and apply to all future I/O until changed. For an idle timeout, set time.Now().Add(d) again before each read.
quiz.hint: It is called a deadline, not a timeout.

lessons.title: UDP: datagrams instead of streams
lessons.concept:
UDP sends individual packets (datagrams): no connection, no
guaranteed delivery, no ordering - but message boundaries ARE kept and
latency is minimal. DNS, game state, metrics (StatsD) and QUIC/HTTP-3
are built on it.

    pc, err := net.ListenPacket("udp", ":9999")
    n, addr, err := pc.ReadFrom(buf)    // one datagram, plus the sender
    pc.WriteTo(reply, addr)

    conn, err := net.Dial("udp", "host:9999")   // a 'connected' socket:
    conn.Write(msg)                             // sets the default peer

▸  TCP vs UDP
    TCP: reliable ordered byte stream, connection setup, congestion
         control. Use by default.
    UDP: independent messages that may be lost, duplicated or
         reordered. Your protocol handles retries if it needs them.

▸  BUFFER SIZE
A datagram bigger than your buffer is truncated. Keep messages well
under ~1200 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation.

▸  net/netip (Go 1.18)
netip.Addr and netip.AddrPort are small comparable value types - use
them as map keys instead of net.IP slices.

ping -> pingping <nil>
go! -> go!go! <nil>
127.0.0.1 true 1

quiz.q: Which property does UDP keep that TCP does not?
options: Message boundaries: one send, one receive
Guaranteed delivery of every packet sent
In-order delivery, even over the internet
Congestion control to avoid flooding a link
quiz.explain: Each UDP datagram arrives whole (or not at all), so one WriteTo matches one ReadFrom. TCP keeps order and reliability but merges everything into one byte stream.
quiz.hint: Compare with the TCP lesson's quiz.

lessons.title: Framing a binary protocol: length-prefixed messages
lessons.concept:
TCP is a byte stream, so every protocol needs FRAMING - a way to know
where one message ends. Two classic approaches:

    delimiter      newline-separated text (HTTP/1 headers, Redis, SMTP);
                   simple, but the payload can't contain the delimiter
    length prefix  a fixed-size length header, then exactly that many
                   bytes - works for any binary payload (Kafka, Postgres,
                   gRPC frames)

▸  WRITING A FRAME
    var hdr [4]byte
    binary.BigEndian.PutUint32(hdr[:], uint32(len(payload)))
    w.Write(hdr[:]); w.Write(payload)       (better: one buffered write)

▸  READING A FRAME
    io.ReadFull(r, hdr[:])                  // exactly 4 bytes, or an error
    n := binary.BigEndian.Uint32(hdr[:])
    if n > maxFrame { reject }              // never trust the length!
    buf := make([]byte, n)
    io.ReadFull(r, buf)

▸  THE SECURITY POINT
Without a maximum, a peer that sends a length of 4 GB makes you
allocate 4 GB. Always cap it.

▸  net.Pipe
An in-memory, synchronous, full-duplex connection - two net.Conn ends
- perfect for testing protocol code without sockets.

frame 19 bytes: "binary\x00safe\npayload"
frame 0 bytes: ""
stop: frame too large: 2147483648 bytes

quiz.q: Why must a length-prefixed reader check the length against a maximum?
options: Lengths are always stored as small integers
A peer could claim a huge size you'd allocate
io.ReadFull cannot read more than 64 KB at once
Big-endian numbers overflow above 65535
quiz.explain: The length comes from an untrusted peer. Allocating whatever it says lets one malicious packet exhaust memory - a classic denial-of-service bug.
quiz.hint: Who wrote the length header?

lessons.title: Streaming responses: Server-Sent Events, WebSockets and gRPC
lessons.concept:
Plain request/response isn't the only shape of network API.

▸  STREAMING HTTP RESPONSES (stdlib)
A handler can send data in pieces and flush each one:
    rc := http.NewResponseController(w)   // Go 1.20
    fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: %s\n\n", msg)
    rc.Flush()
SERVER-SENT EVENTS (text/event-stream) use exactly this: one-way
server-to-browser updates over ordinary HTTP, with automatic reconnect
in browsers (EventSource). Watch r.Context().Done() to stop when the
client leaves.

▸  HTTP/2
net/http negotiates HTTP/2 automatically over TLS. Go 1.24 added
unencrypted HTTP/2 via Server.Protocols / Transport.Protocols.

▸  WEBSOCKETS (third-party)
Full-duplex messages over one upgraded HTTP connection - chat, games,
collaborative editing. Use github.com/coder/websocket or
github.com/gorilla/websocket.

▸  gRPC (third-party)
Typed RPC over HTTP/2 with Protocol Buffers: you write a .proto file,
generate Go code (protoc-gen-go, protoc-gen-go-grpc), and get
streaming, deadlines and cancellation that map onto context.Context.
The default choice between internal services.

The demo implements SSE with the standard library only.

received: step 1 of 3
received: step 2 of 3
received: step 3 of 3

quiz.q: What makes a Go handler send part of a response before it returns?
options: Calling w.WriteHeader(200) a second time
Setting the Content-Length header to 0
Returning early from the ServeHTTP method
Calling Flush on an http.ResponseController
quiz.explain: Written data sits in a buffer until flushed. ResponseController.Flush (or the http.Flusher interface) pushes it to the client immediately - the basis of SSE and other streaming responses.

lessons.title: database/sql: drivers, the connection pool and sql.Open
lessons.concept:
database/sql is a database-NEUTRAL API; a DRIVER plugs in the specific
database (Let's Go 4.2-4.4):

    import (
        "database/sql"
        _ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"   // registers "pgx"
    )
    db, err := sql.Open("pgx", "postgres://user:pw@localhost/app")

Drivers register themselves in init(), which is why they're imported
with the blank identifier _.

▸  sql.Open DOESN'T CONNECT
It only validates arguments. Call db.PingContext(ctx) at start-up to
fail fast when the database is unreachable.

▸  *sql.DB IS A POOL, NOT A CONNECTION
Safe for concurrent use; it opens and reuses connections as needed.
Create ONE at start-up, pass it to your handlers, and Close it on
shutdown. Opening a DB per request exhausts the server.

▸  TUNE THE POOL
    db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)
    db.SetMaxIdleConns(25)
    db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5 * time.Minute)
    db.Stats()                       // in-use, idle, wait count

▸  IN THESE LESSONS
memdb.go (shipped alongside) is a tiny in-memory driver written for
this course: it registers "memdb" and understands a small SQL subset.
With PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite you change only the import and the
sql.Open line - every database/sql call stays the same. (Placeholders
differ: PostgreSQL uses $1, $2; MySQL and SQLite use ?.)
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

func openDB(dsn string) (*sql.DB, error) {
	db, err := sql.Open("memdb", dsn) // validates arguments only
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	db.SetMaxOpenConns(10)
	db.SetMaxIdleConns(10)
	db.SetConnMaxLifetime(5 * time.Minute)

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 2*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil { // actually connects
		db.Close()
		return nil, err
	}
	return db, nil
}

func main() {
	db, err := openDB("shop")
	if err != nil {
		fmt.Println("cannot start:", err)
		return
	}
	defer db.Close()

	_, err = db.Exec("CREATE TABLE products (id, name, price)")
	fmt.Println("create:", err)
	res, err := db.Exec("INSERT INTO products (name, price) VALUES (?, ?)", "keyboard", 4999)
	id, _ := res.LastInsertId()
	n, _ := res.RowsAffected()
	fmt.Println("insert:", id, n, err)

	_, err = sql.Open("no-such-driver", "")
	fmt.Println(err)
	fmt.Println("open connections:", db.Stats().OpenConnections)
}

create: <nil>
insert: 1 1 <nil>
sql: unknown driver "no-such-driver" (forgotten import?)
open connections: 1

quiz.q: How should a web server use *sql.DB?
options: Open one per request and close it afterwards
Open one per goroutine to avoid locking
Open one per table you query
Open one at start-up and share it everywhere
quiz.explain: *sql.DB is a concurrency-safe connection POOL meant to be long-lived. Opening one per request throws away pooled connections and can exhaust the database's connection limit.
quiz.hint: Is *sql.DB a connection, or a pool of them?

lessons.title: Exec, placeholders and SQL injection
lessons.concept:
db.Exec runs statements that don't return rows (INSERT, UPDATE,
DELETE, CREATE) and returns an sql.Result:
    res, err := db.ExecContext(ctx, "UPDATE users SET age = ? WHERE id = ?", 37, 1)
    n, _ := res.RowsAffected()
    id, _ := res.LastInsertId()     (not supported by PostgreSQL: use
                                     INSERT ... RETURNING id with QueryRow)

▸  NEVER BUILD SQL WITH STRING CONCATENATION
    q := "SELECT ... WHERE name = '" + name + "'"   // INJECTION!
With name = x' OR '1'='1 the WHERE clause becomes always-true, and
worse payloads can read or delete anything (100 Go Mistakes #78).

▸  PLACEHOLDERS SEND DATA SEPARATELY
    db.Query("SELECT ... WHERE name = ?", name)
The value never becomes part of the SQL text, so it can't change the
statement's structure. This is the single most important database
habit.

▸  WHAT PLACEHOLDERS CAN'T DO
They replace VALUES only - not table names, column names or ORDER BY
directions. For those, choose from a fixed allow-list in Go code.

They escape any quotes inside the value
They reject any value that contains quotes
They limit values to 255 characters each
quiz.explain: With placeholders the statement text and the data travel separately; the database parses the SQL first and binds the value afterwards, so the value can never alter the query's structure.

lessons.title: QueryRow, Scan and sql.ErrNoRows
lessons.concept:

    var u User
    err := db.QueryRowContext(ctx,
        "SELECT id, name, age FROM users WHERE id = ?", id).
        Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name, &u.Age)

    if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) { return ErrUserNotFound }
Translate it into your own sentinel at the data layer, so handlers
can answer 404 without importing database/sql.

Scan destinations are pointers; database/sql converts between the
driver's values and your Go types (int64 -> int, []byte -> string,
time.Time...). The number of destinations must equal the number of
columns.

QueryRow never returns an error itself - any problem (bad SQL, no
rows) surfaces when you call Scan. Always call Scan.

lessons.title: Query: iterating rows correctly
lessons.concept:
For many rows (Let's Go 4.8; 100 Go Mistakes #79):

    rows, err := db.QueryContext(ctx, "SELECT id, name FROM users")
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer rows.Close()               // 1. ALWAYS close
    for rows.Next() {
        var u User
        if err := rows.Scan(&u.ID, &u.Name); err != nil { return err }
        users = append(users, u)
    }
    if err := rows.Err(); err != nil { return err }   // 2. ALWAYS check

▸  WHY rows.Close MATTERS
An open *sql.Rows holds a connection from the pool. Forget Close (say,
on an early return) and the pool slowly drains until every request
hangs waiting for a connection.

▸  WHY rows.Err MATTERS
rows.Next returns false both at the end AND on a mid-stream failure
(network drop). Only rows.Err tells you which.

▸  RETURN AN EMPTY SLICE OR NIL?
'no rows' from Query is not an error - you just get zero iterations.
Return []User{} if the result is encoded to JSON and clients expect [].

lessons.title: Prepared statements and statement reuse
lessons.concept:
A PREPARED statement is parsed once by the database and executed many
times with different arguments:

    stmt, err := db.PrepareContext(ctx, "INSERT INTO events (kind, ms) VALUES (?, ?)")
    if err != nil { return err }
    defer stmt.Close()
    for _, e := range events {
        if _, err := stmt.ExecContext(ctx, e.Kind, e.Ms); err != nil { ... }
    }

▸  WHEN IT HELPS
Hot statements executed in a loop or on every request: the database
skips re-parsing and re-planning. Placeholders already protect against
injection without preparing.

▸  HOW database/sql HANDLES IT
A *sql.Stmt is bound to the POOL, not one connection: database/sql
re-prepares it transparently on whichever connection runs it. Inside a
transaction use tx.Stmt(stmt) to get a version bound to the tx.

▸  CLOSE IT
Each prepared statement holds resources on the server. Close it when
done - long-lived ones (prepared at start-up in a model's constructor)
are closed at shutdown.

▸  BATCHING
For large imports, wrap the loop in ONE transaction: thousands of
single-row commits are far slower than one commit.

versions already recorded, run the rest, and record each one - ideally
each in its own transaction.

    var migrationsFS embed.FS
The binary carries its own schema: no 'forgot to copy the migrations
folder' deploys.

      one.
    - Make changes backwards-compatible for rolling deploys: add a

lessons.title: The Go memory model: happens-before
lessons.concept:
Without synchronisation, one goroutine is NOT guaranteed to see
another goroutine's writes - ever, or in the order they were made
(gopl 9.4, 100 Go Mistakes #58). Compilers and CPUs reorder memory
operations freely as long as a single goroutine can't tell.

▸  HAPPENS-BEFORE
The memory model lists the events that ORDER memory between
goroutines. If write W happens-before read R, R sees W:
    - a send on a channel happens-before the matching receive completes
    - closing a channel happens-before a receive that sees it closed
    - for unbuffered channels, the receive happens-before the send
      completes
    - mu.Unlock() happens-before the next mu.Lock() returns
    - once.Do(f): f's return happens-before any Do returns
    - wg.Done() happens-before the wg.Wait() it unblocks
    - the go statement happens-before the goroutine starts
    - sync/atomic operations are sequentially consistent

▸  THE BROKEN PATTERN
    var data string; var ready bool
    go func() { data = "hi"; ready = true }()
    for !ready {}          // may spin forever, or see ready
    print(data)            // before data - a DATA RACE

▸  DATA RACE vs RACE CONDITION
A data race: unsynchronised concurrent access with a write - undefined
behaviour, found by -race. A race condition: correct synchronisation
but a wrong ORDER of operations (check-then-act) - a logic bug no tool
finds for you.

quiz.q: Which of these does NOT create a happens-before edge between goroutines?
options: Closing a channel that another goroutine receives from
Unlocking a mutex that another goroutine then locks
Writing a bool variable another goroutine polls
wg.Done() followed by the wg.Wait() it unblocks
quiz.explain: A plain variable write gives no ordering guarantee: the reader may never see it, or may see it before earlier writes. Use a channel, a lock, sync.Once, a WaitGroup or an atomic.
quiz.hint: Which one is not a synchronisation operation at all?

lessons.title: Channels or mutexes? Confinement and stateful goroutines
lessons.concept:
Both are correct tools; choose by the SHAPE of the problem
(100 Go Mistakes #57, Concurrency in Go ch.2):

    MUTEX     protecting shared STATE: a cache, a counter, a map that
              many goroutines read and update
    CHANNEL   transferring OWNERSHIP of data, coordinating steps,
              signalling events (done, results, work to do)

The Go proverb 'Don't communicate by sharing memory; share memory by
communicating' is a design default, not a ban on mutexes.

▸  CONFINEMENT
The safest shared data is data that ISN'T shared. Confine state to one
goroutine and let others ask it to read or change the state through
channels (Go by Example: Stateful Goroutines). No locks, and the owner
can enforce invariants in one place.

    type readOp  struct { key string; resp chan int }
    type writeOp struct { key string; val int; resp chan bool }
    go func() {                     // the owner
        state := map[string]int{}
        for { select {
            case r := <-reads:  r.resp <- state[r.key]
            case w := <-writes: state[w.key] = w.val; w.resp <- true
        } }
    }()

▸  LEXICAL CONFINEMENT
A function that creates a channel and only exposes its receive end
(<-chan T) guarantees nobody else can send - the compiler enforces the
ownership.
lessons.expected:
go 34
rust 33
zig 33

quiz.q: In the stateful-goroutine pattern, why is no mutex needed?
options: Only the owning goroutine ever touches the map
select statements lock the map automatically
Maps are safe for concurrent reads and writes
Each operation copies the whole map first
quiz.explain: The map is confined to one goroutine. Every request arrives over a channel and is handled one at a time, so accesses are serialised by construction.
quiz.hint: How many goroutines hold a reference to state?

lessons.title: sync.Cond: waiting for a condition
lessons.concept:
Sometimes goroutines must wait until some STATE becomes true ('the
queue has room', 'config loaded') - a job for sync.Cond (Concurrency in
Go ch.3, 100 Go Mistakes #72).

    c := sync.NewCond(&mu)

    mu.Lock()
    for !condition() {     // ALWAYS a loop, never an if
        c.Wait()           // atomically unlocks, sleeps, relocks
    }
    ... use the state ...
    mu.Unlock()

    // the side that changes the state:
    mu.Lock(); change(); mu.Unlock()
    c.Signal()             // wake ONE waiter
    c.Broadcast()          // wake ALL waiters

▸  WHY THE LOOP
A woken goroutine must re-check: another goroutine may have consumed
the state first, and wakeups can be spurious.

▸  WHEN NOT TO
For a single event ('done'), close a channel - simpler. Cond shines
when many goroutines wait on repeatedly changing state, and for
Broadcast: a channel can only be closed once, but you can Broadcast
many times.
lessons.expected: received 12 items, sum 1218 queue now 0

quiz.q: Why must c.Wait() be called inside a for loop that re-checks the condition?
options: Wait returns immediately the first time it runs
Another goroutine may have taken the item first
The loop is what actually unlocks the mutex
Signal wakes every waiting goroutine at once
quiz.explain: Being woken only means "something changed". By the time this goroutine re-acquires the lock, another may have taken the item. Re-checking in a loop handles that and spurious wakeups.
quiz.hint: Two consumers wake up for one new item...

lessons.title: sync.Pool: reusing short-lived objects
lessons.concept:
A sync.Pool caches allocated-but-unused objects for reuse, easing
pressure on the garbage collector (Concurrency in Go ch.3, 100 Go
Mistakes #96):

    var bufPool = sync.Pool{
        New: func() any { return new(bytes.Buffer) },
    }
    buf := bufPool.Get().(*bytes.Buffer)
    buf.Reset()                 // objects come back DIRTY
    ... use buf ...
    bufPool.Put(buf)

▸  RULES
    - Always Reset an object you Get: it holds old data.
    - The pool may drop items at ANY garbage collection. It's a cache,
      not a free list - never rely on getting the same object back.
    - Don't pool huge objects of varying size: one 10 MB buffer put
      back keeps 10 MB alive for every future small use. Cap the size
      you return to the pool.
    - Pool objects that are expensive to allocate and used briefly:
      buffers in a hot encoding path, per-request scratch space.

▸  MEASURE FIRST
A pool adds complexity. Use it when a benchmark or profile shows
allocations in a hot path (fmt and encoding/json use pools
internally).

• ada #1
  • bob #2
    • 1002 renders, buffers allocated far fewer: true

quiz.q: What must you do with an object you Get from a sync.Pool?
options: Free it with runtime.GC after use
Nothing - Get always returns a fresh object
Lock it before using it
Reset it, since it may contain old data
quiz.explain: Get returns either a new object or one somebody Put back - still holding whatever it had. Reset (or overwrite) it before use, or old data leaks between requests.
quiz.hint: Where did the object come from?

lessons.title: sync.Map and sharded maps
lessons.concept:
sync.Map is a concurrent map with methods Load, Store, LoadOrStore,
LoadAndDelete, Delete, Swap, CompareAndSwap, Range and Clear (1.23).

▸  IT IS NOT A GENERAL REPLACEMENT
The docs recommend it for two cases only:
    1. keys written once and read many times (a growing cache), or
    2. goroutines working on DISJOINT sets of keys.
Otherwise a plain map + sync.RWMutex is simpler, type-safe (sync.Map
stores any) and often faster.

▸  LoadOrStore: an atomic 'get or create'
    actual, loaded := m.LoadOrStore(key, newValue)
Exactly one goroutine's value wins; the others get the winner's. A
plain map would need lock / check / insert / unlock.

▸  SHARDING
When one mutex is the bottleneck, split the map into N shards, each
with its own lock, choosing the shard by hashing the key. Contention
drops roughly N-fold.

▸  Range IS NOT A SNAPSHOT
Entries changed during Range may or may not be seen.

quiz.q: Which situation is sync.Map designed for?
options: Keys written once and then read many times
Any map shared between two or more goroutines
Maps that need sorted iteration
Small maps updated constantly by every goroutine
quiz.explain: sync.Map optimises read-mostly, append-only caches and disjoint key sets. For general shared state, a map guarded by a (RW)Mutex is clearer and type-safe.
quiz.hint: The documentation lists exactly two use cases.

quiz.q: Why set a channel variable to nil after it is closed, inside a for-select?
options: To let the garbage collector free it
A closed channel is always ready; nil disables the case
To make the next receive panic, signalling the end
Because closed channels cannot be read twice

lessons.title: Generators, or-done and the or-channel
lessons.concept:
Two small combinators from Concurrency in Go ch.4 that keep pipelines
leak-free.

▸  GENERATORS WITH A done CHANNEL
Every stage takes a done (or ctx) so it can stop:
    func repeat(done <-chan struct{}, vals ...int) <-chan int

▸  or-done: range over a channel AND respect cancellation
    for v := range orDone(done, ch) { ... }
Without it, every consumer would need a select with two cases; orDone
packages that select once.

▸  THE or-channel: combine several 'done' signals into one
    <-or(sig1, sig2, sig3)     // closes when ANY input closes
Useful when work should stop on whichever happens first: user cancel,
deadline, or upstream failure. (context.Context covers most of this
today; or-channel is how you'd build it, and is still handy for plain
signal channels.)

▸  take: only the first n values
    for v := range take(done, repeat(done, 1, 2), 5)

These compose: take(done, orDone(done, slowSource), 10).
lessons.expected:
[1 2 3 1 2 3 1]
orDone stopped after 4
or closed on the fastest signal: true

quiz.q: What does the or-channel return?
options: A channel that closes when ALL inputs have closed
A channel carrying values from every input
The first value received from any input
A channel that closes as soon as ANY input closes
quiz.explain: or combines done-signals: the result closes when the first of them closes, so you can wait for "any of these reasons to stop" in a single receive.
quiz.hint: Look at how long the demo waited.

lessons.title: Tee and bridge channels
lessons.concept:
Two more pipeline fittings from Concurrency in Go ch.4:

▸  TEE: split one stream into two
Like the Unix tee command - every value from in goes to BOTH outputs:
    out1, out2 := tee(done, in)
Useful when one stream feeds two consumers (process + audit log). Each
value is only released once both outputs have taken it, so the slower
consumer sets the pace.

▸  BRIDGE: flatten a channel of channels
Some producers emit a SEQUENCE of channels (one per page, per file,
per connection). bridge turns <-chan <-chan T into a single <-chan T,
reading each inner channel to its end before moving to the next:
    for v := range bridge(done, pages) { ... }

▸  THE TRICK IN tee
Inside the loop, both outputs get local copies of the channel
variables. After sending to one, set its local copy to nil, so the
next select iteration can only choose the other - the nil-channel
trick from earlier.
lessons.expected:
process order-1 | audit order-1
process order-2 | audit order-2
process order-3 | audit order-3
p1-a p1-b p2-a p3-a p3-b p3-c

quiz.q: In tee, why are local copies o1, o2 set to nil after a send?
options: To release the values to the garbage collector
To close the output channels early
So the next select can only send to the other output
Because a channel can receive each value only once
quiz.explain: Each value must reach both outputs exactly once. After sending on o1, nil-ing it disables that case, so the second iteration of the inner loop must send on o2.

lessons.title: Heartbeats: detecting stuck goroutines
lessons.concept:
A goroutine that deadlocks or hangs on I/O fails SILENTLY - it simply
stops producing. Heartbeats make health visible (Concurrency in Go
ch.5):

▸  THE IDEA
The worker sends a pulse on a heartbeat channel - on an interval, or
once per unit of work. A supervisor waits for pulses with a timeout;
if none arrives in time, the worker is declared unhealthy and can be
restarted ('healing unhealthy goroutines').

    select {
    case <-heartbeat:          // alive
    case <-time.After(timeout):
        // stuck: cancel it and start a fresh one
    }

▸  SEND PULSES WITHOUT BLOCKING
If nobody is listening, a pulse must not stall the worker:
    select { case heartbeat <- struct{}{}: default: }
with a buffer of 1, so one pending pulse is kept.

▸  ALSO USEFUL IN TESTS
Waiting for the first heartbeat tells a test the goroutine has really
started - deterministic, with no sleep.
lessons.expected:
pulse: finished job 1
pulse: finished job 2
pulse: finished job 3
no heartbeat for 100ms - worker is stuck; restarting
new worker pulse: job 5

quiz.q: Why does the worker send heartbeats with a select that has a default case?
options: So a missing listener never blocks the real work
To send each pulse twice
Because heartbeat channels must be unbuffered
To make the supervisor time out faster
quiz.explain: The heartbeat is advisory. If the supervisor is busy and the buffer is full, dropping a pulse is fine; blocking the worker on its own health report would be absurd.
quiz.hint: What if nobody is reading the heartbeat channel?

lessons.title: Replicated requests: first response wins
lessons.concept:
When latency matters more than load, send the SAME request to several
replicas and take the first answer (Concurrency in Go ch.5). Google's
'The Tail at Scale' showed this tames slow outliers dramatically.

    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(parent)
    defer cancel()                       // stop the losers
    results := make(chan Result, n)      // buffered: losers never block
    for _, r := range replicas {
        go func() { results <- r.Do(ctx) }()
    }
    first := <-results

▸  THE DETAILS THAT MATTER
    - Buffer the results channel to n, or losing goroutines block
      forever on their send (a leak).
    - Cancel the context once you have a winner so the others stop
      wasting resources.
    - Only replicate IDEMPOTENT requests (reads); never 'charge card'.
    - A gentler variant, the 'hedged request', sends the backup only if
      the first hasn't answered within, say, the 95th percentile
      latency.
lessons.expected:
answer from replica 1 | fast: true
losers cancelled: 4

quiz.q: Why must the results channel be buffered with room for every replica?
options: Unbuffered channels are too slow for this
So losing goroutines can send and exit
The context package requires a buffered channel
To keep the answers in their arrival order
quiz.explain: After the winner is read, nobody receives again. With no buffer, every losing goroutine would block forever on its send - a goroutine leak per request.
quiz.hint: Who receives the second, third... results?

lessons.title: Duplicate suppression: a concurrent memo cache
lessons.concept:
gopl 9.7 builds a cache for a slow function f(key) that is safe for
concurrent use AND never calls f twice for the same key - even when
many goroutines ask for it at the same moment.

▸  THE INSIGHT: store an ENTRY, not a result
    type entry struct {
        res   result
        ready chan struct{}   // closed when res is set
    }

    m.mu.Lock()
    e := m.cache[key]
    if e == nil {                 // first request: we compute
        e = &entry{ready: make(chan struct{})}
        m.cache[key] = e
        m.mu.Unlock()
        e.res.value, e.res.err = m.f(key)   // slow, NOT holding the lock
        close(e.ready)                       // broadcast: it's ready
    } else {                      // someone else is computing
        m.mu.Unlock()
        <-e.ready                 // wait for them
    }
    return e.res.value, e.res.err

The lock is held only to look up / insert the entry, never during the
slow call, so different keys proceed in parallel.

▸  IN PRODUCTION
golang.org/x/sync/singleflight provides exactly this 'collapse
duplicate in-flight calls' behaviour (without caching forever) - the
classic defence against a cache stampede.
lessons.expected:
20 requests, slow calls made: 2
keys fetched in parallel: true
content of go.dev | calls still 2

quiz.q: Why does the memo store an entry with a ready channel instead of just the result?
options: Channels are faster to read than plain structs
To limit the cache to one entry per key
So later callers can wait for the first call
Because results cannot be stored in maps
quiz.explain: The entry exists as soon as the first caller starts computing. Others find it, see the computation is in progress, and block on ready instead of starting a duplicate call.
quiz.hint: What happens to the 2nd caller while the 1st is still fetching?

lessons.title: Hidden data races: append, maps behind locks, and formatting
lessons.concept:
Three races that pass code review (100 Go Mistakes #68-#70):

▸  1. append FROM SEVERAL GOROUTINES TO A SHARED SLICE
    base := make([]int, 0, 10)
    go func() { a := append(base, 1) }()
    go func() { b := append(base, 2) }()
Both write the SAME backing-array slot (spare capacity!) - a data race
even though each goroutine has its own result variable. Copy first:
slices.Clone(base) or append(base[:len(base):len(base)], x).

▸  2. RETURNING A REFERENCE FROM BEHIND A LOCK
    func (c *Cache) All() map[string]int {
        c.mu.Lock(); defer c.mu.Unlock()
        return c.m          // caller now reads the map WITHOUT the lock
    }
The lock protected the return statement, not the map. Return a copy
(maps.Clone) or iterate while holding the lock.

▸  3. fmt CALLING YOUR String() METHOD
fmt.Sprintf("%v", c) calls c.String(). If String() locks c.mu and you
call Sprintf while holding c.mu - deadlock. If String() reads fields
without locking - data race.

The race detector catches 1 and 2 when tests exercise them; design
catches all three.

quiz.q: A method locks a mutex and returns the internal map. What is the problem?
options: Maps cannot be returned from methods in Go
The mutex stays locked until the caller is done
The returned map is always empty for callers
Callers then use the map without the lock
quiz.explain: The lock is released when the method returns, but the caller still holds a reference to the same map. Every later read or write by the caller races with other goroutines. Return a copy.
quiz.hint: When is the lock released, and who still has the map?

"go test -race" Under the Hood - Kavya Joshi

lessons.title: When concurrency makes things slower
lessons.concept:
Concurrency isn't free, and it isn't always faster (100 Go Mistakes
#56, #59; Ultimate Go 'Goroutines').

▸  WHAT IT COSTS
Starting a goroutine (~a microsecond and 2-8 KB of stack), channel
operations (tens to hundreds of ns), lock contention, and cache-line
traffic between cores (false sharing - see Performance). If each unit
of work is tiny, the overhead dominates.

▸  KNOW YOUR WORKLOAD
    CPU-BOUND   (hashing, parsing, image work): parallelism helps up to
                about runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0) workers; more just adds
                scheduling overhead.
    I/O-BOUND   (HTTP calls, disk, databases): goroutines mostly wait,
                so far more than the core count is useful - limited by
                the remote side, rate limits and file descriptors.

▸  SPLIT WORK INTO CHUNKS
Don't start one goroutine per element of a million-element slice.
Give each worker a contiguous chunk, and fall back to sequential code
below a size threshold - parallel merge sort with a cut-off is the
classic example.

▸  MEASURE
Write the sequential version first, benchmark both (go test -bench),
and keep the concurrent one only if it wins on realistic inputs.

quiz.q: A function sums 100 integers. Making it start one goroutine per integer will most likely...
options: Make it about 100 times faster
Make it slower, because overhead dwarfs the work
Make it exactly as fast
Make it faster only on 100-core machines
quiz.explain: Adding two integers takes about a nanosecond; starting and synchronising a goroutine costs around a thousand times more. Parallelism pays only when each unit of work is large compared with its coordination cost.
quiz.hint: Compare the cost of one addition with starting a goroutine.

lessons.title: Deadlocks, livelocks and starvation
lessons.concept:
Three ways concurrent programs stop making progress (Concurrency in
Go ch.1):

▸  DEADLOCK - everyone waits for everyone
The four Coffman conditions must ALL hold: mutual exclusion, hold and
wait, no preemption, circular wait. Break any one to prevent it. The
classic case - two goroutines locking two mutexes in opposite orders:
    G1: lock(A); lock(B)        G2: lock(B); lock(A)
Fix: a global LOCK ORDER (always lock the account with the smaller ID
first), or hold only one lock at a time.
The runtime detects deadlock only when EVERY goroutine is blocked; one
stuck pair inside a busy server just hangs silently.

▸  LIVELOCK - everyone is busy, nobody progresses
Two goroutines repeatedly back off and retry in lockstep, like two
people stepping aside in a corridor forever. Fix: randomised backoff.

▸  STARVATION - someone never gets a turn
A greedy goroutine holding a lock for long stretches starves a polite
one. Go's sync.Mutex has a 'starvation mode': a waiter blocked more
than 1ms gets the lock handed to it directly.

▸  DIAGNOSING
A goroutine profile (/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2) shows every
goroutine's stack and how long it has been blocked.
lessons.expected:
1000 1000 2000
TryLock while held: false
TryLock when free: true

quiz.q: Two goroutines each hold one mutex and wait for the other's. Which fix removes the deadlock?
options: Use sync.RWMutex instead of sync.Mutex
Increase GOMAXPROCS so both can run at once
Acquire the locks in one global order everywhere
Add a time.Sleep just before the second Lock
quiz.explain: Deadlock needs a circular wait. If every goroutine locks resources in the same order, no cycle can form. RWMutex, more CPUs or sleeps only change timing.
quiz.hint: Which Coffman condition can you break with discipline?

lessons.title: Channel signaling semantics
lessons.concept:
Bill Kennedy (Ultimate Go 10.1) teaches channels as SIGNALS, chosen by
the guarantee you need:

▸  GUARANTEE OF DELIVERY: unbuffered
The sender blocks until the receiver has taken the signal. The sender
KNOWS it was received. Cost: unknown latency - the sender waits.

▸  DELAYED GUARANTEE: buffered with capacity 1
The sender doesn't wait for this send, but will block on the NEXT one
if the previous signal hasn't been picked up - one step of slack.

▸  NO GUARANTEE: buffered with capacity N > 1
Senders don't wait, until the buffer is full. You trade knowing
'was it received?' for throughput. Size the buffer from a real reason
(the number of senders, a measured burst), not 'to make the deadlock
go away' (100 Go Mistakes #67).

▸  WITH DATA OR WITHOUT
    with data      ch <- v    one-to-one hand-off of a value
    without data   close(ch)  one-to-MANY broadcast ('done', 'start')

▸  NAMED PATTERNS
wait for result, wait for task, pooling, fan out, DROP (non-blocking
send with select-default: shed load instead of slowing down),
cancellation (select on ctx.Done()).

worker got invoice-1
all started: [true true true]
queued 2 dropped 3

quiz.q: You must KNOW that the worker received a task before moving on. Which channel fits?
options: A buffered channel with capacity 100
A nil channel
A buffered channel used with select-default
An unbuffered channel
quiz.explain: An unbuffered send completes only when a receiver takes the value - a guarantee of delivery. Buffered channels let the sender move on before anyone has received.
quiz.hint: Which kind makes the sender wait for the receiver?

lessons.title: Context mistakes: detaching, values and cancellation causes
lessons.concept:
Contexts are easy to misuse (100 Go Mistakes #60-#61):

▸  1. PROPAGATING A CONTEXT THAT WILL BE CANCELLED
A handler starts background work with r.Context(); the request
finishes, its context is cancelled, and the background job dies with
it. Detach it (Go 1.21):
    bg := context.WithoutCancel(r.Context())   // keeps VALUES, drops
                                               // cancellation and deadline
    go audit(bg, event)

▸  2. STORING CONTEXTS IN STRUCTS
Pass ctx as the first PARAMETER of each call; a struct field ties the
context's lifetime to the object's, which is rarely right.

▸  3. WithValue FOR PARAMETERS
Request-scoped data only (trace IDs, the authenticated user), with an
unexported key type. Never optional function arguments.

▸  4. LOSING THE REASON
ctx.Err() only says Canceled or DeadlineExceeded. Record WHY:
    ctx, cancel := context.WithCancelCause(parent)
    cancel(ErrShutdown)          ... context.Cause(ctx) == ErrShutdown
    context.WithTimeoutCause(parent, d, ErrSlowUpstream)  (Go 1.21)

▸  5. FORGETTING CLEANUP HOOKS
context.AfterFunc(ctx, f) (Go 1.21) runs f once ctx is done - useful
for closing a resource when a request is cancelled.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"time"
)

type key int

const requestID key = 0

var ErrSlowUpstream = errors.New("upstream too slow")

func main() {
	reqCtx, cancelReq := context.WithCancel(context.WithValue(context.Background(), requestID, "r-42"))

	detached := context.WithoutCancel(reqCtx) // keeps values, not cancellation
	cancelReq()                               // the request finished
	fmt.Println("request ctx:", reqCtx.Err())
	fmt.Println("detached ctx:", detached.Err(), detached.Value(requestID))

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(context.Background(), 10*time.Millisecond, ErrSlowUpstream)
	defer cancel()
	cleaned := make(chan struct{})
	context.AfterFunc(ctx, func() { close(cleaned) })
	<-ctx.Done()
	<-cleaned
	fmt.Println("err:", ctx.Err(), "| cause:", context.Cause(ctx))
}

request ctx: context canceled
detached ctx: <nil> r-42
err: context deadline exceeded | cause: upstream too slow

lessons.title: Error propagation in concurrent pipelines
lessons.concept:
A goroutine can't return an error to whoever started it. Where should
errors go? (Concurrency in Go ch.4 'Error Handling')

▸  DON'T HANDLE THEM WHERE YOU CAN'T DECIDE
A worker that just logs and continues hides failures from the code
that has the context to react (retry? abort? report to the user?).

▸  SEND RESULTS THAT CARRY ERRORS
    type Result struct {
        Value Response
        Err   error
    }
    results <- Result{Err: err}
The consumer - which knows the whole picture - decides: skip it, stop
after N failures, or cancel everything.

▸  OR USE errgroup
When the first failure should cancel the rest, errgroup (Concurrency
Patterns module) is exactly this.

▸  KEEP ERRORS DESCRIPTIVE
Wrap with the INPUT that failed ("fetch %s: %w") - in a concurrent
system the message is often all you have.

sum of valid inputs: 70
failures: 3
too many failures - the consumer decides to abort
true

options: To a log only - the consumer does not need it
Nowhere - goroutines should panic on errors
Into a package-level error variable
Back to the consumer, alongside the result
quiz.explain: Only the code coordinating the work has enough context to decide what an error means. Bundling errors with results keeps that decision there.

lessons.title: Queues, buffers and Little's Law
lessons.concept:
When should you add a queue (a buffered channel, a job table)?
(Concurrency in Go ch.4 'Queuing'; 100 Go Mistakes #67.)

▸  QUEUES DON'T MAKE A PIPELINE FASTER
They decouple stages so a fast stage isn't held back by a momentarily
slow one. If a downstream stage is SLOWER on average, any queue in
front of it simply fills up - adding latency and memory, and only
delaying the moment you have to apply back-pressure.

▸  LITTLE'S LAW
    L = λ × W
    L  average number of items in the system (queue + in service)
    λ  average arrival rate
    W  average time an item spends in the system
At 200 requests/s and 50 ms each, about 10 requests are in flight; a
worker pool of ~10-15 keeps up. If λ grows to 400/s, either W must
halve or L doubles - the queue grows.

▸  WHERE QUEUES HELP
    - absorbing short BURSTS (size the buffer to the burst)
    - batching (writing 100 rows at once is cheaper than 100 writes)
    - smoothing a stage with variable latency
Put them at the ENTRANCE of the pipeline, where you can reject work
early (429) instead of deep inside where work is half done.

▸  UNBOUNDED QUEUES ARE A BUG
Every queue needs a bound and a policy for 'full': block (back-
pressure), drop, or reject.

quiz.q: A service receives 100 req/s and each takes 200 ms. By Little's Law, about how many requests are in flight?
quiz.explain: L = λ × W = 100/s × 0.2 s = 20 requests in the system on average. Fewer workers than that and a queue will build up.
quiz.hint: Multiply the arrival rate by the time in the system.

lessons.title: The optimisation workflow: measure, then change one thing
lessons.concept:
'Premature optimisation is the root of all evil' - Knuth. In Go the
tools make the disciplined path easy (Ultimate Go 1.2-1.3):

    1. Make it CORRECT, with tests.
    2. Decide what 'fast enough' means (a latency target, a throughput,
       a memory ceiling). No target, no optimisation.
    3. MEASURE realistically: benchmarks for functions, load tests for
       services.
    4. PROFILE to find where time and memory actually go - intuition is
       wrong about hot spots surprisingly often.
    5. Change ONE thing; re-run the benchmark; compare with benchstat
       over -count=10 runs.
    6. Keep the change only if it is a real win AND worth the extra
       complexity.

▸  WHERE THE WINS USUALLY ARE
    - Algorithms and data structures (O(n²) -> O(n log n)) beat any
      micro-optimisation.
    - Fewer allocations (less GC work).
    - Fewer round trips: batch database and network calls.
    - Better memory layout (cache-friendly access).

▸  THE TOOLBOX
go test -bench, -benchmem, -cpuprofile, -memprofile; go tool pprof;
go tool trace; GODEBUG=gctrace=1; -gcflags=-m (escape analysis);
PGO. The following lessons cover each.

Adding goroutines to every function
Profiling to find where time is really spent
Switching every map to a slice
quiz.explain: Profiles show the actual hot spots. Optimising code that accounts for 2% of run time can never make the program more than 2% faster, however clever the change.

lessons.title: Counting allocations with testing.AllocsPerRun
lessons.concept:
Each heap allocation costs time now and garbage-collection work later.
testing.AllocsPerRun(n, f) runs f n times and reports the average
number of heap allocations - usable even outside tests, which makes it
a precise teaching tool.

▸  TECHNIQUES THAT REMOVE ALLOCATIONS (100 Go Mistakes #21, #27, #96)
    - Preallocate: make([]T, 0, n), make(map[K]V, n) when n is known.
    - strconv.Itoa / AppendInt instead of fmt.Sprintf for numbers.
    - strings.Builder (with Grow) instead of += in loops.
    - Append into a caller-provided buffer: AppendXxx(dst []byte, ...)
      APIs (strconv.AppendInt, time.AppendFormat) reuse memory.
    - Return values instead of pointers when the value is small (it can
      stay on the stack).
    - Avoid converting []byte <-> string back and forth.
    - sync.Pool for hot, short-lived buffers.

▸  INTERFACES CAN ALLOCATE
Storing a non-pointer value in an interface (passing an int to
fmt.Println's ...any) usually allocates. Small integers 0-255 and
zero values are special-cased.

Allocation counts are deterministic for a given Go version (they can
shift slightly between releases as the compiler improves).

lessons.title: Stack vs heap in practice
lessons.concept:
Escape analysis (Pointers module) decides whether a value lives on the
cheap goroutine stack or the garbage-collected heap (100 Go Mistakes
#95). You can see the decisions:

    go build -gcflags=-m ./...
    ./main.go:12:9: &Point{...} escapes to heap
    ./main.go:18:7: p does not escape

▸  COMMON ESCAPES
    - returning a pointer to a local:      return &T{...}
    - storing into an interface: fmt.Println(x), any(x)
    - captured by a closure that outlives the function (go func, a
      returned func)
    - slices or maps whose size isn't known at compile time, or that
      are too big for the stack
    - sending a pointer on a channel

▸  'SHARING DOWN' vs 'SHARING UP' (Ultimate Go)
Passing a pointer DOWN the call stack (f(&x)) usually stays on the
stack; returning a pointer UP (return &x) escapes. When a struct is
small, returning it by value is often faster than returning a pointer.

▸  DON'T OBSESS
The heap isn't bad - it's where long-lived data belongs. Look at
escapes only in hot paths a profile has pointed you to.

return value up:   0

box in interface:   0

Returning a copy of it by value
Returning its address from the function

lessons.title: CPU caches and data-oriented design
lessons.concept:
Main memory is ~100x slower than the CPU's L1 cache. Data arrives in
64-byte CACHE LINES, and the CPU prefetches sequential lines. So HOW
you lay out and walk memory can matter more than how many instructions
you run (Ultimate Go 3.1 'Data-Oriented Design', 100 Go Mistakes #91).

▸  PREDICTABLE ACCESS WINS
Walking a slice front to back is as fast as memory gets. Following
pointers through a linked list or tree hops around memory and stalls
on each miss.

▸  ROW-MAJOR TRAVERSAL
A [N][N]int is stored row by row. Looping 'for i { for j { a[i][j] } }'
is sequential; swapping the loops jumps N*8 bytes each step.

▸  STRUCT OF ARRAYS vs ARRAY OF STRUCTS
If a hot loop reads ONE field of a big struct, every cache line also
drags in the fields you don't need:
    []Particle{X, Y, Z, VX, VY, VZ, Mass, Name...}    // AoS
    struct{ X, Y, Z []float64; ... }                   // SoA
SoA packs exactly the bytes the loop reads.

The timings below vary by machine (so this lesson isn't graded); the
RATIO is the lesson. Run it a few times.

quiz.q: Why can summing one field of a slice of large structs be slower than summing a []float64?
options: Struct fields are always stored on the heap
Each cache line also loads fields the loop never uses
Go cannot inline loops over structs
float64 fields in structs are converted on read
quiz.explain: Memory moves in 64-byte lines. With 150-byte structs, each X costs at least one full line of mostly-unused bytes; a dense []float64 delivers 8 useful values per line.
quiz.hint: How many useful bytes does each 64-byte cache line carry?

lessons.title: False sharing and padding
lessons.concept:
Two goroutines writing DIFFERENT variables can still slow each other
down if the variables sit on the SAME cache line (100 Go Mistakes #92,
Ultimate Go 9.1).

▸  WHY
Caches keep lines coherent between cores. When core A writes its
counter, the whole 64-byte line is invalidated in core B's cache, even
though B only uses the neighbouring counter. The line ping-pongs
between cores - 'false sharing'.

    type Counters struct {
        a int64       // goroutine 1 writes this
        b int64       // goroutine 2 writes this - same line!
    }

▸  THE FIX: PAD
    type Counters struct {
        a int64
        _ [56]byte    // push b onto the next 64-byte line
        b int64
    }
(golang.org/x/sys/cpu.CacheLinePad does this portably.) Or avoid the
shared struct: let each goroutine accumulate in a LOCAL variable and
write the result once at the end - usually the best fix.

▸  DATA ALIGNMENT (100 Go Mistakes #94)
Field order also changes struct SIZE through padding (unsafe lesson).
Ordering fields from largest to smallest minimises waste.

Timings vary by machine; this demo isn't graded.

quiz.q: Two goroutines increment two DIFFERENT int64 fields next to each other. What slows them down?
options: Both fields share one cache line between cores
A data race on the two struct fields
The garbage collector scanning the struct
Go serialises all writes to the same struct
quiz.explain: This is false sharing: no data race (the fields are distinct), but cache coherence forces the line containing both fields back and forth between the cores on every write.
quiz.hint: What is the unit the CPU caches in?

lessons.title: Profiling with pprof
lessons.concept:
pprof tells you where CPU time and memory actually go (gopl 11.5,
Ultimate Go 14, 100 Go Mistakes #98).

▸  FROM TESTS (easiest)
    go test -bench=. -cpuprofile=cpu.out -memprofile=mem.out
    go tool pprof cpu.out
    (pprof) top10             the hottest functions
    (pprof) list parseLine    annotated source with per-line costs
    (pprof) web               a call graph in the browser
    go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.out    a full web UI with flame graphs

▸  FROM A PROGRAM
    f, _ := os.Create("cpu.out")
    pprof.StartCPUProfile(f); defer pprof.StopCPUProfile()
    ...
    pprof.WriteHeapProfile(memFile)

▸  FROM A RUNNING SERVER
    import _ "net/http/pprof"     // registers /debug/pprof/ handlers
    go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
    .../debug/pprof/heap, /goroutine, /mutex, /block
Serve it on a separate, internal-only port - never on the public one.

▸  PROFILE TYPES
cpu (sampled 100x per second), heap (in-use and allocated), goroutine
(stacks - great for leaks), block and mutex (contention, need enabling
with runtime.SetBlockProfileRate / SetMutexProfileFraction).

The demo writes a CPU and a heap profile to a temp directory.

lessons.title: The execution tracer
lessons.concept:
A CPU profile shows WHERE time goes; the execution tracer shows WHEN
things happen, per goroutine, on a timeline (100 Go Mistakes #98,
Ultimate Go 14.5):

    - goroutine creation, blocking and unblocking (on channels,
      mutexes, syscalls, network)
    - which goroutine ran on which processor (P) and for how long
    - garbage-collection phases and their effect on your goroutines

▸  CAPTURING
    go test -trace=trace.out
    or in code:  trace.Start(f); defer trace.Stop()
    or from a server: /debug/pprof/trace?seconds=5
    go tool trace trace.out      opens the viewer in a browser

▸  WHEN TO REACH FOR IT
    - Latency spikes the CPU profile can't explain (goroutines WAITING
      rather than computing).
    - Poor parallelism: are all cores busy, or are goroutines
      serialised on a lock?
    - GC pauses and assist time.

▸  ANNOTATE
trace.WithRegion(ctx, "parse", f) and trace.NewTask label your own
operations so they show up in the viewer. Go 1.25 added a flight
recorder (trace.FlightRecorder) that keeps the last few seconds in
memory, so you can snapshot a trace right AFTER something goes wrong.
