lessons.title: Tuning the garbage collector: GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT
lessons.concept:
Go's GC is concurrent and needs little tuning, but two knobs matter
(100 Go Mistakes #99-#100):

▸  GOGC (default 100)
Run a collection when the heap has grown GOGC percent since the last
one. Higher = fewer collections but more memory; GOGC=off disables the
GC (only with a memory limit). debug.SetGCPercent at run time.

▸  GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19)
A SOFT ceiling on total Go memory. As the heap approaches it the GC
runs more often, so a container doesn't get OOM-killed. A common
container setup: GOMEMLIMIT about 90% of the container limit.
debug.SetMemoryLimit at run time.

▸  SEEING THE GC
    GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./app      one line per collection: heap sizes,
                                 pause times, CPU used
    runtime.ReadMemStats(&m)     HeapAlloc, NumGC, PauseTotalNs...
    runtime/metrics              the modern, stable metrics API

▸  GO IN CONTAINERS
GOMAXPROCS used to see all the HOST's CPUs, causing CPU throttling
under a container limit; Go 1.25 made it respect cgroup CPU limits by
default. Set GOMEMLIMIT yourself - Go does not read the container's
memory limit.

▸  THE BEST TUNING IS ALLOCATING LESS
Fewer and smaller allocations beat any knob.

GOGC=800 ran fewer collections: true
memory limit was unlimited: true
GOMAXPROCS: true

GOMAXPROCS=1

lessons.title: Inlining, bounds checks and PGO
lessons.concept:
▸  INLINING (100 Go Mistakes #97)
The compiler copies small functions into their callers, removing call
overhead and enabling further optimisation (including keeping values
on the stack). See its decisions:
    go build -gcflags=-m      'can inline add', 'inlining call to add'
Small, simple functions inline; large ones, or ones with certain
constructs, don't. A 'fast path' split - an inlinable function that
handles the common case and calls a big function for the rare one -
is how sync.Mutex.Lock stays cheap.

▸  BOUNDS-CHECK ELIMINATION
Every s[i] checks i < len(s) unless the compiler can prove it safe.
A hint before a loop can remove the checks inside it:
    _ = s[3]          // one check; then s[0..3] need none
    -gcflags=-d=ssa/check_bce shows remaining checks.
Only bother in measured hot loops.

▸  PGO: PROFILE-GUIDED OPTIMISATION (Go 1.21)
Collect a CPU profile from production, save it as default.pgo in the
main package directory, and go build uses it automatically: hot calls
get inlined more aggressively and interface calls are devirtualised.
Typical gains are 2-14% CPU with zero code changes. Refresh the
profile from time to time.

quiz.q: How do you enable profile-guided optimisation for a Go binary?
options: Add a //go:pgo directive above func main
Build every release with the -race flag
Set GOGC=pgo in the production environment
Save a CPU profile as default.pgo in main
quiz.explain: Since Go 1.21, go build picks up default.pgo from the main package directory (or a file given with -pgo) and uses it to guide inlining and devirtualisation.

lessons.title: Goroutines vs OS threads: the G-M-P scheduler
lessons.concept:
Why can a Go program run 100,000 goroutines when 100,000 OS threads
would crush the machine? (gopl 9.8, Ultimate Go 8.1-8.2)

▸  THREADS ARE HEAVY
An OS thread has a fixed stack (often 1-8 MB), and switching between
threads goes through the kernel (~1-2 microseconds).

▸  GOROUTINES ARE LIGHT
A goroutine starts with a 2 KB stack that grows and shrinks, and
switching between goroutines happens in user space (~100-200 ns).

▸  THE SCHEDULER: G, M, P
    G   a goroutine (its stack, state, instruction pointer)
    M   a machine: an OS thread that actually executes code
    P   a processor: a scheduling context with a local run queue of Gs.
        There are GOMAXPROCS Ps (default: the number of usable CPUs).

An M must hold a P to run Go code. Each P runs Gs from its own queue;
there is also a global queue. When a G blocks in a SYSCALL, its M is
parked with it and the P moves to another M so other Gs keep running.
When a G blocks on a channel or network I/O, it's simply set aside -
no thread is wasted (the netpoller wakes it when data arrives).

▸  YOU RARELY TOUCH THIS
runtime.GOMAXPROCS(n), runtime.NumGoroutine(), runtime.Gosched() (yield)
and runtime.LockOSThread() (for C libraries or OS APIs that care which
thread they run on) are the only knobs most programs ever need.

GOMAXPROCS >= 1: true
goroutines alive: 100001
stack per goroutine under 8 KB: true
all finished; goroutines now: 1

The runtime busy-waits on the socket
quiz.explain: Network I/O goes through the netpoller: the goroutine is parked and its M keeps running other Gs from the P's queue. When the socket becomes readable, the goroutine is made runnable again.

lessons.title: Work stealing and preemption
lessons.concept:
▸  WORK STEALING (Concurrency in Go ch.6)
Each P has its own run queue so most scheduling needs no global lock.
When a P runs out of work it STEALS half of another P's queue (and
checks the global queue and the netpoller). Work spreads itself across
cores without central coordination.

▸  WHERE A NEW GOROUTINE GOES
'go f()' puts the new G in the current P's 'runnext' slot, so a
producer/consumer pair often runs back-to-back on the same core with
hot caches.

▸  PREEMPTION
Before Go 1.14, a goroutine could only be switched out at function
calls, so a tight loop without calls could hog a P - and even stall
the garbage collector. Since 1.14 the runtime uses ASYNCHRONOUS
preemption: a background monitor (sysmon) notices a G running longer
than ~10ms and sends its thread a signal to stop it at a safe point.

▸  WHAT YOU CAN RELY ON
Nothing about ORDER. Which goroutine runs next, and on which core, is
deliberately unspecified. Correct programs synchronise explicitly; they
never depend on the scheduler being fair or prompt.

The demo pins GOMAXPROCS to 1 and starts a goroutine that never calls a
function - yet main still gets to run, thanks to async preemption.

The spinning goroutine is asynchronously preempted
The loop automatically calls runtime.Gosched
It cannot: the program hangs
quiz.explain: Since Go 1.14, sysmon detects a goroutine running too long and signals its thread so the runtime can preempt it at a safe point, even without function calls.

lessons.title: Growable stacks
lessons.concept:
Every goroutine starts with a small stack (2 KB today) that the
runtime GROWS on demand:

    1. Each function's prologue checks whether its frame fits in the
       remaining stack.
    2. If not, the runtime allocates a stack twice as big, COPIES the
       old one into it, adjusts every pointer into the stack, and
       continues.
    3. The GC can shrink stacks that are mostly unused.

▸  CONSEQUENCES
    - Deep recursion that would overflow a fixed-size 8 MB thread stack
      (Python, Java and C programs often crash here) often just works
      in Go. The default maximum is 1 GB on 64-bit
      (runtime/debug.SetMaxStack changes it); beyond that:
      'goroutine stack exceeds 1000000000-byte limit'.
    - Because stacks MOVE, Go can't hand a stack pointer to C code that
      keeps it - one reason for cgo's pointer-passing rules.
    - Pointers to stack variables are fine in Go code: the runtime
      updates them when the stack moves.

▸  THE COST
A copy on growth is O(stack size) but happens rarely (amortised, like
append). Very hot functions that grow the stack every call can show up
in profiles as runtime.morestack.

recursion depth: 1000000
max stack per goroutine: 1000000000 bytes

quiz.q: What does the runtime do when a goroutine needs more stack than it has?
options: Allocates a bigger stack and copies frames
Panics with a stack overflow immediately
Moves the oldest frames out to the heap
Switches the goroutine to a dedicated thread
quiz.explain: Go stacks are contiguous and growable: on overflow the runtime allocates a larger stack, copies the frames and fixes up pointers. Only exceeding the maximum (1 GB by default on 64-bit) is fatal.
quiz.hint: Think of append on a slice.

lessons.title: How channels work inside
lessons.concept:
make(chan T, n) allocates an hchan struct on the heap:

    type hchan struct {
        qcount   uint           // values in the buffer
        dataqsiz uint           // buffer capacity (n)
        buf      unsafe.Pointer // ring buffer of n slots
        sendx, recvx uint       // ring indexes
        recvq, sendq waitq      // goroutines blocked receiving / sending
        closed   uint32
        lock     mutex
    }

A channel VALUE is a pointer to this struct - copying a channel
variable shares the same channel.

▸  A SEND, STEP BY STEP
    1. Lock the hchan.
    2. A receiver is waiting in recvq? Copy the value DIRECTLY onto its
       stack and wake it (no buffer involved).
    3. Else, room in the buffer? Copy into buf[sendx], unlock.
    4. Else, park this goroutine on sendq and let the scheduler run
       something else; whoever receives later takes the value from us.

▸  CONSEQUENCES
    - Unbuffered channels are a direct hand-off between goroutines.
    - Every operation takes a lock: channels are fast (tens of ns
      uncontended) but not free. A mutex is cheaper for simply
      guarding a counter.
    - Values are COPIED in and out. Sending a big struct copies it;
      send a pointer to share instead (and mind ownership).
    - close wakes everyone on recvq (they get zero values) and makes
      any goroutine parked on sendq panic.

quiz.q: A goroutine sends on an unbuffered channel and a receiver is already waiting. What happens?
options: The value goes into a hidden buffer first
The sender blocks until the scheduler runs the receiver
The runtime allocates a new channel
The value is copied straight to the waiting receiver
quiz.explain: The send finds the receiver parked on recvq and copies the value directly into it, then marks it runnable - a hand-off with no buffering.
quiz.hint: Look at step 2 of a send.

lessons.title: How maps work inside
lessons.concept:
A Go map is a hash table managed by the runtime. A map VALUE is a
pointer to the table, which is why maps behave like references.

▸  SWISS TABLES (Go 1.24)
Go 1.24 replaced the bucket-and-overflow design with 'Swiss tables':
keys live in groups of 8 slots, each group has a control word holding
7 bits of every key's hash, and the CPU compares all 8 at once to find
candidates. Lookups and inserts got noticeably faster, especially for
large maps.

▸  WHAT THE DESIGN EXPLAINS
    - RANDOM ITERATION ORDER: iteration starts at a random position,
      deliberately, so nobody depends on an order the implementation
      may change.
    - ELEMENTS AREN'T ADDRESSABLE: &m[k] and m[k].Field = v don't
      compile, because growth moves entries in memory.
    - MAPS DON'T SHRINK: deleting keys frees entries for reuse but the
      table keeps its size (Language Mechanics module).
    - SIZE HINTS HELP: make(map[K]V, n) allocates enough room up front,
      avoiding repeated growth (100 Go Mistakes #27).
    - CONCURRENT WRITES ARE DETECTED: a flag in the table makes the
      runtime abort with 'concurrent map writes' - fatal, not a panic.
    - HASH FLOODING: each map uses a random hash seed, so attackers
      can't precompute keys that all collide.

quiz.q: Why does &m["key"] not compile in Go?
options: Map values are always copied to the stack
Strings cannot be used as map keys at all
Entries move when the map grows
Maps store only pointers, never the values
quiz.explain: The runtime relocates entries when the table grows. A pointer into the old location would dangle, so the language makes map elements non-addressable.
quiz.hint: What happens to entries when the table grows?

lessons.title: How interfaces work inside
lessons.concept:
An interface value is two machine words:

    non-empty interface (io.Reader):  (itab*, data*)
    empty interface (any):            (type*, data*)

▸  THE itab
For each (interface type, concrete type) pair the runtime builds an
itab: the concrete type's descriptor plus a TABLE OF FUNCTION POINTERS
for the interface's methods, in a fixed order. itabs are computed once
and cached.

▸  A METHOD CALL r.Read(p)
    1. load itab from r
    2. load fun[0] (Read's slot) from the itab
    3. call it with r's data pointer as the receiver
An indirect call: cheap, but it usually blocks inlining and makes
escape analysis assume the worst. PGO (Performance module) can
devirtualise hot calls whose concrete type is predictable.

▸  data* AND ALLOCATION
If the concrete value is a pointer, data holds it directly. Otherwise
the value is usually copied to the heap and data points at the copy -
why var a any = bigStruct can allocate.

▸  THE NIL INTERFACE TRAP, EXPLAINED
'iface == nil' checks that the type/itab word is nil. Storing a nil
*MyErr sets that word to *MyErr's itab, so the interface is non-nil
even though data is nil.

▸  TYPE ASSERTIONS
x.(T) compares the type word with T's descriptor - one pointer
comparison for concrete T. Asserting to an interface type looks up (or
builds) an itab.

quiz.q: Why is an interface holding a nil *MyErr not equal to nil?
options: Its type/itab word is set even though its data is nil
Pointers inside interfaces are never nil
The comparison calls the Error method
The runtime replaces nil pointers with zero values
quiz.explain: An interface is nil only when BOTH words are nil. Storing a typed nil pointer fills in the type word, so the comparison with nil fails.
quiz.hint: An interface value has two words. Which one is set?

lessons.title: The garbage collector in depth
lessons.concept:
Go's GC is a CONCURRENT, TRI-COLOUR, MARK-AND-SWEEP collector,
non-generational and non-moving (100 Go Mistakes #99).

▸  TRI-COLOUR MARKING
    white   not yet seen (garbage if still white at the end)
    grey    reachable, but its pointers aren't scanned yet
    black   reachable and fully scanned
Start with roots (globals, every goroutine stack) grey; repeatedly
blacken a grey object and grey its children; when no grey remains,
everything white is garbage.

▸  THE WRITE BARRIER
Because marking runs WHILE your program mutates pointers, the compiler
inserts a write barrier on pointer writes during marking, so a black
object can never hide a pointer to a white one.

▸  PHASES
    1. sweep termination + mark setup     short stop-the-world (STW)
    2. concurrent mark (uses ~25% of CPU via dedicated workers)
    3. mark termination                   short STW
    4. concurrent sweep (lazily, during allocation)
STW pauses are typically well under a millisecond.

▸  MARK ASSIST
A goroutine that allocates fast during marking is drafted to help mark
in proportion to its allocation - the GC's back-pressure. In profiles
this shows as runtime.gcAssistAlloc and is a sign to allocate less.

▸  GREEN TEA (Go 1.25 experiment, default in 1.26)
A redesigned marker that scans memory a page ('span') at a time for
better cache locality, cutting GC CPU for many programs.

▸  PACING
GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT (Performance module) decide WHEN a cycle starts.

quiz.q: Why does Go need a write barrier during concurrent marking?
options: To stop goroutines from allocating while marking
So black objects never hide white ones
To compact the heap once marking is done
To make every pointer write atomic for races
quiz.explain: The program keeps changing pointers while the GC marks. Without the barrier, a pointer could be moved from an unscanned (grey) object into an already-scanned (black) one, and its target would be wrongly freed.
quiz.hint: What could go wrong if the program moves pointers around mid-mark?

lessons.title: Cleanups and weak pointers (Go 1.24)
lessons.concept:
Two Go 1.24 additions let code cooperate with the garbage collector.

▸  runtime.AddCleanup(ptr, fn, arg)
Schedules fn(arg) to run some time AFTER ptr becomes unreachable -
e.g. releasing a C resource or an OS handle owned by a Go object. It
replaces runtime.SetFinalizer, which had sharp edges (it resurrected
the object, broke on cycles, allowed only one per object).
Rules: fn and arg must not reference ptr (or it never becomes
unreachable); cleanups run on a separate goroutine, in no particular
order, and may not run at all if the program exits first. Never rely on
them for correctness - an explicit Close is still the primary path.

▸  weak.Pointer[T]  (package weak)
    wp := weak.Make(obj)
    if p := wp.Value(); p != nil { ... }   // still alive?
A weak pointer doesn't keep its target alive. Value() returns nil once
the object has been collected. Ideal for caches that should never be
the only reason something stays in memory, and for canonicalisation
maps (the unique package is built on this idea).

The demo forces collections with runtime.GC so you can watch both
happen.
lessons.expected:
alive before: true socket-7
alive after GC: false
cleanup ran for socket-7

quiz.q: What does weak.Pointer.Value() return after its target has been garbage collected?
options: A zero-valued copy of the object
It panics with a use-after-free error
The last value, which stays cached
nil
quiz.explain: A weak pointer does not keep its target alive. Once the GC frees the object, Value() returns nil, so callers must always check before using the result.
quiz.hint: Look at the second line of output.

lessons.newhere: • runtime.KeepAlive - KeepAlive marks its argument as currently reachable.

lessons.title: Secrets and tokens from crypto/rand
lessons.concept:
Every secret value - session IDs, API keys, password-reset tokens,
CSRF tokens, salts, nonces, encryption keys - must come from a
CRYPTOGRAPHICALLY SECURE random source:

    import "crypto/rand"
    token := rand.Text()              // Go 1.24: base32, >= 128 bits
    key := make([]byte, 32)
    rand.Read(key)                    // fills from the OS CSPRNG
    n, _ := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(1000000))  // a 6-digit code

▸  HOW MUCH RANDOMNESS?
128 bits (16 bytes) makes guessing infeasible. Encode with
base64.RawURLEncoding or hex for use in URLs and headers.

▸  NEVER math/rand FOR SECRETS
Its output is predictable from a few samples (Standard Library module).
The course linter flags math/rand in files that mention tokens or
passwords.

▸  STORE TOKENS LIKE PASSWORDS
Keep only a SHA-256 hash of long random tokens in the database; compare
hashes when the token comes back. A database leak then exposes no
usable tokens. (Fast hashing is fine here because the token has 128
bits of entropy - unlike a human password.)

▸  COMPARE IN CONSTANT TIME
subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(a, b) == 1 (crypto/subtle) or hmac.Equal.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"encoding/base64"
	"encoding/hex"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
)

func main() {
	text := rand.Text()
	fmt.Println("rand.Text length:", len(text))

	raw := make([]byte, 16)
	rand.Read(raw)
	token := base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(raw)
	fmt.Println("URL-safe token length:", len(token))

	stored := sha256.Sum256([]byte(token)) // keep only the hash
	fmt.Println("stored hash:", len(hex.EncodeToString(stored[:])), "hex chars")

	presented := token
	got := sha256.Sum256([]byte(presented))
	fmt.Println("token valid:", subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(got[:], stored[:]) == 1)

	code, _ := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(1_000_000))
	fmt.Println("6-digit code ok:", len(fmt.Sprintf("%06d", code)) == 6)
}
lessons.expected:
rand.Text length: 26
URL-safe token length: 22
stored hash: 64 hex chars
token valid: true
6-digit code ok: true

quiz.q: Why store only a SHA-256 hash of a random reset token in the database?
options: A database leak then reveals no usable tokens
Hashes are shorter, saving disk space
SHA-256 makes the token expire automatically
It lets you recover the original token later
quiz.explain: Whoever reads the table sees only hashes, which cannot be turned back into working tokens. Because the token has 128 random bits, a fast hash is enough - brute force is hopeless.
quiz.hint: Imagine the users table leaks.

lessons.title: Storing passwords: slow, salted key derivation
lessons.concept:
Never store passwords in plain text, and never as a plain hash
(Let's Go 10.3). Humans pick guessable passwords, and GPUs compute
billions of SHA-256 hashes per second.

▸  USE A PASSWORD-HASHING FUNCTION
It is deliberately SLOW and uses a per-user random SALT:
    - argon2id   (golang.org/x/crypto/argon2) - the current OWASP
                 first choice; memory-hard
    - bcrypt     (golang.org/x/crypto/bcrypt) - very widely used,
                 simplest API: GenerateFromPassword / CompareHashAndPassword
    - scrypt     (x/crypto/scrypt)
    - PBKDF2     (crypto/pbkdf2, in the standard library since Go 1.24)
                 - acceptable with a high iteration count
                 (OWASP: 600,000 for HMAC-SHA-256)

▸  THE SALT
16+ random bytes, different for every user, stored next to the hash.
Two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed
'rainbow tables' become useless.

▸  STORE THE PARAMETERS
Save algorithm, iterations and salt WITH the hash
("pbkdf2-sha256$600000$<salt>$<hash>") so you can raise the cost later
and re-hash on next login.

▸  VERIFY IN CONSTANT TIME
Recompute with the stored salt and compare with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare.

This offline course uses the standard library's PBKDF2; in real
projects bcrypt or argon2id from x/crypto are the usual picks.
lessons.expected:
3 fields; same password, different hashes: true
true <nil>
false <nil>
false unknown hash format

quiz.q: Why does every user get their own random salt?
options: To make the password longer for the user
Salts encrypt the password reversibly
To speed up verification
So identical passwords produce different hashes
quiz.explain: With unique salts, attackers cannot precompute a table of common-password hashes, and two users sharing a password are not revealed by matching hashes. Each guess must be computed per user.
quiz.hint: Compare the two hashes of the same password.

lessons.title: Encrypting data with AES-GCM
lessons.concept:
When data must be SECRET (not just tamper-evident), encrypt it with an
AEAD cipher - Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data. AES-GCM is
the standard choice, built into crypto/cipher:

    block, _ := aes.NewCipher(key)        // key: 16, 24 or 32 random bytes
    gcm, _ := cipher.NewGCM(block)
    nonce := make([]byte, gcm.NonceSize()) // 12 bytes
    rand.Read(nonce)
    sealed := gcm.Seal(nonce, nonce, plaintext, aad)   // nonce || ciphertext || tag
    ...
    plain, err := gcm.Open(nil, nonce, ciphertext, aad) // err if tampered

▸  THE RULES THAT MATTER
    - NEVER reuse a nonce with the same key: GCM's security collapses.
      Random 12-byte nonces are fine for up to ~2^32 messages per key.
    - Authenticated: Open fails if a single bit of the ciphertext, tag
      or associated data changed. Don't use bare CTR/CBC modes.
    - Associated data (aad) is authenticated but not encrypted - bind
      the ciphertext to its context (a user ID, a record ID) so it
      can't be swapped into another record.
    - Keys come from crypto/rand or a KMS, never from a password
      directly (derive with a KDF), and never live in source code.

▸  DON'T INVENT CRYPTO
Use these primitives as documented, or higher-level libraries
(age, NaCl secretbox in x/crypto). Go 1.26 added crypto/hpke for
public-key hybrid encryption.
lessons.expected:
plaintext 24 bytes -> sealed 52 bytes (12 nonce + 16 tag)
"card 4111 1111 1111 1111" <nil>
wrong context: cipher: message authentication failed
tampered: cipher: message authentication failed

quiz.q: What is the most dangerous mistake when using AES-GCM?
options: Using a 32-byte key instead of 16
Prepending the nonce to the ciphertext
Reusing a nonce with the same key
Passing nil associated data
quiz.explain: Repeating a nonce under one key lets an attacker XOR ciphertexts to recover plaintext relationships and forge authentication tags. Generate a fresh random nonce for every Seal.
quiz.hint: N-once: what does the name say?

lessons.title: Digital signatures with ed25519
lessons.concept:
HMAC (Web module) proves a message came from someone who knows a
SHARED secret. Digital signatures use a KEY PAIR: only the private key
can sign, but anyone with the public key can verify - ideal for
licences, software updates, webhooks and tokens checked by many
services.

    pub, priv, _ := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
    sig := ed25519.Sign(priv, message)          // 64 bytes
    ok := ed25519.Verify(pub, message, sig)

▸  WHY ED25519
Small keys (32-byte public key), fast, deterministic signatures (no
random nonce to get wrong - the flaw that broke the PlayStation 3's
ECDSA), and a simple API with no parameters to misconfigure. Prefer it
to RSA and ECDSA for new designs.

▸  STORING KEYS
crypto/x509 marshals keys to PKCS#8/PKIX DER; encoding/pem wraps them
in the familiar '-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----' text.

▸  SIGNING STRUCTURED DATA
Sign the exact BYTES you'll verify. If you sign JSON, sign the
serialised bytes you send - re-encoding on the other side can change
whitespace or key order and break verification.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"crypto/ed25519"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/x509"
	"encoding/pem"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
)

func main() {
	pub, priv, err := ed25519.GenerateKey(rand.Reader)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	fmt.Println("public key:", len(pub), "bytes, private key:", len(priv), "bytes")

	release := []byte(`{"version":"2.0.1","sha256":"9f86d081..."}`)
	sig := ed25519.Sign(priv, release)
	fmt.Println("signature:", len(sig), "bytes")
	fmt.Println("genuine verifies:", ed25519.Verify(pub, release, sig))

	forged := []byte(strings.Replace(string(release), "2.0.1", "6.6.6", 1))
	fmt.Println("forged verifies: ", ed25519.Verify(pub, forged, sig))

	der, _ := x509.MarshalPKIXPublicKey(pub)
	block := pem.EncodeToMemory(&pem.Block{Type: "PUBLIC KEY", Bytes: der})
	fmt.Println(strings.Split(string(block), "\n")[0])
}
lessons.expected:
public key: 32 bytes, private key: 64 bytes
signature: 64 bytes
genuine verifies: true
forged verifies:  false
-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----

quiz.q: When is a digital signature a better fit than an HMAC?
options: When every message is very short
When verifiers must not be able to sign
When the message itself must stay secret
When only one server is ever involved
quiz.explain: With HMAC, anyone who can verify holds the shared secret and can also forge. With signatures, verifiers have only the public key; only the private-key holder can sign. Neither one hides the message.
quiz.hint: Who holds which key?

lessons.title: Path traversal and os.Root (Go 1.24)
lessons.concept:
Serving or writing files named by users invites PATH TRAVERSAL:

    filepath.Join(uploadDir, name)    with name = "../../etc/passwd"

filepath.Join cleans the path - and happily climbs out of uploadDir.
Checking strings.HasPrefix on the result is error-prone (symlinks,
"/srv/up" vs "/srv/uploads-old"...).

▸  os.Root (Go 1.24): a directory you can't escape
    root, err := os.OpenRoot("/srv/uploads")
    defer root.Close()
    f, err := root.Open(name)          // fails if name escapes the root
    root.Create, OpenFile, Mkdir, Remove, Stat, Lstat, OpenRoot, FS()
The OS enforces the boundary (openat-style calls), including through
symlinks - the robust fix.

▸  OTHER HELPERS
    filepath.IsLocal(name)   (Go 1.20) is the path relative, not
                             escaping, and not a reserved name?
    filepath.Base(name)      keep only the last element
    http.Dir / FileServerFS  already reject '..' in URLs

▸  AND STILL
Generate your own stored file names (random IDs) instead of trusting
the client's filename, and limit upload sizes.
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"path/filepath"
)

func main() {
	base, _ := os.MkdirTemp("", "root-*")
	defer os.RemoveAll(base)
	uploads := filepath.Join(base, "uploads")
	os.Mkdir(uploads, 0o755)
	os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(uploads, "photo.txt"), []byte("ok"), 0o644)
	os.WriteFile(filepath.Join(base, "secret.txt"), []byte("TOP SECRET"), 0o644)

	attack := "../secret.txt"
	naive := filepath.Join(uploads, attack)
	data, _ := os.ReadFile(naive)
	fmt.Printf("naive Join reads: %q\n", data)

	fmt.Println("IsLocal:", filepath.IsLocal("photo.txt"), filepath.IsLocal(attack))

	root, err := os.OpenRoot(uploads)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	defer root.Close()
	if f, err := root.Open("photo.txt"); err == nil {
		fmt.Println("root.Open photo.txt: ok")
		f.Close()
	}
	_, err = root.Open(attack)
	fmt.Println("root.Open attack:", err)
}
lessons.expected:
naive Join reads: "TOP SECRET"
IsLocal: true false
root.Open photo.txt: ok
root.Open attack: openat ../secret.txt: path escapes from parent

quiz.q: What does filepath.Join("/srv/uploads", "../secret.txt") return?
options: An error, because the path escapes
"/srv/uploads/secret.txt"
"/srv/secret.txt"
"/srv/uploads/../secret.txt" unchanged
quiz.explain: Join cleans the result, resolving the .. - which walks out of the uploads directory. It is not a security boundary; os.Root is.

lessons.title: Validating untrusted input
lessons.concept:
Every byte from outside your process - HTTP bodies, headers, query
strings, files, environment, other services - is untrusted until
checked.

▸  PRINCIPLES
    - ALLOW-LIST, don't deny-list: accept the known-good shapes
      (^[a-z0-9_]{3,20}$) instead of trying to strip known-bad ones.
    - PARSE INTO TYPES at the boundary: strconv.Atoi with range checks,
      time.Parse, netip.ParseAddr, url.Parse + scheme check. Inner code
      then works with valid values only.
    - LIMIT SIZES: body bytes, field lengths (count runes with
      utf8.RuneCountInString), number of items in arrays.
    - CHECK ENCODING: utf8.ValidString before storing or echoing text.
    - CONTEXT-APPROPRIATE OUTPUT: escape for the destination - SQL via
      placeholders, HTML via html/template, shell via exec arguments
      (never sh -c), URLs via url.Values.

▸  INJECTION, ONE PATTERN
SQL injection, command injection, XSS and header injection all happen
when DATA is mixed into a string that another interpreter parses as
CODE. Every fix is the same idea: keep data and code separate.

▸  REDIRECTS
Never redirect to a user-supplied URL without checking it is relative
or on your own host - open redirects power phishing.
lessons.expected:
accepted {Username:ada_l Age:36 Next:/dashboard}
REJECTED:
username: 3-20 of a-z, 0-9, _
age: a number from 13 to 130
next: must be a local path
REJECTED:
username: 3-20 of a-z, 0-9, _
age: a number from 13 to 130
next: must be a local path

quiz.q: Why prefer an allow-list (e.g. ^[a-z0-9_]{3,20}$) over stripping dangerous characters?
options: Valid input can be fully described; attacks can't
Regular expressions are faster than string functions
Allow-lists automatically escape HTML for you
Deny-lists are not supported by the Go regexp package
quiz.explain: Attackers keep finding encodings and characters a deny-list missed. Describing exactly what is valid rejects everything else by construction, including attacks nobody has invented yet.
quiz.hint: Which list can be complete?

lessons.title: TLS: HTTPS servers and clients
lessons.concept:
TLS encrypts and authenticates connections (Let's Go 9.3-9.5).

▸  SERVING HTTPS
    srv := &http.Server{
        Addr: ":443",
        Handler: mux,
        TLSConfig: &tls.Config{MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12},
    }
    srv.ListenAndServeTLS("cert.pem", "key.pem")
Go's defaults are good: modern cipher suites, TLS 1.3 preferred, HTTP/2
enabled automatically. Get certificates from Let's Encrypt
(golang.org/x/crypto/acme/autocert), or terminate TLS at a proxy.

▸  AS A CLIENT
The default client verifies the server's certificate chain and
hostname. NEVER set InsecureSkipVerify: true in production - it
disables authentication entirely, making man-in-the-middle trivial. To
trust a private CA, add it to tls.Config.RootCAs instead.

▸  USEFUL EXTRAS
    - HSTS header: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000
    - mutual TLS: ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert for
      service-to-service authentication
    - Go 1.24+ supports the post-quantum hybrid key exchange
      X25519MLKEM768 by default

The demo starts an httptest TLS server, which creates a self-signed
certificate and a client (srv.Client()) that trusts it.

Falls back to an older TLS version silently
Makes the handshake faster but equally secure
Turns off all certificate and host checks

  • tls.ConnectionState.Version - Version is the TLS version used by the connection (e.g.

lessons.title: Denial-of-service defences: limits and rate limiting
lessons.concept:
Availability is security too. A Go service should bound every
resource a client can consume:

    - TIME: server timeouts (ReadHeaderTimeout, ReadTimeout,
      WriteTimeout, IdleTimeout), client timeouts, context deadlines.
    - MEMORY: http.MaxBytesReader, io.LimitReader, MaxHeaderBytes,
      caps on JSON array sizes and decompressed sizes (zip bombs).
    - CONCURRENCY: semaphores or worker pools instead of unbounded
      'go handle(x)' per item.
    - RATE: limit requests per client.

▸  TOKEN BUCKET RATE LIMITING
Each client has a bucket of N tokens that refills at R tokens per
second; each request spends one; an empty bucket means 429 Too Many
Requests. Bursts up to N are allowed, sustained traffic is capped at R.
In production use golang.org/x/time/rate (rate.NewLimiter(r, burst))
with one limiter per client key, and evict idle clients so the map
can't grow forever.

▸  IDENTIFYING CLIENTS
r.RemoteAddr is the TCP peer. X-Forwarded-For can be forged unless it's
set by YOUR proxy - trust it only from known proxy addresses.

The demo implements a small token bucket with an injectable clock so
the output is deterministic.
lessons.expected:
burst of 5:    [200 200 200 429 429]
other client:  true
after 0.5s:    true false
after 10s idle: 3 requests allowed

quiz.q: A token bucket has rate 2/s and burst 3. A client was idle for an hour. How many requests pass instantly?
options: 7200, two per second of idle time
3, the bucket is capped at the burst size
2, one second worth of tokens
1, buckets refill one token at a time
quiz.explain: Tokens accumulate at the rate but never beyond the burst capacity, so long idle periods cannot be saved up into a flood.
quiz.hint: Look at min(l.burst, ...) in the refill.

lessons.title: Supply-chain security and secrets hygiene
lessons.concept:
Most code in your binary is other people's. Go's module system has
strong defaults - know them and keep them on.

▸  WHAT GO DOES FOR YOU
    - go.sum pins the cryptographic hash of every dependency version.
    - The checksum database (sum.golang.org) is a public, append-only
      log: a module version can't silently change for one user.
    - The module proxy caches versions, so a deleted or re-tagged
      repository can't break or poison your builds.
    - Builds never run dependency code at build time (no install
      scripts); only 'go generate' runs commands, and only when YOU
      invoke it.

▸  WHAT YOU DO
    - govulncheck ./... in CI: reports known vulnerabilities in code
      your program actually calls (Toolchain module).
    - Keep dependencies few and maintained; read what 'go get' adds
      (go mod graph, go mod why).
    - Upgrade deliberately: go get -u ./... then run the tests; keep
      the Go toolchain current (security fixes ship in point releases).
    - Reproducible builds: -trimpath, pinned toolchain ('toolchain'
      line in go.mod), vendoring for air-gapped audits.

▸  SECRETS
    - Never commit secrets: load from env vars or a secret manager;
      scan history with gitleaks or similar.
    - Never log them: give secret types a String / LogValue that
      redacts (Logging lesson).
    - Rotate anything that leaked - deleting the commit is not enough.

quiz.q: What does the Go checksum database (sum.golang.org) protect against?
options: Dependencies containing known vulnerabilities
Secrets accidentally committed to your repository
A version silently changing for some users
Slow or failed downloads from GitHub servers
quiz.explain: It is a transparent, append-only log of module hashes. Every go command checks downloads against it, so a compromised server cannot serve different code for the same version without detection. Vulnerabilities are govulncheck's job.
quiz.hint: It records hashes, not CVEs.

videos.title: Vulnerability Management for Go - Julie Qiu
Go security pitfalls: lessons from Grafana Labs - Jeremy Matos

lessons.title: cgo: calling C from Go
lessons.concept:
cgo lets Go call C code (gopl 13.4). C code goes in a comment directly
above import "C" - the PREAMBLE:

    /*
    #cgo LDFLAGS: -lm          // linker flags (here: the math library)
    #include <math.h>
    static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }
    */
    import "C"                 // no blank line between comment and import!

    sum := C.add(2, 3)         // C.int
    r := C.sqrt(C.double(2))   // C types: C.int, C.long, C.double,
                               // C.char, C.size_t, *C.char ...
    n := int(sum)              // convert to Go types explicitly

▸  WHEN TO USE IT
Wrapping an existing C library (SQLite, libgit2, OpenSSL, GPU drivers)
or calling OS APIs that have no Go equivalent.

▸  THE COSTS (gopl 13.5)
    - Each Go -> C call costs tens of nanoseconds (vs ~1 ns for a Go
      call): never call C in a tight loop.
    - Builds need a C toolchain; cross-compiling becomes hard; static
      'copy one file' binaries are gone (CGO_ENABLED=0 restores them).
    - C code can crash the whole process with no Go stack trace, and
      the race detector and GC can't see inside it.
'cgo is not Go' (Go proverb): prefer a pure-Go library when one exists.

This lesson is built WITH cgo enabled and needs gcc or clang.

quiz.q: Where must the C code for cgo be written?
options: In a separate .c file only
In a comment immediately before import "C"
Inside a C { } block in main
In a //go:cgo directive at the top of the file
quiz.explain: The comment directly above import "C" (no blank line between them) is the preamble, compiled as C. #cgo lines in it set compiler and linker flags. Separate .c files in the package are also compiled.
quiz.hint: Look at the top of the example.

lessons.title: cgo: strings, memory and the pointer rules
lessons.concept:
Go and C manage memory differently: Go has a garbage collector and
moving stacks; C has malloc and free. Crossing the boundary has rules.

▸  STRINGS
    cs := C.CString(goStr)      // malloc's a NUL-terminated copy in C
    defer C.free(unsafe.Pointer(cs))   // YOU must free it
    gs := C.GoString(cs)        // copies a C string into Go memory
    b := C.GoBytes(ptr, n)      // copies n bytes
C.CString always allocates with malloc - forgetting free is a C memory
leak the Go GC will never clean up.

▸  THE POINTER-PASSING RULES (cmd/cgo docs)
    - Go may pass a pointer to Go memory to C only if that memory
      contains no other Go pointers.
    - C must not KEEP a Go pointer after the call returns (the GC may
      move or free it).
    - C memory (from malloc) is never moved or collected by Go.
GODEBUG=cgocheck=1 (default) catches common violations at run time.

▸  CALLBACKS AND HANDLES
To let C refer to a Go value long-term, pass a runtime/cgo.Handle - an
integer token - instead of a pointer.

▸  THREADS
A C library that keeps per-thread state needs runtime.LockOSThread so
the goroutine stays on one OS thread.
lessons.expected:
strlen: 17
GOPHERS IN C LAND
hello, ada
first element passed by pointer: 3

quiz.q: What must you do with the result of C.CString(s)?
options: Nothing - the Go garbage collector frees it
Convert it back with C.GoString to free it
Pin it with runtime.KeepAlive
Free it with C.free when you are done
quiz.explain: C.CString allocates with C malloc, outside the Go heap. The GC never sees it, so you must C.free it (usually with defer) or leak memory.
quiz.hint: Which allocator created the memory?

lessons.title: Talking to the operating system
lessons.concept:
Most OS interaction goes through PORTABLE packages:

    os           files, dirs, env, process info, signals (os.Process)
    os/exec      run programs                 os/signal   signals
    os/user      user and group lookup        path/filepath  paths
    runtime      GOOS, GOARCH, NumCPU

    os.Getpid(), os.Getppid(), os.Getuid(), os.Hostname()
    os.Executable(), os.UserHomeDir(), os.UserConfigDir(), os.TempDir()

▸  WHEN YOU NEED THE RAW SYSCALL
The syscall package is FROZEN; new code uses golang.org/x/sys/unix and
x/sys/windows, which track every OS's calls and constants:
    unix.Uname(&u), unix.Mmap(...), unix.Setrlimit(...), unix.Prctl(...)
fi.Sys() on an os.FileInfo exposes the OS-specific struct
(*syscall.Stat_t on Unix) for inode numbers, link counts and owners.

▸  REPLACING THE PROCESS
syscall.Exec(path, args, env) replaces the running program entirely
(no return on success) - what a shell's exec does (Go by Example:
Exec'ing Processes).

▸  PLATFORM-SPECIFIC CODE
Put OS-specific calls in files named x_linux.go / x_windows.go (or with
//go:build tags) behind one common function signature (Toolchain
module).

Output differs per machine, so this lesson isn't graded.

quiz.q: New Go code needs a Linux-specific system call. Which package should it use?
options: golang.org/x/sys/unix
syscall, which is frozen but still the recommended home
runtime/internal/syscall
os/exec with the strace command
quiz.explain: The standard syscall package is frozen and will not gain new calls. golang.org/x/sys/unix (and x/sys/windows) is maintained by the Go team and covers each OS completely.
quiz.hint: The syscall package docs say it is frozen.

• user.Current - Current returns the current user.
  • user.User.Username - Username is the login name.
  • user.User.Uid - Uid is the user ID.
  • os.CreateTemp - CreateTemp creates a new temporary file in the directory dir, opens the file for reading and writing, and returns the resulting file.
  • os.Remove - Remove removes the named file or (empty) directory.
  • os.File.Name - Name returns the name of the file as presented to Open.
  • os.File.Chmod - Chmod changes the mode of the file to mode.
  • os.File.Stat - Stat returns the FileInfo structure describing file.
  • fs.FileInfo.Mode - file mode bits

lessons.title: Go 1.18-1.20: generics, fuzzing and errors.Join
lessons.concept:
Old tutorials (and LLM answers!) often predate these releases. Know
what's available so you write current Go.

▸  Go 1.18 (March 2022) - the biggest change since 1.0
    - GENERICS: type parameters, constraints, any, comparable
    - FUZZING built into go test
    - WORKSPACES: go.work for multi-module development
    - strings.Cut / bytes.Cut, net/netip

▸  Go 1.19
    - typed atomics: atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T]
    - GOMEMLIMIT soft memory limit
    - doc comment syntax: links [pkg.Name], lists, headings
    - url.JoinPath

▸  Go 1.20
    - errors.Join and fmt.Errorf with multiple %w
    - slice -> array conversion [N]T(s)
    - context.WithCancelCause / context.Cause
    - PGO preview; bytes.Clone; strings.CutPrefix / CutSuffix
    - time.DateTime, DateOnly, TimeOnly layouts
    - math/rand auto-seeded (rand.Seed deprecated)
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"sync/atomic"
)

func Keys[K comparable, V any](m map[K]V) int { return len(m) } // 1.18

func main() {
	fmt.Println(Keys(map[string]int{"a": 1, "b": 2}))

	before, after, ok := strings.Cut("user=ada", "=") // 1.18
	fmt.Println(before, after, ok)

	var hits atomic.Int64 // 1.19
	hits.Add(3)
	fmt.Println(hits.Load())

	err := errors.Join(errors.New("disk full"), errors.New("retry failed")) // 1.20
	fmt.Println(strings.ReplaceAll(err.Error(), "\n", " | "))
	both := fmt.Errorf("save: %w and %w", context.Canceled, errors.ErrUnsupported)
	fmt.Println(errors.Is(both, context.Canceled), errors.Is(both, errors.ErrUnsupported))

	arr := [3]int([]int{1, 2, 3, 4}) // 1.20
	fmt.Println(arr)

	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancelCause(context.Background()) // 1.20
	cancel(errors.New("user logged out"))
	fmt.Println(ctx.Err(), "/", context.Cause(ctx))

	rest, found := strings.CutPrefix("v1.2.3", "v") // 1.20
	fmt.Println(rest, found)
}

disk full | retry failed

lessons.title: Go 1.21: min, max, clear, slices, maps and slog
lessons.concept:
Go 1.21 (August 2023) turned years of copy-pasted helpers into the
standard library:

▸  NEW BUILT-INS
    min(a, b, ...), max(a, b, ...)   for any ordered type
    clear(m) empties a map; clear(s) zeroes a slice's elements

▸  NEW PACKAGES
    slices   Sort, SortFunc, BinarySearch, Contains, Index, Insert,
             Delete, Compact, Reverse, Max, Min, Equal, Clone...
    maps     Clone, Copy, DeleteFunc, Equal, EqualFunc
    cmp      Compare, Less, Ordered (and cmp.Or in 1.22)
    log/slog structured logging

▸  ALSO
    - sync.OnceFunc / OnceValue / OnceValues
    - context.WithoutCancel, AfterFunc, WithDeadlineCause
    - PGO generally available
    - forward compatibility: the 'toolchain' line in go.mod, and go
      can download a newer toolchain when a module requires it
      (GOTOOLCHAIN)

quiz.q: Before Go 1.21, how did you get the minimum of two ints?
options: With the min built-in, the same as today
With math.Min, which accepted ints too
With slices.Min from the standard library
With an if statement or your own helper

lessons.title: Go 1.22: loop variables, range over ints, smarter routing
lessons.concept:
Go 1.22 (February 2024):

▸  PER-ITERATION LOOP VARIABLES
Each iteration of a for loop now has its OWN variable. Closures and
goroutines that capture the loop variable no longer all see the last
value - the most famous Go gotcha is gone (for modules with go >= 1.22
in go.mod).

▸  RANGE OVER INTEGERS
    for i := range 10 { ... }       // 0..9

▸  ENHANCED http.ServeMux
Method and wildcard patterns: "GET /posts/{id}", r.PathValue("id")
(Web module).

▸  ALSO
    - math/rand/v2 (rand.N, IntN, PCG and ChaCha8 sources)
    - database/sql.Null[T]
    - slices.Concat; cmp.Or
    - go vet: loopclosure check updated for the new semantics
lessons.code:
package main

import (
	"cmp"
	"fmt"
	"slices"
	"sync"
)

func main() {
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	results := make([]int, 3)
	for i := range 3 { // range over an int
		wg.Add(1)
		go func() { // captures this iteration's own i
			defer wg.Done()
			results[i] = i * i
		}()
	}
	wg.Wait()
	fmt.Println(results)

	var printers []func() string
	for _, name := range []string{"ada", "bob"} {
		printers = append(printers, func() string { return name })
	}
	fmt.Println(printers[0](), printers[1]())

	fmt.Println(slices.Concat([]int{1}, []int{2, 3}, []int{4}))
	port := cmp.Or("", "", "8080")
	fmt.Println(port)
}

quiz.q: Before Go 1.22, what would printers[0]() print in this lesson?
options: ada - the behaviour has not changed
An empty string, because name was reset
bob - both closures shared one variable
It would not compile at all before 1.22
quiz.explain: Before 1.22 the range variable was a single variable reused every iteration, so both closures captured the same name, which held "bob" after the loop. Since 1.22 each iteration gets a fresh variable.
quiz.hint: How many name variables existed before 1.22?

lessons.title: Go 1.23: iterators, iter.Pull and unique
lessons.concept:
Go 1.23 (August 2024):

▸  RANGE OVER FUNCTIONS (iterators)
for range accepts func(yield func(V) bool) and friends (Go Deeper
module). The library speaks iterators: maps.Keys, maps.Values,
maps.All, slices.All, slices.Values, slices.Backward, slices.Collect,
slices.Sorted, slices.Chunk.

▸  iter.Pull: turn a push iterator into a pull one
    next, stop := iter.Pull(seq)
    defer stop()
    v, ok := next()            // ask for one value at a time
Needed when you step through TWO sequences in lockstep (merging,
zipping), which a single range loop can't do.

▸  unique: canonicalising values (interning)
    h := unique.Make("eu-west-1")   // a Handle[string]
Equal values give equal handles, and comparing handles is a pointer
comparison - cheap equality for repeated strings like hostnames or
tags, with automatic cleanup when unused.

▸  ALSO
Timer/Ticker garbage-collected when unreferenced and unbuffered
channels (Standard Library module); go telemetry (opt-in); the
//go:linkname crackdown on reaching into the runtime.

[a b c]
[1 2][3 4][5]
ada 36
bob 25
true eu-west-1

quiz.q: What problem does iter.Pull solve?
options: Stepping through two sequences in lockstep
Making iterators run in parallel
Converting a slice into an iterator
Sorting the values of an iterator
quiz.explain: A range loop drives ONE push iterator. To advance a second sequence one value at a time inside that loop (zip, merge), Pull converts it into next()/stop() functions.
quiz.hint: Look at zip.

• iter.Seq2 - Seq2 is an iterator over sequences of pairs of values, most commonly key-value pairs.

lessons.title: Go 1.25 and 1.26: what changed most recently
lessons.concept:
These releases are newer than the Go 1.24 used to verify this
course's examples, so the code below is shown rather than run. Try it
if your toolchain is new enough (go version).

▸  Go 1.25 (August 2025)
    - testing/synctest is generally available: test timers and
      timeouts in a bubble with a fake clock (Concurrency Patterns).
    - sync.WaitGroup.Go:
          var wg sync.WaitGroup
          wg.Go(func() { work() })   // Add(1) + go + Done, in one call
          wg.Wait()
    - GOMAXPROCS respects container (cgroup) CPU limits by default and
      updates if the limit changes.
    - Experimental encoding/json/v2 (GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2) and the
      experimental 'Green Tea' garbage collector.
    - runtime/trace.FlightRecorder: keep the last seconds of trace in
      memory and snapshot them when something goes wrong.
    - go vet: 'waitgroup' (Add inside the goroutine) and 'hostport'
      (fmt.Sprintf("%s:%d") that breaks IPv6 - use net.JoinHostPort).

▸  Go 1.26 (February 2026)
    - new accepts an expression:  p := new(42)  or  new(compute())
      - handy for optional pointer fields.
    - A generic type may refer to itself in its own type-parameter
      constraints.
    - The Green Tea garbage collector is the default.
    - errors.AsType[T](err) - a type-safe, generic errors.As:
          if pe, ok := errors.AsType[*fs.PathError](err); ok { ... }
    - go fix was rebuilt around 'modernizers' that rewrite old idioms
      (interface{} -> any, hand-written loops -> slices functions).
    - reflect gained iterator methods such as Type.Fields().

▸  STAYING CURRENT
Read the release notes at go.dev/doc/devel/release twice a year, run
go fix after upgrading, and keep the 'go' line in go.mod in step.

quiz.q: What does sync.WaitGroup.Go (Go 1.25) replace?
options: The whole WaitGroup type, which is deprecated
The need to call wg.Wait() at the end
wg.Add(1) plus go plus defer wg.Done()
The errgroup package from golang.org/x/sync
quiz.explain: wg.Go(f) increments the counter, starts f in a goroutine and calls Done when it returns - removing the classic Add-inside-the-goroutine bug. You still call Wait.
quiz.hint: It bundles three steps into one call.

lessons.title: Go 1.27: generic methods, a new JSON engine and UUIDs
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Go 1.27 was released in August 2026, six months after 1.26. As with
every release, programs written for older versions keep compiling
and running. This lesson lists what is new. There is no code to run
here: the facts come from the official release notes at
go.dev/doc/go1.27, which is the place to check details.

▸  LANGUAGE: GENERIC METHODS
Until now only functions and types could have TYPE PARAMETERS (the
[T any] part). A method could use the type parameters of its own
type, but could not add new ones. Go 1.27 lifts that: a method may
declare its own type parameters. The release notes' example is in
math/rand/v2, where the generic function rand.N now also exists as a
method on *rand.Rand:

    func (r *Rand) N[Int intType](n Int) Int

So helpers can live on the type they belong to, instead of being
package-level functions.

Two limits remain:
    - a method declared INSIDE AN INTERFACE cannot have type
      parameters
    - a generic method cannot be the method that satisfies an
      interface

This changes the "method rule" taught in module 30.

▸  LANGUAGE: TWO SMALLER CHANGES
    - In a struct literal, a key may now be any valid field
      selector, not only a top-level field name. That lets you set
      a field that comes from an embedded struct directly.
    - Type inference also works when a generic function is assigned
      to, or converted to, a matching function type.

▸  STANDARD LIBRARY
    encoding/json/v2    a new JSON package: Marshal, Unmarshal and
                        stream variants, all taking options. By
                        default it REJECTS invalid UTF-8 and
                        duplicate object names. The old
                        encoding/json now runs on the new engine.
    encoding/json/jsontext   the low-level layer: Encoder, Decoder,
                        Token, Value
    uuid                generates and parses UUIDs (unique 128-bit
                        identifiers), with no outside module needed
    crypto/mldsa        ML-DSA signatures (the FIPS 204 standard): a
                        POST-QUANTUM algorithm, designed to stay
                        safe even against future quantum computers
    simd                experimental processor-vector operations,
                        enabled with GOEXPERIMENT=simd

▸  RUNTIME
    - Small allocations (objects under 80 bytes) are up to 30%
      cheaper, thanks to size-specialised allocation routines.
    - The goroutine LEAK PROFILE is now a normal feature:
      "goroutineleak" in runtime/pprof, and
      /debug/pprof/goroutineleak in net/http/pprof. It can miss
      some leaks, so it complements the habits from module 11.
    - Crash tracebacks show goroutine labels (for modules whose
      go.mod says go 1.27 or later).

▸  TOOLS
    - go fix gained new MODERNIZERS (automatic rewrites to newer
      idioms): atomictypes, embedlit, slicesbackward, unsafefuncs.
    - go doc accepts a version: go doc example.com/pkg@v1.2.3
    - go mod tidy merges duplicate require blocks in go.mod.
    - Fetching modules from bzr (Bazaar) servers is no longer
      supported.

▸  WHAT TO DO WITH THIS
Set "go 1.27" in go.mod when your toolchain is 1.27 or newer, run
go fix ./... and read the diff, and try the leak profile on a
long-running service.

quiz.q: Which of these is still NOT allowed in Go 1.27?
options: A method on a struct declaring its own type parameters
Setting an embedded struct's field by name in a struct literal
An interface declaring a method that has its own type parameters
Using encoding/json without importing the v2 package
quiz.explain: Generic methods are allowed on concrete types, but interface methods cannot declare type parameters, and a generic method cannot satisfy an interface method.
quiz.hint: Re-read the "Two limits remain" list.

lessons.title: The Go proverbs
lessons.concept:
Rob Pike's Go Proverbs (2015) compress Go's design philosophy into
one-liners. Learn what each one means in code:

    Don't communicate by sharing memory, share memory by communicating.
        -> pass data between goroutines over channels; confine state
    Concurrency is not parallelism.
        -> structure vs simultaneous execution
    Channels orchestrate; mutexes serialize.
    The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction.
        -> io.Reader has ONE method and is used everywhere
    Make the zero value useful.
        -> var mu sync.Mutex, var b bytes.Buffer just work
    interface{} says nothing.
        -> any discards type information; be specific
    Gofmt's style is no one's favorite, yet gofmt is everyone's favorite.
    A little copying is better than a little dependency.
    Syscall must always be guarded with build tags.
    Cgo must always be guarded with build tags.
    Cgo is not Go.
    With the unsafe package there are no guarantees.
    Clear is better than clever.
    Reflection is never clear.
    Errors are values.
        -> program with them: wrap, inspect, aggregate
    Don't just check errors, handle them gracefully.
    Design the architecture, name the components, document the details.
    Documentation is for users.
    Don't panic.

Most lessons in this course are one of these proverbs applied.

quiz.q: What does "a little copying is better than a little dependency" advise?
options: Copy a few lines instead of adding an import
Copy entire libraries into your own repository
Never use any third-party modules at all
Copy structs instead of passing pointers
quiz.explain: Every dependency brings its own dependencies, upgrades, security exposure and API churn. For a small helper, a few copied lines are cheaper to own than a module.
quiz.hint: Weigh a three-line function against importing a whole module.

lessons.title: Designing packages: names, boundaries and utility packages
lessons.concept:
▸  NAME BY WHAT THE PACKAGE PROVIDES (100 Go Mistakes #13)
Good: strconv, http, bufio, sql, user, invoice.
Bad: util, common, helpers, misc, base, shared - they say nothing and
become dumping grounds that everything imports.

▸  AVOID STUTTER
The package name is part of every reference: http.Server, not
http.HTTPServer; user.Store, not user.UserStore.

▸  ONE PURPOSE PER PACKAGE
A package should be describable in one sentence. Its exported API is a
promise: keep it small, export only what callers need, and put
implementation details in internal/.

▸  NAME COLLISIONS (100 Go Mistakes #14)
Don't name variables after packages you use:
    redis := redis.NewClient(...)   // now the package is shadowed
Rename the variable (client, rdb) or alias the import.

▸  DEPENDENCY DIRECTION
Packages form a graph with no cycles. Low-level packages (domain
types, storage) must not import high-level ones (HTTP handlers). A
cycle usually means a small shared package - or an interface in the
consumer - is missing.

▸  START SMALL
A single package main is fine until it isn't. Split when a part has a
clear name and a clear API, not in advance.

quiz.q: What is the main problem with a package named "util"?
options: It names no purpose, so unrelated code piles up
The name util is reserved by the go tool
Code in a utility package cannot be exported
Packages named util are slower to compile
quiz.explain: A name like util conveys no purpose, so unrelated helpers pile up and many packages import it, creating coupling. Name packages after what they provide (strconv, httputil-like specific names).
quiz.hint: What would you expect to find inside it?

lessons.title: Project layout: cmd, internal and when to split
lessons.concept:
There is no official layout, and the infamous 'golang-standards/
project-layout' repository is NOT an official standard (100 Go
Mistakes #12). Go's own guide (go.dev/doc/modules/layout) suggests
growing with the project:

▸  A SMALL COMMAND
    myapp/
      go.mod
      main.go
      main_test.go

▸  A PACKAGE (LIBRARY)
    mylib/
      go.mod
      mylib.go        package mylib
      mylib_test.go
      internal/       private helpers

▸  A SERVICE WITH SEVERAL BINARIES
    myservice/
      go.mod
      cmd/
        api/main.go       thin: parse config, wire things, run
        worker/main.go
      internal/
        store/            database access
        billing/          domain logic
        httpapi/          handlers and middleware
      migrations/         SQL, embedded with //go:embed

▸  PRINCIPLES
    - main packages are thin; logic lives in importable packages.
    - internal/ by default - you can always export later; you can't
      un-export without breaking users.
    - pkg/ is optional and adds a path segment for nothing; many
      projects skip it.
    - Organise by DOMAIN (billing, users) rather than by technical
      layer (models, controllers) as the codebase grows.

quiz.q: Why keep cmd/api/main.go thin?
options: main packages cannot contain more than 100 lines
Logic in main cannot be imported or easily tested
The go tool compiles main packages more slowly
cmd directories are ignored by go test
quiz.explain: Nothing can import package main, so code living there can only be tested through the whole binary. Put logic in internal packages and let main just wire configuration and dependencies together.
quiz.hint: Can another package import package main?

lessons.title: Interface pollution: discover interfaces, don't design them
lessons.concept:
Coming from Java or C#, it's tempting to give every type an interface
'for flexibility'. In Go that's INTERFACE POLLUTION (100 Go Mistakes
#5-#7, Ultimate Go 5.4).

▸  SYMPTOMS
    - An interface with exactly one implementation and no test fake.
    - The interface lives next to its implementation (producer side)
      and mirrors all of its methods.
    - Constructors return the interface instead of the concrete type.

▸  WHY IT HURTS
Indirection makes code harder to navigate ('go to definition' lands on
an interface), hides the real API, blocks adding methods (every
implementation must change), and prevents compiler optimisations.

▸  THE GO WAY
    - Return concrete types. Accept interfaces.
    - Let the CONSUMER define the small interface it needs, when it
      needs it - a second implementation or a test fake is the trigger.
    - Abstractions should be DISCOVERED from real use, not designed in
      advance: 'Don't design with interfaces, discover them.'

▸  LEGITIMATE PRODUCER-SIDE INTERFACES
When the library genuinely offers multiple implementations behind one
behaviour (io.Reader, hash.Hash, sql/driver.Driver) or needs a plug-in
point.

quiz.q: A package defines type UserService interface (10 methods) and a single userService struct implementing it. What is the usual Go advice?
options: Add more methods so the interface is complete
Make every method generic for flexibility
Move the interface into an interfaces package
Export the struct; let consumers define interfaces
quiz.explain: An interface with one implementation, declared by the producer, is pollution. Return the concrete type; each consumer can declare the two or three methods it actually uses.
quiz.hint: Who should own an interface in Go?

lessons.title: Generics or interfaces? Choosing the abstraction
lessons.concept:
Both let one piece of code work with many types. They answer
different questions (100 Go Mistakes #8-#9):

▸  INTERFACES: 'what can it DO?'
Use when code calls METHODS and the concrete types behave differently
(Shape.Area, io.Writer.Write). Values of different types can live in
one []Shape.

▸  GENERICS: 'the same code for any TYPE'
Use when the code is identical for every type and only the element
type varies: containers (Stack[T], Set[T]), algorithms over slices and
maps (Map, Filter, Max), channels of T. You keep full static types -
no type assertions, no boxing.

▸  SMELLS
    - any in an API because 'it can be anything' - the compiler can no
      longer help. Use a type parameter or a real interface.
    - A generic function whose body only calls one method on T: a plain
      interface parameter is simpler.
    - Type parameters 'for future flexibility' with one instantiation.
    - Type switches inside generic code to special-case types: the
      abstraction is wrong.

▸  RULE OF THUMB
Write the concrete version first. When you're about to copy it for a
second TYPE, reach for generics; when you need different BEHAVIOUR,
reach for an interface.

pear true

{R:2}

quiz.q: You need one slice holding squares, circles and triangles and a function that sums their areas. Which tool fits?
options: A generic function Sum[T Shape](xs []T)
A slice of any with type switches
An interface Shape with an Area method
reflect, iterating over struct fields
quiz.explain: The values have DIFFERENT types with different behaviour, mixed in one slice. That is exactly an interface: []Shape. A generic []T must hold a single type T.
quiz.hint: Can a []T hold three different concrete types?

lessons.title: Designing error APIs: values, types and behaviour
lessons.concept:
How should callers learn WHAT went wrong? Ultimate Go 6.1-6.4 lists
increasing levels of coupling:

    1. Just the message - err != nil. Callers can only log or return.
    2. SENTINEL VALUES - var ErrNotFound = errors.New(...);
       errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound). Simple, but each one is API.
    3. ERROR TYPES - *ValidationError{Field}; errors.As. Carry data,
       but callers now depend on your concrete type.
    4. BEHAVIOUR - an interface the error satisfies:
           type temporary interface { Temporary() bool }
       Callers ask 'can I retry?' without knowing any of your types.
       Many unrelated packages' errors can answer the same question.

▸  GUIDELINES
    - Export as few error values and types as callers truly need; each
      is a compatibility promise.
    - Wrap with %w to keep the chain inspectable; use %v at a boundary
      where you deliberately hide internals.
    - Handle an error ONCE: either log it or return it, not both
      (100 Go Mistakes #52).
    - Don't ignore errors silently; if you must, write _ = f() with a
      comment explaining why (#53).
lessons.expected:
upload: write: connection reset          retry=true
upload: quota exceeded for ada           retry=false
open config: file does not exist         retry=false

quiz.q: What is the advantage of checking an error for BEHAVIOUR (e.g. Temporary() bool)?
options: It is the only way errors.As can be used
It makes errors print shorter messages
It avoids allocating error values
Callers need not know any concrete error types
quiz.explain: An anonymous interface check couples the caller only to a method, not to a package's exported types. Errors from many unrelated packages can satisfy it.
quiz.hint: Which package does shouldRetry import?

lessons.title: init, globals and package state
lessons.concept:
Package-level state is convenient and costly (100 Go Mistakes #3).

▸  PROBLEMS WITH init()
    - It runs implicitly at import time; tests can't skip it.
    - It can't return an error - only panic or silently continue.
    - It forces global state (it can only set package variables).
    - Order across files depends on file names.

▸  PROBLEMS WITH MUTABLE GLOBALS
    - Hidden dependencies: a function's signature doesn't reveal it.
    - Data races when goroutines touch them.
    - Tests interfere with each other and can't run in parallel.

▸  ACCEPTABLE USES
    - Constants and effectively-constant values:
          var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
          var emailRE = regexp.MustCompile(`...`)
    - Registration that has no failure mode (image formats, database
      drivers via init - convention).
    - sync.OnceValue for lazy, read-only initialisation.

▸  INSTEAD
Create things in main and pass them down (previous lessons), or give a
type a constructor that returns an error.

quiz.q: Which is a reasonable package-level variable?
options: A precompiled regexp used read-only
A *sql.DB opened in init() that every function uses
A map of logged-in users updated by handlers
A counter incremented by many goroutines without a lock
quiz.explain: A regexp compiled once with MustCompile and only read is effectively a constant: safe for concurrent use and with no hidden mutable state. The others hide dependencies, can fail silently, or race.
quiz.hint: Which one never changes after start-up?

lessons.title: Documentation people actually read
lessons.concept:
Every exported name deserves a doc comment (100 Go Mistakes #15).

▸  THE FORMAT
A comment directly above the declaration, starting with the name:
    // Parse parses a duration such as "1h15m". It returns an error
    // if the unit is unknown.
    func Parse(s string) (time.Duration, error)

▸  PACKAGE DOCS
    // Package invoice computes and renders customer invoices.
    package invoice
For long docs, use a doc.go file containing only that comment.

▸  DOC COMMENT SYNTAX (Go 1.19)
    # Heading                   a section heading
    [time.Duration], [Parse]     links to other identifiers
    - item / 1. item            lists
    indented lines              code blocks
    // Deprecated: use [ParseV2].   tools and linters warn on use

▸  WHAT TO WRITE
What it does, what it returns in edge cases (empty input, nil),
whether it's safe for concurrent use, ownership of returned slices,
and the errors callers may want to check. Not HOW it's implemented -
that belongs in comments inside the body.

▸  EXAMPLES ARE DOCS
Example functions (Testing module) appear on pkg.go.dev and are
verified by go test - the best documentation there is.

Browse yours with 'go doc ./...' or 'go doc -http' (Go 1.25).

quiz.q: How do you mark an exported function as deprecated so tools warn users?
options: Rename it with a leading underscore
Begin a doc paragraph with "Deprecated: "
Add a //go:deprecated directive above it
Move it into an internal package instead
quiz.explain: A paragraph beginning with "Deprecated: " in the doc comment is recognised by gopls, staticcheck and pkg.go.dev, which then warn at every use.
quiz.hint: It is a documentation convention, not a directive.

lessons.title: Capstone: an expression evaluator
lessons.concept:
gopl 7.9 builds an arithmetic evaluator - a tiny interpreter. It
combines interfaces, recursion, maps and error handling.

▸  YOUR TASK
Evaluate expressions with + - * / ^, parentheses, unary minus,
variables and the functions sqrt, min and max. Precedence: ^ binds
tightest (right-associative), then unary minus, then * /, then + -.
Report errors (unknown variable, division by zero, syntax) instead of
panicking. Match YOUR TASK exactly.

▸  THE DESIGN
    1. LEXER: turn "2*(x+1)" into tokens: 2 * ( x + 1 ).
    2. PARSER: recursive descent, one function per precedence level:
           expr   = term   { ("+" | "-") term }
           term   = unary  { ("*" | "/") unary }
           unary  = "-" unary | power
           power  = atom [ "^" unary ]
           atom   = number | name | name "(" args ")" | "(" expr ")"
    3. AST: an Expr interface { Eval(env Env) (float64, error) } with
       num, varRef, unary, binary and call types.
    4. EVAL walks the tree.

▸  STRETCH
Add a String() method to every node to pretty-print the tree; check
for unknown functions at parse time rather than eval time.
lessons.expected:
1 + 2 * 3                    = 7
(1 + 2) * 3                  = 9
2 ^ 3 ^ 2                    = 512
-2 ^ 2                       = -4
pi * r ^ 2                   = 12.5664
sqrt(x*x + 16)               = 5
max(1, x, min(10, 7)) / 2    = 3.5
y + 1                        eval error: undefined variable "y"
10 / (x - 3)                 eval error: division by zero
2 * (3 + 4                   parse error: missing )
5 $ 2                        parse error: unexpected character '$'

quiz.q: In a recursive-descent parser, how is operator precedence expressed?
options: By sorting the tokens before parsing them
One function per level, each calling the next
By a lookup table consulted during evaluation
By evaluating left to right, then fixing it up
quiz.explain: expr handles + and - by calling term for its operands, term handles * and / by calling unary, and so on. Tighter-binding operators are parsed deeper, so they end up lower in the tree and are evaluated first.
quiz.hint: Look at which function expr calls for its operands.

lessons.title: Capstone: a concurrent log analyzer
lessons.concept:
Combine a pipeline, a worker pool, parsing and aggregation.

▸  YOUR TASK
Parse web-server log lines of the form
    METHOD PATH STATUS DURATION_MS
with 4 worker goroutines, and report:
    - total requests and the number of malformed lines,
    - requests per status class (2xx, 3xx, 4xx, 5xx),
    - the 3 slowest paths by AVERAGE duration (ties by path),
    - the error rate (5xx / total) as a percentage with one decimal.
Match YOUR TASK exactly.

▸  THE STRUCTURE
    lines -> [ 4 parser workers ] -> records -> aggregator (main)
    - A producer goroutine sends lines and closes the channel.
    - Workers parse with strings.Fields + strconv and send either a
      record or a parse error on separate channels... or one channel
      of a result struct.
    - Close the results channel after the WaitGroup finishes.
    - The aggregator (one goroutine) owns all the maps: no locks.
    - Sort for stable output.

Only the aggregating goroutine uses them

quiz.explain: Workers only send results; a single goroutine (main) receives them and owns every map. Confinement removes the need for locks entirely.

lessons.title: API responses: envelopes, errors and status codes
lessons.concept:
A JSON API is a contract. Make every response predictable:

▸  ENVELOPES

breaking clients:

    app.notFound(w, r)                 404
    app.badRequest(w, r, err)          400
    app.failedValidation(w, r, errs)   422 {"error": {"field": "message"}}
    app.serverError(w, r, err)         500: log the details, send a
                                       GENERIC message (never leak
                                       internals or stack traces)
    app.methodNotAllowed               405

▸  STATUS CODES CLIENTS RELY ON
200 GET/PUT/PATCH success, 201 Created (+ Location header), 204 No
Content (DELETE), 400 malformed input, 401 not authenticated, 403
not allowed, 404, 409 conflict, 422 validation failed, 429 rate
limited, 500.

▸  JSON DETAILS
Set Content-Type: application/json; consider json.MarshalIndent for
human-friendly APIs (slower, bigger); end with a newline for curl.

The full database error, to help them debug

A 404, since the data could not be found
quiz.explain: Internal error details (SQL, hostnames, stack traces) help attackers and confuse clients. Log them with context on the server; send a stable, generic message and a 500.

lessons.title: Filtering, sorting and pagination
lessons.concept:
List endpoints need query parameters, validated as carefully as
bodies (Let's Go Further ch.9):

    GET /v1/movies?genre=drama&sort=-year&page=2&page_size=20

▸  READ WITH DEFAULTS, VALIDATE, COLLECT ERRORS
    page      integer, 1..10,000,000, default 1
    page_size integer, 1..100, default 20
    sort      from an ALLOW-LIST: id, title, year, -id, -title, -year
              ('-' means descending). Never interpolate a raw sort
              value into SQL.
Return 422 with all problems at once.

▸  PAGINATION
OFFSET pagination: LIMIT page_size OFFSET (page-1)*page_size. Simple,
but deep pages get slow and rows can shift between requests.
KEYSET (cursor) pagination: WHERE id > last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n -
stable and fast; return an opaque 'next' cursor.

▸  METADATA
Tell clients where they are:
    "metadata": {"current_page": 2, "page_size": 20, "first_page": 1,
                 "last_page": 7, "total_records": 132}

▸  STABLE ORDERING
Always add a tiebreaker (usually the id) so equal sort keys don't
shuffle between pages.
lessons.expected:
""                        Casablanca(1942), Alien(1979), Heat(1995) | page 1/3 of 7 records
"sort=-year"              Dune(2021), Arrival(2016), Moonlight(2016) | page 1/3 of 7 records
"sort=-year&page=2"       Up(2009), Heat(1995), Alien(1979) | page 2/3 of 7 records
"genre=scifi&sort=title"  Alien(1979), Arrival(2016), Dune(2021) | page 1/1 of 3 records
"page=0&sort=rating"      422 map[page:must be an integer from 1 to 10000000 sort:invalid sort value]

quiz.q: Why add the id as a tiebreaker when sorting by year for pagination?
options: Databases cannot sort by the year column alone
It forces the query to use the primary index
Clients require the id field to be sorted
Equal years could swap order between pages
quiz.explain: Without a total order, rows with the same sort key may come back in any order, so a row can appear on two pages or none. A unique tiebreaker makes the ordering deterministic.
quiz.hint: Arrival and Moonlight are both 2016.

lessons.title: Partial updates with PATCH
lessons.concept:
PUT replaces a resource; PATCH changes only the fields the client
sends. In Go the challenge is telling 'field absent' from 'field set to
its zero value':

    {"title": "Up"}              update the title only
    {"runtime": 0}               set runtime to 0 (maybe invalid!)

▸  POINTER FIELDS IN THE INPUT STRUCT
    var input struct {
        Title   *string  `json:"title"`
        Year    *int32   `json:"year"`
        Genres  []string `json:"genres"`   // nil = absent
    }
A nil pointer means the key was absent; a non-nil pointer means the
client sent a value - even "" or 0.

    if input.Title != nil { movie.Title = *input.Title }

▸  THEN VALIDATE THE RESULT
Apply the changes to a copy of the stored record, validate the WHOLE
record, and only then save it.

▸  ALTERNATIVES
JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396: null means 'delete') and JSON Patch (RFC
6902: a list of operations) are standard formats - pointer fields
implement the simple common case.

quiz.q: How does a PATCH handler tell "year was not sent" from "year was sent as 0"?
options: By checking whether Year == 0 after decoding
By decoding into a *int: nil means it was absent
By reading the raw request body a second time
It can't - JSON cannot represent the difference
quiz.explain: A plain int is 0 in both cases. A pointer field stays nil when the key is absent and points at 0 when the client sent 0, so the handler can distinguish them.
quiz.hint: Which Go type has a "nothing here" value distinct from zero?
