lessons.title: Intervals and an LRU cache
lessons.concept:
▸  MERGE INTERVALS
Sort by start, then sweep: if the next interval starts before the
current one ends, extend; otherwise start a new one.
    slices.SortFunc(iv, func(a, b [2]int) int { return cmp.Compare(a[0], b[0]) })

▸  LRU CACHE (container/list + map)
A doubly linked list keeps entries from most to least recently used; a
map gives O(1) access to each list element:
    Get:  move the element to the front.
    Put:  update and move to front, or insert at front; if over
          capacity, remove the BACK element and its map entry.
container/list stores values as 'any', so you type-assert on the way
out: e.Value.(*entry). (For production, hashicorp/golang-lru adds
generics, TTLs and thread safety.)

▸  YOUR TASK
    1. Merge [[8 10] [1 3] [2 6] [15 18] [17 20] [6 7]] and print the
       result.
    2. An LRU with capacity 2. Do: Put(a,1) Put(b,2) Get(a) Put(c,3)
       Get(b) Put(d,4) Get(a) Get(c) Get(d). Print each Get as
       'get X: value ok' (value 0 when missing), then print the keys
       from most to least recently used as 'order: ...'.
lessons.expected:
[[1 7] [8 10] [15 20]]
get a: 1 true
get b: 0 false
get a: 0 false
get c: 3 true
get d: 4 true
order: d c

quiz.q: Why does the LRU cache combine a map with a doubly linked list?
options: The list keeps the keys sorted alphabetically
Map: O(1) lookup; list: O(1) reorder and evict
Maps cannot store more than a few thousand keys
The linked list is what makes it thread-safe
quiz.explain: Lookup needs the map; "move to most recent" and "remove least recent" need O(1) list operations. Neither structure alone gives both.
quiz.hint: Two operations, two data structures.

lessons.title: Gym: Luhn and ISBN-10 checksums
lessons.concept:
▸  YOUR TASK
Two checksum validators used in the real world:

LUHN (credit card numbers). Spaces are allowed and ignored; any other
non-digit, or fewer than 2 digits, is invalid. From the RIGHT, double
every second digit; if doubling gives more than 9, subtract 9. The
number is valid when the sum is divisible by 10.

ISBN-10. Dashes are ignored. There must be exactly 10 characters left:
nine digits, then a digit or 'X' (meaning 10) as the last. Valid when
    (d1*10 + d2*9 + d3*8 + ... + d10*1) % 11 == 0

Print 'input: true/false' for each, one per line:
    Luhn:  "4539 3195 0343 6467", "8273 1232 7352 0569", "0", "059a"
    ISBN:  "3-598-21508-8", "3-598-21507-X", "3-598-21508-9", "3-598-2X507-9"

quiz.q: In the Luhn loop, why is the string read from the right (s[len(s)-1-i])?
options: Go strings can only be indexed from the end
It avoids converting the string to runes
Reading from the left gives the same, slower
Doubling starts from the rightmost digit
quiz.explain: Luhn doubles the second, fourth... digits from the RIGHT. Numbers of odd and even length would be handled differently if you counted from the left.
quiz.hint: Try a 3-digit and a 4-digit number.

lessons.title: Gym: a Clock value type
lessons.concept:
▸  YOUR TASK
Design a Clock that handles times without dates:

    func New(h, m int) Clock         - any ints, even negative or huge;
                                       New(25, 0) is 01:00, New(0, -1) is 23:59
    func (c Clock) Add(min int) Clock
    func (c Clock) Subtract(min int) Clock
    func (c Clock) String() string   - "HH:MM"

Make Clock a small VALUE type (store minutes since midnight, 0..1439) so
that two clocks showing the same time are equal with ==, and so it can
be a map key. Beware: Go's % keeps the sign of the left operand
(-1 % 1440 == -1), so normalise with ((x % n) + n) % n.

Print, one per line:
    New(8, 0), New(11, 9), New(25, 160), New(-1, 15), New(0, -1441)
      (space separated)
    New(10, 0).Add(3*60 + 25) and New(10, 0).Subtract(3000)
    New(15, 37) == New(-9, 37*1 + 0*60)   and   New(0, 0) == New(24, 0)
    the number of distinct keys in a map after adding New(1,0),
      New(25,0) and New(1,1440)

quiz.q: Why store a Clock as normalised minutes rather than separate hour and minute fields set directly from New's arguments?
options: Structs are unable to hold two int fields
It uses less memory than two ints by design
One canonical value makes == and map keys work
fmt is unable to print two separate fields
quiz.explain: New(25, 0) and New(1, 0) must be equal. Normalising to a single canonical value means the compiler-generated == compares like-for-like.

▸  YOUR TASK
Score a complete ten-pin bowling game from the list of rolls (pins
knocked down per roll):

    - A frame is normally two rolls.
    - STRIKE (10 on the first roll): the frame is one roll and scores
      10 + the next TWO rolls.
    - SPARE (both rolls add to 10): scores 10 + the next ONE roll.
    - Open frame: the sum of its two rolls.
    - The 10th frame's strike or spare earns its bonus rolls at the end
      of the list.

Write Score(rolls []int) int that walks frame by frame with an index.
Print the score for each game, one per line:
    all gutter balls:  20 zeros
    all ones:          20 ones
    one spare:         5 5 3 then 17 zeros
    one strike:        10 3 4 then 16 zeros
    perfect game:      12 strikes
    all spares:        21 fives

quiz.q: Why does the loop run exactly 10 times instead of looping over all rolls?
options: A game has 10 frames; extra rolls are bonuses
range cannot loop over a slice of ints
There are always exactly 10 rolls in a game
It is purely a performance optimisation
quiz.explain: A game has 10 frames. The extra rolls after a 10th-frame strike or spare are read as bonuses via i+1/i+2, but they never start a new frame.
quiz.hint: A perfect game has 12 rolls.

goroutine per text, each building its own map[rune]int, then merge.

    func Frequency(text string) map[rune]int     (letters only, lowercased)
    func ConcurrentFrequency(texts []string) map[rune]int

Do NOT share one map between goroutines (that is a data race). Instead,
send each partial map on a channel and merge them in the caller.

Use these three texts:
    "Freude schöner Götterfunken"
    "Tochter aus Elysium,"
    "Wir betreten feuertrunken"

'same: true'.

Concurrent map writes race and can crash
Go limits each map to one goroutine at compile time
Separate maps always use less memory overall
quiz.explain: Go maps are not safe for concurrent writes; the runtime may even abort with "concurrent map writes". Per-goroutine maps merged by one goroutine need no locks.

lessons.title: Gym: a concurrency-safe bank account
lessons.concept:
▸  YOUR TASK
Implement an account that many goroutines use at once:

    func Open(initial int64) *Account     - nil if initial < 0
    func (a *Account) Balance() (int64, bool)        ok=false if closed
    func (a *Account) Deposit(amt int64) (int64, bool)
         negative amt = withdrawal; fails (false) if it would make the
         balance negative or the account is closed
    func (a *Account) Close() (int64, bool)  - returns the final balance;
         false if already closed

Protect the state with a sync.Mutex. Then:
    1. Open with 3000. Start 1000 goroutines that each deposit 5 and
       1000 that each withdraw 3 (Deposit(-3)); wait for all.
       Print 'balance: N'.
    2. Print the results of Deposit(-10000) as 'value ok'.
    3. Close the account and print the result, then Close again and
       Balance, each as 'value ok' on its own line.
    4. Print Open(-5) == nil.
lessons.expected:
balance: 5000
5000 false
5000 true
0 false
0 false
true

quiz.q: Why is the final balance always 5000, whatever order the 2000 goroutines run in?
options: Atomic updates, and 3000 covers every withdrawal
Goroutines always run in the order started
Withdrawals are queued until deposits finish
The race detector forces a fixed order
quiz.explain: The mutex prevents lost updates. And because the opening 3000 covers all 1000 withdrawals of 3, no withdrawal can be refused in any interleaving. With an opening balance of 100, some withdrawals could fail depending on scheduling, and the result would vary from run to run.
quiz.hint: What if every withdrawal ran before any deposit?

lessons.title: Design patterns in Go: what changes, what stays
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A DESIGN PATTERN is a named, reusable answer to a problem that keeps
coming back ("how do I make this optional?", "how do I swap this part
out?"). The names let programmers talk quickly: saying "use a
decorator" is shorter than describing it.

▸  WHY GO'S PATTERNS LOOK SMALLER
Most pattern books were written for languages built on CLASSES and
INHERITANCE (one type extending another). Go has neither. It has
three tools that replace most of that machinery:

    - functions are values: you can store one in a variable, pass it
      to another function, and return it
    - interfaces are satisfied implicitly: a type fits an interface
      just by having the right methods, with no "implements" word
    - embedding: put one type inside another to reuse its methods

So a pattern that needs four classes elsewhere is often one function
type in Go.

▸  THE CODE BELOW
One problem solved twice. A greeter must say hello in different
styles. First with an interface and two types (the classic shape),
then with a plain function type. Both give the same output; the
second is shorter. Each lesson in this module shows where the longer
shape is still worth it.

▸  RULE OF THUMB
Reach for a pattern only after you have felt the problem it solves.
A pattern added "just in case" is extra code to read and no benefit.
lessons.expected:
Good day, Ada.
HEY ADA!
Good day, Ada.
HEY ADA!

quiz.q: Why do many classic design patterns need less code in Go?
options: Go compiles faster than older languages
Functions are values and interfaces are implicit
Go forbids writing more than one type per file
Go has a built-in keyword for each pattern
quiz.explain: A function value can carry a behaviour without a class around it, and a type satisfies an interface without declaring it. Those two features remove most of the scaffolding.
quiz.hint: Re-read "WHY GO'S PATTERNS LOOK SMALLER".

lessons.title: Functional options: optional settings without a pile of parameters
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
A constructor (a function that builds a value, by convention named
NewX) starts simple: NewServer(addr). Then you need a timeout. Then a
retry count. Then a logger. Go has no default parameter values and no
function overloading (two functions with one name), so you end up
with NewServer(addr, 0, 0, nil) and nobody knows what the zeros mean.

▸  THE PATTERN
An OPTION is a function that changes the thing being built:

    type Option func(*Server)

    func WithTimeout(d time.Duration) Option {
        return func(s *Server) { s.timeout = d }
    }

The constructor takes any number of options. "opts ...Option" is a
VARIADIC parameter: the caller may pass zero, one or many, and inside
the function opts is a slice.

    func NewServer(addr string, opts ...Option) *Server {
        s := &Server{addr: addr, timeout: 30 * time.Second} // defaults
        for _, opt := range opts {
            opt(s)                                          // apply
        }
        return s
    }

▸  WHY IT WORKS WELL
    - Defaults live in ONE place, the constructor.
    - Each call names what it changes: WithTimeout(5*time.Second).
    - Adding a new option later breaks no existing caller.

▸  HOW WithTimeout WORKS
It returns a CLOSURE: a function that remembers the variable d from
the call that created it. Nothing happens until NewServer calls it.

▸  WHEN NOT TO USE IT
For two or three settings a plain Config struct is simpler. Options
earn their keep on public APIs that will grow.
lessons.expected:
:8080  timeout=30s  retries=3 name=default
:9090  timeout=5s   retries=3 name=api
:7070  timeout=30s  retries=0 name=default

quiz.q: In NewServer(addr string, opts ...Option), what is opts inside the function?
options: A map from option name to value
A single Option that may be nil
A slice of Option values, possibly empty
A pointer to the Server being built
quiz.explain: A variadic parameter collects all the extra arguments into a slice. Passing none gives an empty slice, so the range loop simply runs zero times and the defaults stay.
quiz.hint: Look at how the constructor loops over opts.

lessons.title: The builder: assemble a value step by step
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
Some values are made from many optional parts in a meaningful order:
a database query, an email, an HTTP request. Writing the final string
by hand is error-prone. A BUILDER is a helper value that collects the
parts through small method calls and produces the result at the end.

▸  METHOD CHAINING
If every method returns the builder itself, calls can be chained on
one expression:

    q := Select("name").From("users").Where("age > ?", 30).Build()

Each method has a POINTER RECEIVER (b *Builder) so it changes the one
shared builder, and ends with "return b".

▸  ERRORS IN A CHAIN
A chain cannot stop halfway to return an error, because each method
must return the builder. The Go answer: REMEMBER the first error
inside the builder and report it once, in the final Build call.

    func (b *Builder) Limit(n int) *Builder {
        if n < 0 && b.err == nil {
            b.err = errors.New("limit must not be negative")
        }
        b.limit = n
        return b
    }

The standard library does the same in bufio.Scanner (check
Scanner.Err() once, after the loop).

▸  PLACEHOLDERS
The "?" marks are PLACEHOLDERS: the values travel separately in args
and the database fills them in. That keeps user input out of the SQL
text itself, which is what prevents SQL injection (an attacker
sneaking their own SQL into your query).
lessons.expected:
SELECT name, email FROM users WHERE age > ? AND city = ? LIMIT 10
[30 Cairo] <nil>
error: limit must not be negative
error: no table: call From

quiz.q: Why does the builder store an error in a field instead of returning it from Limit?
options: Go methods are not allowed to return errors
Stored errors are faster than returned errors
The field makes the error visible to other packages
Returning an error would break the method chain
quiz.explain: Each chained method must return the builder so the next call can follow. Saving the first error and reporting it in Build keeps the chain intact and the error is still never lost.
quiz.hint: What must every method return for chaining to work?

lessons.title: Strategy: swap an algorithm at run time
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
One job, several ways to do it, chosen while the program runs: how to
price an order, how to sort a list, how to compress a file. Without a
pattern you get a growing switch statement inside the function, and
every new way means editing that function again.

▸  THE PATTERN
A STRATEGY is the changeable part pulled out and passed in. In Go the
simplest strategy is a function type:

    type Pricing func(cents int) int

    func Checkout(items []int, price Pricing) int

Checkout does the fixed part (add up the items). The Pricing function
does the part that varies.

▸  STRATEGIES THAT NEED SETTINGS
"10% off" and "25% off" are the same rule with a different number.
Write a function that RETURNS a strategy:

    func PercentOff(p int) Pricing {
        return func(c int) int { return c - c*p/100 }
    }

▸  COMBINING STRATEGIES
Because strategies are values, you can build one out of others.
Chain(a, b) below returns a strategy that applies a, then b.

▸  FUNCTION OR INTERFACE?
Use a function type when the strategy is ONE operation. Use an
interface when it needs several methods or carries state you want to
inspect. sort.Slice takes a function; sort.Sort takes an interface
with three methods. Both are the strategy pattern.

▸  MONEY NOTE
Prices are kept in cents as int. Floating-point numbers (float64)
cannot store 0.1 exactly, so they drift when you add money.

quiz.q: When is an interface a better strategy type than a function type?
options: When the strategy must run faster
When the strategy is used only once
When the strategy needs several methods
When the strategy takes no parameters
quiz.explain: A function type expresses exactly one operation. If the changeable part needs several operations (like Len, Less and Swap for sorting), an interface groups them.
quiz.hint: Compare sort.Slice with sort.Sort.

lessons.title: Decorator: add behaviour by wrapping
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
You have a working component and want to add something around it:
logging, caching, timing, retries. Editing the component mixes two
jobs in one place. Copying it creates two versions to maintain.

▸  THE PATTERN
A DECORATOR is a value that has the SAME interface as the thing it
wraps, holds that thing inside, and adds work before or after passing
the call on.

    type Store interface { Get(key string) (string, error) }

    type logged struct{ next Store }

    func (l logged) Get(key string) (string, error) {
        v, err := l.next.Get(key)   // pass the call on
        fmt.Println("get", key)     // added behaviour
        return v, err
    }

The caller only knows it has a Store. It cannot tell, and does not
care, how many layers are inside.

▸  LAYERS STACK
Because a decorator IS a Store, a decorator can wrap a decorator:

    s := Logged(Cached(slowStore))

Read it from the outside in: a call reaches Logged first, then
Cached, then the real store. ORDER MATTERS. In the code below logging
is outside the cache, so every call is logged. Swap them and only
cache misses would reach the logger.

▸  YOU ALREADY KNOW ONE
HTTP middleware (module 16) is this pattern for http.Handler.
bufio.NewReader(file) decorates an io.Reader with buffering.
gzip.NewWriter(w) decorates an io.Writer with compression.

▸  CACHE
A CACHE keeps answers it has already computed so the slow work is
done once. A HIT means the answer was in the cache; a MISS means it
was not and the real store had to be asked.
lessons.expected:
log: Get("go") -> "gopher", err=<nil>
  log: Get("go") -> "gopher", err=<nil>
  log: Get("py") -> "snake", err=<nil>
  log: Get("go") -> "gopher", err=<nil>
  log: Get("rust") -> "", err=not found: rust
calls that reached the slow store: 3

quiz.q: What must be true of a decorator for it to be stackable (one wrapping another)?
options: It must be declared in the same file as the thing it wraps
It must copy all the data of the thing it wraps
It must use a pointer receiver on every method
It must satisfy the same interface as the thing it wraps
quiz.explain: Each layer accepts a Store and is itself a Store, so the output of one wrapping step is a valid input to the next. That shared interface is the whole trick.
quiz.hint: What type does Cached take, and what type does it return?

lessons.title: Observer: an event bus with subscribe and publish
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
When an order is placed, the program must send an email, update the
stock and write an audit line. If PlaceOrder calls all three directly
it must know about all three, and every new reaction means editing
PlaceOrder. The parts are COUPLED: a change in one forces a change in
another.

▸  THE PATTERN
An OBSERVER is code that asks to be told when something happens. The
thing that tells them is here called a BUS:

    bus.Subscribe("order.placed", sendEmail)   // "tell me"
    bus.Publish("order.placed", "order 17")    // "it happened"

The publisher does not know who is listening. Listeners do not know
who published. They share only the TOPIC name (a string label for a
kind of event) and the shape of the data.

▸  A HANDLER
The function a subscriber registers is called a HANDLER. Here:

    type Handler func(data string)

▸  UNSUBSCRIBING
Go cannot compare two function values with ==, so you cannot remove a
handler by passing the same function again. The usual answer:
Subscribe RETURNS a function that removes exactly that subscription.

    stop := bus.Subscribe("order.placed", audit)
    stop()   // audit no longer receives events

Each subscription gets a number (id) and the returned closure
remembers its own id.

▸  ORDER OF DELIVERY
Handlers are kept in a slice, not a map, so they run in the order
they subscribed. Map iteration order in Go is deliberately random; a
slice keeps the output predictable.

▸  LIMITS
This bus calls handlers one after another on the publisher's
goroutine. A slow handler delays the rest. Real systems often give
each subscriber a channel and its own goroutine (module 12).
lessons.expected:
email: confirmation for order 17
  audit: order 17
delivered to 2
  email: confirmation for order 18
delivered to 1
  email: on its way, order 17
delivered to 1
delivered to 0

quiz.q: Why does Subscribe return an unsubscribe function instead of offering Unsubscribe(fn)?
options: Returning a function uses less memory than a method
Function values cannot be compared with == in Go
Methods cannot take function parameters in Go
A handler may only ever be registered once
quiz.explain: Go only allows comparing a function value to nil. Without ==, the bus cannot find "the same function" again, so it hands back a closure that remembers the subscription's id.
quiz.hint: Re-read "UNSUBSCRIBING".

lessons.title: State machines: make illegal moves impossible
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
An order can be new, paid, shipped, delivered or cancelled. Code that
tracks this with loose booleans (isPaid, isShipped, isCancelled)
allows nonsense such as "shipped and cancelled", and the rules for
what may happen next end up scattered across many if statements.

▸  THE PATTERN
A STATE MACHINE has:
    - a fixed list of STATES (it is in exactly one at a time)
    - a fixed list of EVENTS (things that can happen)
    - a TRANSITION TABLE: for each (state, event) pair that is
      allowed, the state that comes next

Anything not in the table is rejected. All the rules sit in one
place that you can read like a diagram.

▸  STATES AS A TYPE
    type State int

    const (
        New State = iota   // 0
        Paid               // 1
        Shipped            // 2
    )

iota numbers the constants 0, 1, 2 ... A String method on State makes
fmt print the name instead of the number.

▸  THE TABLE AS A MAP
A struct with comparable fields can be a map KEY:

    type key struct { from State; ev Event }

    var table = map[key]State{
        {New, Pay}: Paid,
        {Paid, Ship}: Shipped,
    }

Looking up table[key{s, ev}] with the "comma ok" form tells you both
the next state and whether the move is allowed.

▸  WHERE YOU MEET THEM
Network connections (connecting, open, closing, closed), parsers,
game characters, traffic lights, payment flows.
lessons.expected:
pay      -> Paid
rejected: order 7: cannot pay while Paid
ship     -> Shipped
rejected: order 7: cannot cancel while Shipped
deliver  -> Delivered
rejected: order 7: cannot ship while Delivered

quiz.q: In the transition table, what happens for a (state, event) pair that is not listed?
options: The order moves to the Cancelled state
The program panics with a missing-key error
The lookup reports ok == false and Apply returns an error
The order stays put and Apply returns nil
quiz.explain: Reading a missing map key never panics. The comma-ok form returns the zero value and false, and Apply turns that false into a descriptive error, leaving the state unchanged.
quiz.hint: Look at the first three lines of Apply.

lessons.title: Adapter: make a type fit an interface it was not written for
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
Your code expects one shape (an interface). A type you want to use,
perhaps from another package you cannot edit, has the right ability
under the wrong method name or with different parameters.

▸  THE PATTERN
An ADAPTER is a small type that sits between them. It holds the
foreign value and offers the method your code expects, translating
the call:

    type Notifier interface { Notify(user, msg string) error }

    type smsAdapter struct{ c *SMSClient }

    func (a smsAdapter) Notify(user, msg string) error {
        return a.c.SendText(lookupPhone(user), msg)   // translate
    }

▸  ADAPTER vs DECORATOR
They look alike (both wrap a value) but have different goals:
    - a decorator keeps the SAME interface and ADDS behaviour
    - an adapter CHANGES the interface and adds nothing else

▸  FUNCTION ADAPTERS
The standard library's most famous adapter is one line long:

    type HandlerFunc func(ResponseWriter, *Request)
    func (f HandlerFunc) ServeHTTP(w ResponseWriter, r *Request) { f(w, r) }

It gives a plain function a method, so the function satisfies the
http.Handler interface. The code below does the same with
NotifierFunc: a defined function type with a method that calls
itself.

▸  WHY THIS MATTERS IN GO
Because interfaces are implicit, you define the interface where it is
USED, as small as you need, and adapt outside types to it. Your core
code then never imports the outside package, which keeps it easy to
test and to swap.
lessons.expected:
EMAIL from=shop@example.com to=ada@example.com subject="Notice" body="Order shipped"
  SMS to=+20-100-555-0100 text="Order shipped"
  CONSOLE ADA: Order shipped
  EMAIL from=shop@example.com to=ada@example.com subject="Notice" body="Your order has been delivered"
  SMS to=+20-100-555-0100 text="Your order has been delivered"
  failed: sms to ada: message too long (29 bytes)
  CONSOLE ADA: Your order has been delivered

quiz.q: What is the difference between an adapter and a decorator?
options: An adapter is a function and a decorator is a struct
An adapter is faster because it copies less data
An adapter changes the interface; a decorator keeps it
An adapter may wrap only types from other packages
quiz.explain: Both wrap a value. A decorator presents the same interface and adds behaviour; an adapter presents a different interface so the wrapped value can be used where it otherwise would not fit.
quiz.hint: Re-read "ADAPTER vs DECORATOR".

lessons.title: Registry: plug-ins that register themselves
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
A program supports several formats (or drivers, or commands) and you
want adding one to be a matter of adding a file, with no edit to a
central switch statement.

▸  THE PATTERN
A REGISTRY is a table from a name to an implementation, plus two
functions: Register(name, impl) to add and Lookup(name) to find.

    var codecs = map[string]Codec{}

    func Register(name string, c Codec) { codecs[name] = c }

Each implementation registers ITSELF from an init function. Go runs
every init function automatically, after the package's variables are
set up and before main starts.

    func init() { Register("upper", upperCodec{}) }

▸  YOU HAVE USED THIS
    import _ "image/png"

The underscore import means "run this package's init functions; I
will not use its names". image/png's init calls image.RegisterFormat,
and from then on image.Decode understands PNG files. Database drivers
register with database/sql the same way.

▸  RULES THAT KEEP IT SAFE
    - Registering the same name twice is a bug: panic at start-up so
      it is found immediately.
    - Register only during init. Then the map is never written while
      goroutines read it and needs no lock.
    - Offer a way to LIST names, sorted, so error messages can say
      what is available.

▸  THE COST
A registry is a package-level variable: hidden shared state. It makes
"what does this program support?" depend on which packages were
imported. Use it for true plug-in points, not as a general way to
pass things around.
lessons.expected:
registered: [reverse rot13 upper]
upper    HELLO, GOPHER
rot13    Uryyb, Tbcure
reverse  rehpoG ,olleH
error: unknown codec "base99" (have: reverse, rot13, upper)

quiz.q: What does the import line  import _ "image/png"  do?
options: It imports the package under the short name _
It imports the package only when tests are run
It runs the package's init functions without using its names
It tells the compiler to skip the package if unused
quiz.explain: The blank identifier _ keeps the import even though no name from the package is used. Its init functions still run, and that is where the package registers itself.
quiz.hint: Re-read "YOU HAVE USED THIS".

lessons.title: Challenge: undo and redo with the command pattern
lessons.concept:
▸  THE COMMAND PATTERN
A COMMAND is an action turned into a value. Instead of just calling
doc.Append("x"), you build a small value that knows how to DO the
action and how to UNDO it:

    type Command interface {
        Do(d *Doc)
        Undo(d *Doc)
    }

Once actions are values you can store them. That is how editors
implement undo.

▸  TWO STACKS
A STACK is a list where you add and remove at the same end (last in,
first out). A slice is a stack: append pushes, and
s = s[:len(s)-1] pops.

    - Run(cmd):  cmd.Do, then push cmd on the undo stack and EMPTY
                 the redo stack (a new action discards redo history)
    - Undo():    pop from undo, call Undo, push on the redo stack
    - Redo():    pop from redo, call Do, push on the undo stack

Undo and Redo on an empty stack do nothing and return false.

▸  YOUR TASK
Build a text document with two commands:
    - Append{Text}: adds Text at the end
    - DeleteLast{N}: removes the last N characters (it must remember
      what it removed so Undo can put it back)

Then run this script, printing the document in quotes after each
step with fmt.Printf("%-8s %q\n", label, text):

    append   "Hello"
    append   ", Go"
    delete 4 characters
    undo, undo, undo, undo   (the fourth finds nothing: print
                              "undo     nothing to undo")
    redo, redo
    append   "!"
    redo                     (print "redo     nothing to redo")

▸  HINTS
    - DeleteLast needs a pointer receiver, or a field that Do can
      write to, because Do must store the removed text.
    - If N is larger than the text, remove everything.
lessons.expected:
append   "Hello"
append   "Hello, Go"
delete   "Hello"
undo     "Hello, Go"
undo     "Hello"
undo     ""
undo     nothing to undo
redo     "Hello"
redo     "Hello, Go"
append   "Hello, Go!"
redo     nothing to redo

quiz.q: Why does running a new command empty the redo stack?
options: The redo stack would otherwise use too much memory
Go slices cannot hold more than one kind of command
Undo would stop working on the newest command
The redone actions were made for a document that no longer exists
quiz.explain: Redo replays actions that followed a certain state. After a new action the document has moved on in a different direction, so replaying the old ones would produce nonsense.
quiz.hint: Think about what "redo" would apply to after you type something new.

lessons.title: Ring buffer: a fixed-size queue that never moves its data
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A QUEUE is a line: items leave in the order they arrived (first in,
first out, "FIFO"). The obvious Go queue is a slice: append to add,
q = q[1:] to remove. It works, but the front of the backing array is
never reused, so a long-running queue keeps allocating new memory.

▸  THE IDEA
A RING BUFFER (also "circular buffer") is a fixed array plus two
numbers:

    head   index of the oldest item
    size   how many items are stored

The newest item goes at index (head + size) % len(buf). The % sign is
the REMAINDER operator: it makes the index "wrap around" to 0 after
the last slot, as if the array were bent into a ring.

    cap 4:   [ c | d | a | b ]      head = 2, size = 4
                       ^ oldest

▸  OPERATIONS (all take the same tiny time, however full it is)
    Push   write at the tail slot, size++
    Pop    read buf[head], head = (head+1) % len(buf), size--

▸  WHEN IT IS FULL
You must choose a policy. This one OVERWRITES the oldest item, which
is what you want for "keep the last N log lines". Another policy is
to refuse the push and return false, which is what a buffered channel
does by blocking.

▸  GENERICS REMINDER
Ring[T any] is a generic type: T is a TYPE PARAMETER, a placeholder
for whatever element type the user picks, such as Ring[int] or
Ring[string]. "var zero T" declares a variable holding T's zero
value, used here to return something when the ring is empty.

▸  BIG-O REMINDER
O(1), said "constant time", means the work does not grow with the
number of items stored.
lessons.expected:
push boot   overwrote=false items=[boot] raw=["boot" "" ""] head=0
push login  overwrote=false items=[boot login] raw=["boot" "login" ""] head=0
push query  overwrote=false items=[boot login query] raw=["boot" "login" "query"] head=0
push error  overwrote=true  items=[login query error] raw=["error" "login" "query"] head=1
push retry  overwrote=true  items=[query error retry] raw=["error" "retry" "query"] head=2
pop: query true left: [error retry]
pop on empty: "" false

quiz.q: In a ring buffer with len(buf) == 8, head == 6 and size == 3, at which index is the next pushed item stored?
quiz.explain: The tail slot is (head + size) % len(buf) = (6 + 3) % 8 = 9 % 8 = 1. Slots 6, 7 and 0 hold the three stored items, so slot 1 is next.
quiz.hint: Use the formula (head + size) % len(buf).

lessons.title: Building a binary heap by hand
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
Module 7 used container/heap. Here you build the heap yourself, so
you know what Push and Pop cost and why.

▸  WHAT A HEAP IS
A MIN-HEAP is a binary tree (each node has up to two children) with
one rule: every parent is less than or equal to its children. So the
smallest item is always at the top, the ROOT. Nothing is promised
about left versus right; a heap is NOT fully sorted.

▸  THE ARRAY TRICK
The tree is stored in a slice with no pointers at all. For the item
at index i:

    parent       (i - 1) / 2
    left child   2*i + 1
    right child  2*i + 2

        index:  0  1  2  3  4  5
        value:  1  3  2  8  5  4

              1
            /   \
           3     2
          / \   /
         8   5 4

▸  PUSH: "SIFT UP"
Append at the end, then swap it with its parent while it is smaller
than the parent.

▸  POP: "SIFT DOWN"
Save the root. Move the LAST item to index 0, shrink the slice, then
swap it with its smaller child while that child is smaller.

▸  COST
The tree has about log2(n) levels, and each operation walks one path
from top to bottom or back, so Push and Pop are O(log n). With a
million items that is about 20 steps. Reading the minimum is O(1).

▸  USES
Priority queues (always handle the most urgent job next), Dijkstra's
shortest paths, merging many sorted files, "top K" problems, timers
inside the Go runtime.

▸  THE less FUNCTION
The heap takes a less(a, b) function. Pass a < b for a min-heap, or
a > b to get a max-heap with the same code.
lessons.expected:
push 5 -> [5]
push 3 -> [3 5]
push 8 -> [3 5 8]
push 1 -> [1 3 8 5]
push 4 -> [1 3 8 5 4]
push 2 -> [1 3 2 5 4 8]
pop order: 1 2 3 4 5 8
9 restore database
5 resize images
1 send newsletter

quiz.q: In a heap stored in a slice, where are the children of the item at index 3?
options: Indexes 4 and 5
Indexes 6 and 7
Indexes 7 and 8
Indexes 1 and 2
quiz.explain: Left child is 2*i + 1 = 7 and right child is 2*i + 2 = 8. Index 1 is its parent, (3 - 1) / 2.
quiz.hint: Apply 2*i + 1 and 2*i + 2 with i = 3.

lessons.title: Bloom filter: "definitely not" or "probably yes"
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
You have a huge set (every username taken, every URL already
crawled) and want to ask "is X in it?" without keeping every item in
memory or asking the disk each time.

▸  THE IDEA
A BLOOM FILTER is a row of bits (each bit is 0 or 1), all starting at
0, plus k HASH FUNCTIONS. A hash function turns any data into a
number; the same input always gives the same number.

    Add(x):   compute k positions from x, set those bits to 1
    Has(x):   compute the same k positions;
              if ANY bit is 0  ->  x was never added. Certain.
              if ALL are 1     ->  x was PROBABLY added.

"Probably" because other items may have set those same bits. That
wrong "yes" is called a FALSE POSITIVE. A false "no" is impossible.

▸  WHY THAT IS USEFUL
A database asks the filter first. On "no" it skips the disk read
completely. On "yes" it reads the disk, and is occasionally
disappointed. Most lookups for missing keys become free.

▸  THE COST
    - You cannot remove an item (clearing its bits could erase others).
    - You cannot list the items.
    - More bits per item means fewer false positives. About 10 bits
      per item with 7 hashes gives roughly 1% false positives.

▸  GETTING k HASHES FROM ONE
Computing k different hash functions is slow. A standard trick: take
two numbers h1 and h2 from one 64-bit hash and use
h1 + i*h2 for i = 0, 1, ... k-1.

▸  BITS IN GO
The bits live in a []uint64. Bit number p is in word p/64, at
position p%64 inside that word.
    set:   words[p/64] |= 1 << (p % 64)
    test:  words[p/64] & (1 << (p % 64)) != 0
|= is "OR and assign" (turn a bit on); & is AND (keep only that bit).

▸  THE HASH USED HERE
hash/fnv is FNV-1a, a small fast hash in the standard library. It is
fine for tables and filters and NOT for security.
lessons.expected:
added items reported missing: 0
false positives: 10 of 1000 never-added items (1.0%)
memory used: 128 bytes for 100 items

quiz.q: A Bloom filter answers "no" for a key. What do you know?
options: The key was probably never added
The key was certainly never added
The key was added and later removed
Nothing; the filter may be wrong either way
quiz.explain: Adding a key sets all of its bits to 1 and bits are never cleared. If any of its bits is 0, that key cannot have been added. Only "yes" answers can be wrong.
quiz.hint: Which kind of wrong answer is impossible?

lessons.newhere:
• fnv.New64a - New64a returns a new 64-bit FNV-1a hash.Hash.
  • hash.Hash64.Sum64 - returns the 64-bit hash of everything written so far

lessons.title: Fenwick tree: running totals that survive updates
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
You have a list of numbers and two operations that keep coming, mixed
together:
    - add something to one position
    - ask for the sum of a range of positions

A plain slice makes the update instant but each sum walks the range,
O(n). A PREFIX-SUM array (where p[i] is the total of everything up to
i) makes each sum instant but every update must fix all later
entries, O(n). With a million numbers and a million operations,
either way is too slow.

▸  THE IDEA
A FENWICK TREE (also "binary indexed tree") makes BOTH operations
O(log n). It is a slice where each cell stores the sum of a block of
the input, and the block sizes are powers of two chosen from the
index's binary form.

Positions are counted from 1. Cell i covers the last (i & -i)
positions ending at i. "i & -i" keeps only the lowest 1-bit of i:

    i = 6  is 110 in binary   ->  lowest bit is 10  = 2  -> covers 5..6
    i = 8  is 1000            ->  lowest bit is 1000 = 8 -> covers 1..8

▸  THE TWO LOOPS
    Add(i, d):    for ; i <= n; i += i & -i { tree[i] += d }
                  climb to every block that contains position i

    Prefix(i):    for ; i > 0;  i -= i & -i { sum += tree[i] }
                  jump back block by block to position 0

Each loop changes one bit of i per step, so it runs at most about
log2(n) times: 20 steps for a million items.

▸  RANGE SUM
Sum(l..r) = Prefix(r) - Prefix(l-1).

▸  WHERE IT IS USED
Live leaderboards ("how many players score below me?"), counting
inversions, cumulative frequency tables in compression.

▸  WHY 1-BASED
With 0-based indexes, 0 & -0 is 0 and the loops would never move.
The public methods below accept ordinary 0-based indexes and add 1
inside.
lessons.expected:
data:       [5 2 9 -3 6 1 4 7]
tree cells: [5 7 9 13 6 7 4 31]
sum 0..7 = 31
sum 2..4 = 12
after adding 10 at index 3:
sum 0..7 = 41
sum 2..4 = 22
sum 4..7 = 18
i= 1 binary=0001 lowest bit i&-i=1
i= 6 binary=0110 lowest bit i&-i=2
i= 8 binary=1000 lowest bit i&-i=8
i=12 binary=1100 lowest bit i&-i=4

quiz.q: What does the expression i & -i give for i = 12 (binary 1100)?
quiz.explain: i & -i isolates the lowest 1-bit. 12 is 1100 in binary; its lowest set bit is the 100 place, which is 4. So cell 12 covers 4 positions: 9 to 12.
quiz.hint: Write 12 in binary and find the rightmost 1.

lessons.title: Segment tree: range questions with updates
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
Same setting as the Fenwick tree (a list that changes, with range
questions in between), but now the question is "what is the MINIMUM
between positions l and r?". A Fenwick tree needs an operation that
can be undone by subtraction; minimum cannot. A SEGMENT TREE handles
any operation that can combine two answers into one: min, max, sum,
greatest common divisor.

▸  THE IDEA
Build a binary tree over the list:
    - each LEAF (a node with no children) holds one item
    - each inner node holds the combined answer of its two children

                 min(0..3)=1
                /           \
        min(0..1)=2      min(2..3)=1
          /    \           /    \
         5      2         9      1

▸  QUERY
To answer a range, walk down from the root. At each node:
    - its span is completely inside the range -> use its stored value
    - its span is completely outside          -> ignore it
    - otherwise                               -> ask both children
Only about 2*log2(n) nodes are touched.

▸  UPDATE
Change the leaf, then recompute each ancestor on the way back up:
log2(n) nodes.

▸  STORAGE
Like a heap, the tree lives in a slice: node i has children 2*i and
2*i+1, with the root at index 1. A slice of size 4*n is always large
enough.

▸  IDENTITY VALUE
A node outside the range must return something that changes nothing
when combined. For min that is a huge number (math.MaxInt); for sum
it would be 0. This is called the IDENTITY of the operation.

▸  RECURSION
build, update and query each call themselves on the two halves. Every
call receives the node index and the span [lo, hi] that node covers;
mid := (lo + hi) / 2 splits it.

quiz.q: Why can a segment tree answer range-minimum queries when a Fenwick tree cannot?
options: A segment tree stores the items in sorted order
A segment tree uses less memory per item
A segment tree combines whole blocks and never needs to subtract
A segment tree works on 0-based indexes
quiz.explain: A Fenwick range answer is prefix(r) minus prefix(l-1), which needs an operation that can be undone. Minimum has no "un-min". A segment tree only ever combines the stored answers of blocks inside the range.
quiz.hint: How does the Fenwick tree turn two prefix answers into a range answer?

lessons.title: Self-balancing trees: an AVL tree
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
A BINARY SEARCH TREE (module 7) keeps smaller keys on the left and
larger keys on the right, so a lookup discards half the tree at each
step. But insert the keys 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 in order and every node gets
only a right child: the "tree" is a linked list and a lookup walks
every node. Sorted input is common, so this matters.

▸  THE IDEA
A SELF-BALANCING tree repairs its shape after every insert. An AVL
tree (named after its inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis) keeps this
rule for every node:

    height(left subtree) and height(right subtree) differ by at most 1

HEIGHT is the number of nodes on the longest path down to a leaf.
The difference (left minus right) is the BALANCE FACTOR.

▸  ROTATIONS
When an insert pushes a balance factor to +2 or -2, the tree is fixed
by a ROTATION: a local re-linking of three nodes that keeps the
left-smaller / right-larger order but shortens the tall side.

        z                 y
       /                 / \
      y       ->        x   z        (rotate right at z)
     /
    x

There are four cases, named by where the new key went:
    left-left     rotate right
    right-right   rotate left
    left-right    rotate left on the child, then right
    right-left    rotate right on the child, then left

▸  RESULT
The height stays close to log2(n). A million keys give a tree about
20 levels deep, whatever order they arrived in. Search, insert and
delete are all O(log n).

▸  IN PRACTICE
Go's standard library has no balanced tree; sorted slices with binary
search or maps cover most needs. Databases use a relative, the
B-tree. You build one here because rotations appear in interviews
and in every ordered-map library.

▸  CODE NOTES
insert returns the (possibly new) root of the subtree it was given.
That is how a rotation replaces a node: the caller stores the result
back with n.left = insert(n.left, key).
lessons.expected:
tree turned on its side (root at the left):
        7
    6
        5
4
        3
    2
        1
root: 4 height: 3
1000 sorted keys -> height 10 (a plain BST would have height 1000)
in-order walk is sorted: [10 20 25 30 50 60]

quiz.q: What does the AVL rule guarantee about the tree?
options: Every node has exactly two children
The keys are stored in the order they were inserted
Its height stays close to log2 of the number of keys
The root always holds the smallest key
quiz.explain: Keeping the two subtrees of every node within one level of each other prevents long thin branches, so the height grows only logarithmically and operations stay O(log n).
quiz.hint: What goes wrong in a plain BST with sorted input, and what does balancing prevent?

lessons.title: Skip list: a sorted list with express lanes
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
A sorted linked list is simple to insert into (re-link two pointers)
but slow to search: there is no jumping to the middle, so you walk
node by node, O(n). Balanced trees fix the speed but need rotations.

▸  THE IDEA
A SKIP LIST is a sorted linked list with extra "express" levels on
top. Every node is on level 0. About half of them are also on level
1, a quarter on level 2, and so on.

    level 2:  head ----------------> 30 -----------------> nil
    level 1:  head ------> 10 -----> 30 ------> 50 ------> nil
    level 0:  head -> 5 -> 10 -> 20 -> 30 -> 40 -> 50 ---> nil

▸  SEARCH
Start at the top level of the head. Move right while the next key is
smaller than the target; when it is not, drop down one level. You
skip large stretches on the upper levels and arrive on level 0 next
to the answer. On average that takes O(log n) steps.

▸  INSERT
Search as above, remembering at each level the last node you stood
on (the "update" list). Then pick the new node's height by flipping
a coin: keep adding a level while it comes up heads. Link the new
node in after the remembered node on each of its levels.

▸  WHY RANDOM WORKS
No rebalancing is ever needed. The coin flips make tall nodes rare
in just the right proportion, whatever order the keys arrive in.

▸  WHO USES IT
Redis sorted sets, LevelDB and RocksDB memtables, and concurrent
ordered maps (inserting touches only a few neighbours, which makes
locking simple).

▸  CODE NOTES
    - Each node has next []*node: one "next" pointer per level.
    - rand.New(rand.NewPCG(1, 2)) creates a random generator with a
      FIXED SEED, so this lesson prints the same thing on every run.
      A seed is the starting number of a random sequence; real code
      would use the default generator, which is seeded randomly.
lessons.expected:
level 6: 30
level 5: 30
level 4: 30
level 3: 30
level 2: 30
level 1: 5 10 20 30 35 50
level 0: 5 10 20 30 35 40 50 60
Contains(40) = true
Contains(45) = false
10000 keys: finding the last one visited 92 nodes; a plain list visits 9999

quiz.q: How does a skip list decide how many levels a new node gets?
options: It uses the number of nodes already in the list
It gives every node one more level than the last
It copies the level of the node before it
It flips a coin until the first tails
quiz.explain: Each extra level is added with probability one half. That makes about half the nodes reach level 1, a quarter level 2, and so on, which is exactly the shape that gives O(log n) searches.
quiz.hint: Look at randomLevel.

lessons.newhere: • rand.Rand - A Rand is a source of random numbers.

lessons.title: Deque and the sliding-window maximum
lessons.concept:
▸  DEQUE
A DEQUE (say "deck", short for double-ended queue) lets you add and
remove at BOTH ends. On a Go slice:

    push back    d = append(d, x)
    pop back     d = d[:len(d)-1]
    pop front    d = d[1:]

▸  THE PROBLEM
Given readings and a window size k, report the maximum of every run
of k neighbours: positions 0..k-1, then 1..k, and so on. The plain
way looks at k items for each window: O(n*k). For a day of
per-second data and a one-hour window that is 300 million steps.

▸  THE TRICK: A MONOTONIC DEQUE
Keep a deque of INDEXES whose values are in decreasing order
("monotonic" means always going one way). For each new item:

    1. Pop from the BACK every index whose value is <= the new value.
       They are older AND not larger, so they can never be a maximum
       again.
    2. Push the new index at the back.
    3. Pop from the FRONT if that index has slid out of the window.
    4. The front is now the maximum of the current window.

▸  WHY IT IS FAST
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total work
is O(n) regardless of k. This style of counting (total work across
the whole run, not per step) is called AMORTISED analysis.

▸  WHY INDEXES, NOT VALUES
Step 3 needs to know WHERE the front item is, to tell whether it has
left the window.

▸  SAME PATTERN ELSEWHERE
Sliding minimum (flip the comparison), "next greater element" with a
stack, stock-span problems, rate graphs in dashboards.
lessons.expected:
input:     [3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5]
window 3:  [4 4 5 9 9 9 6 6 5]
slow way:  [4 4 5 9 9 9 6 6 5]
window 1:  [3 1 4 1 5 9 2 6 5 3 5]
window 11: [9]
i=0 value=3 deque indexes=[0]
i=1 value=1 deque indexes=[0 1]
i=2 value=4 deque indexes=[2]
i=3 value=1 deque indexes=[2 3]
i=4 value=5 deque indexes=[4]
i=5 value=9 deque indexes=[5]

quiz.q: Why may the algorithm throw away an index at the back whose value is <= the new value?
options: Smaller values are never needed in any window
The deque must not grow beyond k entries
It leaves the window sooner and is not larger, so it can never be a maximum again
Removing it keeps the deque sorted in increasing order
quiz.explain: The new item stays in the window longer than everything already in the deque. Any older item that is not larger will always be beaten by it for as long as both are in a window.
quiz.hint: Compare how long the old item and the new item remain in the window.

lessons.title: Challenge: an LFU cache
lessons.concept:
▸  BACKGROUND
A cache has limited room. When it is full and a new key arrives, one
old key must be thrown out: this is EVICTION. Module 7 built an LRU
cache, which evicts the Least Recently Used key. An LFU cache evicts
the Least FREQUENTLY Used key: the one that has been read or written
the fewest times.

▸  RULES
    - Get(key) returns the value and true, and adds 1 to that key's
      use count. A missing key returns 0 and false.
    - Put(key, value) on an existing key replaces the value and adds
      1 to its use count.
    - Put on a new key when the cache is full first evicts the key
      with the smallest use count. On a tie, evict the one that was
      used LEAST RECENTLY among them.
    - A new key starts with a use count of 1.

▸  A SIMPLE DESIGN THAT IS ENOUGH HERE
Keep, for every key: its value, its use count, and a "tick" (a
counter you increase on every operation, standing in for time). To
evict, scan all entries for the smallest (count, tick) pair. That
scan is O(n); production LFU caches use linked lists per count to
make it O(1), but get the rules right first.

▸  YOUR TASK
With capacity 2, run exactly these steps and print each result:

    Put(1, 10)
    Put(2, 20)
    Get(1)        -> print "get 1: 10 true"
    Put(3, 30)    -> evicts key 2 (count 1; key 1 has count 2)
    Get(2)        -> print "get 2: 0 false"
    Get(3)        -> print "get 3: 30 true"
    Put(4, 40)    -> keys 1 and 3 both have count 2; 1 is older
    Get(1)        -> print "get 1: 0 false"
    Get(3)        -> print "get 3: 30 true"
    Get(4)        -> print "get 4: 40 true"

After each Put that evicts, print "evicted K" with the key. Finish by
printing the keys still in the cache in increasing order.
lessons.expected:
get 1: 10 true
evicted 2
get 2: 0 false
get 3: 30 true
evicted 1
get 1: 0 false
get 3: 30 true
get 4: 40 true
keys: [3 4]

quiz.q: An LFU cache holds key A (used 5 times, long ago) and key B (used 2 times, just now). It is full and a new key arrives. Which is evicted?
options: A, because it was used least recently
B, because it has been used fewer times
Both, to make room for future keys
Neither; the new key is rejected
quiz.explain: LFU compares use counts first. B's count of 2 is lower than A's 5, so B goes, even though B was touched more recently. Recency only breaks ties between equal counts.
quiz.hint: Which does LFU look at first: how often, or how recently?

lessons.title: How a language works: the three stages
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A programming language is itself a program. Building a small one is
the fastest way to stop seeing compilers as magic, and it uses nearly
everything you have learned: structs, interfaces, recursion, maps,
slices and errors. This module builds a calculator language and grows
it into one with variables, functions and its own virtual machine.

▸  THE THREE STAGES
Source text goes through a pipeline. Each stage has one job.

    "1 + 2 * 3"                        SOURCE: just characters
         |
       LEXER      (also "tokenizer" or "scanner")
         |
    [1] [+] [2] [*] [3]                TOKENS: the words of the language
         |
       PARSER
         |
           +                           AST: the structure
          / \
         1   *
            / \
           2   3
         |
       EVALUATOR  (or a COMPILER that produces instructions)
         |
         7                             RESULT

▸  THE WORDS
    TOKEN      one meaningful piece: a number, a name, an operator
    AST        "abstract syntax tree": the program as a tree, where
               an operator is a node and its operands are children
    INTERPRETER  runs the program directly by walking the tree
    COMPILER     translates the program into another form (machine
               code, or BYTECODE for a virtual machine) to run later

Go itself is compiled: go build runs a lexer, a parser, a type
checker and a code generator. You met Go's own lexer and parser as
packages in module 28 (go/scanner, go/parser, go/ast).

▸  THE CODE BELOW
A complete, tiny language in 40 lines: whole numbers and + only. All
three stages are there. The next lessons replace each stage with a
real one.
lessons.expected:
"1 + 2"      tokens=["1" "+" "2"] = 3
"10+20 + 12" tokens=["10" "+" "20" "+" "12"] = 42
"7"          tokens=["7"] = 7
"1 + + 2"    tokens=["1" "+" "+" "2"] error: expected a number but found "+"
"4 +"        tokens=["4" "+"] error: incomplete expression

quiz.q: What does a parser produce?
options: A list of tokens from the source characters
A tree showing the structure of the program
The final result of running the program
Machine code for the computer's processor
quiz.explain: The lexer makes tokens. The parser arranges those tokens into a tree (the AST) that shows which operator applies to which operands. Running it is a later stage.
quiz.hint: Follow the pipeline diagram: what comes out of PARSER?

lessons.title: The lexer: turning characters into tokens
lessons.concept:
▸  THE JOB
The lexer reads the source one character at a time and groups
characters into tokens. It throws away what the parser does not need
(spaces) and attaches a KIND to each token so later stages never look
at raw characters again.

    "price = (2 + 30) * 4"

    IDENT "price"   ASSIGN "="   LPAREN "("   NUMBER "2"   PLUS "+"
    NUMBER "30"     RPAREN ")"   STAR "*"     NUMBER "4"   EOF ""

▸  THE WORDS
    IDENT   an IDENTIFIER: a name chosen by the programmer
    EOF     "end of file": a final token that tells the parser there
            is nothing more, so it never reads past the end

▸  HOW IT WORKS
One loop with a position (pos) into the input:

    1. Skip spaces.
    2. Look at the current character and decide which token starts
       here.
    3. For one-character tokens (+, *, parentheses) emit it and move
       one step.
    4. For numbers and names, keep moving while the characters still
       belong (digits for a number; letters, digits or _ for a name),
       then emit the whole stretch src[start:pos].

Reading on while characters match is called MAXIMAL MUNCH: the lexer
always takes the longest token it can, so "count1" is one name and
not "count" followed by "1".

▸  POSITIONS
Every token records where it started. Without that, an error message
can only say "unexpected character"; with it, the message can say
"at column 9", which is what makes a language pleasant to use.

▸  ERRORS
A character that starts no token (such as $ here) becomes an ILLEGAL
token. The lexer keeps going so that one run can report every bad
character.

▸  CODE NOTES
    - Kind is a string type so tokens print readably with no extra
      String method.
    - The input is treated as bytes. That is enough for digits,
      ASCII letters and operators; a real lexer for a language that
      allows accented names would decode runes with
      utf8.DecodeRuneInString.

source: price = (2 + 30) * 4
  col  1  IDENT   "price"
  col  7  ASSIGN  "="
  col  9  LPAREN  "("
  col 10  NUMBER  "2"
  col 12  PLUS    "+"
  col 14  NUMBER  "30"
  col 16  RPAREN  ")"
  col 18  STAR    "*"
  col 20  NUMBER  "4"
  col 21  EOF     ""
source: count1/x_2 - 7
  col  1  IDENT   "count1"
  col  7  SLASH   "/"
  col  8  IDENT   "x_2"
  col 12  MINUS   "-"
  col 14  NUMBER  "7"
  col 15  EOF     ""
source: 3 $ 4
  col  1  NUMBER  "3"
  col  3  ILLEGAL "$"
  col  5  NUMBER  "4"
  col  6  EOF     ""

quiz.q: Why does the lexer add an EOF token at the end?
options: To mark where the lexer found an illegal character
To tell the operating system the file can be closed
So the parser can detect the end without reading past the slice
So that every token list has an even number of tokens
quiz.explain: With an explicit end marker the parser can always ask "what is the next token?" and get a real answer. Without it, every look-ahead would need a bounds check first.
quiz.hint: What would the parser otherwise have to check before each look at the next token?

lessons.title: The parser: precedence with Pratt parsing
lessons.concept:
▸  THE JOB
Turn tokens into a tree that respects PRECEDENCE (which operator
binds tighter) and ASSOCIATIVITY (how operators of equal precedence
group).

    1 + 2 * 3     must become   1 + (2 * 3)      * binds tighter
    8 - 3 - 2     must become   (8 - 3) - 2      - groups to the left
    2 ^ 3 ^ 2     must become   2 ^ (3 ^ 2)      ^ groups to the right

▸  PRATT PARSING
A method by Vaughan Pratt (1973) that handles all of this with one
short recursive function. Give every operator a number, its BINDING
POWER: higher binds tighter.

    +  -   10
    *  /   20
    ^      30

    parseExpr(minPower):
        left = parsePrefix()            // a number, (expr), or -expr
        while power(next operator) > minPower:
            op = take the operator
            right = parseExpr(power(op))    // recursive call
            left = Binary{op, left, right}
        return left

Read the loop as a question: "is the next operator strong enough to
grab what I have built so far?" If not, return and let the caller
have it.

▸  WHY 1 + 2 * 3 WORKS
parseExpr(0) reads 1, sees + (10 > 0), and calls parseExpr(10) for
the right side. That call reads 2, sees * (20 > 10), so * grabs the
2 first and builds 2*3. Back in the outer call the right side of +
is the whole (2 * 3).

▸  ASSOCIATIVITY
For a LEFT-associative operator the right side is parsed with the
operator's own power, so an equal operator is NOT strong enough and
the loop in the caller takes it: (8 - 3) - 2. For a RIGHT-associative
operator, parse the right side with power - 1, so an equal operator
IS taken by the inner call: 2 ^ (3 ^ 2).

▸  PREFIX AND GROUPING
parsePrefix handles what can START an expression:
    - a number: a leaf
    - "(" : parse a full expression with parseExpr(0), then require ")"
    - "-" : a UNARY minus (one operand), parsed with a high power so
      that -2 * 3 means (-2) * 3

▸  ERRORS WITHOUT if err != nil EVERYWHERE
The parser calls panic with its own error type on bad input, and
Parse recovers it at the top and returns a normal error. Inside one
package this keeps deep recursive code readable; the panic never
escapes to callers. encoding/json and text/template do the same.

▸  CODE NOTES
The tree is printed in fully parenthesised form so you can SEE the
grouping the parser chose. The lexer is cut down to keep the focus
on parsing.
lessons.expected:
1 + 2 * 3          (1 + (2 * 3))
8 - 3 - 2          ((8 - 3) - 2)
2 ^ 3 ^ 2          (2 ^ (3 ^ 2))
(1 + 2) * 3        ((1 + 2) * 3)
-2 * 3             ((-2) * 3)
-2 ^ 2             (-(2 ^ 2))
1 + 2 * 3 - 4 / 2  ((1 + (2 * 3)) - (4 / 2))
1 +                parse error: unexpected end of input
(1 + 2             parse error: expected ) but found ""
1 2                parse error: unexpected "2" after expression

quiz.q: In a Pratt parser, how is a right-associative operator such as ^ handled?
options: Its binding power is set lower than every other operator
Its operands are swapped after the tree is built
Its right side is parsed with a minimum power one lower than its own
The parser reads the tokens from right to left
quiz.explain: Lowering the minimum by one lets the recursive call accept another operator of the same power, so 2 ^ 3 ^ 2 groups as 2 ^ (3 ^ 2). Left-associative operators pass their own power, which refuses an equal operator.
quiz.hint: Re-read "ASSOCIATIVITY".

videos.title: Implementing a bignum calculator - Rob Pike

lessons.title: The evaluator: environments, functions and closures
lessons.concept:
▸  THE JOB
An EVALUATOR walks the AST and computes a value for each node. It is
a recursive function with one case per node type:

    Num           its own value
    Var           look the name up
    Binary        evaluate both sides, then apply the operator
    Let           evaluate a value, bind it to a name, evaluate a body
    Fn            create a function value
    Call          evaluate the function and argument, run the body
    If            evaluate the condition, then ONE of two branches

To keep the focus on evaluation, the trees in this lesson are written
directly as Go struct values; the previous lesson showed how a parser
would produce them from text.

▸  ENVIRONMENTS
Where do variables live? In an ENVIRONMENT: a table from names to
values, with a link to the environment outside it.

    type Env struct {
        vars   map[string]Value
        parent *Env
    }

Looking a name up checks this table, then the parent's, and so on
outward. That chain IS the scope rule: inner names hide outer names,
and when an inner block ends its table is simply dropped.

▸  FUNCTIONS ARE VALUES
Evaluating Fn{Param, Body} does NOT run the body. It produces a
CLOSURE value holding three things: the parameter name, the body,
and the environment where the function was CREATED.

Calling a closure makes a new environment whose parent is that saved
environment (not the caller's), binds the parameter there, and
evaluates the body in it.

▸  WHY THE SAVED ENVIRONMENT MATTERS
    let makeAdder = fn(n) { fn(x) { x + n } }
    let add5 = makeAdder(5)
    add5(10)                 -> 15

When add5 runs, makeAdder has already returned. The inner function
still finds n because it kept a pointer to the environment where n
was bound to 5. This is exactly how Go closures work; here you can
see the mechanism, because you wrote it.

▸  RECURSION
A function can call itself only if its own name is visible in the
environment it captured. So when the value is a function, Let
evaluates it in the NEW environment (the one that will hold the
name). For any other value it uses the outer environment, so that
"let x = x + 1" reads the old x.

▸  VALUES
The language has two kinds of value, integers and functions. Value is
an interface with no methods (any), and a TYPE SWITCH tells them
apart at run time.

quiz.q: When a closure is called, what is the parent of the new environment created for the call?
options: The environment of the code that is calling it
The global environment, always
The environment where the function was created
No parent; the call starts with an empty chain
quiz.explain: The closure saved its defining environment. Using that as the parent is what lets add5 still find n after makeAdder has returned. Using the caller's environment instead would be "dynamic scope", which almost no modern language uses.
quiz.hint: Look at the line that builds callEnv.

lessons.title: A bytecode compiler and a stack machine
lessons.concept:
▸  WHY NOT JUST WALK THE TREE?
Tree walking is simple but slow: every step follows pointers, does a
type switch and makes a recursive Go call. Faster interpreters
(Python, Lua, Ruby, the Java virtual machine) first COMPILE the tree
into a flat list of tiny instructions, then run that list in a tight
loop.

▸  BYTECODE
An INSTRUCTION is an OPCODE (a small number naming the operation)
optionally followed by an OPERAND (extra data, such as which constant
to load). A program is a slice of them.

▸  A STACK MACHINE
The VIRTUAL MACHINE (VM) here keeps intermediate values on a STACK,
a slice it pushes to and pops from at the end:

    PUSH n      push the constant n
    LOAD i      push the value of variable number i
    STORE i     pop a value into variable number i
    ADD         pop two values, push their sum   (SUB and MUL likewise)
    PRINT       pop a value and print it

    (2 + 3) * 4   compiles to   PUSH 2, PUSH 3, ADD, PUSH 4, MUL

    step     stack
    PUSH 2   [2]
    PUSH 3   [2 3]
    ADD      [5]
    PUSH 4   [5 4]
    MUL      [20]

▸  THE COMPILER IS A TREE WALK TOO
To compile a Binary node: compile the left side, compile the right
side, then emit the operator. Emitting children before the operator
is called POST-ORDER, and it produces exactly the order a stack
machine needs.

▸  VARIABLES BECOME NUMBERS
The compiler keeps a table from each variable name to a slot number
and emits LOAD 0 or STORE 1. The VM never sees a name and never does
a map lookup while running. Work done once at compile time instead
of repeatedly at run time is the main reason compiled code is fast.

▸  THE VM LOOP
    for pc := 0; pc < len(code); pc++ {
        switch code[pc].Op { ... }
    }

pc is the PROGRAM COUNTER: the index of the instruction being run. A
jump instruction (for if and loops) would simply assign to pc.

▸  SUB AND THE ORDER OF OPERANDS
For "a - b", a is pushed first, so b is on TOP. The VM pops b, then
a, and computes a - b. Getting this backwards is the classic stack
machine bug.
lessons.expected:
compiled to 14 instructions, variables: 2
   0 PUSH 2   stack=[2]
   1 PUSH 3   stack=[2 3]
   2 ADD      stack=[5]
   3 PUSH 4   stack=[5 4]
   4 MUL      stack=[20]
   5 STORE 0  stack=[]
   6 LOAD 0   stack=[20]
   7 PUSH 5   stack=[20 5]
   8 SUB      stack=[15]
   9 STORE 1  stack=[]
  10 LOAD 1   stack=[15]
  11 LOAD 0   stack=[15 20]
  12 MUL      stack=[300]
  output: 300
  13 PRINT    stack=[]

quiz.q: To compile  a - b  for a stack machine, in what order are the instructions emitted?
options: SUB, then code for a, then code for b
Code for b, then code for a, then SUB
Code for a, then SUB, then code for b
Code for a, then code for b, then SUB
quiz.explain: Children first, operator last (post-order). After both operands are on the stack, SUB pops b (on top) and then a, and pushes a - b.
quiz.hint: The operator can only run when both of its inputs are already on the stack.

lessons.title: Challenge: a constant-folding optimizer
lessons.concept:
▸  OPTIMIZATION
An OPTIMIZER rewrites a program into an equivalent one that does less
work. The simplest and most common one is CONSTANT FOLDING: if both
operands of an operator are known numbers, compute the result at
compile time and replace the whole subtree with it.

    x * (2 + 3)        becomes      x * 5
    (4 * 5) - (6 / 2)  becomes      17

The Go compiler does this for you; that is why const seconds = 60 *
60 * 24 costs nothing at run time.

▸  ALGEBRAIC SIMPLIFICATION
Some rules hold even when one side is unknown:

    e + 0   and   0 + e    ->   e
    e * 1   and   1 * e    ->   e
    e * 0   and   0 * e    ->   0

▸  THE SHAPE OF THE SOLUTION
Write  func Fold(n Node) Node  that returns a NEW tree:

    1. For a Binary node, FIRST fold the left and right children
       (work from the leaves up: this is post-order again).
    2. If both folded children are Num, return Num with the computed
       value.
    3. Otherwise try the algebraic rules.
    4. Otherwise return a Binary with the folded children.
    5. Num and Var return themselves.

Do not fold a division by a constant zero: leave it in the tree so
the error still happens at run time, where it belongs.

▸  YOUR TASK
The node types and a String method are given in the reference
solution's shape:  Num{V int}, Var{Name string},
Binary{Op byte; L, R Node}. Binary prints as "(L op R)".

For each expression below print  before  ->  after:

    (2 + 3) * x
    (x + 0) * (1 * y)
    (4 * 5) - (6 / 2)
    x * (2 - 2)
    (x + 1) + (2 * 3)
    8 / (3 - 3)

quiz.q: Why must Fold process a node's children before the node itself?
options: Go evaluates function arguments from left to right
The String method only works on folded trees
Children are stored before parents in memory
A node can only be folded once its children have become constants
quiz.explain: Folding (2 - 2) to 0 is what reveals that x * (2 - 2) is x * 0. Working from the leaves up lets each simplification enable the next one above it.
quiz.hint: Try folding x * (2 - 2) from the top down. What do you see at the * node?

lessons.title: The simplest database: an append-only log
lessons.concept:
▸  THE POINT
A database has one promise that a map in memory cannot make: after
the program stops, or the power fails, the data is still there. This
property is called DURABILITY. This module builds the machinery
behind that promise, one piece per lesson, the way real storage
engines (the part of a database that reads and writes the disk) are
built.

▸  THE IDEA
Never change what is already in the file. Only ADD to the end. Each
change is written as one RECORD (one self-contained entry):

    set   name    Ada
    set   city    Cairo
    set   name    Grace       <- the old "name" line is still above
    del   city

This file is called a LOG. To find the current state, read it from
the top and apply every record in order to a map: later records win.
Doing that at start-up is called REPLAY.

▸  WHY APPEND-ONLY
    - Appending is the fastest thing a disk can do: no searching for
      the right place, no moving of old data.
    - A crash can only damage the END of the file (the record being
      written). Everything before it is untouched.
    - The file is a complete history. Nothing is ever overwritten.

Almost every database uses this idea somewhere. PostgreSQL calls it
the write-ahead log, MySQL the redo log, Kafka is nothing but a log.

▸  DELETING
You cannot remove a line from the middle, so a delete is itself a
record: "del city". Such a marker is called a TOMBSTONE.

▸  CODE NOTES
    - os.OpenFile takes FLAGS joined with | (the OR operator):
      O_RDWR read and write, O_CREATE make the file if missing,
      O_APPEND every write goes to the end.
    - 0o644 is the file's permission bits, written in octal (base 8):
      the owner may read and write, everyone else may read.
    - Fields are separated by a TAB character, written "\t".
    - f.Sync() asks the operating system to really push the bytes to
      the disk. Without it they may sit in memory for a while and be
      lost if the power fails.

▸  WHAT IS WRONG WITH THIS VERSION
A value containing a tab or a newline would break the format, and a
half-written last line would be read as a real record. The next
lesson fixes both.
lessons.expected:
the file on disk:
set | name | Ada
set | city | Cairo
set | name | Grace
del | city
set | lang | Go
after restart:
  lang = Go
  name = Grace
city present: false

quiz.q: In an append-only log, how is a key deleted?
options: Its line is erased from the middle of the file
The file is rewritten without that key
A new "delete" record is appended to the end
The key's value is overwritten with spaces
quiz.explain: Nothing already written is ever changed. A delete is one more record (a tombstone), and replay removes the key from the map when it reaches that record.
quiz.hint: Re-read "DELETING".

lessons.title: Binary records and checksums: surviving a crash
lessons.concept:
▸  THE PROBLEM
If the power fails while a record is being written, the file ends
with half a record: a TORN WRITE. Disks can also, rarely, flip a bit
on their own. On restart the database must tell good records from
damaged ones, and must never treat garbage as data.

▸  A BINARY RECORD FORMAT
Instead of text lines, each record says how long it is, so keys and
values may contain ANY bytes (tabs, newlines, images):

    | checksum | key length | value length |   key   |  value  |
    |  4 bytes |  4 bytes   |   4 bytes    | n bytes | m bytes |

The first 12 bytes are the HEADER: fixed-size information that tells
the reader how to read the rest.

▸  CHECKSUM
A CHECKSUM is a small number computed from the data. The writer
stores it; the reader computes it again and compares. If one bit of
the record changed, the two numbers differ.

CRC-32 (hash/crc32) is the usual choice: fast, and very good at
catching accidental damage. It is NOT protection against a person
who changes the data on purpose; that needs a cryptographic hash or
signature (module 22).

▸  BYTE ORDER
A number such as 300 needs more than one byte. LITTLE-ENDIAN stores
the low byte first, BIG-ENDIAN the high byte first. It does not
matter which you pick, as long as writer and reader agree.
encoding/binary does the conversion:

    binary.LittleEndian.PutUint32(buf, n)     number -> 4 bytes
    n := binary.LittleEndian.Uint32(buf)      4 bytes -> number

▸  RECOVERY
Read records from the start. Stop at the first one that is
    - too short to hold a header or the lengths it announces, or
    - has a checksum that does not match.
Everything BEFORE that point is good. Cut the file there (TRUNCATE
it) and carry on. A record that was not completely written was never
reported as saved, so dropping it breaks no promise.

▸  CODE NOTES
The demo works on byte slices in memory so you can see the damage
being done; a real engine would do the same on a file with
io.ReadFull and os.Truncate.
lessons.expected:
intact log:            80 bytes, 80 good (clean end), drop 0 bytes
    "name" = "Ada"
    "note" = "line one\nline two\ttabbed"
    "city" = "Cairo"
torn last record:      77 bytes, 59 good (torn record), drop 18 bytes
    "name" = "Ada"
    "note" = "line one\nline two\ttabbed"
bit flip in record 2:  80 bytes, 19 good (checksum mismatch), drop 61 bytes
    "name" = "Ada"

quiz.q: During recovery the third of five records fails its checksum. What does the database keep?
options: All five records, marking the third as suspect
Records one, two, four and five
Records one and two only
Nothing; the whole file is discarded
quiz.explain: After a damaged record the reader can no longer trust where the next record starts, because the lengths themselves may be wrong. Everything before the damage is known good; the file is cut there.
quiz.hint: Why can the reader not simply skip to record four?

lessons.title: An index and compaction: reading without replaying everything
lessons.concept:
▸  TWO PROBLEMS WITH THE PLAIN LOG
    1. All values live in memory (in the map). A 100 GB database
       needs 100 GB of RAM.
    2. The file grows forever: setting one key a million times keeps
       a million records, of which only the last matters.

▸  FIX 1: AN INDEX
Keep in memory only WHERE each value is, not the value itself:

    index:   key  ->  (offset in the file, length)

An OFFSET is a position counted in bytes from the start of the file.
Get looks up the key in the index and reads exactly those bytes with
f.ReadAt(buf, offset): one disk read, however large the file is.
Memory now holds only the keys and two numbers each.

This design is called BITCASK (it comes from the Riak database). Its
rule of thumb: all keys must fit in memory; values need not.

▸  FIX 2: COMPACTION
From time to time, write a NEW file containing only the newest
record of every live key, then replace the old file with it. This is
COMPACTION: the garbage (overwritten and deleted records) is
dropped.

▸  THE SAFE REPLACE
    1. write everything to "data.tmp"
    2. Sync it, so it is really on disk
    3. os.Rename("data.tmp", "data.log")

Rename is ATOMIC on normal filesystems: at every instant the name
"data.log" refers either to the complete old file or to the complete
new one, never to a mixture. A crash at any step leaves a usable
database.

▸  CODE NOTES
    - Record layout here: key length (4 bytes), value length
      (4 bytes), key, value. The checksum from the last lesson is
      left out to keep the code short.
    - The file is opened once with O_APPEND for writing; the
      position of each new record is tracked in db.size.
    - Compaction writes keys in sorted order only so that this
      lesson's output is the same on every run.
lessons.expected:
counter = 999 at {17887 3}
file size before compaction: 17922 bytes for 2 keys
file size after compaction:  35 bytes
counter = 999 at {15 3} | name = Grace
error: key "missing" not found

quiz.q: Why does compaction write a new file and rename it, instead of editing the old file in place?
options: Editing a file in place is not possible in Go
A renamed file is read faster than an edited one
A crash part-way through leaves either the whole old file or the whole new one
The operating system limits how often a file may be edited
quiz.explain: Rename is atomic: there is no moment at which the name points to a half-finished file. Editing in place could be interrupted in the middle and leave neither a valid old nor a valid new database.
quiz.hint: Re-read "THE SAFE REPLACE".
